Through extensive experiments across multiple environments (Atari, MuJoCo, and real-world robotic control tasks) and algorithms (DQN, PPO, and SAC), we demonstrate that poisoned agents perform normally under standard conditions but exhibit targeted suboptimal behaviors when triggers are activated during deployment. Our analysis reveals that even modest poisoning rates (≤5% of training episodes) can lead to successful attacks with trigger detection rates below 15% for state-of-the-art anomaly detectors. We further characterize the transferability of these attacks across different network architectures and training paradigms, providing insights into potential defensive strategies. These findings highlight fundamental security challenges for DRL systems in safety-critical applications and emphasize the need for robust training procedures that can identify and mitigate in-distribution poisoning attacks.

Video Trajectory Classification and Anomaly Detection Using Hybrid CNN-VAE

This paper introduces a novel hybrid architecture combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) for video trajectory classification and anomaly detection. The proposed CNN-VAE framework leverages the feature extraction capabilities of CNNs with the generative modeling strengths of VAEs to learn compact latent representations of normal motion patterns in video sequences. Our approach first extracts trajectory data from video frames, then employs the CNN component to capture spatial-temporal dependencies while the VAE component learns a probabilistic latent space of normal movement patterns. By measuring the reconstruction error between original and regenerated trajectories, the system effectively identifies anomalous movements that deviate from learned normal patterns. Experiments conducted on multiple public datasets, including UCSD Ped1, Avenue, and ShanghaiTech, demonstrate that our hybrid CNN-VAE architecture outperforms state-of-the-art methods with improvements of 3.7% in AUC and 2.9% in EER metrics. The model shows particular robustness in detecting subtle anomalies and maintaining performance across varying environmental conditions. Our approach offers promising applications in surveillance systems, traffic monitoring, and crowd behavior analysis with minimal computational overhead during inference.

Time-Series Event Prediction with Evolutionary State Graph

This paper introduces the Evolutionary State Graph (ESG), a novel framework for time-series event prediction that addresses the limitations of existing approaches in capturing both temporal dynamics and evolving state dependencies. Unlike traditional methods that treat time-series data as sequential patterns, our approach models the data as a dynamic graph structure where nodes represent states and edges capture transition probabilities that evolve over time. The ESG framework incorporates three key components: (1) a state identification mechanism that adaptively clusters similar temporal patterns, (2) a temporal evolution module that captures how state transitions change across different time scales, and (3) a prediction layer that leverages both historical state trajectories and current contextual information. We evaluate our approach on multiple real-world datasets spanning healthcare monitoring, financial market events, and urban transportation systems. Results demonstrate that ESG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving 17% improvement in prediction accuracy and 23% reduction in false alarm rates. Furthermore, the interpretable nature of our graph representation provides valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms driving event occurrences. Our work contributes a powerful new paradigm for time-series analysis that effectively balances predictive performance with model explainability.

RICE: Refining Instance Masks in Cluttered Environments with Graph Neural Networks

Instance segmentation in cluttered environments remains a significant challenge in computer vision, as objects with complex occlusions and varying densities often lead to imprecise mask boundaries. In this paper, we present RICE (Refining Instance masks in Cluttered Environments), a novel post-processing framework that leverages Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to enhance the quality of instance segmentation masks. Our approach constructs a graph representation where nodes correspond to mask regions and edges represent spatial relationships between them. The GNN learns to reason about object boundaries by aggregating contextual information across the graph, enabling more accurate refinement decisions even in highly cluttered scenes. We introduce a boundary-aware attention mechanism that focuses computational resources on ambiguous regions while preserving well-defined object contours. Extensive experiments on challenging datasets including COCO-Cluttered, Cityscapes, and our newly introduced ClutterNet benchmark demonstrate that RICE consistently improves mask quality across multiple baseline instance segmentation models, achieving up to 5.2% improvement in mask AP and 7.8% in boundary precision. Ablation studies confirm that our graph-based approach outperforms conventional CNN-based refinement methods, particularly in scenes with high object density and occlusion. RICE offers a model-agnostic solution that can be seamlessly integrated into existing instance segmentation pipelines with minimal computational overhead.

SGL: Spectral Graph Learning from Measurements

This paper introduces Spectral Graph Learning (SGL), a novel framework for inferring graph structure from observational data measurements. Our approach leverages spectral graph theory to recover underlying network connectivity patterns without requiring explicit knowledge of the graph generation process. SGL formulates graph learning as an optimization problem in the spectral domain, where we jointly estimate the graph Laplacian eigenvectors and eigenvalues that best explain observed measurements across nodes. Unlike existing methods that impose structural constraints directly in the spatial domain, our spectral formulation naturally incorporates smoothness properties while remaining computationally efficient. We provide theoretical guarantees on recovery performance under various sampling regimes and noise conditions. Experiments on both synthetic networks and real-world datasets—including brain connectivity networks, social interaction graphs, and sensor networks—demonstrate that SGL outperforms state-of-the-art graph learning methods, particularly when measurements are limited or contaminated with noise. The proposed framework offers a principled approach to graph structure discovery with applications in network science, signal processing, and machine learning on graphs.

On the ability of neural nets to express distributions

This paper investigates the expressive power of neural networks in modeling probability distributions. We analyze the theoretical capabilities and limitations of various neural network architectures in approximating complex probability distributions with finite parameters. Our work establishes formal bounds on the approximation error as a function of network depth and width, demonstrating that deep networks can efficiently represent a broader class of distributions compared to shallow counterparts. We prove that for certain distribution families, the required parameter count grows only polynomially with the desired approximation accuracy, while for others, an exponential number of parameters is necessary. Through empirical validation on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that properly designed neural density estimators can capture multimodal, heavy-tailed, and hierarchically structured distributions with remarkable fidelity. Our findings provide theoretical foundations for neural network-based probabilistic modeling and offer practical insights for designing architectures tailored to specific distributional properties.

Semantic Graph Based Place Recognition for 3D Point Clouds

This paper presents a novel approach to place recognition in 3D point clouds by leveraging semantic information through graph-based representations. While traditional point cloud place recognition methods rely primarily on geometric features, our approach incorporates semantic understanding to enhance robustness against environmental changes and viewpoint variations. We propose a hierarchical semantic graph structure that encodes both the spatial relationships between semantic objects and their distinctive attributes within urban environments. Our method first segments point clouds into semantic entities, constructs a graph representation preserving their topological relationships, and then employs a graph matching algorithm optimized for place recognition tasks. Extensive experiments on multiple large-scale urban datasets demonstrate that our semantic graph-based approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art geometric methods, achieving 87% recall at 95% precision in challenging scenarios including seasonal changes, dynamic objects, and partial observations. The computational efficiency of our graph matching paradigm also enables real-time performance suitable for autonomous navigation systems. This work bridges the gap between semantic scene understanding and place recognition, establishing a promising direction for robust localization in complex 3D environments.

Learning Dual Convolutional Neural Networks for Low-Level Vision

In this paper, we propose a general dual convolutional neural network (DualCNN) architecture for tackling low-level vision problems. The DualCNN consists of two parallel branches, each dedicated to recovering complementary image components. By explicitly modeling the inherent duality in various low-level vision tasks, our approach effectively decomposes the original problem into two simpler sub-problems. We implement this architecture through weight-sharing and dual-objective regularization strategies that enable the two branches to work collaboratively while maintaining their specialization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our DualCNN achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple challenging tasks including image denoising, super-resolution, and JPEG artifacts removal. The proposed architecture not only improves quantitative metrics but also produces visually superior results with better preservation of structural details and fewer artifacts. Furthermore, our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the dual-branch design compared to single-branch alternatives with equivalent parameter counts. The DualCNN presents a simple yet powerful framework that can be easily adapted to various low-level vision applications without task-specific architectural modifications.

Illuminated Decision Trees with Lucid

This paper introduces a novel visualization framework for interpreting decision trees using Lucid, an open-source interpretability library. Despite the inherent interpretability of decision trees compared to other machine learning models, understanding complex trees remains challenging, particularly when they contain numerous nodes or feature high-dimensional data. Our approach, "Illuminated Decision Trees," leverages Lucid's capabilities to provide dynamic, interactive visualizations that elucidate decision boundaries, feature importance, and prediction pathways. We demonstrate how these visualizations can reveal previously obscured patterns in the model's decision-making process across various datasets. The framework supports both classification and regression trees, with customizable visualization parameters to accommodate different analysis needs. Experimental results show that data scientists using our visualization framework identified model weaknesses and potential improvements 37% faster than with traditional tree visualization methods. This work contributes to the growing field of explainable AI by making decision tree models more transparent and accessible to both technical and non-technical stakeholders.

NAS-FCOS: Fast Neural Architecture Search for Object Detection

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has demonstrated remarkable success in automating the design of deep neural networks for various computer vision tasks, yet its application to object detection remains challenging due to computational constraints and task complexity. In this paper, we present NAS-FCOS, a novel and efficient neural architecture search framework specifically designed for anchor-free object detection. Building upon the FCOS (Fully Convolutional One-Stage) detector, our approach systematically explores the architectural design space of detection networks while maintaining real-time inference capabilities. We introduce a detection-specific search space that encompasses critical components including feature pyramid networks, multi-scale feature fusion, and detection heads. To address the computational burden of architecture search, we employ a gradient-based search strategy with weight sharing, reducing search time from thousands of GPU days to just a few days on a single GPU. Extensive experiments on the MS COCO dataset demonstrate that our automatically discovered architectures outperform manually designed counterparts, achieving state-of-the-art results among anchor-free detectors with comparable inference speeds. NAS-FCOS achieves 44.2% AP on COCO test-dev, surpassing the original FCOS by 3.5% while maintaining similar computational efficiency. Our work demonstrates the potential of automated architecture design for object detection tasks and provides insights for future research in this direction.

Improved Inference via Deep Input Transfer

This paper introduces Deep Input Transfer (DIT), a novel approach to enhance inference performance across diverse machine learning tasks. By reformulating the traditional input processing pipeline, DIT creates optimized intermediate representations that significantly reduce computational overhead while preserving essential information content. Our method leverages a learnable transfer function that maps raw inputs to a more efficient representation space, enabling downstream models to achieve comparable or superior performance with reduced computational resources. Experiments across computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal tasks demonstrate that DIT reduces inference latency by 37-52% while maintaining accuracy within 0.5% of baseline models. For resource-constrained environments, our approach enables deployment of sophisticated models that would otherwise be prohibitively expensive. We provide theoretical analysis of the information preservation properties of DIT and release an open-source implementation to facilitate adoption across various domains. This work represents a significant advancement in making deep learning models more efficient and accessible for real-world applications.

DeepPerimeter: Indoor Boundary Estimation from Posed Monocular Sequences

This paper presents DeepPerimeter, a novel approach for estimating indoor architectural boundaries from posed monocular video sequences. While existing methods for indoor reconstruction often focus on complete 3D modeling, our system specifically targets the extraction of structural perimeters—the walls, floor, and ceiling that define the architectural envelope of indoor spaces. DeepPerimeter employs a two-stage deep learning architecture: first, a feature extraction network processes individual frames to identify boundary cues, then a temporal integration module fuses these features across multiple viewpoints using the known camera poses. We leverage geometric priors specific to indoor environments, such as Manhattan world assumptions and typical room configurations, to regularize the prediction. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard datasets including ScanNet and Matterport3D, with a 27% improvement in boundary precision compared to existing methods. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DeepPerimeter can accurately recover complex floor plans even in challenging scenarios with occlusions, varying illumination, and minimal texture. The resulting boundary models provide a lightweight yet informative representation of indoor spaces that can support applications in floor plan generation, navigation, and augmented reality.

Leverage Score Sampling for Complete Mode Coverage in Generative Adversarial Networks

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated remarkable capability in generating high-quality synthetic data across various domains. However, a persistent challenge in GAN training is mode collapse, where the generator fails to capture the full diversity of the target distribution. This paper introduces a novel approach to address this limitation through leverage score sampling, a technique borrowed from randomized numerical linear algebra. We propose a framework that dynamically identifies underrepresented modes in the training distribution by computing leverage scores that quantify the importance of individual data points. By strategically oversampling these high-leverage regions during training, our method encourages the generator to explore the entire data manifold. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that our approach provides probabilistic guarantees for complete mode coverage under certain conditions. Experimental results across synthetic distributions and real-world datasets show that our leverage score sampling technique significantly outperforms existing methods in capturing multimodal distributions, achieving up to 35% improvement in mode coverage while maintaining comparable sample quality. The proposed method requires minimal modifications to existing GAN architectures and introduces negligible computational overhead, making it a practical solution for enhancing the diversity of GAN-generated samples.

Abstract: Logically-Constrained Neural Fitted Q-Iteration

This paper introduces Logically-Constrained Neural Fitted Q-Iteration (LC-NFQ), a novel reinforcement learning approach that integrates formal logical constraints into the neural fitted Q-learning framework. While deep reinforcement learning has demonstrated remarkable success across various domains, ensuring that learned policies satisfy critical safety requirements and logical constraints remains challenging. Our method addresses this limitation by embedding temporal logic specifications directly into the Q-function approximation process, effectively shaping the policy search space to prioritize constraint satisfaction while optimizing for reward. 

We formalize LC-NFQ as a constrained optimization problem where logical requirements are transformed into differentiable loss terms that guide neural network training. This approach allows the agent to learn policies that provably satisfy specified logical properties while maintaining performance objectives. We evaluate our method across diverse environments, including robotic navigation tasks with safety constraints and resource management problems with temporal dependencies. Results demonstrate that LC-NFQ consistently outperforms unconstrained methods and alternative constraint-handling approaches in terms of constraint satisfaction while achieving comparable or superior reward performance. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees on constraint satisfaction under certain conditions and analyze the trade-offs between constraint strictness and exploration capabilities.

Characterizing Policy Divergence for Personalized Meta-Reinforcement Learning

Meta-reinforcement learning (Meta-RL) enables agents to quickly adapt to new tasks by leveraging knowledge from previously encountered similar tasks. However, standard Meta-RL approaches often struggle to personalize policies effectively when faced with heterogeneous task distributions. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for characterizing policy divergence in personalized Meta-RL settings. We formalize the concept of policy divergence as a measure of the distance between task-specific optimal policies, and demonstrate how this characterization can be used to improve adaptation efficiency. Our approach explicitly models the trade-off between maintaining a generalizable meta-policy and allowing task-specific policy specialization. Through theoretical analysis, we establish bounds on the sample complexity of adaptation based on our divergence metrics. Experimental results across diverse environments, including MuJoCo locomotion tasks and multi-user recommendation systems, show that our divergence-aware personalization approach achieves up to 45% faster adaptation and 32% higher asymptotic performance compared to state-of-the-art Meta-RL methods. These findings provide new insights into the fundamental limitations of meta-learning in heterogeneous task spaces and offer practical solutions for more efficient personalized reinforcement learning.

Sketch-Guided Object Localization in Natural Images

This paper presents a novel approach for localizing objects in natural images using hand-drawn sketches as queries. Unlike traditional object detection methods that rely on predefined categories or bounding box annotations, our sketch-guided framework enables flexible and intuitive object localization based on visual similarity to user-provided sketches. We propose a dual-branch neural architecture that learns a shared embedding space between sketches and natural images, bridging the substantial domain gap between these modalities. Our model employs a cross-modal attention mechanism to focus on structural similarities while being robust to variations in sketch quality, style, and detail. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing sketch-based retrieval methods when adapted for localization tasks, achieving mean average precision improvements of 12.3% over the state-of-the-art. Additionally, we introduce a new benchmark dataset containing diverse sketch-image pairs with ground-truth localization annotations. User studies confirm that our system enables more intuitive object discovery compared to text-based queries, particularly for objects with distinctive shapes but ambiguous verbal descriptions. The proposed method has promising applications in content-based image retrieval, interactive image editing, and visual search systems.

S4RL: Surprisingly Simple Self-Supervision for Offline Reinforcement Learning

We introduce S4RL, a surprisingly simple yet effective approach for offline reinforcement learning that leverages self-supervision to enhance performance on tasks with limited or suboptimal demonstration data. Unlike complex methods that require elaborate architectures or auxiliary objectives, S4RL incorporates lightweight self-supervised learning techniques into standard offline RL algorithms. Our method creates additional training signals by applying data augmentation and contrastive learning to the state representations, enabling more robust policy learning from fixed datasets. Through extensive experiments on standard offline RL benchmarks including D4RL, we demonstrate that S4RL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios with sparse rewards or low-quality demonstrations. The simplicity of our approach makes it easily integrable with existing offline RL frameworks while significantly improving sample efficiency and final performance. Our analysis reveals that the self-supervised components help mitigate common challenges in offline RL such as distributional shift and value overestimation, suggesting that simple self-supervision may be a fundamental missing piece in effective offline reinforcement learning.

On Completeness-aware Concept-Based Explanations in Deep Neural Networks

Concept-based explanations have emerged as a promising approach for interpreting deep neural networks by mapping latent representations to human-understandable concepts. However, existing methods often lack guarantees regarding the completeness of the identified concepts, raising questions about whether these explanations capture all relevant information used in model decisions. This paper introduces a novel framework for completeness-aware concept-based explanations that quantitatively measures and optimizes for explanation completeness. We formalize completeness as the degree to which concept-based explanations preserve the model's original predictive power and propose metrics to evaluate this property. Our approach leverages information-theoretic principles to identify a minimal set of concepts that maximally explain model behavior while maintaining fidelity to the original decision boundary. Through extensive experiments on image classification, natural language processing, and healthcare datasets, we demonstrate that our method produces more comprehensive explanations than existing techniques while maintaining interpretability. Additionally, we show how completeness-aware explanations can detect potential shortcomings in model reasoning and concept annotation. This work represents a significant step toward trustworthy AI systems that provide complete and faithful explanations of their decision-making processes.

GTEA: Representation Learning for Temporal Interaction Graphs via Edge Aggregation

Temporal interaction graphs, which capture time-stamped interactions between entities, have become increasingly important for modeling dynamic relationships in various domains such as social networks, financial transactions, and recommendation systems. This paper introduces GTEA (Graph Temporal Edge Aggregation), a novel framework for learning representations in temporal interaction graphs that effectively captures both structural and temporal patterns. Unlike previous approaches that primarily focus on node-level representations or treat time as a simple additional feature, GTEA explicitly models the evolution of interactions through a specialized edge aggregation mechanism. Our method employs a hierarchical attention architecture that first aggregates temporal information at the edge level before integrating structural context, allowing the model to capture complex temporal dependencies while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that GTEA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on various downstream tasks, including link prediction, node classification, and temporal pattern detection. Furthermore, we provide theoretical analysis showing that GTEA's representation capacity generalizes several existing temporal graph embedding approaches. Our framework offers a flexible and powerful approach for modeling dynamic interactions, with significant implications for applications requiring temporal reasoning on graph-structured data.

Grid Partitioned Attention: Efficient Transformer Approximation with Inductive Bias for High Resolution Detail Generation

This paper introduces Grid Partitioned Attention (GPA), a novel attention mechanism that addresses the computational challenges of transformer models when processing high-resolution data while preserving fine-grained detail generation capabilities. Traditional transformer architectures face quadratic complexity with respect to sequence length, limiting their application in high-resolution image synthesis, video generation, and other domains requiring detailed local feature representation. GPA implements a spatially-aware partitioning strategy that divides input tokens into overlapping grid regions, enabling efficient local attention computation while maintaining global context through a hierarchical information exchange framework. Our approach incorporates inductive biases about spatial locality and multi-scale feature relationships, significantly reducing computational complexity from O(n²) to O(n·k), where k represents a constant region size regardless of input resolution. Extensive experiments across image generation, video synthesis, and 3D rendering tasks demonstrate that GPA achieves comparable or superior quality to full attention models while requiring only a fraction of the computational resources. At high resolutions (1024×1024 and beyond), our method generates substantially more coherent fine details than existing efficient transformer approximations. The proposed method scales linearly with input size, enabling transformer-based architectures to process previously prohibitive resolutions while maintaining the representational advantages of attention mechanisms.

Locally Private Graph Neural Networks

This paper introduces a novel approach to preserving privacy in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) through the application of local differential privacy (LDP) techniques. While GNNs have demonstrated remarkable performance in various graph-based learning tasks, they pose significant privacy concerns as they typically require access to sensitive structural information and node features. Our framework, Locally Private Graph Neural Networks (LP-GNNs), provides rigorous privacy guarantees at the individual node level by incorporating LDP mechanisms directly into the message-passing operations of GNNs. We develop privacy-preserving variants of neighborhood aggregation functions that allow nodes to communicate perturbed representations while maintaining utility. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that our approach achieves an optimal privacy-utility tradeoff under the LDP model. Extensive experiments on benchmark graph datasets show that LP-GNNs maintain competitive performance on node classification, link prediction, and graph classification tasks while providing strong privacy guarantees. Our results indicate that LP-GNNs effectively balance the trade-off between model utility and privacy protection, offering a practical solution for privacy-preserving graph representation learning in decentralized environments where traditional privacy-preserving techniques are insufficient.

Short-Term Wind-Speed Forecasting Using Kernel Spectral Hidden Markov Models

This paper introduces a novel approach for short-term wind-speed forecasting based on Kernel Spectral Hidden Markov Models (KS-HMMs). Wind power generation has emerged as a critical renewable energy source, yet its integration into power grids remains challenging due to the inherent variability and limited predictability of wind patterns. We propose a non-parametric spectral learning framework that leverages the representational power of kernel methods within an HMM structure to capture the complex temporal dynamics of wind-speed time series. Our method transforms wind-speed data into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, allowing for more flexible state representations than traditional HMM approaches. Experiments conducted on wind-speed datasets from multiple geographical locations demonstrate that KS-HMMs outperform existing forecasting methods, including ARIMA, standard HMMs, and neural network-based approaches, reducing mean absolute percentage error by 12-18% for forecasting horizons of 1-6 hours. The proposed model shows particular strength in capturing sudden changes in wind patterns and maintaining accuracy during periods of high volatility. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence properties of our spectral learning algorithm. These results suggest that KS-HMMs offer a promising framework for improving the reliability of short-term wind-speed forecasts, potentially enhancing the economic and operational efficiency of wind power integration.

When Autonomous Systems Meet Accuracy and Transferability through AI: A Survey

This survey provides a comprehensive analysis of the intersection between autonomous systems, accuracy demands, and transferability challenges in artificial intelligence applications. We examine how modern AI techniques address the critical balance between achieving high accuracy in controlled environments and maintaining performance when deployed across diverse, often unpredictable real-world scenarios. The paper systematically reviews recent advancements in transfer learning, domain adaptation, and robust AI architectures that enable autonomous systems to generalize effectively beyond their training environments. We analyze key challenges including distribution shifts, sim-to-real transfer, and performance degradation in novel contexts across multiple domains including autonomous vehicles, robotics, unmanned aerial systems, and smart infrastructure. Our findings highlight emerging methodologies that promote transferability without compromising accuracy, including meta-learning frameworks, self-supervised representation learning, and continual adaptation mechanisms. We identify persistent research gaps and propose future directions toward developing autonomous systems that maintain reliable performance across varying operational conditions while meeting stringent accuracy requirements. This survey serves as a foundational resource for researchers and practitioners working at the critical interface of autonomous system reliability and AI transferability.

On the Universality of Invariant Networks

This paper investigates the expressive power and universality properties of neural networks designed to respect group invariances. We establish theoretical foundations for understanding when invariant networks can universally approximate any continuous invariant function. Our analysis reveals that the architecture of invariant networks significantly influences their approximation capabilities, with certain designs achieving universal approximation within the class of invariant functions while others face fundamental limitations. We prove that properly constructed invariant networks can maintain universality while respecting symmetries for a wide class of compact groups. Furthermore, we characterize the minimal architectural requirements needed to achieve this universality. Through both theoretical analysis and empirical validation, we demonstrate that our proposed architectural principles lead to invariant networks that efficiently learn complex invariant functions with fewer parameters than conventional approaches. These results provide important insights for designing neural networks in domains where symmetry and invariance are essential, such as physics, chemistry, and computer vision.

Unsupervised Diverse Colorization via Generative Adversarial Networks

This paper presents a novel approach to image colorization using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in an unsupervised learning framework. Unlike previous colorization methods that produce a single deterministic output or require user guidance, our approach generates diverse and plausible colorizations for a given grayscale image without requiring any human intervention. We introduce a conditional GAN architecture that learns to model the distribution of possible colorizations rather than just regressing to a single solution. Our model incorporates a diversity-promoting objective function that encourages the generation of multiple distinct yet realistic color versions while preserving structural integrity. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of diversity metrics while maintaining comparable quality measures. User studies further confirm that our colorizations are often indistinguishable from real color images. The proposed approach has significant applications in image restoration, content creation, and data augmentation, offering a fully automated solution for generating multiple colorization variants with high perceptual quality and semantic plausibility.

Unsupervised Learning of Visual Representations using Videos

This paper presents a novel approach for learning visual representations from unlabeled video data. We propose a self-supervised learning framework that leverages the rich temporal structure inherent in videos to learn meaningful and generalizable visual features without human annotation. Our method exploits the natural coherence between consecutive video frames to create a pretext task of predicting future frames or frame sequences. By training deep convolutional neural networks to solve this prediction task, the networks learn to capture semantic and structural visual information that transfers well to various downstream computer vision tasks. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our video-based unsupervised approach achieves competitive performance compared to supervised pre-training on ImageNet when the learned representations are fine-tuned for object detection, semantic segmentation, and action recognition. Notably, our method outperforms previous unsupervised learning techniques that rely solely on static images. These results highlight the potential of using the vast amounts of unlabeled video data available online for learning general-purpose visual representations, reducing the dependency on expensive manual annotations for computer vision applications.

Test-Time Adaptation for Super-Resolution: You Only Need to Overfit on a Few More Images

Deep learning-based super-resolution (SR) models often suffer from performance degradation when deployed on real-world images with distribution shifts from their training data. To address this challenge, we propose a novel test-time adaptation framework for super-resolution that requires minimal computational overhead and no prior knowledge of the target domain. Our approach, which we call SR-OTTO (Super-Resolution with Overfitting On Test-Time Only), leverages the observation that overfitting on a small set of test images can effectively adapt pre-trained SR models to new domains. By fine-tuning only a subset of model parameters on the test image itself and a few additional similar images, SR-OTTO captures domain-specific degradation patterns while preserving the general super-resolution capabilities of the base model. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms traditional SR approaches and existing test-time adaptation techniques, achieving up to 2.1 dB PSNR improvement on challenging real-world images. Furthermore, SR-OTTO maintains efficiency with an adaptation time of less than 10 seconds per image on standard hardware. Our findings suggest that controlled overfitting can serve as a powerful mechanism for rapid adaptation in image restoration tasks, opening new possibilities for deployment-efficient super-resolution systems.

Learning Dual Semantic Relations with Graph Attention for Image-Text Matching

Image-text matching is a fundamental task in vision-language understanding that aims to measure the semantic similarity between visual and textual content. In this paper, we propose a novel Dual Semantic Relations Graph Attention Network (DSR-GAN) that explicitly models both intra-modal and cross-modal semantic relationships for more effective image-text matching. Our approach constructs dual relation graphs—one capturing fine-grained relationships between visual regions in images, and another modeling linguistic dependencies between words in text descriptions. The key innovation lies in our graph attention mechanism that dynamically learns to weight these semantic relations based on their relevance to the matching task. Through this dual-graph representation, our model can better align semantically related components across modalities while preserving structural information within each modality. Extensive experiments on MS-COCO and Flickr30K datasets demonstrate that DSR-GAN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on bidirectional retrieval tasks. Ablation studies further confirm the effectiveness of our dual semantic relation modeling approach. Our work provides new insights into the importance of structured semantic representations for cross-modal understanding tasks.

Deeper and Wider Siamese Networks for Real-Time Visual Tracking

This paper addresses fundamental limitations of Siamese networks for visual object tracking. While Siamese trackers have demonstrated impressive performance balancing accuracy and speed, their potential has been constrained by architectural restrictions that limit network depth and adaptability. We identify and overcome two key constraints: spatial invariance caused by excessive pooling operations, and receptive field limitations that restrict target discrimination. We propose a novel architecture that enables deeper and wider backbone networks without sacrificing real-time performance. Our approach introduces layer-wise adjustments to preserve spatial resolution in deep layers and employs dilated convolutions to expand the effective receptive field. Extensive experiments on major tracking benchmarks including OTB-100, VOT-2018, and LaSOT demonstrate that our deeper and wider Siamese networks achieve state-of-the-art performance while maintaining real-time tracking speeds exceeding 50 FPS. The proposed architectural improvements provide a 10% relative gain in accuracy compared to previous Siamese trackers without requiring additional training data or complex optimization strategies. Our work establishes a new foundation for Siamese tracking frameworks that can effectively leverage the representational power of modern deep networks.

Boosting Template-based SSVEP Decoding by Cross-domain Transfer Learning

Steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) have emerged as a promising paradigm for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) due to their high signal-to-noise ratio and information transfer rate. Template-based methods have demonstrated superior performance in SSVEP decoding; however, they typically require substantial calibration data from each user to achieve optimal accuracy, limiting their practical applicability. This study introduces a novel cross-domain transfer learning framework to enhance template-based SSVEP decoding while minimizing calibration requirements. Our approach leverages knowledge from existing datasets (source domain) to improve classification performance on new users (target domain) with limited training samples. We propose a two-stage transfer learning strategy that first aligns the feature distributions between domains through domain adaptation techniques, then fine-tunes subject-specific templates using minimal calibration data. Experiments conducted on a multi-subject SSVEP dataset demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms traditional template-matching approaches, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 15.2% when using only 20% of the calibration data typically required. Furthermore, the proposed framework shows robust performance across subjects with varying signal quality and maintains effectiveness even with inter-session variability. These findings suggest that cross-domain transfer learning offers a promising solution to the calibration bottleneck in SSVEP-based BCIs, potentially facilitating more practical and user-friendly applications.

Definition and evaluation of model-free coordination of electrical vehicle charging with reinforcement learning

This paper presents a novel model-free approach for coordinating electric vehicle (EV) charging using reinforcement learning (RL) techniques. As EV adoption accelerates globally, efficient charging coordination becomes critical to prevent grid congestion, reduce peak loads, and optimize electricity costs. Unlike traditional model-based methods that require extensive knowledge of grid dynamics and user behavior, our approach leverages RL to learn optimal charging policies directly from interactions with the environment. We formulate the EV charging coordination problem as a Markov Decision Process and implement several state-of-the-art RL algorithms, including Deep Q-Networks (DQN) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), to discover effective charging strategies. Our framework considers multiple objectives including minimizing electricity costs, reducing grid impact, and maximizing user satisfaction. Extensive evaluations using real-world EV charging data from urban charging stations demonstrate that our model-free approach achieves 18% cost reduction and 23% peak load reduction compared to uncoordinated charging, while maintaining comparable performance to model-based methods. Additionally, our solution shows robust adaptability to varying grid conditions and charging demands without requiring system recalibration. These results highlight the potential of reinforcement learning as a scalable and adaptive solution for large-scale EV charging coordination in future smart grid systems.

Limits of End-to-End Learning

End-to-end learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm in machine learning, enabling models to map directly from raw inputs to desired outputs without explicit feature engineering or intermediate representations. While this approach has yielded remarkable successes across domains including computer vision, natural language processing, and robotics, this paper examines its fundamental limitations. We identify several critical constraints: the requirement for massive labeled datasets, challenges in incorporating prior knowledge and domain expertise, difficulties in providing interpretability and explanations for predictions, and diminished performance in low-data regimes. Through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation across multiple domains, we demonstrate scenarios where hybrid approaches that combine end-to-end learning with modular components, symbolic reasoning, or structured representations outperform pure end-to-end systems. Our findings suggest that future research should focus on developing frameworks that preserve the representation learning capabilities of end-to-end systems while addressing their inherent limitations through judicious integration of complementary approaches. This work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of when to apply end-to-end learning and how to overcome its constraints in practical applications.

Exploiting Color Name Space for Salient Object Detection

This paper presents a novel approach to salient object detection by leveraging the perceptual and linguistic characteristics of color name space. While traditional methods often rely on low-level color features in RGB or other standard color spaces, we demonstrate that color naming models—which map colors to linguistic terms—provide powerful cues for identifying visually salient regions. Our framework transforms input images into a color name space representation where each pixel is characterized by its association with universal color terms (e.g., red, green, blue, yellow). We introduce a Color Name Saliency (CNS) model that exploits the distinctiveness and categorical perception of colors to enhance saliency detection. Experiments conducted on five benchmark datasets show that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 3.8% in F-measure and 2.5% in Mean Absolute Error. Further analysis reveals that color name features are particularly effective for images where salient objects exhibit distinctive colorization or appear against complex backgrounds. The proposed method is computationally efficient and provides more interpretable saliency maps aligned with human perceptual understanding. This work establishes color naming as an important higher-level feature for saliency detection and offers new directions for incorporating linguistic color representations in computer vision tasks.

AFS: An Attention-based mechanism for Supervised Feature Selection

Feature selection remains a critical challenge in machine learning, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional datasets where many features may be irrelevant or redundant. This paper introduces AFS (Attention-based Feature Selection), a novel supervised feature selection framework that leverages attention mechanisms to identify the most informative features for classification and regression tasks. Unlike traditional feature selection methods that rely on statistical measures or wrapper approaches, AFS learns feature importance through an end-to-end differentiable attention layer integrated within a neural network architecture. The model assigns attention weights to input features during training, naturally identifying relevant features while suppressing uninformative ones. Our experimental evaluation across diverse datasets demonstrates that AFS consistently outperforms classical feature selection techniques including filter methods, wrapper methods, and embedded approaches. Furthermore, AFS offers interpretability by providing clear feature importance rankings while maintaining competitive computational efficiency. The proposed method shows particular strength in handling datasets with complex feature interactions and noisy features, making it a promising approach for real-world applications where feature selection is crucial for model performance and interpretability.

Adapting Models to Signal Degradation using Distillation

This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance model robustness against signal degradation through knowledge distillation techniques. As machine learning systems increasingly operate in real-world environments where input signals are subject to noise, compression artifacts, and other forms of degradation, maintaining performance becomes challenging. We propose a distillation framework that transfers knowledge from models trained on pristine signals to student models specifically optimized for degraded inputs. Our method employs a two-stage process: first, a teacher model is trained on high-quality data; second, this knowledge is distilled into a student model while systematically exposing it to various degradation patterns. Experimental results across multiple domains—including speech recognition, computer vision, and sensor data analysis—demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms both standard training and conventional data augmentation techniques. Models trained with our distillation approach maintain up to 92% of their original performance under severe degradation conditions where baseline approaches drop below 65%. We provide theoretical insights into why distillation is particularly effective for this adaptation problem and offer practical guidelines for implementing this approach in resource-constrained environments.

SSPC-Net: Semi-supervised Semantic 3D Point Cloud Segmentation Network

This paper presents SSPC-Net, a novel semi-supervised learning framework for semantic segmentation of 3D point cloud data. While point cloud segmentation has advanced significantly with deep learning approaches, these methods typically require large amounts of labeled data, which is costly and time-consuming to obtain. Our proposed SSPC-Net addresses this challenge by effectively leveraging both labeled and unlabeled point cloud data in a semi-supervised learning paradigm. The network architecture consists of a teacher-student model with a feature consistency regularization mechanism that propagates knowledge from labeled to unlabeled samples. We introduce a dynamic confidence thresholding strategy for pseudo-label generation and a point-wise contrastive learning module that enhances feature discrimination across semantic categories. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including S3DIS, ScanNet, and SemanticKITTI demonstrate that SSPC-Net achieves competitive performance with only 20% labeled data compared to fully-supervised approaches. Furthermore, our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each proposed component. The results indicate that SSPC-Net provides a promising solution for real-world applications where annotated 3D point cloud data is limited but unlabeled data is abundant.

Regression Prior Networks

This paper introduces Regression Prior Networks (RPNs), a novel framework for uncertainty-aware regression that explicitly models both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. While existing approaches often struggle to disentangle these uncertainty types or require separate model components, RPNs provide a unified solution by placing a prior distribution over the parameters of the predictive distribution. Our approach extends the Prior Networks paradigm from classification to regression tasks, enabling the model to express uncertainty through a higher-order distribution over predictive distributions. We demonstrate that RPNs can effectively capture out-of-distribution inputs without explicit training on outliers, provide well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, and maintain competitive predictive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Extensive empirical evaluation on both synthetic datasets and real-world regression benchmarks shows that RPNs offer robust uncertainty quantification while maintaining computational efficiency. Furthermore, we establish theoretical connections between RPNs and other uncertainty estimation approaches, providing insights into when and why our method offers advantages. These properties make RPNs particularly suitable for safety-critical applications where reliable uncertainty estimation is essential.

Prototype Guided Federated Learning of Visual Feature Representations

This paper introduces a novel approach to federated learning for visual feature representation that addresses the challenges of data heterogeneity and communication efficiency in distributed learning environments. We propose Prototype Guided Federated Learning (PGFL), a framework that leverages class-specific prototypes to guide the learning of robust visual representations across decentralized clients without sharing raw data. PGFL employs a dual-level knowledge distillation mechanism: locally, each client aligns its feature space with prototype-based references, while globally, a prototype aggregation strategy ensures consistent feature representations across the federation. Our experiments across multiple vision datasets with varying degrees of non-IID distribution demonstrate that PGFL significantly outperforms existing federated learning methods, achieving up to 7.2% improvement in classification accuracy on heterogeneous data while reducing communication costs by 35%. Furthermore, PGFL shows remarkable resilience to statistical heterogeneity and client drift, maintaining representation consistency even with highly skewed data distributions. The proposed approach not only advances the state-of-the-art in federated visual representation learning but also provides insights into effective knowledge transfer in privacy-preserving distributed learning systems.

A Deep Actor-Critic Reinforcement Learning Framework for Dynamic Multichannel Access

This paper introduces a novel deep actor-critic reinforcement learning framework to address the challenge of dynamic multichannel access in wireless communication systems. We formulate the channel selection problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) where the agent must learn to navigate a time-varying radio environment with partial observability. Our proposed framework combines a deep neural network-based actor that determines channel selection policies with a critic network that evaluates action quality, enabling efficient learning in complex channel environments. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our approach outperforms conventional methods such as multi-armed bandit algorithms and Q-learning approaches, achieving up to 35% higher throughput and 42% lower collision rates in highly dynamic spectrum environments. The framework shows remarkable adaptability to changing channel conditions and scalability to systems with large numbers of channels. Furthermore, we provide theoretical convergence guarantees and practical implementation considerations for deployment in real-world wireless systems. This work represents a significant advancement in intelligent spectrum access techniques for next-generation wireless networks facing increasingly congested and unpredictable spectrum conditions.

Distortion Estimation Through Explicit Modeling of the Refractive Surface

This paper presents a novel approach to estimating optical distortion by explicitly modeling the underlying refractive surface. Unlike traditional methods that treat distortion as a black-box phenomenon, our approach incorporates physical principles of light refraction to create a more accurate and interpretable model. We develop a parametric representation of the refractive surface that can account for complex distortion patterns in imaging systems, including those found in underwater photography, through-glass imaging, and medical endoscopy. By solving the inverse problem of determining the refractive surface parameters from observed distortion patterns, our method achieves superior correction accuracy compared to polynomial distortion models. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach reduces geometric distortion by an average of 37% compared to state-of-the-art techniques, while providing physically meaningful insights into the optical system. Additionally, the explicit nature of our model enables effective distortion prediction under varying imaging conditions. This work bridges the gap between physical optics and computational imaging, offering both theoretical contributions and practical applications for computer vision systems operating in environments with refractive distortion.

A Comprehensive Comparison of End-to-End Approaches for Handwritten Digit String Recognition

This paper presents a systematic evaluation of various end-to-end approaches for recognizing handwritten digit strings. We compare traditional segmentation-based methods with modern segmentation-free deep learning architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and attention-based transformer models. Experiments were conducted on multiple benchmark datasets including MNIST-Strings, SVHN, and IAM-Digits, encompassing various challenges such as connected digits, varying string lengths, and different writing styles. Our results demonstrate that attention-based encoder-decoder architectures consistently outperform other approaches, achieving a 97.3% sequence-level accuracy on complex digit strings. We also observe that while segmentation-free methods generally perform better, hybrid approaches that incorporate weak segmentation cues show promise for challenging cases. Furthermore, we analyze the computational requirements and inference speeds of each method, providing practical insights for real-world deployment scenarios. This comprehensive comparison establishes new baselines for the field and offers guidance for selecting appropriate recognition techniques based on specific application constraints.

Temporal Knowledge Consistency for Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning

This paper introduces Temporal Knowledge Consistency (TKC), a novel framework for unsupervised visual representation learning that leverages the temporal coherence inherent in video data. Unlike previous approaches that rely on instance discrimination or contrastive learning between individual frames, our method exploits the consistency of knowledge extracted across temporal sequences to learn robust visual representations without human supervision. We propose a teacher-student architecture where a slowly evolving teacher network distills consistent knowledge to a student network across temporally augmented views of the same video sequence. The key innovation of TKC lies in enforcing consistency at the knowledge level rather than the feature level, allowing the model to focus on semantically meaningful information that persists through time while being invariant to transient visual changes. Through extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including ImageNet classification, COCO object detection, and action recognition tasks, we demonstrate that TKC outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised learning methods while requiring less computational resources. Our approach shows particular strength in scenarios with limited labeled data, suggesting that temporal knowledge consistency effectively captures fundamental visual representations that generalize across diverse visual understanding tasks.

Fast and Accurate 3D Medical Image Segmentation with Data-swapping Method

This paper introduces a novel data-swapping method for 3D medical image segmentation that significantly improves both computational efficiency and segmentation accuracy. Current approaches to 3D medical image segmentation often face challenges balancing processing speed with precision, particularly when handling large volumetric datasets. Our proposed method addresses these limitations by implementing an innovative data-swapping technique that dynamically exchanges information between adjacent image slices during the segmentation process. The approach leverages contextual similarities in neighboring regions while reducing redundant computations. Experiments conducted across multiple medical imaging modalities, including MRI, CT, and ultrasound volumes, demonstrate that our method achieves up to 40% reduction in processing time while simultaneously improving segmentation accuracy by 8-12% compared to state-of-the-art methods. The data-swapping technique proves particularly effective for structures with complex morphologies and indistinct boundaries. Furthermore, our approach requires minimal additional memory overhead, making it suitable for deployment in resource-constrained clinical settings. These results suggest that the proposed data-swapping method represents a significant advancement in 3D medical image segmentation, offering potential benefits for time-sensitive clinical applications such as intraoperative guidance and rapid diagnostics.

Risk Bounds for Unsupervised Cross-Domain Mapping with IPMs

This paper addresses the fundamental challenge of unsupervised cross-domain mapping, where the goal is to learn transformations between domains without paired examples. We develop a theoretical framework leveraging Integral Probability Metrics (IPMs) to establish rigorous risk bounds for this setting. Our approach provides a principled alternative to existing adversarial methods by explicitly quantifying the statistical guarantees of domain mapping functions. We first characterize the relationship between the true mapping risk and its empirical counterpart using IPM-based discrepancy measures, demonstrating how these bounds tighten as sample size increases. The framework accommodates various IPM instantiations, including Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and Wasserstein distances, allowing flexibility in capturing domain-specific characteristics. Theoretical analysis reveals that our bounds achieve minimax optimal rates under standard assumptions. Empirical validation across synthetic distributions and real-world domain adaptation tasks demonstrates that our IPM-based mapping approach not only provides theoretical guarantees but also achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. These results establish a theoretical foundation for unsupervised domain mapping that balances statistical rigor with practical effectiveness.

Dynamics-Aware Unsupervised Discovery of Skills

This paper presents a novel framework for unsupervised skill discovery that explicitly incorporates environmental dynamics awareness. While previous approaches to learning diverse skills without external rewards have shown promise, they often fail to discover behaviors that effectively exploit the underlying dynamics of the environment. Our method, Dynamics-Aware Skill Discovery (DASD), addresses this limitation by jointly learning a dynamics model alongside the skill discovery process. We introduce a mutual information objective that encourages skills to not only be distinguishable but also to interact meaningfully with the environment's physical properties. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that our approach leads to the emergence of skills that exhibit both diversity and dynamical consistency. Experiments across various continuous control environments show that DASD discovers more functional and transferable skills compared to dynamics-agnostic methods. Furthermore, when these discovered skills are used as primitives for hierarchical reinforcement learning, agents achieve significantly faster learning on downstream tasks. Our results suggest that dynamics awareness is a crucial component for unsupervised discovery of useful behavioral primitives in embodied agents.

Cryptocurrency Portfolio Management with Deep Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces a novel deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach for cryptocurrency portfolio management that addresses the unique challenges of this highly volatile and complex market. We develop a framework that combines a deep neural network architecture with reinforcement learning algorithms to dynamically allocate assets across multiple cryptocurrencies. Our model incorporates market microstructure features, sentiment analysis from social media, and on-chain metrics to capture the multidimensional nature of cryptocurrency valuations. Through extensive backtesting on historical data from 2017 to 2023, covering both bull and bear market cycles, we demonstrate that our DRL approach significantly outperforms traditional portfolio optimization methods and benchmark strategies, achieving 18.3% higher risk-adjusted returns while reducing maximum drawdown by 12.5%. The model exhibits particular strength in rapidly adapting to market regime changes and extreme volatility events characteristic of cryptocurrency markets. We further analyze the interpretability of the model's decision-making process and discuss practical implementation considerations including transaction costs and liquidity constraints. Our findings suggest that DRL-based portfolio management offers a promising solution for institutional and retail investors seeking to navigate the cryptocurrency asset class effectively.

Panoster: End-to-end Panoptic Segmentation of LiDAR Point Clouds

This paper introduces Panoster, a novel end-to-end framework for panoptic segmentation of LiDAR point clouds that simultaneously addresses instance and semantic segmentation in 3D space. While previous approaches typically handle these tasks separately or through complex multi-stage pipelines, our method unifies them in a single architecture that operates directly on raw point cloud data. Panoster employs a point-based backbone with a dual-head architecture that jointly predicts semantic classes for each point while generating instance embeddings that cluster points belonging to the same object. We propose a new loss function that effectively balances the semantic and instance learning objectives, addressing the inherent challenges of varying object sizes and point densities in LiDAR data. Extensive experiments on the SemanticKITTI and nuScenes datasets demonstrate that Panoster achieves state-of-the-art performance in panoptic quality metrics while maintaining real-time inference capabilities critical for autonomous driving applications. Our ablation studies highlight the importance of our unified approach over traditional methods that treat semantic and instance segmentation as separate problems. The proposed framework provides a more efficient and accurate solution for scene understanding from LiDAR data, with potential applications in autonomous navigation, robotic perception, and environmental mapping.

Reward Propagation Using Graph Convolutional Networks

This paper introduces a novel approach to reward propagation in reinforcement learning using Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). Traditional reinforcement learning algorithms often struggle with sparse rewards and long-term credit assignment. We formulate the reward propagation problem as a graph-based learning task, where states and actions are represented as nodes in a graph with their relationships encoded as edges. Our proposed method, RP-GCN (Reward Propagation GCN), leverages the power of graph convolutional networks to efficiently propagate reward signals through this state-action graph. Experimental results across various domains, including grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and complex game environments, demonstrate that RP-GCN significantly outperforms baseline methods in terms of sample efficiency and final performance. The approach shows particular promise in environments with delayed rewards, where it accelerates learning by 45-60% compared to standard methods. Additionally, we provide theoretical analysis establishing convergence guarantees under certain conditions. Our work bridges deep learning on graphs with reinforcement learning, opening new avenues for addressing fundamental challenges in reward-based learning systems.

Abstract: How to Simplify Search: Classification-wise Pareto Evolution for One-shot Neural Architecture Search

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has demonstrated remarkable success in automating the design of neural networks, yet its computational demands remain a significant challenge. In this paper, we introduce Classification-wise Pareto Evolution (CPE), a novel approach to one-shot NAS that substantially reduces search complexity while maintaining performance. Our method decomposes the architecture search space into classification-wise subspaces and employs Pareto optimization to efficiently navigate the trade-offs between accuracy and computational cost. Unlike conventional approaches that evaluate entire architectures, CPE optimizes architectural components specific to different classification tasks, enabling more targeted exploration. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, we demonstrate that CPE achieves comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art NAS methods while reducing search time by up to 70%. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the architectures discovered through CPE exhibit better generalization across diverse tasks. The proposed approach not only simplifies the search process but also provides insights into the relationship between architectural components and specific classification challenges, offering a more interpretable framework for neural architecture design.

Group Collaborative Learning for Co-Salient Object Detection

Co-salient object detection (CoSOD) aims to identify common salient objects shared across multiple related images. Despite recent advances in deep learning-based CoSOD methods, effectively modeling inter-image relationships while maintaining intra-image saliency remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Group Collaborative Learning (GCL), a novel framework that addresses these challenges by treating CoSOD as a collaborative learning problem among image groups. Our approach employs a dual-stream architecture: a group-aware feature extraction module that captures group-level semantic consistency, and an adaptive collaboration mechanism that dynamically weighs inter-image relationships based on semantic similarity. The GCL framework incorporates a group consensus loss that explicitly encourages consistent predictions across related images while preserving distinctive object features. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets—CoSOD3k, CoCA, and CoSal2015—demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving improvements of 2.3%, 3.1%, and 1.8% in F-measure scores, respectively. Further ablation studies validate the effectiveness of each component in our proposed framework. The GCL approach not only advances CoSOD performance but also provides insights into collaborative representation learning for group-based visual tasks.

HRegNet: A Hierarchical Network for Large-scale Outdoor LiDAR Point Cloud Registration

Point cloud registration is a fundamental task in 3D computer vision with critical applications in autonomous driving, robotics, and mapping. In this paper, we present HRegNet, a novel hierarchical deep learning framework designed specifically for large-scale outdoor LiDAR point cloud registration. Unlike existing approaches that struggle with the complexity and scale of outdoor environments, our method employs a multi-resolution hierarchical architecture that efficiently processes point clouds while preserving both local geometric details and global structural context. HRegNet consists of three main components: (1) a hierarchical feature extraction module that leverages downsampling and local aggregation to capture multi-scale representations, (2) a cross-attention mechanism that establishes reliable correspondences between point clouds at different hierarchical levels, and (3) a coarse-to-fine registration refinement strategy that progressively improves alignment accuracy. Extensive experiments on large-scale outdoor datasets, including KITTI and nuScenes, demonstrate that HRegNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of registration accuracy, robustness to noise and sparse scanning patterns, and computational efficiency. Our approach achieves an average rotation error reduction of 23% and translation error reduction of 18% compared to previous methods, while maintaining real-time performance suitable for autonomous navigation systems. The code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available.

Precision and Recall for Time Series

Traditional precision and recall metrics, widely used in information retrieval and classification tasks, face significant challenges when applied to time series data due to temporal dependencies, alignment issues, and the continuous nature of time-based measurements. This paper introduces a novel framework for evaluating precision and recall specifically designed for time series analysis. Our approach addresses the fundamental question of how to meaningfully quantify true positives, false positives, and false negatives in the temporal domain while accounting for time shifts, amplitude variations, and different sampling rates. We propose a distance-based similarity measure that incorporates temporal warping and defines adaptive thresholds for determining matches between predicted and actual events. Through extensive experiments on diverse datasets including financial indicators, sensor measurements, and physiological signals, we demonstrate that our metrics provide more nuanced and actionable performance assessments than conventional techniques. The proposed framework enables more accurate model comparison and selection in time series forecasting, anomaly detection, and pattern recognition tasks. Our results indicate that this approach better reflects human judgment of similarity in time series and provides robust performance evaluation across various temporal resolutions and data characteristics.

Road Mapping In LiDAR Images Using A Joint-Task Dense Dilated Convolutions Merging Network

This paper presents a novel approach to road mapping in LiDAR point clouds using a Joint-Task Dense Dilated Convolutions Merging Network (JT-DDCMNet). Road extraction from LiDAR data remains challenging due to varying point densities, occlusions, and complex urban environments. Our proposed architecture addresses these challenges by simultaneously performing road segmentation and boundary detection through a dual-stream network architecture with shared feature learning. The network leverages dense dilated convolutions to capture multi-scale contextual information while maintaining spatial resolution, crucial for precise road boundary delineation. We introduce a feature merging module that effectively combines complementary information from both tasks, enhancing overall performance through mutual reinforcement. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including KITTI Road and Toronto-3D demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance with 94.7% F1-score for road segmentation and 92.3% for boundary detection, outperforming existing methods by 3.2% and 4.5% respectively. Additionally, our model demonstrates robust generalization capabilities across different urban environments and sensor configurations while maintaining real-time inference speeds suitable for autonomous driving applications. The proposed joint-task learning framework provides a promising direction for enhancing road mapping accuracy in LiDAR-based perception systems.

Semantic Palette: Guiding Scene Generation with Class Proportions

This paper introduces Semantic Palette, a novel approach for controlled scene generation that allows users to specify desired semantic class distributions in generated images. Unlike existing methods that rely on spatial layouts or text prompts, our framework enables intuitive control through simple class proportion inputs (e.g., 30% sky, 25% building, 20% vegetation). We propose a two-stage architecture that first translates class proportions into compatible semantic layouts and then renders these layouts into photorealistic images. Our key technical contribution is a proportion-conditioned diffusion model that learns to generate diverse, realistic layouts adhering to specified class distributions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Semantic Palette generates high-quality images that accurately reflect user-specified class proportions while maintaining scene coherence across diverse environments including urban, natural, and indoor settings. Comparative evaluations show our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of proportion fidelity, image quality, and user control. Semantic Palette offers an intuitive interface for non-expert users to guide scene generation through simple numerical inputs, enabling applications in content creation, architectural visualization, and environmental design.

All You Can Embed: Natural Language based Vehicle Retrieval with Spatio-Temporal Transformers

This paper introduces a novel approach to natural language-based vehicle retrieval in complex urban environments using spatio-temporal transformers. Current vehicle identification systems primarily rely on structured queries like license plate recognition or appearance-based matching, which fail to accommodate natural language descriptions that humans naturally use to identify vehicles. We present a multimodal framework that jointly encodes visual vehicle features alongside their motion patterns and contextual information through a spatio-temporal transformer architecture. Our model, AYCE-VR (All You Can Embed Vehicle Retrieval), learns dense embeddings that align free-form textual descriptions with corresponding vehicle instances across multiple camera views and time periods. The approach incorporates temporal attention mechanisms to capture vehicle dynamics and spatial context encoders to model relationships between vehicles and their surroundings. Extensive experiments on large-scale urban traffic datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous approaches, achieving 23.7% higher recall@1 on complex queries involving motion descriptions, spatial references, and appearance details. We further show that our embeddings generalize effectively to unseen query formulations and transfer well across different urban environments. This work represents a substantial advancement in natural human-machine interaction for intelligent transportation systems and urban surveillance applications.

Fully Steerable 3D Spherical Neurons
