We introduce Fully Steerable 3D Spherical Neurons (FS3D-SN), a novel neural network architecture designed to process 3D data with inherent rotational equivariance. Unlike conventional 3D convolutional networks that struggle with orientation variations, our approach leverages spherical harmonic transformations to create steerable feature representations that maintain consistent predictions regardless of input orientation. By decomposing 3D signals onto a spherical harmonic basis and applying learnable weight functions that respect SO(3) symmetry constraints, FS3D-SN achieves rotation equivariance by design rather than through data augmentation. Our experiments demonstrate superior performance on 3D object classification, molecular property prediction, and medical image segmentation tasks, with particular advantages in data-limited regimes where orientation invariance cannot be effectively learned through augmentation alone. The model requires significantly fewer parameters than comparable architectures while maintaining computational efficiency through optimized spherical convolution operations. This work bridges theoretical insights from group representation theory with practical deep learning architectures, offering a principled approach to building rotation-equivariant 3D neural networks.

Fighting Deepfake by Exposing the Convolutional Traces on Images

The proliferation of deepfake technology poses significant threats to information integrity and public trust in visual media. This paper presents a novel approach to deepfake detection by identifying and analyzing the unique convolutional traces left on images during the generation process. Our method leverages the observation that deepfake algorithms, which primarily rely on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), leave distinct fingerprints in the frequency domain of manipulated images. We develop a detection framework that extracts these forensic traces through multi-scale frequency analysis and employs a custom-designed neural network architecture to classify authentic versus synthetic content. Experiments conducted on multiple state-of-the-art deepfake datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves 97.3% detection accuracy, outperforming existing methods by 4.8%. Notably, our technique maintains robust performance even when confronted with post-processing operations designed to conceal manipulation, such as compression and blurring. Additionally, we provide visualization tools that highlight manipulated regions, enhancing the interpretability of detection results. This research contributes a powerful, generalizable approach to combating the growing sophistication of deepfake technologies while requiring minimal computational resources for deployment.

BEV-Seg: Bird's Eye View Semantic Segmentation Using Geometry and Semantic Point Cloud

This paper presents BEV-Seg, a novel approach for bird's eye view (BEV) semantic segmentation that effectively leverages both geometric and semantic information from 3D point clouds. Unlike existing methods that rely primarily on perspective image data or raw point clouds, our approach integrates semantic features with precise geometric information to generate accurate top-down scene representations. We propose a two-stream architecture that processes LiDAR point clouds through a geometric branch while simultaneously extracting rich semantic features through a dedicated semantic encoding pathway. These complementary representations are fused through our proposed Cross-Modal Attention Module (CMAM) that dynamically emphasizes relevant features from both modalities. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes and Argoverse datasets demonstrate that BEV-Seg achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) by 3.2% compared to previous methods. Our approach shows particular strength in segmenting small objects and disambiguating semantically similar classes in the bird's eye view perspective. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive ablation study that validates the contribution of each component in our framework. BEV-Seg offers a robust solution for autonomous driving perception systems requiring accurate environmental understanding from a top-down viewpoint.

Sketch-based Normal Map Generation with Geometric Sampling

This paper presents a novel approach for generating high-quality normal maps directly from hand-drawn sketches using geometric sampling techniques. We introduce a framework that bridges the gap between simple line drawings and detailed surface information by leveraging geometric priors to infer plausible surface orientations. Our method employs a two-stage process: first, a geometric feature extraction phase identifies key structural elements from input sketches; second, an adaptive sampling strategy propagates normal information across the surface while preserving artistic intent. Unlike previous approaches that rely solely on data-driven learning, our geometric sampling technique explicitly models the relationship between sketch lines and surface gradients, resulting in more consistent and predictable normal reconstructions. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and coherence metrics, while qualitative assessments confirm improved visual fidelity. The system enables real-time feedback and intuitive controls for artists to refine results, making it suitable for integration into existing digital content creation pipelines. Our work contributes to the growing field of sketch-based modeling by providing a robust solution for rapidly converting 2D drawings into 3D surface details with minimal user intervention.

Generative Cooperative Net for Image Generation and Data Augmentation

This paper introduces Generative Cooperative Net (GCN), a novel framework for high-fidelity image generation and effective data augmentation. Unlike traditional generative adversarial networks that rely on competition between generator and discriminator, our approach establishes a cooperative mechanism where multiple subnetworks collaborate to optimize image synthesis. GCN employs a hierarchical architecture with specialized components for structure preservation, texture refinement, and semantic consistency, enabling the generation of diverse yet realistic images across various domains. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods on standard benchmarks, achieving an FID score improvement of 18.7% on CIFAR-10 and 22.3% on ImageNet. Furthermore, when used for data augmentation in downstream classification tasks, GCN-generated samples boost model accuracy by an average of 4.2% in limited data scenarios. The cooperative design also exhibits enhanced training stability and mitigates mode collapse issues common in adversarial frameworks. Our approach provides a promising direction for generative modeling with particular benefits for applications requiring both high-quality image synthesis and effective data augmentation.

Bootstrapping Structure into Language: Alignment-Based Learning

This paper introduces Alignment-Based Learning (ABL), a novel computational framework for bootstrapping structural representations into language models without explicit supervision. We demonstrate how structural patterns can emerge through iterative alignment procedures that identify and reinforce recurring patterns across linguistic data. Our approach leverages the principle that language acquisition involves discovering hierarchical regularities through pattern matching and distributional analysis. By implementing a self-organizing system that identifies, abstracts, and generalizes structural alignments, we show that models can develop linguistically plausible representations that capture syntactic and semantic relationships. Experiments across multiple languages demonstrate that ABL successfully induces grammatical categories, phrase structures, and dependencies that closely match linguistic analyses, despite having no prior grammatical knowledge encoded. The resulting representations not only improve performance on downstream tasks but also exhibit better generalization to novel linguistic constructions compared to traditional supervised approaches. Our findings suggest that structural bootstrapping through alignment mechanisms may be a fundamental process in both natural language acquisition and computational language learning.

Stereo Vision-based Semantic 3D Object and Ego-motion Tracking for Autonomous Driving

This paper presents a novel framework for joint 3D object detection and ego-motion estimation using stereo vision for autonomous driving applications. Our approach integrates semantic understanding with geometric reasoning to simultaneously track vehicle movement and surrounding objects in complex urban environments. By leveraging deep neural networks for semantic segmentation and stereo matching, we generate semantically enriched 3D point clouds that serve as input to our tracking system. The proposed method introduces a multi-task optimization scheme that jointly estimates camera ego-motion and tracks dynamic objects, incorporating semantic cues to improve robustness against occlusions and appearance changes. Extensive experiments on the KITTI and nuScenes datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in both 3D object tracking and ego-localization, with average precision improvements of 7.2% for vehicle detection and 5.3% reduced drift in ego-motion estimation compared to existing methods. Our system operates in real-time at 18 frames per second on standard GPU hardware, making it suitable for deployment in autonomous driving systems. The results highlight how integrating semantic information with geometric constraints enhances the accuracy and reliability of vision-based perception for autonomous navigation.

Neural Oblivious Decision Ensembles for Deep Learning on Tabular Data

Despite the significant success of deep learning in various domains such as computer vision and natural language processing, its application to tabular data has remained challenging, with traditional machine learning methods like gradient boosting decision trees (GBDT) often outperforming neural networks in this context. In this paper, we introduce Neural Oblivious Decision Ensembles (NODE), a novel deep learning architecture specifically designed for tabular data. NODE combines the strengths of both decision tree ensembles and neural networks by implementing differentiable oblivious decision trees within a neural network framework. This approach allows for end-to-end gradient-based optimization while maintaining the inductive biases that make decision trees effective for tabular data. Through extensive experimentation on a diverse range of tabular datasets, we demonstrate that NODE consistently outperforms both traditional GBDT implementations and existing deep learning approaches. Our model shows particular strength in handling heterogeneous features, categorical variables, and complex feature interactions, while maintaining interpretability through its tree-based structure. Additionally, NODE exhibits improved robustness to noise and missing values compared to alternative methods. These results suggest that our approach represents a significant advancement in applying deep learning techniques to tabular data problems across various domains including finance, healthcare, and recommendation systems.

Simple, Accurate, and Robust Nonparametric Blind Super-Resolution

This paper introduces a novel nonparametric approach to blind super-resolution (SR) that addresses key limitations of existing methods. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on parametric blur kernel models or extensive training data, our method operates without prior assumptions about the degradation process. We propose a simple yet effective framework that iteratively refines both the high-resolution image and the unknown blur kernel through a nonparametric estimation procedure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves superior reconstruction quality across diverse degradation scenarios, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by an average of 2.3dB PSNR on benchmark datasets. The method exhibits remarkable robustness to noise, compression artifacts, and severe blur conditions where parametric models typically fail. Additionally, our algorithm maintains computational efficiency with linear scaling relative to image size. The simplicity of our approach, combined with its accuracy and robustness, makes it particularly suitable for real-world applications where degradation parameters are unknown and variable. Code and pre-trained models are made publicly available to facilitate further research in this direction.

PointShuffleNet: Learning Non-Euclidean Features with Homotopy Equivalence and Mutual Information

Point cloud analysis remains challenging due to the inherent non-Euclidean structure and irregular sampling of 3D data. This paper introduces PointShuffleNet, a novel deep learning framework designed to capture topological and geometric features of point clouds through the lens of homotopy equivalence and information theory. Our approach leverages channel shuffling operations inspired by ShuffleNet architecture, but uniquely adapted to preserve topological invariants across point cloud transformations. We propose a mutual information maximization objective that ensures learned representations maintain both local geometric details and global topological structures. Experimental results demonstrate that PointShuffleNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets for classification, segmentation, and shape completion tasks, outperforming previous methods by 2.3% on ModelNet40 and 3.1% on ShapeNet. Ablation studies confirm that our homotopy-aware feature extraction and information-theoretic learning objectives significantly contribute to the model's robustness against non-uniform sampling, noise, and partial occlusions. PointShuffleNet provides a theoretically grounded framework for understanding non-Euclidean data while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time applications.

Deep PDF: Probabilistic Surface Optimization and Density Estimation

This paper introduces Deep PDF, a novel framework that combines deep learning with probabilistic density function estimation for optimizing surface representations and estimating probability distributions from complex data. Our approach leverages neural networks to learn continuous probability density functions that can accurately model the underlying distribution of high-dimensional data while simultaneously optimizing surface representations in 3D space. By formulating surface optimization as a density estimation problem, Deep PDF provides a unified mathematical framework that bridges geometric processing and statistical learning. We demonstrate that our method can effectively handle noisy, incomplete data and generate high-quality surface reconstructions with quantified uncertainty. Experiments across diverse applications—including 3D shape completion, point cloud processing, and generative modeling—show that Deep PDF outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of reconstruction accuracy, generalization capability, and computational efficiency. The probabilistic nature of our framework enables robust handling of ambiguous regions and principled quantification of uncertainty, making it particularly valuable for applications in computer vision, graphics, and scientific computing where data may be sparse or noisy.

A Taxonomy of Similarity Metrics for Markov Decision Processes

This paper presents a comprehensive taxonomy of similarity metrics for Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), addressing the growing need for principled comparison methods in reinforcement learning and decision theory. We systematically categorize existing metrics based on their mathematical foundations, computational properties, and preservation of decision-relevant structures. Our taxonomy distinguishes between state-space metrics, transition dynamics metrics, reward-based metrics, value-function metrics, and policy-based similarity measures. For each category, we analyze theoretical guarantees, computational complexity, and sensitivity to MDP parameterizations. Through extensive empirical evaluation across diverse domains, we demonstrate how different metrics capture various aspects of behavioral equivalence between MDPs. Our framework unifies previously disparate approaches and provides practical guidance for selecting appropriate similarity measures based on specific application requirements. This taxonomy not only clarifies the relationships between existing metrics but also identifies promising directions for developing new similarity measures that better capture the decision-theoretic essence of MDPs.

Temporal Context Aggregation for Video Retrieval with Contrastive Learning

This paper introduces a novel approach to video retrieval that addresses the critical challenge of effectively modeling temporal relationships within video content. Our proposed Temporal Context Aggregation (TCA) framework enhances video representation by explicitly capturing and aggregating temporal contextual information across frames. Unlike previous methods that treat videos as collections of independent frames or rely on simple temporal pooling, TCA leverages a multi-head attention mechanism that dynamically weighs the importance of temporal relationships at different scales. We integrate this temporal modeling approach within a contrastive learning paradigm, where video-text pairs are aligned in a joint embedding space through a dual-encoder architecture. Extensive experiments on standard video retrieval benchmarks, including MSR-VTT, MSVD, and DiDeMo, demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 6.2% improvement in R@1 on MSR-VTT. Ablation studies confirm that the performance gains stem from our temporal context aggregation module's ability to capture complex temporal dynamics while maintaining computational efficiency. Our work provides new insights into the importance of temporal modeling for cross-modal video understanding tasks.

Tackling the Unannotated: Scene Graph Generation with Bias-Reduced Models

Scene Graph Generation (SGG) aims to detect objects and their relationships in images, providing structured representations crucial for visual reasoning tasks. However, current SGG models often exhibit strong biases toward frequently observed relationship patterns in training data, while struggling with rare but valid relationships—a problem exacerbated by the inherent incompleteness of relationship annotations in benchmark datasets. This paper introduces a novel bias-reduction framework that addresses both the annotation sparsity and the long-tailed distribution challenges in SGG. Our approach combines contrastive learning with a debiasing mechanism that distinguishes between truly negative relationships and those that are merely unannotated. Through extensive experiments on the Visual Genome dataset, we demonstrate that our method significantly improves performance on tail relationships without compromising overall accuracy, achieving state-of-the-art results across standard metrics. Notably, our model shows a 14.3% relative improvement in Recall@K for rare relationship categories compared to previous methods. We further validate our approach through qualitative analysis and ablation studies, confirming its effectiveness in generating more comprehensive and accurate scene graphs in real-world scenarios where annotation completeness cannot be guaranteed.

T2Net: Synthetic-to-Realistic Translation for Solving Single-Image Depth Estimation Tasks

Single-image depth estimation is a fundamental computer vision problem that remains challenging due to the difficulty of obtaining large-scale ground truth depth data in real-world scenarios. While synthetic data offers precise depth annotations, models trained on synthetic datasets often fail to generalize to real-world images due to the domain gap. In this paper, we propose T2Net (Translation-to-Reality Network), a novel unsupervised domain adaptation framework that bridges the synthetic-to-realistic domain gap for depth estimation tasks. Our approach consists of two main components: (1) an image-translation network that transforms synthetic images to appear more realistic while preserving geometric structure, and (2) a depth estimation network that leverages both the translated synthetic data and unlabeled real data through a carefully designed consistency loss. The key innovation of T2Net is its ability to perform end-to-end training without requiring paired cross-domain data or real-world depth annotations. Extensive experiments on indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches trained on synthetic data alone, and achieves competitive results compared to supervised methods trained on real data with ground truth. Our code and pre-trained models are available to facilitate future research in this direction.

Structure-Aware Network for Lane Marker Extraction with Dynamic Vision Sensor

This paper introduces a novel structure-aware network architecture for lane marker extraction utilizing Dynamic Vision Sensors (DVS). Unlike conventional frame-based cameras, DVS captures asynchronous events triggered by brightness changes, offering advantages in high dynamic range, low latency, and reduced data redundancy—critical properties for robust lane detection in autonomous driving systems. Our proposed network leverages the unique spatiotemporal characteristics of event data while explicitly modeling the structural properties of lane markers. We incorporate a structure-aware feature extraction module that captures the geometric constraints of lanes through directional convolutions and a topology-preserving loss function. Experimental results on both public event-based datasets and our newly collected challenging scenarios demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 12.7% in F1-score and 18.3% in accuracy while maintaining real-time performance (95 fps on standard hardware). Additionally, our method shows remarkable robustness in challenging lighting conditions where traditional vision systems typically fail. The proposed architecture bridges the gap between event-based sensing and structured prediction tasks, opening new possibilities for neuromorphic vision in intelligent transportation systems.

Weakly Supervised Video Moment Retrieval From Text Queries

This paper addresses the challenging task of retrieving specific temporal moments in videos based on natural language queries without relying on expensive temporal boundary annotations during training. We propose a novel weakly supervised framework that learns to align textual queries with relevant video segments using only video-level text descriptions as supervision. Our approach employs a cross-modal attention mechanism that dynamically captures the semantic relationships between visual and textual features, enabling fine-grained localization of moments described in queries. To overcome the lack of temporal annotations, we introduce a multiple instance learning strategy that treats each video as a bag of temporal segments and optimizes a ranking-based objective function to identify the most relevant segments. Extensive experiments on the Charades-STA and ActivityNet Captions datasets demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance compared to fully supervised approaches while significantly outperforming existing weakly supervised alternatives. Notably, our model shows robust generalization to queries with complex linguistic structures and videos containing multiple activities. This work represents an important step toward scalable video moment retrieval systems that can be trained without labor-intensive temporal annotations.

FusiformNet: Extracting Discriminative Facial Features on Different Levels

This paper introduces FusiformNet, a novel deep learning architecture designed specifically for hierarchical facial feature extraction across multiple levels of abstraction. Inspired by the fusiform face area in the human brain, which specializes in face perception, our network employs a multi-pathway structure to simultaneously capture low-level textural details, mid-level facial components, and high-level holistic representations. Through an innovative feature fusion mechanism, FusiformNet dynamically weights the importance of features at different levels based on their discriminative power for the task at hand. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including LFW, CelebA, and CASIA-WebFace demonstrate that FusiformNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods in face recognition, facial attribute prediction, and facial expression analysis. Our ablation studies confirm that the multi-level feature extraction approach significantly contributes to the model's robustness against variations in pose, illumination, and occlusion. The proposed architecture not only advances the performance of automated facial analysis systems but also provides insights into how hierarchical representations can enhance deep learning models for fine-grained visual recognition tasks.

Wasserstein Dependency Measure for Representation Learning

This paper introduces a novel dependency measure for learning robust representations based on the Wasserstein distance. While mutual information has been widely used as an objective for representation learning, it suffers from limitations in capturing the geometry of the underlying data space. We propose the Wasserstein Dependency Measure (WDM), which leverages optimal transport theory to quantify dependencies between variables while respecting the metric structure of the data. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that WDM exhibits desirable properties including sensitivity to non-linear dependencies and robustness to noise. We develop computationally efficient estimators for WDM and incorporate them into representation learning frameworks. Extensive experiments on synthetic data, image classification, and reinforcement learning tasks show that WDM-based representations consistently outperform those trained with mutual information and other dependency measures, particularly in settings with complex geometric structures or limited data. Our approach provides a principled alternative for representation learning that better preserves the underlying data geometry while maintaining computational tractability.

Text2Video: Text-driven Talking-head Video Synthesis with Personalized Phoneme-Pose Dictionary

This paper presents Text2Video, a novel framework for synthesizing realistic talking-head videos driven directly from text input. Unlike existing approaches that rely on intermediate representations such as audio or 3D face models, our method establishes a direct mapping from text to video through a personalized phoneme-pose dictionary. We decompose the text-to-video synthesis task into two key components: (1) a phoneme-to-facial pose mapping that captures speaker-specific articulation patterns, and (2) a neural rendering module that transforms these poses into photorealistic video frames. The core of our approach is the personalized dictionary that associates phonetic units with corresponding facial configurations, learned from a small corpus of target speaker footage. Experimental results demonstrate that Text2Video generates highly realistic talking-head videos with accurate lip synchronization while preserving the identity and speaking style of the target individual. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both objective metrics and subjective human evaluations, particularly in maintaining temporal consistency and natural facial dynamics. Furthermore, we show that our framework can generalize to unseen text inputs and can be fine-tuned with minimal data for new identities. The proposed Text2Video framework offers promising applications in content creation, accessibility services, and human-computer interaction.

3D Ultrasound Image Segmentation: A Survey

This survey provides a comprehensive review of three-dimensional ultrasound (3D US) image segmentation techniques developed over the past two decades. 3D ultrasound imaging has emerged as a valuable non-invasive modality in clinical diagnosis and image-guided interventions due to its real-time capability, absence of ionizing radiation, and relatively low cost. However, the inherent characteristics of ultrasound images—including speckle noise, acoustic shadows, and intensity inhomogeneities—make segmentation particularly challenging. This paper systematically categorizes and analyzes segmentation approaches for 3D ultrasound data, including traditional methods (region-growing, watershed, active contours, level sets), machine learning techniques (random forests, support vector machines), and more recent deep learning architectures (CNNs, U-Net variants, transformer-based models). We discuss the relative advantages and limitations of each method, examining their performance across various anatomical structures and clinical applications. Additionally, we review publicly available datasets, evaluation metrics, and validation strategies specific to 3D ultrasound segmentation. Finally, we identify current research gaps and suggest promising future directions, including multimodal fusion, weakly supervised learning, and real-time segmentation for interventional guidance. This survey aims to serve as a reference for researchers and clinicians working with 3D ultrasound image analysis.

Accelerating Minibatch Stochastic Gradient Descent using Typicality Sampling

This paper introduces a novel approach to improve the efficiency of minibatch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) through a technique we call "typicality sampling." While traditional minibatch SGD randomly selects training examples, our method strategically identifies and selects "typical" examples that better represent the underlying data distribution, reducing variance in gradient estimates. We formalize the notion of typicality in the context of optimization and demonstrate how samples closer to distributional centroids can accelerate convergence. Our theoretical analysis establishes convergence guarantees and provides bounds on the expected improvement in convergence rates. Experimental results across various deep learning benchmarks, including image classification and natural language processing tasks, show that typicality sampling consistently achieves faster convergence than uniform sampling, reducing training time by 15-30% while maintaining or improving generalization performance. The method requires minimal computational overhead and can be easily integrated into existing deep learning frameworks, making it a practical enhancement to standard training procedures.

Pre-training strategies and datasets for facial representation learning

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of pre-training strategies and datasets for facial representation learning. We investigate how different self-supervised and supervised pre-training approaches affect the quality and generalizability of facial representations across various downstream tasks. Our study evaluates multiple architectural designs, loss functions, and data augmentation techniques on large-scale facial datasets comprising over 10 million images with diverse demographic distributions. Results demonstrate that contrastive learning frameworks with carefully designed facial-specific augmentations outperform traditional supervised approaches on face verification, facial attribute prediction, and expression recognition tasks. We identify that pre-training dataset diversity significantly impacts model fairness across demographic groups, while dataset scale influences performance on low-resource downstream tasks. Furthermore, we introduce a novel curriculum learning strategy that progressively increases the complexity of identity discrimination tasks during pre-training, yielding representations that capture both fine-grained identity features and generalizable facial attributes. Our findings provide practical guidelines for developing robust facial representation models that balance task performance, computational efficiency, and fairness considerations.

Dynamic Refinement Network for Oriented and Densely Packed Object Detection

Detecting oriented and densely packed objects remains a significant challenge in computer vision, particularly when objects exhibit arbitrary orientations and severe overlapping. This paper introduces the Dynamic Refinement Network (DRNet), a novel two-stage detection framework specifically designed to address these challenges. DRNet incorporates a dynamic refinement module that adaptively adjusts detection parameters based on contextual information and object density. Our approach features a rotation-invariant feature extraction backbone coupled with an oriented proposal generation mechanism that effectively captures objects at various orientations. To handle dense packing scenarios, we propose a density-aware non-maximum suppression algorithm and an overlap-guided feature enhancement strategy that preserves detection accuracy even under severe occlusion. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks, including DOTA, HRSC2016, and our newly introduced Dense Orientation Dataset (DOD), demonstrate that DRNet significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance with improvements of 3.2% mAP on densely packed scenes while maintaining computational efficiency. The proposed method shows particular strength in scenarios with arbitrary object orientations and high density, making it applicable to critical domains such as aerial imagery analysis, industrial inspection, and logistics management.

A Fully Pipelined FPGA Accelerator for Scale Invariant Feature Transform Keypoint Descriptor Matching

This paper presents a novel hardware architecture for accelerating Scale Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) keypoint descriptor matching implemented on Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs). SIFT descriptor matching is computationally intensive but essential for numerous computer vision applications including object recognition, image stitching, and 3D reconstruction. Our proposed design employs a fully pipelined architecture that exploits the inherent parallelism of FPGAs to achieve significant speedup over software implementations. The accelerator utilizes a hierarchical processing structure with multiple parallel matching units that compute Euclidean distances between 128-dimensional SIFT descriptors. We introduce an optimized nearest-neighbor search algorithm specifically tailored for hardware implementation that maintains matching accuracy while reducing computational complexity. Experimental results demonstrate that our design achieves up to 45× speedup compared to CPU implementations and 3.2× speedup over existing GPU solutions, while consuming only 7.8 watts of power. The accelerator can process over 100,000 descriptor pairs per second, enabling real-time performance for many computer vision applications. This work represents a significant advancement in hardware acceleration for feature matching algorithms, providing an efficient solution for embedded vision systems with strict power and performance requirements.

BRPO: Batch Residual Policy Optimization

This paper introduces Batch Residual Policy Optimization (BRPO), a novel approach to reinforcement learning that leverages offline data to improve policy performance. BRPO extends traditional residual policy learning by operating in a batch setting, allowing it to efficiently learn from fixed datasets without requiring additional environment interactions. Our method combines the strengths of batch reinforcement learning with residual policy techniques to address the limitations of each approach individually. By iteratively refining a base policy through the addition of residual corrections, BRPO demonstrates improved sample efficiency and stability compared to standard batch learning methods. We provide theoretical guarantees on the performance improvement bounds of our approach and empirically validate BRPO across a diverse set of continuous control tasks. Experimental results show that BRPO significantly outperforms state-of-the-art batch reinforcement learning algorithms, particularly in scenarios with limited or suboptimal data. Additionally, we demonstrate that BRPO is robust to various forms of dataset composition and can effectively leverage mixed-quality demonstration data. Our work contributes a practical framework for policy improvement in settings where online environment interaction is costly or infeasible.

Debiased Distributed Learning for Sparse Partial Linear Models in High Dimensions

This paper addresses the challenge of distributed statistical inference for sparse partial linear models in high-dimensional settings. We propose a novel debiased distributed estimation framework that enables efficient parameter estimation and inference when data is distributed across multiple machines or computing nodes. Our approach combines local debiased estimators through a carefully designed aggregation procedure that preserves statistical efficiency while reducing computational burden. We establish theoretical guarantees for the proposed estimator, demonstrating that it achieves the same asymptotic efficiency as the oracle centralized estimator under mild conditions, even when the dimension of the parameter space grows exponentially with the sample size. Specifically, we prove that our distributed estimator attains a convergence rate of O(√(log p/n)) and enables valid statistical inference through confidence intervals and hypothesis testing. Extensive numerical simulations and real-data applications demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing distributed approaches in terms of estimation accuracy and inference validity, while maintaining computational efficiency. This work provides a practical solution for analyzing high-dimensional partially linear data in modern distributed computing environments without sacrificing statistical optimality.

Temporal Graph Network Embedding with Causal Anonymous Walks Representations

This paper introduces a novel approach for learning representations in temporal graphs by leveraging causal anonymous walks. Temporal graphs, where both nodes and edges evolve over time, present unique challenges for traditional embedding techniques that fail to capture the temporal dynamics and causal dependencies inherent in these structures. Our proposed method, Temporal Graph Network Embedding with Causal Anonymous Walks Representations (TGCAWR), addresses these limitations by incorporating time-respecting random walks that preserve the causal ordering of interactions. We extend the concept of anonymous walks to the temporal domain, capturing structural patterns while maintaining temporal sensitivity and node privacy. The approach generates embeddings that encode both topological information and temporal evolution through a carefully designed sampling strategy and representation learning framework. Extensive experiments on several real-world temporal networks, including communication, transportation, and social interaction datasets, demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art temporal graph embedding techniques on downstream tasks such as link prediction, node classification, and temporal community detection. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees on the expressiveness of our representations with respect to temporal graph isomorphism. TGCAWR offers an efficient and interpretable approach for modeling dynamic networks while respecting causal constraints inherent in temporal data.

Attentional Separation-and-Aggregation Network for Self-supervised Depth-Pose Learning in Dynamic Scenes

Self-supervised depth and ego-motion estimation from monocular videos has shown promising results, but remains challenging in dynamic environments where moving objects violate the static world assumption. In this paper, we propose an Attentional Separation-and-Aggregation Network (ASANet) that effectively handles dynamic scenes by decomposing the scene into static and dynamic components. Our approach introduces a novel attention mechanism that first separates scene features into static and dynamic branches, processes them independently, and then adaptively aggregates them to produce accurate depth maps and camera pose estimates. The separation module employs a motion-aware attention gate that identifies dynamic objects without explicit supervision, while the aggregation module intelligently combines the processed features based on their motion characteristics. Extensive experiments on KITTI and Cityscapes datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving significant improvements in depth accuracy and pose estimation, particularly in scenes with multiple moving objects. Furthermore, our qualitative results show that ASANet successfully handles occlusions and complex motion patterns that challenge existing methods. The proposed framework requires no additional supervision beyond monocular video sequences, making it applicable to real-world scenarios where annotated data is scarce.

Zero-Shot Instance Segmentation

Instance segmentation, the task of detecting and delineating each distinct object of interest in an image, has traditionally relied on large annotated datasets with pixel-level labels. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for Zero-Shot Instance Segmentation (ZSIS) that eliminates the need for instance-level annotations during training. Our approach leverages semantic knowledge transfer between seen and unseen object categories by embedding visual features and semantic descriptions in a shared latent space. We introduce a dual-branch architecture that combines a class-agnostic proposal mechanism with a semantic alignment module that can generalize to previously unseen object categories. The framework employs contrastive learning to maximize the similarity between visual features and their corresponding semantic embeddings while maintaining spatial awareness critical for precise mask generation. Extensive experiments on challenging benchmarks, including COCO and ADE20K, demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing zero-shot approaches, achieving up to 24% improvement in mask AP on unseen categories. Additionally, we present a comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between generalization capability and segmentation accuracy. Our ZSIS framework represents an important step toward flexible visual systems that can identify and segment novel objects without requiring exhaustive annotation efforts.

An Improved Evaluation Framework for Generative Adversarial Networks

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generating realistic data across various domains, yet their evaluation remains challenging due to the lack of standardized, comprehensive assessment methodologies. This paper introduces a novel evaluation framework that addresses the limitations of existing metrics by combining quantitative measures with qualitative assessments in a structured, reproducible manner. Our framework incorporates three key innovations: (1) a multi-faceted quality assessment that evaluates sample diversity, fidelity, and mode coverage through an ensemble of complementary metrics; (2) a task-specific relevance scoring system that weighs evaluation criteria according to application requirements; and (3) a computational efficiency analysis that considers training stability and convergence properties. Through extensive experimentation across multiple datasets and GAN architectures, we demonstrate that our framework provides more consistent rankings of generative models compared to traditional evaluation approaches, with stronger correlation to human perception studies. Furthermore, we release an open-source implementation of our framework to facilitate standardized benchmarking and accelerate progress in GAN research and applications.

Edge-similarity-aware Graph Neural Networks

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning on graph-structured data, yet most existing approaches focus primarily on node features and topological structure while overlooking the semantic relationships between edges. In this paper, we introduce Edge-similarity-aware Graph Neural Networks (ES-GNNs), a novel framework that explicitly incorporates edge similarity information into the message passing mechanism. Our approach constructs an edge similarity matrix that captures the semantic relatedness between edges in the graph, allowing for more nuanced information propagation. By leveraging this additional structural information, ES-GNNs can better distinguish between different types of connections and their relative importance in the underlying data. Through extensive experimentation on various benchmark datasets including citation networks, molecular graphs, and social networks, we demonstrate that ES-GNNs consistently outperform state-of-the-art GNN variants across node classification, link prediction, and graph classification tasks. Our ablation studies further confirm that the edge similarity component significantly contributes to the model's expressive power, particularly in graphs with heterogeneous edge types. The proposed framework provides a principled approach to incorporating edge semantics into graph representation learning while maintaining computational efficiency.

TxT: Crossmodal End-to-End Learning with Transformers

We present TxT (Transformers crossing Transformers), a novel end-to-end architecture for crossmodal learning that leverages the power of transformer models across different data modalities. Our approach unifies vision and language processing within a single framework by employing specialized transformer encoders for each modality, followed by a crossmodal attention mechanism that enables rich information exchange between domains. Unlike previous methods that rely on separate pre-trained models or complex fusion techniques, TxT processes raw inputs from multiple modalities simultaneously, learning joint representations through shared self-attention layers. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets for tasks including visual question answering, image captioning, and multimodal sentiment analysis demonstrate that TxT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods while requiring fewer parameters. Our ablation studies further reveal that the crossmodal attention mechanism effectively captures complementary information across modalities, leading to more robust representations. The proposed architecture provides a unified framework for various multimodal applications while maintaining computational efficiency, paving the way for more integrated approaches to crossmodal learning.

Is Homophily a Necessity for Graph Neural Networks?

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various graph-based learning tasks, with much of their effectiveness traditionally attributed to the homophily assumption—the tendency of connected nodes to share similar features or labels. This paper critically examines whether homophily is truly a necessary condition for GNN performance. Through systematic experiments on both synthetic and real-world heterophilous graphs, we demonstrate that carefully designed GNN architectures can achieve competitive performance even in settings where the homophily assumption is significantly violated. We propose a theoretical framework that explains how message-passing mechanisms can effectively capture useful structural information regardless of homophily levels. Our analysis reveals that the key to GNN success lies not in homophily itself, but in the ability to learn appropriate feature transformations and neighborhood aggregation strategies that align with the underlying graph properties. We introduce a homophily-agnostic architecture that adapts to varying levels of homophily without prior knowledge of the graph structure. Experimental results across diverse datasets show that our approach consistently outperforms homophily-dependent models, challenging the conventional wisdom that homophily is a prerequisite for effective graph representation learning.

Unit Ball Model for Embedding Hierarchical Structures in the Complex Hyperbolic Space

This paper introduces a novel approach for embedding hierarchical data structures in complex hyperbolic space using the unit ball model. While Euclidean embeddings have been widely employed for representing hierarchical relationships, they often struggle to efficiently capture both hierarchical and similarity relationships simultaneously. We propose a complex hyperbolic embedding framework that leverages the unique geometric properties of the unit ball model of complex hyperbolic space, which naturally accommodates hierarchical structures through its exponentially expanding volume. Our model extends traditional real hyperbolic embeddings by utilizing complex dimensions, allowing for richer representations of asymmetric relationships and circular patterns within hierarchies. We develop specialized optimization techniques that respect the geometry of complex hyperbolic space and ensure stable training. Experimental evaluations on diverse hierarchical datasets—including taxonomies, knowledge graphs, and organizational structures—demonstrate that our complex hyperbolic embeddings significantly outperform both Euclidean and real hyperbolic alternatives, particularly for hierarchies with complex branching patterns. The proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on hierarchy reconstruction tasks while maintaining computational efficiency, making it suitable for large-scale applications. Our work opens new directions for geometric representation learning by establishing complex hyperbolic geometry as a powerful framework for modeling hierarchical data.

Dual-Neighborhood Deep Fusion Network for Point Cloud Analysis

This paper introduces the Dual-Neighborhood Deep Fusion Network (DN-DFNet), a novel architecture for point cloud analysis that effectively captures both local and global geometric structures. Our approach addresses the inherent challenges of point cloud data—sparsity, irregularity, and permutation invariance—by simultaneously exploiting complementary neighborhood information at different scales. DN-DFNet employs two parallel neighborhood construction strategies: a distance-based spherical neighborhood that preserves local geometric details, and a feature-based semantic neighborhood that captures contextual relationships. The core innovation lies in our adaptive fusion module, which dynamically integrates these dual neighborhood representations based on their relative importance for different regions and tasks. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that DN-DFNet achieves state-of-the-art performance in classification, part segmentation, and semantic segmentation tasks. Notably, our method shows significant improvements in handling complex scenes with varying point densities and object boundaries. Ablation studies confirm that the dual-neighborhood mechanism substantially enhances feature representation compared to single-neighborhood approaches, while maintaining computational efficiency. The proposed architecture provides a promising direction for robust point cloud understanding in various applications including autonomous driving, robotics, and 3D scene understanding.

Spectral-Spatial Graph Reasoning Network for Hyperspectral Image Classification

This paper presents a novel Spectral-Spatial Graph Reasoning Network (SSGRN) for hyperspectral image (HSI) classification that effectively leverages both spectral and spatial information through graph-based reasoning. Traditional HSI classification methods often struggle to simultaneously capture complex spectral correlations across bands and spatial dependencies among neighboring pixels. Our proposed SSGRN addresses this challenge by constructing dual graph representations: a spectral graph that models relationships between spectral bands and a spatial graph that encodes pixel neighborhoods. The framework employs graph convolutional networks to perform reasoning on both graphs, enabling the extraction of rich spectral-spatial features. We introduce an adaptive fusion mechanism that dynamically integrates information from both domains based on their relative importance for different land cover types. Extensive experiments on four benchmark HSI datasets (Indian Pines, Pavia University, Houston-2013, and Salinas) demonstrate that our SSGRN outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 2.3-4.1% in overall accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. The proposed approach shows particular robustness in scenarios with limited training samples, highlighting its potential for practical remote sensing applications.

Geometry in Active Learning for Binary and Multi-class Image Segmentation

This paper introduces a novel geometric approach to active learning for image segmentation tasks across both binary and multi-class settings. We propose a framework that leverages the geometric properties of decision boundaries in feature space to identify the most informative samples for annotation, thereby reducing labeling costs while maintaining high segmentation accuracy. Our method analyzes the curvature and spatial distribution of boundaries between regions of interest, prioritizing pixels that lie in areas of high geometric complexity or uncertainty. Through extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets including PASCAL VOC, Cityscapes, and medical imaging collections, we demonstrate that our geometry-aware sampling strategy consistently outperforms conventional uncertainty-based and random sampling approaches, achieving comparable segmentation performance with up to 60% fewer labeled pixels. Furthermore, we extend our approach to handle multi-class segmentation problems by incorporating class relationship modeling within the geometric framework. The proposed method is architecture-agnostic and can be integrated with various deep learning segmentation models. Our results suggest that geometric information provides valuable cues for active learning that complement traditional uncertainty measures, particularly in scenarios with limited annotation budgets.

CM3: Cooperative Multi-goal Multi-stage Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces CM3, a novel framework for addressing complex cooperative multi-agent tasks requiring the achievement of multiple goals across distinct stages. Traditional multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approaches often struggle with scenarios demanding both coordinated behavior and sequential goal completion. CM3 addresses these challenges through a hierarchical architecture that decomposes the overall problem into manageable sub-tasks while maintaining coordination among agents. Our approach incorporates a goal-conditioned policy structure where agents learn to prioritize objectives dynamically based on the current stage of task progression. We formulate a multi-stage reward mechanism that provides appropriate learning signals for both immediate actions and long-term goal achievement. Extensive experiments across diverse environments, including resource allocation, collaborative construction, and strategic team games, demonstrate that CM3 significantly outperforms existing MARL methods in terms of task completion rate, coordination efficiency, and adaptability to changing goals. Results show up to 45% improvement in multi-goal achievement compared to state-of-the-art baselines, with particularly strong performance in scenarios requiring complex sequential decision-making. CM3 provides a promising direction for scaling cooperative multi-agent systems to increasingly complex real-world applications requiring coordinated sequential goal achievement.

Neural Rule Ensembles: Encoding Sparse Feature Interactions into Neural Networks

This paper introduces Neural Rule Ensembles (NREs), a novel approach that combines the interpretability of rule-based models with the expressive power of neural networks. While deep neural networks excel at learning complex patterns, they often struggle to efficiently capture sparse feature interactions that are naturally represented by logical rules. Our framework addresses this limitation by explicitly encoding rule-based feature interactions within a neural architecture. We propose a two-phase learning process where an initial rule discovery phase identifies meaningful sparse feature interactions, which are then incorporated into a neural network through a specialized rule encoding layer. This architecture allows the model to leverage both the interpretability of discrete logical rules and the continuous optimization capabilities of neural networks. Through extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that NREs achieve superior performance compared to standard neural networks and traditional rule-based methods, particularly on problems characterized by sparse feature interactions. Additionally, the resulting models maintain a level of interpretability by exposing the learned rules and their contributions to predictions. Our approach offers a promising direction for developing models that balance predictive performance with human-understandable decision logic.

3D Multi-Object Tracking: A Baseline and New Evaluation Metrics

This paper addresses the critical yet under-explored domain of 3D multi-object tracking (MOT) in autonomous driving and robotic vision applications. While significant progress has been made in 2D MOT, the transition to 3D space introduces unique challenges that existing metrics and methodologies fail to adequately capture. We present a straightforward yet effective baseline approach for 3D MOT that combines state-of-the-art 3D object detection with a nearest-neighbor association strategy based on 3D Kalman filtering. To properly evaluate 3D MOT systems, we introduce novel evaluation metrics that specifically account for the spatial accuracy of trajectories in 3D space, addressing limitations in traditional MOT metrics that were designed for 2D scenarios. Our comprehensive experiments on the KITTI and nuScenes datasets demonstrate that our baseline outperforms existing methods while providing insights into the unique challenges of 3D tracking. The proposed metrics offer a more complete assessment of tracking performance by considering both detection accuracy and trajectory consistency in three-dimensional space. This work establishes a foundation for future research in 3D MOT by providing both a strong baseline and appropriate evaluation tools for the research community.

Improving Transferability of Deep Neural Networks

This paper addresses the critical challenge of enhancing the transferability of deep neural networks (DNNs) across diverse domains and tasks. Despite their remarkable performance in specific contexts, DNNs often struggle to generalize knowledge to novel environments, limiting their practical utility. We propose a comprehensive framework that systematically improves transferability through three complementary approaches: architectural modifications, training methodology enhancements, and representation learning techniques. Our architectural innovations include a modular transfer-aware design that separates domain-specific and domain-invariant features. We introduce a progressive regularization strategy during training that gradually enforces feature invariance while preserving task-specific discriminative power. Extensive experiments across multiple domains—including computer vision, natural language processing, and cross-modal tasks—demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms traditional transfer learning methods, reducing the required target domain data by up to 75% while maintaining comparable performance. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights into the transferability-specificity trade-off and establish guarantees on transfer performance bounds. Our framework offers a promising direction for developing more adaptable deep learning systems that can effectively leverage knowledge across domains with minimal supervision.

Multiresolution Convolutional Autoencoders

This paper presents a novel deep learning architecture called Multiresolution Convolutional Autoencoders (MCA), which extends traditional convolutional autoencoders by incorporating multiresolution analysis principles. Our approach integrates wavelet-inspired decomposition techniques within the autoencoder framework, enabling the network to simultaneously process information at multiple scales and resolution levels. The proposed architecture employs specialized encoding pathways that capture features at different resolutions, followed by a fusion mechanism that combines these representations before reconstruction through the decoder. Experiments on diverse datasets including natural images, medical imagery, and satellite data demonstrate that MCAs outperform standard convolutional autoencoders in reconstruction quality, feature extraction, and denoising tasks. The multiresolution approach proves particularly effective for capturing both fine-grained details and global structures, leading to a 15% improvement in reconstruction PSNR and significant enhancements in downstream tasks when used for representation learning. Additionally, we show that the learned multiresolution representations exhibit better generalization capabilities when transferred to tasks with limited training data. Our work provides a promising direction for representation learning that effectively leverages scale-space information through architectural design.

Action-dependent Control Variates for Policy Optimization via Stein's Identity

Policy optimization methods for reinforcement learning often suffer from high variance in gradient estimates, leading to slow convergence and training instability. In this paper, we introduce a novel variance reduction technique using action-dependent control variates derived from Stein's identity. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on state-value functions as baselines, our method leverages the geometry of the action space and the policy's structure to construct control variates that explicitly depend on actions. By applying Stein's identity, we develop a framework that automatically generates zero-mean control variates tailored to the specific policy parameterization without requiring additional value function approximation. We provide theoretical analysis showing that our approach provably reduces variance under mild conditions while maintaining unbiased gradient estimates. Empirical evaluations across continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves faster convergence, improved sample efficiency, and more stable learning compared to state-of-the-art policy gradient methods. The action-dependent nature of our control variates makes them particularly effective for policies with complex action distributions, offering a promising direction for enhancing policy optimization algorithms.

FAHT: An Adaptive Fairness-aware Decision Tree Classifier

Machine learning models often perpetuate or amplify existing societal biases present in training data, raising significant ethical concerns when deployed in high-stakes decision-making scenarios. This paper introduces FAHT (Fairness-Aware Hoeffding Tree), a novel adaptive decision tree classifier designed to maintain prediction accuracy while ensuring fairness across protected demographic groups. Unlike conventional approaches that apply post-processing corrections or preprocessing transformations, FAHT incorporates fairness constraints directly into the learning process through a modified information gain splitting criterion that penalizes discriminatory branching decisions. Our approach dynamically adapts to evolving data distributions in streaming environments while maintaining fairness guarantees. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that FAHT successfully reduces disparate impact and equalized odds violations by an average of 43% compared to standard Hoeffding Trees, with minimal impact on overall accuracy (less than 3% reduction). Furthermore, FAHT exhibits superior computational efficiency compared to existing fairness-aware classifiers, making it particularly suitable for real-time applications. We also provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence properties of our fairness-aware splitting criteria and analyze the trade-offs between different fairness metrics in various domains.

Autoregressive Score Matching

This paper introduces Autoregressive Score Matching (ASM), a novel approach for training generative models that combines the strengths of autoregressive modeling with score-based generative techniques. Unlike traditional score matching methods that estimate gradients of the log-density function across the entire data space simultaneously, ASM decomposes the score function autoregressively, enabling more efficient and accurate density estimation in high-dimensional spaces. By factorizing the joint distribution into a sequence of conditional distributions, our method addresses the challenges of capturing complex dependencies while maintaining tractable computation. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that ASM converges to the true data distribution under mild assumptions and demonstrate empirically that it outperforms existing score matching and autoregressive approaches across multiple benchmarks. Experiments on image, audio, and text generation tasks show that ASM achieves state-of-the-art sample quality while enabling faster sampling compared to diffusion models and better handling of long-range dependencies than traditional autoregressive models. Our approach offers a promising direction for scalable generative modeling that balances computational efficiency with expressive power.

Boundary-Seeking Generative Adversarial Networks

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have emerged as powerful frameworks for unsupervised learning, but they continue to face challenges related to training instability and mode collapse. This paper introduces Boundary-Seeking Generative Adversarial Networks (BSGANs), a novel approach that reformulates the generator's objective to explicitly target the decision boundary of the discriminator. Unlike traditional GANs that rely on gradient signals that may vanish in regions where the discriminator is confident, BSGANs directly optimize the generator to produce samples that lie on the decision boundary between real and generated data distributions. This boundary-seeking behavior provides consistent and meaningful gradients throughout training, even when the discriminator reaches near-optimal performance. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that this approach implicitly minimizes the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the data and generator distributions. Extensive experiments on image generation benchmarks, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA, show that BSGANs achieve improved training stability, reduced mode collapse, and competitive sample quality compared to state-of-the-art GAN variants. Furthermore, our approach is compatible with existing GAN architectures and regularization techniques, making it a versatile enhancement to the GAN framework.

Full-Duplex Strategy for Video Object Segmentation

This paper introduces a novel full-duplex strategy for video object segmentation (VOS) that enables bidirectional information exchange throughout the segmentation process. Unlike traditional unidirectional approaches that propagate features solely from previous to current frames, our method establishes a two-way communication channel that simultaneously leverages both historical and future frame information. We propose a dual-stream architecture with forward and backward pathways that dynamically exchange complementary features through specially designed cross-temporal attention modules. Experimental results on benchmark datasets DAVIS 2016, DAVIS 2017, and YouTube-VOS demonstrate that our full-duplex approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 3.2%, 2.8%, and 2.5% in J&F scores respectively. The bidirectional information flow proves particularly effective in handling challenging scenarios involving occlusions, deformations, and appearance changes. Additionally, our ablation studies confirm that the full-duplex strategy maintains temporal consistency while reducing error accumulation common in sequential processing methods. The proposed approach represents a fundamental shift in VOS methodology, offering a more robust framework for accurate and temporally coherent video object segmentation.

Fed-TGAN: Federated Learning Framework for Synthesizing Tabular Data

This paper introduces Fed-TGAN, a novel federated learning framework for generating synthetic tabular data across distributed environments. Traditional tabular data synthesis approaches require centralized data collection, raising significant privacy concerns in sensitive domains such as healthcare and finance. Fed-TGAN addresses these challenges by enabling multiple organizations to collaboratively train a tabular generative adversarial network (TGAN) without sharing their raw data. Our framework implements a secure aggregation protocol where only model parameters are exchanged while raw data remains local, preserving privacy while leveraging the collective knowledge across institutions. Experimental evaluation on multiple real-world datasets demonstrates that Fed-TGAN produces synthetic data with statistical properties closely matching the original distributed data, while maintaining comparable utility for downstream machine learning tasks. The synthetic data generated by Fed-TGAN successfully preserves complex relationships between features and achieves high fidelity scores, within 5-7% of centralized approaches, while providing formal privacy guarantees. Fed-TGAN offers a promising solution for privacy-preserving collaborative data synthesis in regulated industries where data sharing is restricted by legal and ethical constraints.

Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Explicit Policy Estimates

This paper introduces a novel approach to inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) that incorporates explicit policy estimates to enhance reward function recovery. Traditional IRL methods infer reward functions from expert demonstrations but often struggle with ambiguity and computational inefficiency. Our proposed framework, Explicit Policy-guided IRL (EP-IRL), leverages direct policy estimates as an additional information source to constrain the reward function search space. By explicitly modeling the expert's policy alongside reward inference, we demonstrate improved sample efficiency and more accurate reward recovery compared to conventional methods that rely solely on demonstrations. We provide theoretical guarantees for our approach and empirically validate its performance across various continuous control environments, showing particular advantages in scenarios with limited demonstration data. Our results indicate that EP-IRL achieves up to 40% improvement in reward recovery accuracy and 30% reduction in computational cost compared to state-of-the-art IRL methods, while maintaining robust performance under noisy observations. This work bridges the gap between direct policy imitation and reward inference, offering a promising direction for more efficient and accurate inverse reinforcement learning.

Polarimetric SAR Image Semantic Segmentation with 3D Discrete Wavelet Transform and Markov Random Field

This paper presents a novel approach for semantic segmentation of polarimetric synthetic aperture radar (PolSAR) imagery by integrating three-dimensional discrete wavelet transform (3D-DWT) with Markov Random Field (MRF) modeling. PolSAR images contain rich scattering information but present unique challenges due to speckle noise and complex scattering mechanisms. Our method leverages the multi-resolution analysis capabilities of 3D-DWT to effectively decompose PolSAR data across different scales and orientations while preserving polarimetric information. The wavelet coefficients serve as discriminative features that capture both spatial textures and polarimetric characteristics. We then employ an MRF framework to model spatial contextual dependencies between neighboring pixels, thereby improving segmentation coherence. The MRF optimization is solved using graph cuts to efficiently determine the optimal class labels. Experimental results on several benchmark PolSAR datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy, boundary preservation, and robustness to speckle noise. The proposed framework achieves an average improvement of 4.3% in overall accuracy and 3.8% in mean intersection over union compared to existing techniques, while maintaining computational efficiency. This work provides a promising direction for exploiting both polarimetric and spatial information in PolSAR image interpretation tasks.

Bandwidth-Adaptive Feature Sharing for Cooperative LIDAR Object Detection

This paper presents a novel bandwidth-adaptive approach for cooperative LIDAR-based object detection in multi-agent perception systems. While collaborative perception significantly improves detection performance, it faces critical challenges in bandwidth-constrained environments where agents cannot freely share complete sensor data. Our proposed framework dynamically adjusts the granularity and quantity of shared features based on available network bandwidth, network conditions, and scene complexity. We introduce an adaptive feature compression mechanism that intelligently prioritizes the most informative spatial regions and semantic features while discarding redundant information. Through extensive experiments on the V2X-Sim and OPV2V datasets, we demonstrate that our approach achieves up to 40% bandwidth reduction with minimal performance degradation (<3% mAP) compared to full-feature sharing methods. Furthermore, our system exhibits robust performance across varying bandwidth conditions, from high-capacity fixed infrastructure to constrained mobile networks. The proposed adaptive sharing strategy outperforms static compression methods by intelligently allocating bandwidth resources according to real-time perception needs, making it particularly suitable for dynamic autonomous driving scenarios where communication resources fluctuate. Our work addresses a critical gap in cooperative perception by enabling effective collaboration even under severe bandwidth limitations.

A Novel Approach to Curiosity and Explainable Reinforcement Learning via Interpretable Sub-Goals

This paper introduces a novel framework that integrates intrinsic curiosity mechanisms with explainable reinforcement learning (XRL) through the identification and utilization of interpretable sub-goals. While traditional reinforcement learning approaches often struggle with sparse reward environments and produce black-box policies, our method addresses both challenges simultaneously. We propose a hierarchical architecture that decomposes complex tasks into human-interpretable sub-goals, which serve dual purposes: driving curiosity-based exploration and providing explanations for agent behavior. Our approach leverages semantic information from the environment to generate sub-goals that are both meaningful to humans and useful for exploration. Through extensive experiments across diverse environments, including Atari games, robotic manipulation tasks, and procedurally generated worlds, we demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art curiosity-driven approaches while providing human-understandable explanations of learned policies. Results show a 37% improvement in sample efficiency and a 42% increase in task success rate in sparse reward settings compared to baseline methods. Additionally, user studies confirm that the generated explanations substantially improve human understanding and trust in the agent's decision-making process. This work represents an important step toward reinforcement learning systems that are both efficient and transparent.

An efficient scheme based on graph centrality to select nodes for training for effective learning

This paper proposes a novel node selection strategy for graph-based machine learning tasks that optimizes training efficiency while maintaining high model performance. Traditional approaches often rely on random sampling or domain-specific heuristics to select training nodes, which can be suboptimal and computationally expensive. Our method leverages graph centrality measures to identify the most influential nodes in a network, creating a more representative and informative training set. We evaluate multiple centrality metrics—including degree, betweenness, eigenvector, and PageRank centrality—and introduce a hybrid selection algorithm that balances local and global network properties. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets across various domains (citation networks, social networks, and molecular graphs) demonstrate that our centrality-based selection scheme requires up to 40% fewer training nodes while achieving comparable or superior performance to random sampling baselines. Furthermore, our approach shows particular effectiveness in scenarios with limited labeled data, making it valuable for semi-supervised learning applications. The computational overhead of centrality calculations is mitigated through efficient approximation techniques, resulting in an overall reduction in training time. These findings suggest that graph structural properties provide valuable signals for optimizing the node selection process in graph-based learning tasks.

Flood-Filling Networks

We present Flood-Filling Networks (FFNs), a novel deep learning architecture designed for instance segmentation of complex, densely interconnected structures in 3D image volumes. Unlike traditional convolutional neural networks that process entire images at once, FFNs operate through an iterative growth process, expanding segmentation one object at a time through a recurrent flood-filling mechanism. The network focuses on a specific seed point and progressively extends the segmentation boundary by repeatedly analyzing local context and predicting the probability of voxel inclusion. This approach enables FFNs to resolve intricate boundary patterns and accurately separate closely adjacent objects, which is particularly valuable in challenging domains such as connectomics for neural circuit reconstruction. Our experiments on electron microscopy datasets of brain tissue demonstrate that FFNs significantly outperform previous state-of-the-art methods, reducing segmentation errors by more than 30% and achieving previously unattainable accuracy levels in automated neural membrane segmentation.
