We formulate erosion, dilation, opening, and closing operators that preserve the probabilistic nature of categorical distributions while enabling meaningful shape transformations in the probability simplex. Our approach defines structuring elements as probability kernels and leverages optimal transport metrics to ensure that morphological operations maintain statistical coherence. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed operators satisfy key properties including idempotence and preservation of distribution constraints. Experimental results on synthetic data and real-world applications in natural language processing and computer vision demonstrate the utility of our framework for tasks such as noise reduction in categorical data, feature extraction, and distribution smoothing. This work establishes a foundation for morphological processing in probabilistic categorical domains, bridging the gap between traditional image processing and modern statistical learning approaches.

K+ Means: An Enhancement Over K-Means Clustering Algorithm

This paper presents K+ Means, a novel enhancement to the traditional K-Means clustering algorithm that addresses several fundamental limitations of its predecessor. While K-Means remains one of the most widely used clustering techniques due to its simplicity and efficiency, it suffers from sensitivity to initial centroid selection, vulnerability to outliers, and difficulty in determining the optimal number of clusters. Our proposed K+ Means algorithm incorporates an adaptive centroid initialization strategy, a robust distance metric that minimizes outlier influence, and an automatic cluster number optimization mechanism. Experimental evaluations conducted on diverse datasets demonstrate that K+ Means consistently outperforms traditional K-Means, achieving an average improvement of 27% in clustering accuracy and 35% reduction in iteration count until convergence. Furthermore, K+ Means exhibits enhanced stability across multiple runs and greater resilience when processing noisy data. The algorithm maintains computational efficiency comparable to standard K-Means while delivering significantly improved clustering quality. These results suggest that K+ Means represents a valuable advancement for clustering applications across various domains including image segmentation, customer segmentation, and document classification.

Legacy Photo Editing with Learned Noise Prior

This paper introduces a novel approach for editing legacy photographs by leveraging a learned noise prior. Historical photographs often suffer from degradation, film grain, and artifacts that challenge modern editing algorithms. We present a framework that disentangles the intrinsic image content from its noise characteristics, enabling high-quality editing while preserving the authentic aesthetic of the original photograph. Our method employs a deep generative model trained on a diverse dataset of vintage photographs to learn the statistical properties of period-specific noise patterns. This learned noise prior serves as a regularization term during editing operations, allowing for seamless manipulations such as colorization, inpainting, and object removal while maintaining period-consistent noise distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms conventional editing techniques that either strip away the characteristic noise or fail to properly account for it during manipulation. User studies confirm that edited images retain the perceived authenticity of historical photographs while accommodating modern editing capabilities. The proposed framework opens new possibilities for digital restoration and creative reinterpretation of photographic archives while respecting their historical visual character.

Cats or CAT scans: transfer learning from natural or medical image source datasets?

Transfer learning has become a cornerstone technique in medical image analysis, yet the optimal choice of source dataset remains an open question. This study investigates whether pre-training on natural images (e.g., ImageNet) or domain-specific medical images yields superior performance for medical image classification tasks. We conducted extensive experiments across five medical imaging modalities (X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and histopathology) using identical network architectures with weights initialized from either natural image datasets or medical image collections. Our results demonstrate that while natural image pre-training provides a strong foundation, domain-specific medical pre-training offers statistically significant improvements in classification accuracy (+3.8%), sensitivity (+4.2%), and convergence speed (1.7× faster) across most tasks. Interestingly, the performance gap narrows for larger target datasets but remains substantial for limited training data scenarios common in medical applications. We further analyze feature representations through visualization techniques, revealing that medical image pre-training captures more relevant anatomical structures and pathological patterns. These findings suggest that as curated medical image repositories continue to grow, domain-specific pre-training may increasingly outperform traditional natural image transfer learning approaches for medical image analysis tasks.

A Literature Study of Embeddings on Source Code

This literature study presents a comprehensive review of embedding techniques applied to source code representations. As software engineering increasingly leverages machine learning approaches, the effective representation of code as numerical vectors has become crucial for tasks such as code completion, bug detection, and program synthesis. This paper systematically analyzes the evolution of code embedding methods, from traditional feature engineering approaches to modern neural network-based techniques including recurrent neural networks, transformer architectures, and graph neural networks. We examine how these embeddings capture syntactic structure, semantic information, and program behavior across different programming languages and application domains. The review highlights key research trends, comparing embedding performance across various downstream tasks and identifying the trade-offs between model complexity, interpretability, and effectiveness. Additionally, we discuss current challenges in the field, including handling of out-of-vocabulary tokens, cross-language generalization, and the incorporation of execution context. Our findings suggest that hybrid approaches combining structural and semantic representations yield the most promising results for complex code understanding tasks, while domain-specific pre-training continues to push performance boundaries. This study provides a foundation for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand the landscape of code embeddings and identify promising directions for future work.

Dynamic Routing on Deep Neural Network for Thoracic Disease Classification and Sensitive Area Localization

Accurate classification and localization of thoracic diseases in chest radiographs remain challenging tasks in computer-aided diagnosis systems. This paper presents a novel approach that integrates dynamic routing mechanisms with deep neural networks to enhance both disease classification and sensitive area localization in chest X-ray images. Our proposed architecture employs a capsule network-based dynamic routing strategy that adaptively determines the optimal information flow paths through the network based on input features. This approach allows the model to focus on relevant anatomical structures while maintaining spatial relationships critical for accurate diagnosis. Using the ChestX-ray14 dataset containing 112,120 frontal-view radiographs with 14 disease categories, we demonstrate that our dynamic routing approach achieves superior classification performance (AUC of 0.867) compared to traditional convolutional neural networks. Furthermore, without explicit bounding box annotations during training, our method generates class-specific activation maps that precisely localize disease-relevant regions, validated by radiologists to align with clinically significant areas. The proposed architecture shows particular strength in identifying subtle pathological changes and distinguishing between visually similar conditions. These results suggest that dynamic routing mechanisms can significantly improve thoracic disease classification accuracy while providing interpretable visualization of pathological regions, potentially enhancing clinical decision support systems.

Sparse Adversarial Attack to Object Detection

This paper introduces a novel sparse adversarial attack framework specifically designed to compromise object detection systems. Unlike traditional adversarial attacks that modify entire images, our approach strategically perturbs only a minimal set of carefully selected pixels, making the attack both more efficient and harder to detect. We formulate this as a constrained optimization problem that balances attack effectiveness with sparsity requirements. Our method systematically identifies critical regions that influence detector performance and concentrates perturbations there, achieving high attack success rates while modifying less than 1% of the image pixels. Extensive evaluations on popular detection frameworks including Faster R-CNN, YOLO, and SSD across multiple datasets demonstrate that our sparse attacks can successfully cause misdetection, misclassification, and bounding box regression errors. Notably, these attacks remain effective under various defense mechanisms and show strong transferability across different detection architectures. Our findings highlight significant vulnerabilities in current object detection systems and emphasize the need for robust defenses against sparse adversarial perturbations in safety-critical applications.

Pix2Shape: Towards Unsupervised Learning of 3D Scenes from Images using a View-based Representation

This paper presents Pix2Shape, a novel framework for unsupervised learning of 3D scene representations from 2D images without explicit 3D supervision. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on volumetric or mesh-based 3D representations, we introduce a view-based representation that decomposes 3D understanding into a collection of 2D views with corresponding depth maps. Our key insight is that learning to predict consistent multi-view representations from single images implicitly encodes 3D structure while being more computationally tractable and better aligned with the 2D supervision signal. Pix2Shape employs a neural architecture that jointly learns to extract view-invariant scene features and to generate novel viewpoints with consistent geometry through a differentiable rendering module. We demonstrate that our approach can effectively disentangle shape, appearance, and viewpoint without explicit 3D supervision. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that Pix2Shape outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised 3D reconstruction methods in terms of novel view synthesis quality, shape consistency, and generalization to unseen objects. Furthermore, we show that the learned representations transfer effectively to downstream tasks such as object recognition and scene understanding, highlighting the potential of view-based representations for unsupervised 3D scene understanding.

Multi-modal Egocentric Activity Recognition using Audio-Visual Features

This paper presents a novel approach to egocentric activity recognition by leveraging the complementary nature of audio and visual data streams captured from wearable devices. While traditional activity recognition systems often rely solely on visual information, our multi-modal framework integrates audio features to enhance recognition accuracy and robustness, particularly in scenarios where visual cues alone are insufficient. We propose a deep learning architecture that effectively fuses audio-visual features at multiple levels, capturing both temporal dynamics and cross-modal relationships. Our approach employs a combination of convolutional neural networks for spatial feature extraction from video frames, and recurrent networks with attention mechanisms to process audio spectrograms and temporal patterns. Experiments conducted on three egocentric datasets demonstrate that our multi-modal system achieves a significant improvement of 8.2% in average recognition accuracy compared to unimodal baselines. Furthermore, we provide detailed analysis showing how audio cues particularly enhance performance for activities with distinctive sound signatures but similar visual appearances. The proposed framework offers a more comprehensive understanding of human activities in real-world environments and shows promising applications in assistive technologies, augmented reality, and human-computer interaction systems.

Causality in Neural Networks -- An Extended Abstract

This extended abstract explores the intersection of causality theory and neural network architectures, addressing the fundamental challenge of moving beyond correlation to establish causal relationships in deep learning systems. We review recent advances in causal inference mechanisms within neural networks, highlighting approaches that enable models to discover and leverage causal structures in data. Our analysis covers causal representation learning, interventional techniques, and counterfactual reasoning frameworks that enhance the interpretability and robustness of neural networks. We demonstrate that causally-aware neural architectures can mitigate issues of distribution shift, improve generalization to unseen scenarios, and provide more reliable explanations for their predictions. Preliminary results indicate that incorporating causal structures into neural networks leads to significant performance improvements on tasks requiring reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals. We conclude by outlining open challenges and promising research directions for advancing causal understanding in deep learning systems, emphasizing the potential for these approaches to bridge the gap between statistical learning and causal reasoning.

High Dynamic Range Image Forensics Using CNN

High Dynamic Range (HDR) imaging has become increasingly prevalent in modern photography, presenting new challenges for digital image forensics. This paper proposes a novel approach to HDR image forensics using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to detect manipulation and authenticate HDR content. Our method addresses the unique characteristics of HDR images, including their extended luminance range and tone mapping operations, which traditional forensic techniques often fail to properly analyze. We develop a specialized CNN architecture that extracts discriminative features from both the structural and tonal aspects of HDR images, enabling the detection of various tampering operations such as splicing, copy-move forgeries, and artificial HDR generation from Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images. Experiments conducted on a diverse dataset of authentic and manipulated HDR images demonstrate that our approach achieves an accuracy of 94.7%, significantly outperforming conventional forensic methods. Furthermore, our model shows robustness against anti-forensic techniques and maintains effectiveness across different HDR formats and tone mapping operators. This work contributes to the emerging field of HDR image forensics and provides a reliable authentication tool for the growing ecosystem of HDR content.

EffiScene: Efficient Per-Pixel Rigidity Inference for Unsupervised Joint Learning of Optical Flow, Depth, Camera Pose and Motion Segmentation

This paper presents EffiScene, a novel unsupervised learning framework that jointly estimates optical flow, depth, camera pose, and motion segmentation from monocular video sequences. Unlike previous approaches that treat these tasks separately or use computationally expensive two-stage pipelines, our method introduces an efficient per-pixel rigidity inference mechanism that enables end-to-end training. The key innovation of EffiScene is a lightweight rigidity estimation module that differentiably distinguishes between static and dynamic regions in the scene, allowing the network to appropriately apply geometric constraints. Our framework leverages the complementary nature of these tasks: depth and camera motion explain the static scene structure, while optical flow captures both rigid and non-rigid motion. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including KITTI and Cityscapes demonstrate that EffiScene achieves state-of-the-art performance across all four tasks while requiring significantly less computational resources than existing methods. Furthermore, we show that our joint learning approach improves generalization to unseen environments, as the integrated tasks provide strong self-supervisory signals to one another. The proposed method represents an important step toward efficient scene understanding in dynamic environments for autonomous systems.

Deep Multi-Task Augmented Feature Learning via Hierarchical Graph Neural Network

This paper presents a novel approach to multi-task learning through a hierarchical graph neural network framework that effectively captures complex relationships between tasks and features. We introduce Deep Multi-Task Augmented Feature Learning (DMTAFL), which leverages a two-tier hierarchical graph structure to model both task-level interactions and feature-level dependencies simultaneously. Our method constructs a meta-graph where nodes represent individual tasks, while each task node contains a subgraph capturing the feature relationships specific to that task. This hierarchical representation enables knowledge transfer across related tasks while preserving task-specific feature importance. The proposed framework employs attention mechanisms to dynamically weight task relationships and feature contributions, allowing for adaptive knowledge sharing during training. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets across various domains, including computer vision, natural language processing, and recommendation systems, demonstrate that DMTAFL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art multi-task learning approaches. Our method shows particular strength in scenarios with limited training data and when handling tasks with varying degrees of relatedness. Additionally, we provide theoretical analysis on the model's convergence properties and the conditions under which cross-task knowledge transfer is most beneficial. The hierarchical graph structure of DMTAFL not only improves prediction accuracy but also enhances model interpretability by explicitly modeling the relationships between tasks and features.

Model Agnostic Multilevel Explanations

This paper introduces a novel framework for generating explanations of machine learning model predictions at multiple levels of abstraction. While existing explainable AI (XAI) approaches typically provide explanations at a single level of granularity, we propose a model-agnostic approach that generates complementary explanations across different conceptual levels, from feature-level attributions to higher-level semantic concepts. Our multilevel explanation framework adapts to various stakeholder needs, allowing users to seamlessly transition between technical feature importance explanations and more abstract concept-based interpretations. Through extensive experiments on image classification, natural language processing, and tabular data tasks, we demonstrate that our approach maintains explanation fidelity while significantly improving human understanding and trust across diverse user groups with varying technical expertise. The framework is compatible with any black-box prediction model and addresses key limitations in current XAI methods by providing contextually appropriate explanations that bridge the gap between technical precision and conceptual clarity. Our user studies confirm that multilevel explanations enable more effective human-AI collaboration by supporting both detailed technical debugging and high-level decision justification within a unified explanation system.

What can I do here? A Theory of Affordances in Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces a theoretical framework for incorporating affordances into reinforcement learning (RL) systems. Affordances, a concept from ecological psychology describing action possibilities available in an environment, offer a promising approach to address key challenges in RL including sample efficiency, exploration, and transfer learning. We formalize affordances as state-dependent action filters that constrain the action space to contextually relevant options, thereby reducing the complexity of the learning problem. Our theory defines affordance-aware Markov Decision Processes and demonstrates how learning and utilizing affordance models can accelerate policy acquisition across diverse environments. Through theoretical analysis, we establish convergence guarantees for affordance-guided RL algorithms and derive bounds on sample complexity improvements. Empirical evaluations across simulated robotic manipulation tasks, navigation problems, and game environments demonstrate that affordance-aware agents learn 35-60% faster than traditional RL approaches while developing more robust and transferable policies. This work bridges ecological psychology and reinforcement learning, establishing a foundation for more efficient and human-like artificial agents that can rapidly identify and leverage action possibilities in novel environments.

SkrGAN: Sketching-rendering Unconditional Generative Adversarial Networks for Medical Image Synthesis

Medical image synthesis remains a critical challenge in healthcare applications due to limited data availability, privacy concerns, and the need for diverse training examples. In this paper, we present SkrGAN, a novel unconditional generative adversarial network that employs a two-stage sketching-rendering approach for high-fidelity medical image synthesis. Our architecture first generates anatomical sketches capturing essential structural information, followed by a rendering stage that transforms these sketches into realistic medical images while preserving clinically relevant features. Experiments conducted across multiple imaging modalities (MRI, CT, and X-ray) demonstrate that SkrGAN outperforms existing state-of-the-art GANs in terms of image quality, diversity, and preservation of pathological features. Quantitative evaluation using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), and radiologist assessment confirms the superior performance of our approach. Furthermore, we show that synthetic images generated by SkrGAN can effectively augment training datasets, improving downstream segmentation and classification tasks by up to 17%. The proposed method offers a promising solution for addressing data scarcity in medical imaging while maintaining patient privacy through the generation of realistic yet synthetic medical images.

Toward Joint Image Generation and Compression using Generative Adversarial Networks

This paper explores a novel framework that unifies image generation and compression within a single Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture. While traditional image compression methods and generative models have evolved along separate trajectories, we propose that these tasks share fundamental characteristics that can be jointly optimized. Our approach leverages the generative capabilities of GANs to simultaneously learn compact latent representations and high-fidelity image reconstruction. We introduce a dual-purpose network that encodes images into a highly compressed latent space while maintaining the ability to generate realistic novel images from random samples in this same space. Experimental results demonstrate that our joint model achieves compression ratios comparable to state-of-the-art dedicated compression algorithms while preserving generative capabilities with minimal quality degradation. The framework shows particular promise for applications requiring both efficient storage and image synthesis, such as content creation platforms and augmented reality systems. We analyze the trade-offs between compression efficiency, reconstruction quality, and generative diversity, providing insights into the shared information bottleneck that connects these traditionally separate domains.

Multi-Goal Reinforcement Learning environments for simulated Franka Emika Panda robot

This paper introduces a comprehensive suite of multi-goal reinforcement learning (RL) environments for the simulated Franka Emika Panda robot, designed to accelerate research in robotic manipulation. We implement these environments following the OpenAI Gym interface, allowing for seamless integration with existing RL algorithms while specifically addressing the challenges of goal-conditioned learning in robotic tasks. Our framework features configurable reward structures, variable goal spaces, and realistic physics simulation to bridge the gap between simulation and real-world deployment. We benchmark several state-of-the-art RL algorithms, including Hindsight Experience Replay (HER), Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), and Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3), across diverse manipulation tasks ranging from simple reach-and-grasp scenarios to complex sequential object manipulations. Experimental results demonstrate that our environments enable efficient learning of generalizable policies capable of achieving multiple goals with the same underlying model. Additionally, we provide performance analysis on the sample efficiency and generalization capabilities of these algorithms, establishing baseline results for future research. This work contributes a valuable resource to the robotics and RL communities by providing standardized environments that facilitate the development of versatile manipulation skills for robotic systems.

Screen Content Image Segmentation Using Least Absolute Deviation Fitting

This paper presents a novel approach to screen content image (SCI) segmentation using Least Absolute Deviation (LAD) fitting. Unlike traditional image segmentation methods that often struggle with the unique characteristics of screen content images—such as sharp edges, text, graphics, and natural image regions—our proposed method leverages the robustness of LAD fitting to handle the heterogeneous nature of SCIs. We formulate the segmentation problem as a piecewise fitting optimization that minimizes the L1-norm of residuals, making it inherently resistant to outliers commonly found in screen content. Our algorithm effectively distinguishes between textual, graphical, and photographic regions by adaptively modeling the local image structure through LAD-based region growing. Experimental results on standard SCI datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, achieving 15% higher segmentation accuracy and 20% better boundary preservation while maintaining computational efficiency. The proposed approach enables more effective compression, rendering, and content adaptation of screen content images, making it particularly valuable for applications in remote desktop sharing, mixed-content document processing, and online education platforms.

Visual Time Series Forecasting: An Image-driven Approach

This paper introduces a novel approach to time series forecasting by recasting the traditional numerical prediction problem as a visual task. Our method, which we call VisualForecast, transforms time series data into image representations that capture temporal patterns, seasonal variations, and trend components through specialized encoding techniques. By leveraging recent advances in computer vision and deep learning architectures originally designed for image processing, we demonstrate that these visual representations enable more effective extraction of complex temporal dependencies than conventional time series models. Our experiments across diverse datasets—including financial markets, energy consumption, and climate measurements—show that VisualForecast outperforms state-of-the-art statistical and deep learning forecasting methods, reducing prediction error by 17-23% on long-horizon forecasts while demonstrating enhanced robustness to noise and missing data. Furthermore, the visual nature of our approach provides interpretable insights through attention maps that highlight which historical patterns most strongly influence predictions. This research opens new pathways for cross-modal learning in time series analysis and demonstrates the untapped potential of computer vision techniques in forecasting applications.

RadarScenes: A Real-World Radar Point Cloud Data Set for Automotive Applications

We present RadarScenes, a comprehensive radar point cloud dataset specifically designed for automotive applications. This dataset addresses the critical need for high-quality radar data to advance the development of perception algorithms for autonomous driving systems. RadarScenes comprises over 100 hours of real-world driving scenarios captured using automotive-grade radar sensors mounted on vehicles operating in diverse urban, suburban, and highway environments. The dataset includes synchronized point cloud data with precise temporal and spatial annotations, capturing various traffic participants, weather conditions, and driving scenarios. Each radar point is labeled with classification information, making RadarScenes particularly valuable for object detection, tracking, and classification tasks. Unlike existing datasets that primarily focus on camera or LiDAR data, RadarScenes emphasizes radar's unique capabilities in adverse weather conditions and varying lighting scenarios. The dataset also provides detailed sensor calibration information and evaluation metrics to facilitate fair comparison of algorithms. By releasing RadarScenes to the research community, we aim to accelerate the development of robust radar-based perception systems that can enhance the safety and reliability of autonomous vehicles in real-world conditions.

Coordinate Independent Convolutional Networks -- Isometry and Gauge Equivariant Convolutions on Riemannian Manifolds

This paper introduces a principled framework for constructing coordinate-independent convolutional neural networks on Riemannian manifolds. While traditional convolutional networks on Euclidean spaces have achieved remarkable success, their extension to general manifolds has been hindered by the inherent coordinate dependency of conventional approaches. We address this fundamental challenge by developing a mathematically rigorous formulation of gauge equivariant convolutions that respect the intrinsic geometry of the manifold.

Our framework leverages differential geometry to define convolution operations that are equivariant to both isometries of the manifold and local gauge transformations. By working with vector- and tensor-valued features in local coordinate frames, we establish convolution kernels that transform appropriately under changes of coordinates, ensuring that network predictions depend only on the intrinsic geometry rather than the arbitrary choice of coordinate system.

We prove several theoretical properties of our approach, including equivariance guarantees and stability bounds with respect to deformations of the underlying manifold. Experiments on tasks involving spherical data, curved surfaces, and general Riemannian manifolds demonstrate the effectiveness of our method compared to existing approaches. The results show significant improvements in accuracy, generalization, and robustness to different mesh discretizations and coordinate choices. Our framework provides a foundation for developing geometric deep learning methods that respect the mathematical structure of manifold-valued data across diverse applications in computer vision, graphics, and physical sciences.

Reward-Conditioned Policies

This paper introduces a novel framework for reinforcement learning called Reward-Conditioned Policies (RCPs), which explicitly incorporates reward targets as conditioning inputs to the policy. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning approaches that implicitly optimize for maximum rewards, our method enables agents to modulate their behavior based on specified reward objectives at inference time. We formalize RCPs as policies that map state observations and desired reward targets to actions, allowing for flexible control over the reward-performance trade-off. Through extensive experiments across diverse environments, including robotic manipulation tasks, game-playing domains, and simulated navigation scenarios, we demonstrate that RCPs can effectively achieve targeted reward levels while maintaining appropriate behavioral characteristics. Our approach shows particular promise in safety-critical applications where maximum reward pursuit may lead to undesirable risk-taking behaviors. Additionally, we show that RCPs can be efficiently trained using a modified version of standard policy gradient methods, with minimal computational overhead compared to conventional approaches. This work opens new avenues for developing more controllable and interpretable reinforcement learning systems that can adapt to varying reward preferences and constraints.

RayNet: Real-time Scene Arbitrary-shape Text Detection with Multiple Rays

This paper introduces RayNet, a novel end-to-end framework for real-time arbitrary-shape text detection in natural scenes. Unlike previous methods that rely on polygon or segmentation-based representations, our approach models text instances using multiple rays emitting from central points, enabling efficient and accurate detection of curved, rotated, and irregular text shapes. RayNet employs a lightweight backbone with a feature pyramid network, followed by a ray prediction head that simultaneously determines text centroids and corresponding ray endpoints. We propose a dynamic ray allocation mechanism that adaptively assigns more rays to complex text shapes while using fewer for simpler instances, optimizing computational resources. Experiments on challenging benchmarks including Total-Text, CTW1500, and MSRA-TD500 demonstrate that RayNet achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining real-time inference speeds (26 FPS on a single GPU). Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our multi-ray representation and dynamic allocation strategy. RayNet's ability to precisely capture arbitrary-shape text with minimal computational overhead makes it particularly suitable for resource-constrained applications such as mobile devices and real-time video analysis.

Learning Objectness from Sonar Images for Class-Independent Object Detection

This paper presents a novel approach to class-independent object detection in sonar imagery, addressing the unique challenges posed by underwater environments. Unlike traditional object detection methods that rely on class-specific training, we propose an objectness-based framework that can identify generic objects without prior knowledge of their specific categories. Our method leverages deep learning techniques to learn intrinsic objectness properties from sonar images, effectively distinguishing objects from the complex acoustic backgrounds typical in underwater sensing. We introduce a custom network architecture that combines multi-scale feature extraction with attention mechanisms specifically designed to handle the noise, reverberation, and low signal-to-noise ratio characteristics of sonar data. Extensive experiments conducted on diverse sonar datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance in detecting previously unseen object types compared to conventional class-specific detectors. The proposed framework shows particular promise for underwater robotics applications where novel objects are frequently encountered and training data for specific classes may be limited. This work represents a significant step toward more flexible and robust underwater object detection systems that can operate effectively in unexplored environments.

Multimodal Reward Shaping for Efficient Exploration in Reinforcement Learning

Exploration is a critical challenge in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in environments with sparse rewards or large state-action spaces. This paper introduces Multimodal Reward Shaping (MRS), a novel framework that leverages diverse information sources to guide agent exploration more efficiently. Our approach integrates visual, semantic, and dynamic environmental cues to construct auxiliary reward signals that complement the sparse environmental rewards. By combining these modalities through an adaptive weighting mechanism, MRS creates a rich reward landscape that encourages both targeted exploration and exploitation. We evaluate our method across diverse domains including navigation tasks, robotic manipulation, and game environments, demonstrating that MRS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art exploration methods in terms of sample efficiency and final performance. Ablation studies confirm that the integration of multiple modalities provides complementary guidance that is more effective than any single modality alone. Additionally, we show that MRS is compatible with existing RL algorithms and can be easily incorporated into various policy optimization frameworks. Our results suggest that multimodal reward shaping represents a promising direction for addressing the exploration challenge in reinforcement learning.

Reducing Unintended Bias of ML Models on Tabular and Textual Data

Machine learning models deployed in high-stakes domains often exhibit unintended biases that can lead to discriminatory outcomes against protected groups. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for detecting, measuring, and mitigating bias in ML models operating on both tabular and textual data. We first establish a taxonomy of bias types across structured and unstructured data, then propose a suite of pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing techniques tailored to each data modality. For tabular data, we introduce a novel reweighting algorithm that preserves model performance while reducing disparate impact. For text data, we develop a counterfactual augmentation approach that neutralizes latent biases in embeddings without compromising semantic coherence. Experiments across financial, healthcare, and content moderation applications demonstrate that our methods reduce bias metrics by 45-68% compared to baseline approaches, with minimal impact on overall accuracy (≤3% reduction). Furthermore, we provide practical guidelines for bias auditing throughout the ML development lifecycle and discuss the inherent trade-offs between fairness, model performance, and interpretability. Our framework enables practitioners to systematically address bias concerns while maintaining the utility of ML systems across diverse real-world applications.

Safe Reinforcement Learning in Constrained Markov Decision Processes

This paper addresses the critical challenge of ensuring safety in reinforcement learning (RL) systems by formalizing and analyzing safety-constrained optimization within Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs). While traditional RL focuses on maximizing cumulative rewards, many real-world applications require adherence to safety constraints during both learning and deployment phases. We propose a novel framework that integrates safety constraints directly into the optimization objective through a constrained policy optimization approach. Our method maintains a probabilistic safety guarantee during the learning process by employing a two-timescale update mechanism that simultaneously improves reward performance while enforcing constraint satisfaction. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees and establish bounds on constraint violations during training. Extensive empirical evaluation across diverse environments demonstrates that our approach achieves comparable reward performance to unconstrained methods while significantly reducing safety violations. The framework proves particularly effective in high-dimensional continuous control tasks where safety considerations are paramount. This work contributes to the development of RL systems that can be reliably deployed in safety-critical domains such as autonomous vehicles, healthcare, and industrial robotics.

Combining Ensemble Kalman Filter and Reservoir Computing to predict spatio-temporal chaotic systems from imperfect observations and models

This study presents a novel hybrid approach for predicting spatio-temporal chaotic systems when faced with both imperfect observations and incomplete model knowledge. We combine the strengths of Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF), a sequential data assimilation method, with Reservoir Computing (RC), a machine learning technique particularly effective for time series prediction. Our framework leverages EnKF's ability to optimally integrate noisy observations with model forecasts while exploiting RC's capacity to learn the underlying dynamics from data without explicit knowledge of the governing equations. We evaluate this hybrid methodology on benchmark chaotic systems, including the Lorenz-96 model and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, under various scenarios of observation sparsity, noise contamination, and model error. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms either method used independently, extending the prediction horizon by 30-45% and reducing forecast error by up to 60% compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the combined framework shows remarkable robustness to systematic model biases and observation gaps. This work provides a promising direction for improving predictions in complex systems where perfect models or complete observations are unavailable, with potential applications in weather forecasting, turbulence modeling, and other complex dynamical systems.

Regret Bound Balancing and Elimination for Model Selection in Bandits and RL

This paper introduces a novel approach to model selection in bandit problems and reinforcement learning (RL) by combining two fundamental techniques: regret bound balancing and elimination. We address the challenge of selecting the optimal model from a candidate set when the complexity of the underlying environment is unknown a priori. Our proposed algorithm, Balanced Elimination for Model Selection (BEMS), dynamically allocates resources between promising models while systematically eliminating underperforming ones based on their empirical regret bounds. We establish theoretical guarantees showing that BEMS achieves near-optimal regret with respect to the best model in hindsight, with only logarithmic overhead compared to an oracle with advance knowledge of the optimal model. Empirical evaluations across diverse bandit environments and RL tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing model selection methods, particularly in non-stationary and complex environments. The framework is general enough to accommodate various base algorithms while maintaining computational efficiency. Our results provide important insights into the fundamental trade-offs between exploration, exploitation, and model complexity in sequential decision-making problems.

FreeAnchor: Learning to Match Anchors for Visual Object Detection

Modern object detection frameworks rely heavily on predefined anchor boxes as regression references, but the assignment strategies between anchors and ground-truth objects remain largely heuristic and sub-optimal. In this paper, we propose FreeAnchor, a novel anchor-matching mechanism that reformulates the object detection problem from a maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) perspective. Our approach models the anchor assignment process as a latent variable optimization problem, where anchors are allowed to freely match with objects in a probabilistic manner. The proposed framework consists of two key components: (1) a detection-customized likelihood function that evaluates the quality of anchor-object pairs, and (2) an expectation-maximization (EM) based learning procedure that dynamically optimizes anchor assignments during training. Through extensive experiments on the MS COCO dataset, FreeAnchor consistently improves the performance of various detector architectures, achieving significant gains over their baseline counterparts. Our single-model detector achieves 44.9% mAP on COCO test-dev, outperforming many state-of-the-art methods while maintaining inference efficiency. The results demonstrate that learning to match anchors with a principled probabilistic formulation leads to more accurate and robust object detection systems.

Deep Multi-view Depth Estimation with Predicted Uncertainty

This paper presents a novel approach to multi-view depth estimation that explicitly models uncertainty in predicted depth maps. While deep learning has significantly advanced the state of multi-view stereo reconstruction, most existing methods do not provide reliable confidence measures for their predictions, limiting their applicability in safety-critical systems. Our method addresses this gap by introducing a probabilistic framework that jointly estimates depth and its associated uncertainty from multiple input views. We develop a two-headed neural architecture that predicts both depth values and their uncertainty distributions through a cost volume-based feature extraction pipeline. The uncertainty predictions are supervised using a specialized loss function that encourages calibrated probability estimates. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including ScanNet, ETH3D, and KITTI demonstrate that our approach not only achieves competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods but also provides well-calibrated uncertainty estimates that strongly correlate with actual depth errors. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our uncertainty modeling approach across varying numbers of input views and different scene complexities. The predicted uncertainty enables downstream applications to make informed decisions about the reliability of depth estimates, making our method particularly valuable for robotics and autonomous navigation systems where safety guarantees are essential.

A Shapelet Transform for Multivariate Time Series Classification

Time series classification is a fundamental task in data mining with applications spanning healthcare, finance, and industrial monitoring. While shapelet-based approaches have proven effective for univariate time series classification, their extension to multivariate time series presents significant challenges. In this paper, we propose a novel Multivariate Shapelet Transform (MST) that effectively captures discriminative subsequences across multiple dimensions of multivariate time series data. Our approach extends the traditional shapelet transform by incorporating both intra-channel and inter-channel relationships, enabling the identification of complex patterns that may exist across multiple variables simultaneously. We introduce an efficient algorithm for extracting candidate shapelets from multivariate time series and a distance measure that accounts for cross-dimensional dependencies. Extensive experiments on 20 multivariate time series datasets from the UEA repository demonstrate that our MST approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average improvement of 4.7% in classification accuracy. Additionally, our method provides interpretable insights by identifying the most discriminative subsequences across variables, making it particularly valuable for domains requiring explainable predictions. The computational efficiency of our approach also makes it suitable for real-time classification tasks on high-dimensional time series data.

DeepHMap++: Combined Projection Grouping and Correspondence Learning for Full DoF Pose Estimation

This paper presents DeepHMap++, a novel deep learning framework for estimating the full 6 Degree of Freedom (DoF) pose of objects from single RGB-D images. Unlike traditional methods that rely on either template matching or correspondence-based techniques, our approach integrates projection grouping with correspondence learning in an end-to-end trainable architecture. We introduce a hierarchical feature extraction module that captures both local geometric details and global contextual information, enabling robust performance across varying lighting conditions and partial occlusions. The framework employs a two-stage process: first, a projection grouping network identifies candidate pose hypotheses through a voting-based mechanism; second, a correspondence refinement network establishes precise point-to-point matches between the input and the object model to optimize the final pose estimation. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including LineMOD, Occlusion LineMOD, and YCB-Video demonstrate that DeepHMap++ outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average rotation error of 2.7° and translation error of 0.8 cm. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of our integrated approach compared to using either projection grouping or correspondence learning alone. The proposed method maintains real-time performance while significantly improving accuracy for challenging pose estimation scenarios.

Graph Networks with Spectral Message Passing

This paper introduces a novel approach to graph representation learning through Spectral Message Passing (SMP), a framework that leverages spectral graph theory to enhance information propagation in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Unlike traditional spatial message passing techniques, our method operates in the graph spectral domain, enabling more effective capture of global graph properties and long-range dependencies. We formulate message passing as a spectral filtering operation on graph signals, allowing for adaptive frequency-dependent information exchange between nodes. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that SMP overcomes fundamental limitations of conventional GNNs, including over-smoothing and the bottleneck effect in capturing complex structural patterns. Our empirical evaluation across diverse benchmarks—including node classification, graph classification, and link prediction tasks—shows that SMP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art GNN architectures, with particularly significant improvements on graphs with complex topological structures. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees on the expressive power of our approach and analyze its computational complexity, demonstrating that SMP achieves an effective balance between model expressivity and computational efficiency. These results establish Spectral Message Passing as a powerful paradigm for graph representation learning with broad applications across domains.

TransTailor: Pruning the Pre-trained Model for Improved Transfer Learning

Transfer learning from large pre-trained models has become the de facto approach for addressing a wide range of downstream tasks. However, these models often contain redundant parameters that are unnecessary for specific target tasks, leading to increased computational costs and potential overfitting. In this paper, we introduce TransTailor, a novel pruning framework that systematically removes task-irrelevant parameters from pre-trained models to enhance transfer learning performance. Our approach integrates importance scoring mechanisms that consider both the intrinsic properties of the pre-trained representations and their relevance to the target task. Through extensive experiments across multiple domains including computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal tasks, we demonstrate that TransTailor achieves comparable or superior performance to full model fine-tuning while reducing model size by 30-70%. Notably, our pruned models show improved generalization on low-resource tasks and faster inference times. We also provide theoretical insights into why selective pruning before fine-tuning can mitigate negative transfer and overfitting problems. TransTailor offers a practical solution for deploying efficient, task-specific models derived from large-scale pre-trained architectures.

CrossATNet - A Novel Cross-Attention Based Framework for Sketch-Based Image Retrieval

Sketch-based image retrieval (SBIR) remains a challenging computer vision task due to the significant domain gap between free-hand sketches and natural images. This paper presents CrossATNet, a novel cross-attention based framework that effectively bridges this modality gap by learning robust cross-domain feature representations. Our approach leverages a dual-branch architecture with specialized encoders for sketch and image inputs, connected through innovative cross-attention modules that facilitate bidirectional information exchange between modalities. Unlike previous methods that rely on triplet loss or contrastive learning alone, CrossATNet employs a hybrid loss function that combines cross-modal attention supervision with feature embedding alignment. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including Sketchy, TU-Berlin, and QuickDraw, demonstrate that CrossATNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins, achieving improvements of 4.7%, 5.2%, and 3.8% in mean Average Precision (mAP) respectively. Further ablation studies validate the effectiveness of our cross-attention mechanism and hybrid loss formulation. The proposed framework not only excels in category-level SBIR but also shows promising results for fine-grained retrieval tasks, making it a versatile solution for practical applications in image search and retrieval systems.

CNN Profiler on Polar Coordinate Images for Tropical Cyclone Structure Analysis

This study presents a novel Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture designed specifically for analyzing tropical cyclone structure using polar coordinate imagery. Traditional CNN approaches applied to satellite imagery of tropical cyclones often struggle with the radial nature of these weather systems. Our proposed "CNN Profiler" transforms conventional satellite imagery into polar coordinate representations, where the storm center serves as the origin, enabling more effective feature extraction of cyclone structural characteristics. The model was trained on a comprehensive dataset of 3,000 tropical cyclone images from multiple ocean basins, converted to polar coordinates. Results demonstrate that our approach achieves 87% accuracy in classifying cyclone intensity categories and significantly outperforms standard CNN architectures applied to Cartesian imagery by 23% when identifying key structural features such as eyewalls, rainbands, and asymmetries. Additionally, the model successfully extracts quantitative structural profiles that strongly correlate (r = 0.83) with in-situ measurements from aircraft reconnaissance. This approach provides meteorologists with an automated, objective tool for tropical cyclone structure analysis that can be operationally implemented in regions lacking aircraft reconnaissance capabilities, potentially improving intensity forecasts and enhancing our understanding of cyclone dynamics.

A Worrying Analysis of Probabilistic Time-series Models for Sales Forecasting

This study presents a critical evaluation of probabilistic time-series models commonly deployed for retail sales forecasting. Through rigorous analysis of 15 probabilistic forecasting methods across diverse retail datasets spanning 5 years and 8 market sectors, we uncover concerning patterns in model performance and uncertainty quantification. Our findings reveal that while these models often produce acceptable point forecasts, their uncertainty estimates exhibit systematic miscalibration, with 78% of the examined models demonstrating significant overconfidence in their predictions. Furthermore, we document a troubling inverse relationship between forecast accuracy and uncertainty estimation quality, with the best-performing models for point predictions frequently producing the least reliable prediction intervals. The consequences of these unreliable uncertainty estimates are substantial, potentially leading to suboptimal inventory management decisions costing retailers an estimated 12-18% in excess inventory costs or stockouts. We propose a novel evaluation framework specifically designed to assess probabilistic forecast calibration in retail contexts and offer practical recommendations for practitioners to mitigate these issues. This work serves as an important caution regarding the uncritical adoption of probabilistic forecasting methods without careful consideration of their uncertainty quantification properties.

Generation For Adaption: A GAN-Based Approach for 3D Domain Adaption with Point Cloud Data

Domain adaptation for 3D point cloud data remains challenging due to the irregular structure and varying density of point clouds across different domains. In this paper, we propose a novel Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) based approach that addresses the domain shift problem in 3D point cloud classification and segmentation tasks. Our method, Generation For Adaption (GFA), leverages the generative capabilities of GANs to create synthetic target-like point cloud data while preserving semantic information from the source domain. The framework consists of a point cloud generator that transforms source domain features into the target domain style, and a discriminator network that distinguishes between real target domain data and generated samples. We introduce a geometric consistency loss that maintains structural integrity during domain transfer and a feature alignment module that minimizes the distribution discrepancy between domains in the feature space. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including ModelNet40, ShapeNet, and KITTI demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 4.2% in classification accuracy and 5.7% in segmentation mIoU. Additionally, our qualitative results show that GFA successfully preserves fine-grained geometric details while adapting to different domain characteristics. The proposed method provides a promising direction for unsupervised domain adaptation in 3D point cloud processing with potential applications in autonomous driving, robotics, and augmented reality.

A Coupled Manifold Optimization Framework to Jointly Model the Functional Connectomics and Behavioral Data Spaces

This paper introduces a novel coupled manifold optimization framework that simultaneously models the relationship between functional brain connectomics and behavioral data. While traditional approaches analyze these domains separately or employ simplistic correlation methods, our framework leverages the intrinsic geometric structure of both data spaces to discover their complex interdependencies. We represent functional connectivity as elements on a Riemannian manifold of positive definite matrices and behavioral measures within their appropriate geometric constraints, then develop a coupled optimization approach that preserves the topological properties of each manifold while identifying meaningful cross-domain relationships. Through experiments on large-scale neuroimaging datasets including the Human Connectome Project, we demonstrate that our framework outperforms conventional methods in predicting behavioral outcomes from connectivity data and in identifying neurobiologically plausible brain-behavior associations. The proposed methodology reveals multivariate patterns linking specific brain network configurations to clusters of behavioral traits, offering insights into the neural underpinnings of human cognition and behavior. This work provides a mathematically rigorous foundation for jointly analyzing multimodal brain-behavior data that respects the geometric constraints inherent in each domain.

Interpreting Spatially Infinite Generative Models

This paper introduces a novel framework for interpreting generative models that operate on unbounded spatial domains. While traditional generative models typically produce outputs with fixed dimensions, spatially infinite generative models present unique challenges for interpretation due to their theoretical capacity to generate content extending infinitely in all directions. We develop a formal mathematical characterization of these models and propose metrics to evaluate their coherence, consistency, and contextual awareness across arbitrary spatial extensions. Our approach introduces the concept of "spatial interpretability fields" that quantify how model semantics and feature representations evolve across unbounded domains. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our interpretation framework successfully identifies emergent patterns, discontinuities, and semantic drift in infinite canvas generations. Furthermore, we show how these insights can guide architectural improvements in spatially infinite models, leading to enhanced generation quality and more predictable behavior at extreme spatial coordinates. Our work provides fundamental theoretical and practical tools for understanding the behavior of this increasingly important class of generative models.

Automatic Cross-Domain Transfer Learning for Linear Regression

This paper introduces a novel framework for automatic cross-domain transfer learning in linear regression tasks. We address the fundamental challenge of leveraging knowledge from source domains to improve prediction performance on target domains with limited labeled data. Our approach automatically identifies transferable structures between seemingly disparate domains by learning domain-invariant feature representations while simultaneously adapting domain-specific components. The proposed method employs a two-stage optimization process: first discovering shared parameter subspaces across domains, then fine-tuning domain-specific coefficients using a regularized objective function that balances knowledge transfer with target domain adaptation. Theoretical analysis provides generalization bounds that characterize the trade-off between transfer benefit and negative transfer risk. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms traditional linear regression and existing transfer learning approaches, particularly when target domain samples are scarce. Results show average error reductions of 18-35% compared to baseline methods across diverse application domains including healthcare, finance, and environmental monitoring. Our framework requires minimal hyperparameter tuning and automatically determines when and how much to transfer, making it practical for real-world applications where domain expertise may be limited.

Manipulating Identical Filter Redundancy for Efficient Pruning on Deep and Complicated CNN

This paper introduces a novel approach to neural network compression by exploiting identical filter redundancy in deep and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). We observe that modern CNN architectures often contain redundant filters that learn nearly identical feature representations, creating computational inefficiency without providing additional discriminative power. Our method, termed Identical Filter Redundancy Pruning (IFRP), systematically identifies and eliminates these redundancies through a two-phase process: first detecting clusters of similar filters using a specialized similarity metric, then selectively pruning redundant filters while preserving network expressivity. Experiments conducted on state-of-the-art architectures including ResNet, DenseNet, and EfficientNet demonstrate that IFRP achieves compression rates of up to 65% with minimal accuracy degradation (less than 0.5% on ImageNet). Additionally, our approach complements existing pruning methods and requires significantly less computational overhead for retraining compared to conventional pruning techniques. The proposed method is particularly effective for very deep networks where redundancy accumulates across layers. Our work provides new insights into the internal representations of CNNs and offers a practical solution for deploying efficient deep learning models in resource-constrained environments.

DECOR-GAN: 3D Shape Detailization by Conditional Refinement

We present DECOR-GAN, a novel generative adversarial network designed for enhancing 3D shape representations with fine-grained geometric details. While existing 3D shape generation methods excel at producing coarse structures, they often struggle to capture intricate surface details that are crucial for realism. Our approach addresses this limitation through a two-stage conditional refinement process. First, DECOR-GAN learns a latent space of geometric details from high-resolution 3D scans. Then, it applies these details to low-resolution shapes through a conditional generation framework that respects the underlying structure while adding appropriate fine-grained features. Experiments show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both quantitative metrics and user studies across diverse object categories. DECOR-GAN can effectively transfer details between shapes of different classes and generate multiple plausible detailizations for a single coarse input. This capability enables applications in content creation, virtual reality, and simulation where detailed 3D assets are essential. Our code and pre-trained models are available to facilitate further research in this direction.

Decision Forest: A Nonparametric Approach to Modeling Irrational Choice

Traditional economic models often rely on the assumption of rational decision-making, yet empirical evidence consistently demonstrates that human choices frequently deviate from rational norms. This paper introduces Decision Forest, a novel nonparametric framework designed to capture and predict irrational choice patterns without imposing restrictive assumptions about utility maximization or preference consistency. Our approach leverages ensemble learning techniques to accommodate preference reversals, context-dependent valuations, and other behavioral anomalies that challenge conventional choice models. By analyzing data from multiple experimental settings, including intertemporal choices, risky decisions, and framing-sensitive scenarios, we demonstrate that Decision Forest significantly outperforms parametric alternatives in predictive accuracy. The model's flexibility allows it to identify decision boundaries that reflect actual choice patterns rather than normative theories, while its interpretability features provide insights into the psychological mechanisms underlying seemingly irrational decisions. These results suggest that nonparametric approaches may offer a more productive path toward modeling real-world decision-making than continued refinements of rational choice frameworks.

Probing Transfer Learning with a Model of Synthetic Correlated Datasets

Transfer learning has become a cornerstone technique in modern machine learning, enabling models trained on one task to perform effectively on related tasks. However, the theoretical underpinnings of when and why transfer learning succeeds remain incompletely understood. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for systematically investigating transfer learning dynamics using synthetically generated correlated datasets. Our approach allows precise control over dataset similarity through a parameterized correlation structure, enabling rigorous examination of how different correlation patterns affect transfer learning outcomes. We demonstrate that performance improvements from transfer learning follow predictable patterns based on the correlation structure between source and target domains. Through extensive experiments with both linear and deep neural network models, we identify critical correlation thresholds that determine when transfer learning outperforms training from scratch. Furthermore, we provide theoretical bounds on expected performance gains as a function of dataset correlation properties. Our findings offer practical guidance for practitioners on when to apply transfer learning and contribute to the fundamental understanding of representation transfer across related tasks. This synthetic dataset framework provides a valuable testbed for future research on transfer learning mechanisms and optimization.

Constraining Implicit Space with Minimum Description Length: An Unsupervised Attention Mechanism across Neural Network Layers

Deep neural networks learn complex internal representations, yet the organization and flow of information across layers remains poorly understood. We introduce a novel unsupervised attention mechanism that leverages the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle to constrain the implicit space of neural representations. Our approach dynamically attends to the most information-efficient features across network layers without requiring explicit supervision. By formalizing neural attention through an information-theoretic framework, we demonstrate how MDL-based constraints enable networks to develop more compact and interpretable representations while maintaining or improving performance. Experiments across vision, language, and multimodal architectures show that our method: (1) significantly reduces representation redundancy between layers, (2) creates emergent attention maps that align with human-interpretable features, and (3) improves generalization on out-of-distribution tasks. Theoretical analysis reveals connections between our approach and Bayesian inference, suggesting that MDL-constrained attention approximates optimal posterior inference over latent representations. Our work provides both a practical unsupervised attention mechanism and deeper insights into information flow within neural networks.

Schema-Aware Deep Graph Convolutional Networks for Heterogeneous Graphs

Heterogeneous graphs, which contain multiple types of nodes and edges, represent a prevalent data structure in real-world applications ranging from social networks to knowledge graphs. However, traditional graph convolutional networks (GCNs) often fail to capture the complex semantic relationships inherent in these graphs. In this paper, we propose Schema-Aware Deep Graph Convolutional Networks (SA-DGCN), a novel framework that explicitly incorporates graph schema information into the learning process. Our approach leverages the meta-paths defined by the schema to guide the message passing mechanism, enabling more effective feature propagation across heterogeneous node and edge types. We introduce a schema-aware attention mechanism that dynamically weights different meta-path-based neighbors according to their relevance, allowing the model to capture both local and global semantic relationships. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SA-DGCN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in node classification, link prediction, and graph classification tasks, with improvements of up to 15% in accuracy. Furthermore, our model exhibits enhanced interpretability by revealing the importance of different meta-paths for specific prediction tasks. The proposed approach provides a principled way to integrate domain knowledge encoded in graph schemas into deep learning models for heterogeneous graphs.

Anomaly Detection with Generative Adversarial Networks for Multivariate Time Series

This paper presents a novel approach to anomaly detection in multivariate time series data using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We introduce a framework that leverages the adversarial learning paradigm to model complex temporal dependencies and inter-variable correlations in multivariate time series. Our method, which we call TS-GAN, employs a specialized architecture where the generator learns to produce realistic time series sequences while the discriminator is trained to distinguish between real and generated data. By utilizing the trained discriminator's output and reconstruction error as anomaly scores, our approach can effectively identify anomalous patterns that deviate from normal behavior across multiple variables simultaneously. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets from various domains, including industrial systems, healthcare monitoring, and financial transactions, demonstrate that TS-GAN outperforms traditional statistical methods and recent deep learning approaches, achieving up to 15% improvement in F1-score and significantly reducing false positive rates. Additionally, our model exhibits robust performance in scenarios with limited labeled anomalies, making it particularly suitable for real-world applications where anomalous samples are scarce. The proposed method also provides interpretable results by highlighting the contributing variables and temporal segments that lead to anomaly detection, thus facilitating root cause analysis.

Non-uniform Motion Deblurring with Blurry Component Divided Guidance

This paper presents a novel approach to non-uniform motion deblurring through a framework we call Blurry Component Divided Guidance (BCDG). Traditional deblurring methods often struggle with spatially varying blur caused by camera shake, object movement, or depth variations. Our method addresses this challenge by decomposing blurry images into distinct component layers based on blur characteristics and utilizing these components to guide the restoration process. We first develop a component division network that separates the image into regions with similar blur patterns. These components are then processed through parallel restoration branches with adaptive convolutional filters optimized for specific blur types. A guidance mechanism integrates information across components while preserving spatial coherence at region boundaries. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our BCDG framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods by an average of 2.3dB PSNR on complex non-uniform blur scenarios, with particularly significant improvements in regions containing multiple blur types. The proposed method maintains computational efficiency while effectively handling diverse real-world blurring conditions without requiring explicit blur kernel estimation.

Occlusion-aware Unsupervised Learning of Depth from 4-D Light Fields

This paper presents a novel unsupervised learning framework for depth estimation from 4-D light fields that explicitly addresses the challenges posed by occlusions. Unlike previous approaches that either require ground truth depth supervision or struggle with depth discontinuities at object boundaries, our method incorporates an occlusion-aware consistency loss that enables accurate depth estimation without labeled data. We leverage the rich angular information inherent in light field data to detect occlusion regions and develop specialized handling for these areas during training. Our network architecture employs a multi-scale feature extraction pathway that processes both spatial and angular dimensions of the light field, followed by a refinement module that preserves sharp depth boundaries. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world light field datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods by significant margins, particularly in regions with complex occlusions. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our occlusion-aware components, and qualitative results showcase the method's ability to recover fine geometric details even in challenging scenes. The proposed framework advances unsupervised light field depth estimation toward practical applications in computational photography, autonomous navigation, and mixed reality.

Evaluation of Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks for data augmentation of chest X-ray images

Deep learning approaches for medical image analysis frequently face challenges related to limited data availability, particularly for rare pathologies. This study evaluates the efficacy of Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs) for synthetic data augmentation of chest X-ray images. We trained a DCGAN model on 10,000 chest radiographs from publicly available datasets and generated synthetic images to supplement training data for a convolutional neural network (CNN) classifier designed to detect five common thoracic pathologies. The quality of synthetic images was assessed using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and through evaluation by three board-certified radiologists. Classification models trained with augmented datasets (original plus synthetic images) were compared against baseline models trained solely on original images. Results demonstrate that DCGAN-based augmentation improved classification performance, with the augmented model achieving a mean increase in accuracy of 4.7% (p<0.01) and AUC improvement of 0.056 across all pathologies. Performance gains were most pronounced for conditions with fewer training examples. While radiologists could distinguish synthetic from real images with 83% accuracy, they confirmed the clinical plausibility of the generated pathologies. Our findings suggest that DCGANs offer a promising approach for medical image data augmentation, particularly in scenarios with limited training data, though challenges remain in generating images indistinguishable from real radiographs. This technique may help address data scarcity issues in medical imaging and improve the performance of diagnostic AI systems.

Augmented Mitotic Cell Count using Field Of Interest Proposal

Accurate mitotic cell counting is crucial for cancer grading and prognosis, yet remains challenging due to the rarity and morphological variability of mitotic figures in histopathological slides. This study presents a novel approach called Field Of Interest Proposal (FOIP) to augment mitotic cell detection and counting in histopathological images. Our two-stage framework first identifies potential regions containing mitotic activity using a lightweight region proposal network, followed by detailed classification within these fields of interest. We evaluated our method on the TUPAC16 and MIDOG datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over traditional whole-slide analysis approaches. The FOIP technique achieved 87.3% sensitivity and 91.2% specificity, with a 43% reduction in false positives compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, our approach reduced computational requirements by 65%, enabling more efficient processing of whole-slide images. The proposed methodology addresses the class imbalance problem inherent in mitotic cell detection and provides pathologists with an interpretable tool that highlights relevant regions for review. This work contributes to more accurate cancer grading and has potential applications in computational pathology beyond mitotic figure assessment.

Word-Class Embeddings for Multiclass Text Classification

This paper introduces a novel approach to multiclass text classification using word-class embeddings, a technique that incorporates class-specific information directly into word representations. Traditional word embeddings capture semantic relationships between words but fail to encode class-relevant distinctions that are crucial for classification tasks.
