Our proposed method extends standard embedding architectures by jointly learning word representations and their associations with target classes, creating embeddings that are inherently discriminative for classification purposes. We develop a neural architecture that combines these specialized embeddings with attention mechanisms to emphasize class-indicative terms during document representation. Experiments conducted on four benchmark datasets—Reuters-21578, 20Newsgroups, ArXiv abstracts, and Amazon product reviews—demonstrate that our word-class embedding approach significantly outperforms traditional classification methods using standard word embeddings, with average improvements of 4.7% in F1-score. Further analysis reveals that our method is particularly effective for datasets with subtle semantic distinctions between classes and performs robustly even with limited training data. The approach also provides interpretable insights into class-specific vocabulary importance, enhancing model explainability. Our findings suggest that explicitly modeling word-class relationships creates more discriminative features for multiclass text classification tasks.

The Chan-Vese Algorithm

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the Chan-Vese algorithm, an influential active contour model for image segmentation that operates without relying on gradient information. Unlike traditional edge-based segmentation methods, the Chan-Vese algorithm utilizes a level set formulation based on the Mumford-Shah functional to identify objects whose boundaries are not necessarily defined by gradient. The algorithm minimizes an energy functional that partitions an image into regions of approximately piecewise-constant intensities, making it particularly effective for segmenting images with weak or diffuse boundaries. We review the mathematical foundation of the method, examine its implementation through numerical schemes, and discuss various extensions that address multi-phase segmentation, texture discrimination, and adaptations for different imaging modalities. Experimental results demonstrate the algorithm's robustness to noise and effectiveness across diverse image types. Furthermore, we explore recent developments incorporating machine learning techniques to enhance the algorithm's performance. This work highlights the Chan-Vese algorithm's continuing significance in image analysis and computer vision applications despite the emergence of deep learning approaches to segmentation.

Variational Learning Across Domains with Triplet Information

This paper presents a novel variational learning framework that leverages triplet information to facilitate knowledge transfer across multiple domains. Traditional domain adaptation methods often struggle with heterogeneous feature spaces and limited labeled data. Our approach addresses these challenges by encoding relative similarity relationships through triplets—consisting of an anchor, a positive, and a negative example—to learn domain-invariant representations. We formulate a variational objective that jointly optimizes a triplet-based contrastive loss and a domain-specific reconstruction term, enabling the model to preserve both discriminative and domain-specific information. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that our method minimizes an upper bound on the cross-domain generalization error while maintaining local structure consistency. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets across image recognition, natural language processing, and cross-modal tasks show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods, particularly in scenarios with limited supervision. The proposed framework demonstrates robust performance in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings, offering a flexible solution for knowledge transfer across heterogeneous domains.

Deep Semi-Supervised Learning for Time Series Classification

Time series classification presents unique challenges due to temporal dependencies and the often limited availability of labeled data. This paper introduces a novel deep semi-supervised learning framework specifically designed to address these challenges in time series classification tasks. Our approach leverages both labeled and unlabeled time series data through a dual-branch neural network architecture that combines supervised classification with self-supervised representation learning. The framework incorporates temporal consistency regularization and contrastive learning mechanisms tailored to the sequential nature of time series data. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms traditional supervised approaches, especially in scenarios with limited labeled data. With only 20% labeled samples, our model achieves classification accuracy comparable to fully supervised methods trained on complete datasets. Furthermore, we show that the learned representations effectively capture temporal patterns and are transferable across related time series tasks. This work provides both theoretical insights into semi-supervised learning for sequential data and practical solutions for real-world time series classification problems where labeled data acquisition is costly or limited.

Structured Sparsity Inducing Adaptive Optimizers for Deep Learning

This paper introduces a novel family of adaptive optimization algorithms designed to induce structured sparsity in deep neural networks during training. While existing adaptive optimizers like Adam and AdaGrad have proven effective for training dense networks, they do not explicitly encourage sparsity patterns that align with hardware efficiency constraints. Our proposed optimizers incorporate regularization terms that promote structured sparsity—including channel-wise, filter-wise, and block-wise patterns—directly into the parameter update rules. Through theoretical analysis, we establish convergence guarantees for our methods under standard assumptions. Extensive experiments on image classification, natural language processing, and recommendation system benchmarks demonstrate that our optimizers simultaneously achieve model compression rates of 70-90% with negligible accuracy loss compared to dense baselines, while maintaining training stability. Furthermore, we show that the resulting sparse structures translate to practical speedups of 2.5-3.8× on commodity hardware without requiring specialized sparse computation libraries. Our approach offers a promising direction for training efficient deep learning models that are inherently compatible with deployment constraints, eliminating the need for post-training pruning or specialized sparse architecture design.

GDDR: GNN-based Data-Driven Routing

This paper presents GDDR (GNN-based Data-Driven Routing), a novel approach to network routing that leverages Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to learn optimal routing policies from network traffic data. Traditional routing algorithms rely on predefined heuristics and often fail to adapt to the dynamic nature of modern network environments. GDDR addresses this limitation by formulating the routing problem as a graph learning task where nodes learn to make forwarding decisions based on both local and global network conditions. Our model captures complex spatial dependencies in network topologies and temporal patterns in traffic flows through a specialized message-passing architecture. Extensive evaluations on both simulated and real-world network datasets demonstrate that GDDR achieves up to 27% reduction in end-to-end latency and 35% improvement in throughput compared to conventional routing protocols. Furthermore, GDDR exhibits robust performance under various network conditions including congestion, link failures, and bursty traffic patterns. The data-driven nature of our approach enables continuous adaptation to changing network dynamics without manual reconfiguration, making it particularly suitable for large-scale, heterogeneous networks. Our work establishes a promising direction for intelligent networking systems that can learn and optimize routing decisions from experience.

ARMDN: Associative and Recurrent Mixture Density Networks for eRetail Demand Forecasting

Accurate demand forecasting is critical for eRetail businesses to optimize inventory management, pricing strategies, and operational planning. This paper introduces the Associative and Recurrent Mixture Density Network (ARMDN), a novel deep learning architecture specifically designed to address the complex challenges of eRetail demand forecasting. ARMDN combines the expressive power of mixture density networks with recurrent neural components to capture temporal dependencies and associative learning mechanisms to incorporate cross-product relationships. Unlike traditional forecasting methods that produce point estimates, our approach generates complete probability distributions over future demand, effectively modeling the inherent uncertainty in eRetail sales patterns. We evaluate ARMDN on large-scale datasets from multiple eRetail platforms, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art forecasting methods, with a 17.3% reduction in mean absolute percentage error and a 21.5% improvement in quantile loss metrics. Additionally, we show that ARMDN effectively captures complex demand patterns including seasonality, promotional effects, product cannibalization, and complementary product relationships. Our model's probabilistic forecasts provide valuable insights for inventory optimization, reducing stockouts by 14.2% and overstock situations by 9.7% in real-world deployments. These results highlight ARMDN's potential as a powerful tool for eRetail demand planning in uncertain and dynamic market environments.

Learning Models for Visual 3D Localization with Implicit Mapping

This paper presents a novel approach to visual 3D localization that leverages implicit neural representations for mapping. While traditional visual localization methods rely on explicit feature matching or dense reconstruction, our approach learns an implicit mapping function that encodes scene geometry and appearance in the weights of a neural network. We introduce a two-stage architecture consisting of an implicit mapping network that represents the 3D environment and a localization network that predicts 6-DoF camera poses from RGB images. By representing scenes implicitly, our method eliminates the need for explicit point cloud storage or feature databases, resulting in a compact scene representation that captures multi-scale environmental details. Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable or superior localization accuracy to state-of-the-art explicit methods while requiring significantly less memory. Additionally, our implicit mapping enables robust performance under challenging conditions such as viewpoint changes, lighting variations, and partial scene occlusions. We further analyze the emergent properties of the learned representations and discuss the scalability of our approach to large environments through a hierarchical mapping strategy.

An Improvement of Object Detection Performance using Multi-step Machine Learnings

This study proposes a novel multi-step machine learning approach to enhance object detection performance across diverse environments and conditions. While current object detection methods achieve impressive results in controlled settings, they often struggle with real-world challenges such as occlusion, varying lighting conditions, and complex backgrounds. Our approach addresses these limitations by implementing a cascaded architecture of specialized machine learning models, each designed to handle specific aspects of the detection process. The framework consists of three key stages: initial region proposal refinement, feature enhancement through adaptive learning, and contextual reasoning for final detection optimization. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our multi-step approach achieves a significant improvement in detection accuracy (average precision increased by 8.7%) and robustness compared to single-model approaches, particularly for challenging cases involving small objects and partial occlusions. The computational overhead remains manageable through efficient model design and selective processing, making the system viable for practical applications. This work contributes to the field by establishing that strategically decomposing the object detection task into specialized sub-problems can yield substantial performance gains while maintaining reasonable computational requirements.

Class-incremental Learning via Deep Model Consolidation

Class-incremental learning remains a significant challenge in deep learning, where models must continually adapt to new classes while maintaining performance on previously learned ones. In this paper, we propose Deep Model Consolidation (DMC), a novel framework that addresses catastrophic forgetting in class-incremental scenarios without requiring access to the original training data. Our approach leverages knowledge distillation techniques to consolidate the representations from a new-class model and a previously trained model into a unified architecture that preserves performance across all classes. We introduce a double-distillation loss that balances the transfer of decision boundaries from both constituent models while maintaining discriminative feature representations. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including CIFAR-100, ImageNet-Subset, and Caltech-101 demonstrate that DMC significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving up to 13.2% improvement in average accuracy under challenging incremental learning settings. Moreover, our approach exhibits robust performance even with substantial class additions and maintains computational efficiency during the consolidation process. These results highlight the potential of DMC as an effective solution for real-world applications requiring continuous knowledge acquisition without catastrophic forgetting.

Towards the Unification and Robustness of Perturbation and Gradient Based Explanations

Explanations of neural network predictions have become increasingly important as these models are deployed in critical domains. Two prominent families of explanation methods have emerged: perturbation-based approaches that analyze model behavior when inputs are modified, and gradient-based methods that examine the sensitivity of outputs to infinitesimal input changes. While these approaches appear fundamentally different, this paper demonstrates their underlying connections and proposes a unified theoretical framework. We establish formal relationships between perturbation methods (e.g., LIME, SHAP) and gradient techniques (e.g., Integrated Gradients, SmoothGrad), showing how they can be viewed as different approximations of the same underlying attribution principle. Our framework reveals that the apparent distinctions between these methods stem primarily from implementation choices rather than conceptual differences. Building on these insights, we develop a novel hybrid approach that leverages the complementary strengths of both paradigms, achieving superior robustness to input noise and adversarial manipulations. Extensive experiments across image, text, and tabular data demonstrate that our unified method produces more stable and faithful explanations compared to existing techniques. This work not only advances our theoretical understanding of explanation methods but also provides practical tools for more reliable model interpretability in real-world applications.

Visual Attention for Behavioral Cloning in Autonomous Driving

This paper presents a novel approach to behavioral cloning for autonomous driving that leverages visual attention mechanisms to improve driving policy learning from human demonstrations. While traditional end-to-end behavioral cloning methods have shown promise, they often struggle with generalization and interpretability. Our approach incorporates a multi-head attention network that explicitly models which regions of the visual input are most relevant for driving decisions. By analyzing the attention patterns of expert human drivers, our system learns not only what actions to take but also which visual cues are important for those decisions. We evaluate our approach on both simulated and real-world driving datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in driving performance metrics compared to attention-free baselines. Our method reduces off-road incidents by 37% and improves adherence to traffic rules by 28% in challenging scenarios. Furthermore, the learned attention maps provide interpretable visualizations of the decision-making process, enhancing transparency and facilitating debugging. These results suggest that incorporating human-inspired visual attention mechanisms can substantially improve the robustness and explainability of behavioral cloning approaches for autonomous driving.

Gaze Estimation using Transformer

This paper presents a novel approach to gaze estimation utilizing Transformer architecture, which has shown remarkable success in various computer vision tasks. Traditional gaze estimation methods often rely on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that struggle to capture long-range dependencies and contextual information critical for accurate gaze prediction. Our proposed Transformer-based model addresses these limitations by leveraging self-attention mechanisms to better understand the relationship between facial features and gaze direction. We introduce a specialized vision transformer that processes facial images at multiple scales while incorporating positional encoding adapted specifically for the gaze estimation task. Experiments conducted on benchmark datasets including MPIIGaze, GazeCapture, and ETH-XGaze demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, reducing angular error by 15% compared to previous methods. Additionally, our model shows improved robustness to variations in head pose, illumination conditions, and occlusions. Ablation studies confirm the importance of the attention mechanism in capturing subtle eye region details crucial for precise gaze estimation. This work establishes Transformers as a powerful framework for gaze estimation with potential applications in human-computer interaction, virtual reality, and driver monitoring systems.

INTEL-TUT Dataset for Camera Invariant Color Constancy Research

We present INTEL-TUT, a novel dataset designed to address the challenge of camera invariance in computational color constancy research. This dataset consists of images captured under diverse illumination conditions using multiple camera models with different sensor characteristics. Unlike existing color constancy benchmarks that focus on algorithm performance for specific camera sensors, INTEL-TUT enables the investigation of cross-camera generalization capabilities of color constancy algorithms. The dataset includes precisely calibrated ground truth illumination data, raw image files, and camera spectral sensitivity information for each device. We provide over 7,000 images captured across indoor and outdoor environments using five distinct camera models, ensuring significant variations in sensor responses to identical scenes. Preliminary experiments demonstrate that algorithms trained on single-camera datasets experience significant performance degradation when applied to images from unseen cameras, highlighting the importance of camera-invariant approaches. The INTEL-TUT dataset serves as a valuable resource for developing robust color constancy algorithms capable of generalizing across different imaging devices, advancing both practical applications and theoretical understanding in the field of computational color constancy.

Query-guided Regression Network with Context Policy for Phrase Grounding

Phrase grounding, the task of localizing objects in an image based on natural language descriptions, remains challenging due to the complex interplay between visual features and linguistic semantics. In this paper, we present a novel Query-guided Regression Network with Context Policy (QRNCP) that effectively bridges the gap between textual queries and visual context. Our approach introduces a query-guided regression mechanism that directly predicts bounding box coordinates by leveraging fine-grained language features, eliminating the need for predefined anchor boxes or region proposals. To enhance localization accuracy, we develop a context policy module that dynamically determines the optimal utilization of contextual information based on query characteristics. Extensive experiments on Flickr30K Entities, ReferIt, and Visual Genome datasets demonstrate that our QRNCP approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins (4.2%, 3.7%, and 5.1% respectively). Further ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of both our regression network and context policy components. The proposed framework not only achieves superior performance but also offers improved inference efficiency, making it suitable for real-world applications requiring accurate phrase grounding.

Understanding Negative Samples in Instance Discriminative Self-supervised Representation Learning

Self-supervised representation learning, particularly instance discriminative approaches, has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning transferable visual features without manual annotations. While recent methods have achieved impressive results, the theoretical understanding of why these approaches work remains limited. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the role of negative samples in instance discriminative self-supervised learning frameworks. We investigate how the quantity, quality, and diversity of negative samples affect the learned representations and downstream performance. Through systematic experiments, we demonstrate that the composition of negative samples significantly influences the feature space geometry and the semantic relationships captured during training. Our theoretical analysis reveals that negative samples serve as implicit regularizers that prevent representational collapse while encouraging features to encode task-relevant semantic information. We further propose a novel negative sampling strategy that adaptively selects informative negatives based on their difficulty and relevance to the anchor sample, yielding consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks. Our findings provide valuable insights into the fundamental mechanisms of instance discrimination and offer practical guidelines for designing more effective self-supervised learning algorithms.

Large-scale Simple Question Answering with Memory Networks

This paper presents a novel approach to question answering using Memory Networks applied to large-scale knowledge bases. We address the challenge of answering simple factoid questions by developing a memory architecture that efficiently stores and retrieves facts from knowledge bases containing millions of entities and relationships. Our model employs a multi-step attention mechanism that learns to focus on relevant facts while filtering irrelevant information, enabling accurate answers even when faced with ambiguous questions or incomplete information. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets including WebQuestions, SimpleQuestions, and our newly introduced LargeQA dataset, demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods. Experimental results show that our memory-augmented neural network achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particular advantages in handling questions requiring multi-hop reasoning. Furthermore, we provide detailed analysis of the model's attention mechanisms, revealing insights into how the system reasons through complex factual relationships. This work represents an important step toward scalable question answering systems capable of leveraging extensive knowledge bases while maintaining computational efficiency.

SPSG: Self-Supervised Photometric Scene Generation from RGB-D Scans

We present SPSG, a novel self-supervised approach for generating photorealistic 3D scene representations from RGB-D scan data. While existing methods for scene reconstruction often struggle with incomplete scans, view-dependent effects, and textureless regions, our approach leverages a self-supervised learning framework to overcome these limitations. SPSG employs a neural rendering pipeline that decomposes scene geometry and appearance, enabling high-quality novel view synthesis without requiring ground truth supervision. Our method first constructs a coarse geometric representation from the input RGB-D scans, then refines both geometry and appearance through a differentiable rendering process optimized via photometric consistency across multiple views. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPSG outperforms state-of-the-art methods in reconstruction quality, novel view synthesis, and scene completion tasks. The self-supervised nature of our approach makes it particularly valuable for real-world applications where ground truth 3D data is unavailable. We evaluate SPSG on standard indoor scene datasets, showing significant improvements in visual fidelity and geometric accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for practical applications.

Conditional Teacher-Student Learning

This paper introduces Conditional Teacher-Student Learning (CTSL), a novel framework that enhances traditional teacher-student knowledge distillation by incorporating conditional dependencies between teacher guidance and student learning. Unlike conventional approaches where knowledge transfer is uniform across all training instances, CTSL enables adaptive knowledge distillation based on specific conditions such as input complexity, task difficulty, or domain characteristics. We formalize this conditional relationship through a probabilistic framework that dynamically adjusts the teacher's influence based on measurable conditions. Our experiments across image classification, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning tasks demonstrate that CTSL consistently outperforms standard knowledge distillation methods, with particularly significant improvements on complex or out-of-distribution samples. The conditional approach allows student models to benefit from teacher expertise where needed while developing independent problem-solving capabilities in familiar scenarios. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence properties of CTSL and analyze the trade-offs between computational efficiency and performance. This work offers a flexible and principled approach to knowledge distillation that can be integrated with existing architectures to improve model compression and transfer learning outcomes.

Learning Knowledge Graph-based World Models of Textual Environments

This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling text-based environments using knowledge graph representations as world models. Text-based environments present unique challenges for reinforcement learning agents due to their partially observable nature and complex state spaces. We propose a framework that dynamically constructs and updates knowledge graphs to represent the agent's understanding of the environment, capturing entities, relationships, and state changes as the agent interacts with the text world. Our knowledge graph-based world model (KG-WM) enables effective reasoning about the environment's structure and dynamics, facilitating both exploration and planning. Through extensive experiments on multiple text-based game benchmarks, we demonstrate that agents equipped with our KG-WM significantly outperform baseline approaches in terms of task completion, sample efficiency, and generalization to unseen scenarios. The results show that structured knowledge representations provide a strong inductive bias for learning in language-grounded environments, offering interpretable insights into agent decision-making processes. This work bridges techniques from knowledge representation, natural language understanding, and reinforcement learning to advance the capabilities of agents in text-based interactive environments.

DSAC: Distributional Soft Actor Critic for Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces Distributional Soft Actor Critic (DSAC), a novel algorithm that extends the Soft Actor Critic framework to address risk-sensitive reinforcement learning problems. While traditional reinforcement learning methods focus on optimizing expected returns, many real-world applications require consideration of the entire distribution of possible outcomes to manage risk appropriately. DSAC combines the sample efficiency and stability of SAC with distributional reinforcement learning techniques to learn and reason about the full return distribution rather than just its expectation. By modeling uncertainty explicitly, our approach enables risk-sensitive policy optimization through various risk measures such as conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) and entropic risk. We derive the distributional policy gradient theorem for the maximum entropy framework and develop a practical algorithm that estimates return distributions using quantile regression. Empirical evaluations across various continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that DSAC achieves superior performance in risk-sensitive scenarios compared to conventional methods, while maintaining competitive performance in risk-neutral settings. Our results highlight DSAC's ability to effectively balance expected returns and risk, making it particularly suitable for safety-critical applications where reliability and robustness are paramount.

Bayesian Optimisation for Sequential Experimental Design with Applications in Additive Manufacturing

This paper presents a novel approach to sequential experimental design in additive manufacturing (AM) using Bayesian optimisation techniques. The complex parameter spaces and high costs associated with AM experiments create significant challenges for process optimisation and material development. We propose a framework that leverages Gaussian process surrogate models to efficiently navigate the design space while systematically reducing uncertainty in regions of interest. Our method employs acquisition functions that balance exploration and exploitation, enabling rapid convergence toward optimal process parameters with minimal experimental trials. The framework is validated through case studies in selective laser melting and directed energy deposition processes, demonstrating significant reductions in experimental iterations (approximately 65%) compared to traditional design of experiments approaches. Results show particular efficacy in optimising mechanical properties and geometric accuracy while identifying critical process-structure-property relationships. The proposed methodology provides a generalizable approach for accelerating AM development cycles, reducing material waste, and enabling more efficient exploration of novel materials and process configurations. This work contributes to the broader goal of making AM process optimisation more accessible and economically viable for industrial applications.

Attention-based Conditioning Methods for External Knowledge Integration

This paper explores novel attention-based conditioning techniques for integrating external knowledge into neural network architectures. We propose a framework that enables deep learning models to selectively attend to and incorporate domain-specific knowledge sources while maintaining their generalization capabilities. Our approach introduces a multi-head cross-attention mechanism that dynamically weighs the relevance of external knowledge based on the input context. Through extensive experimentation across natural language processing, computer vision, and multimodal tasks, we demonstrate that our conditioning methods significantly outperform traditional knowledge integration approaches. Results show consistent improvements in performance metrics, with particularly notable gains on tasks requiring specialized domain knowledge. The proposed architecture maintains computational efficiency while enhancing model interpretability through attention visualization. We further analyze the trade-offs between knowledge depth and model flexibility, providing guidelines for implementing these techniques across various applications. Our work addresses the fundamental challenge of leveraging structured external knowledge within deep learning systems, offering a flexible framework that can be adapted to diverse knowledge sources and model architectures.

Predicting Traffic Signals on Transportation Networks Using Spatio-Temporal Correlations on Graphs

This study presents a novel framework for predicting traffic signal states across large-scale transportation networks by leveraging spatio-temporal correlations encoded in graph structures. Traffic signal prediction remains a challenging problem due to complex interdependencies between intersections, time-varying traffic patterns, and the need for real-time applications. Our approach models the transportation network as a directed graph where nodes represent intersections and edges capture road segments connecting them. We introduce a graph neural network architecture that explicitly accounts for both spatial dependencies between adjacent intersections and temporal evolution of traffic patterns. By incorporating attention mechanisms that dynamically weight the influence of neighboring signals, our model effectively captures the propagation of traffic flows through the network. Experiments conducted on real-world traffic data from three metropolitan areas demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional time series models and state-of-the-art deep learning methods, achieving 17% lower prediction error and 23% improved accuracy in predicting signal phase transitions. The proposed method shows particular strength in handling complex scenarios such as rush hour congestion and special events. These results suggest significant potential for enhancing traffic management systems, reducing congestion, and supporting the development of intelligent transportation infrastructure.

LEAF-QA: Locate, Encode & Attend for Figure Question Answering

Visual Question Answering (VQA) for figures and charts presents unique challenges compared to natural image VQA due to the structured information and specialized visual elements in scientific and business visualizations. In this paper, we introduce LEAF-QA, a novel framework designed specifically for Figure Question Answering that leverages a three-stage approach: Locate, Encode, and Attend. Our model first localizes relevant visual elements within figures using a specialized detection module, then encodes these elements along with their spatial and semantic relationships, and finally employs a multi-modal attention mechanism to integrate textual queries with visual information. We evaluate LEAF-QA on multiple figure QA datasets, including FigureQA, DVQA, and PlotQA, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance with improvements of 5.7%, 4.3%, and 6.2% respectively over previous methods. Further analysis reveals that our approach is particularly effective for complex reasoning tasks requiring numerical understanding and relative comparisons between visual elements. LEAF-QA represents a significant advancement in multimodal reasoning for structured visual content, with potential applications in scientific document understanding, business intelligence, and educational technology.

Human Extraction and Scene Transition utilizing Mask R-CNN

This paper presents a novel approach for human extraction and scene transition effects using Mask R-CNN, a state-of-the-art instance segmentation framework. Our method enables precise isolation of human subjects from video frames and facilitates seamless integration into new backgrounds or scenes. We extend the capabilities of Mask R-CNN by implementing a specialized post-processing pipeline that refines human silhouette masks, preserves fine details such as hair and clothing edges, and maintains temporal consistency across video sequences. The system demonstrates robust performance in challenging scenarios including complex lighting conditions, occlusions, and diverse human poses. Experimental results show that our approach achieves an average precision of 92.3% for human extraction and significantly outperforms traditional chroma keying techniques. We further demonstrate the practical applications of our method in video production workflows, augmented reality environments, and interactive media installations. The proposed framework operates at near real-time speeds on consumer hardware, making it accessible for content creators without specialized equipment. Our contributions include a comprehensive evaluation dataset and an optimized implementation that balances computational efficiency with high-quality visual results.

Is a Good Representation Sufficient for Sample Efficient Reinforcement Learning?

Representation learning has emerged as a promising approach to improve sample efficiency in reinforcement learning (RL). While prior work has demonstrated that good representations can accelerate learning in certain contexts, this paper investigates the fundamental question of whether a high-quality representation alone is sufficient to guarantee sample-efficient RL across diverse environments. Through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that even with access to optimal state representations, RL algorithms may still require substantial environment interaction to converge to effective policies. We identify key factors that influence sample efficiency beyond representation quality, including reward sparsity, long-horizon dependencies, and exploration challenges. Our experiments across both continuous and discrete domains reveal that representation quality exhibits a non-linear relationship with sample efficiency, with diminishing returns beyond certain thresholds. We propose a framework for characterizing when representations are most beneficial and introduce a hybrid approach that adaptively balances representation learning with direct policy optimization. These findings suggest that while good representations are valuable, they must be complemented by effective exploration strategies and planning mechanisms to achieve truly sample-efficient reinforcement learning.

A Bayesian Decision Tree Algorithm

This paper introduces a novel Bayesian approach to decision tree learning that addresses the limitations of traditional decision tree algorithms. Our proposed Bayesian Decision Tree Algorithm (BDTA) incorporates prior knowledge and uncertainty quantification into the tree construction process, resulting in more robust models with improved generalization capabilities. Unlike conventional algorithms that make hard splits based on information gain or Gini impurity, BDTA employs a probabilistic framework that considers the full posterior distribution over possible tree structures. Through Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling techniques, our method effectively explores the space of decision trees while avoiding overfitting through automatic complexity regularization inherent in the Bayesian formulation. Empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate that BDTA achieves competitive predictive performance compared to state-of-the-art ensemble methods while providing interpretable models with reliable uncertainty estimates. Additionally, our approach offers natural handling of missing data and mixed variable types without extensive preprocessing. The theoretical properties and practical advantages of BDTA make it a valuable contribution to both the machine learning toolkit and applications requiring transparent, uncertainty-aware decision-making.

A2Log: Attentive Augmented Log Anomaly Detection

Log anomaly detection is a critical component of system reliability and security monitoring, yet existing approaches often struggle with the high dimensionality and semantic complexity of log data. This paper introduces A2Log, a novel framework for log anomaly detection that leverages attention mechanisms and data augmentation techniques to improve detection accuracy and robustness. A2Log employs a dual-attention architecture that captures both local sequential patterns within log entries and global contextual relationships across the log corpus. We enhance this architecture with specialized log augmentation strategies that address the common challenge of imbalanced datasets in anomaly detection tasks. Our approach generates synthetic anomalous patterns while preserving the semantic integrity of log sequences. Extensive evaluations on public benchmark datasets (HDFS, BGL, Thunderbird, and Spirit) demonstrate that A2Log outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 97.8% F1-score and reducing false positive rates by an average of 34% compared to existing techniques. Furthermore, A2Log shows superior generalization capabilities when detecting previously unseen anomaly types. The proposed framework offers a promising solution for robust, real-time anomaly detection in large-scale distributed systems.

Depth-Aware Arbitrary Style Transfer Using Instance Normalization

This paper introduces a novel depth-aware approach to arbitrary style transfer that preserves spatial relationships while allowing for flexible stylization. Our method extends instance normalization techniques by incorporating depth information as a structural prior, enabling more coherent style transformations that respect the original content's spatial layout. We propose a Depth-Aware Instance Normalization (DAIN) module that adaptively modulates feature statistics based on estimated depth maps, maintaining foreground-background relationships during stylization. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art arbitrary style transfer methods on standard benchmarks, achieving higher structural consistency scores while maintaining stylistic fidelity. User studies confirm that our depth-aware stylizations are perceived as more natural and spatially coherent. Additionally, our method introduces minimal computational overhead compared to existing approaches, making it practical for real-time applications. The proposed technique addresses a fundamental limitation in style transfer by explicitly modeling spatial relationships, resulting in visually compelling transformations that preserve the structural integrity of the original content.

Scalable Centralized Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Policy Gradients

This paper presents a novel approach to centralized multi-agent reinforcement learning that addresses the scalability challenges inherent in coordinating multiple agents. We introduce a policy gradient-based framework that enables efficient learning of cooperative behaviors while maintaining computational tractability as the number of agents increases. Our method leverages a centralized critic with decentralized actors, where the critic has access to global state information during training, while individual agents execute policies based solely on local observations during deployment. To overcome the curse of dimensionality in multi-agent settings, we develop a hierarchical attention mechanism that dynamically focuses on relevant agent interactions and efficiently processes joint action spaces. Extensive experiments on benchmark environments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of sample efficiency, convergence speed, and final performance, particularly in scenarios with large agent populations. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence properties of our algorithm. These results suggest that our framework provides a promising direction for scaling centralized training to complex multi-agent systems with practical real-world applications.

GMAT: Global Memory Augmentation for Transformers

We present Global Memory Augmentation for Transformers (GMAT), a novel architecture that addresses the limitations of traditional transformer models in handling long-range dependencies and large-scale knowledge integration. GMAT introduces a persistent, external memory module that exists independently of input sequences, enabling transformers to store and retrieve information across arbitrary contexts. Unlike conventional attention mechanisms that are limited to the current input, our approach allows models to access a global memory space that persists throughout training and inference. Through extensive experiments on language modeling, question answering, and long-context reasoning tasks, we demonstrate that GMAT significantly outperforms standard transformers and existing memory-augmented architectures. Our approach shows particular strength in knowledge-intensive applications, reducing hallucination rates by 37% while improving factual consistency. GMAT also demonstrates enhanced sample efficiency, requiring fewer parameters to achieve comparable performance on benchmark datasets. This work represents an important step toward transformer architectures that can effectively maintain and utilize information across diverse contexts, opening new possibilities for more reliable and capable language models.

Subgraph Federated Learning with Missing Neighbor Generation

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in various graph-based applications, but their deployment in federated settings faces significant challenges due to privacy constraints and incomplete subgraph structures. In this paper, we propose Subgraph Federated Learning with Missing Neighbor Generation (SFL-MNG), a novel framework that addresses the critical issue of missing neighborhood information when training GNNs across distributed subgraphs. Our approach introduces a generative model that synthesizes plausible neighboring structures for nodes at subgraph boundaries, effectively completing the local graph topology without requiring explicit data sharing between clients. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that SFL-MNG preserves the essential spectral properties of the original graph while maintaining privacy guarantees. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including Cora, Citeseer, and PubMed, as well as large-scale industrial graphs, show that SFL-MNG outperforms existing federated GNN methods by an average of 8.3% in node classification accuracy while reducing communication costs by up to 47%. Our method proves particularly effective in scenarios with high graph partition heterogeneity, offering a practical solution for privacy-preserving, communication-efficient federated learning on graph-structured data.

Mutual Information-driven Subject-invariant and Class-relevant Deep Representation Learning in BCI

Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) face significant challenges due to substantial inter-subject variability in brain signals, which often necessitates lengthy calibration procedures for new users. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework that leverages mutual information principles to simultaneously extract subject-invariant and class-relevant features from electroencephalography (EEG) data. Our approach employs a dual-branch neural architecture: one branch maximizes mutual information between EEG representations and class labels while the second branch minimizes mutual information between representations and subject identities. This mutual information-driven optimization enables the model to learn discriminative features that generalize across subjects while remaining sensitive to task-relevant neural patterns. Extensive experiments on three public BCI datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art transfer learning approaches, achieving an average improvement of 8.7% in cross-subject classification accuracy. Furthermore, our approach reduces calibration data requirements by 75% while maintaining performance comparable to fully-calibrated systems. The proposed framework represents a substantial advance toward practical, plug-and-play BCI systems that can adapt to new users with minimal training data, potentially expanding the accessibility and utility of BCI technology across clinical and consumer applications.

Machine Learning for Visual Navigation of Unmanned Ground Vehicles

This paper presents a comprehensive review and analysis of machine learning techniques for visual navigation in Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs). We explore how deep learning approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and reinforcement learning frameworks, have revolutionized autonomous navigation capabilities in complex and unstructured environments. Our research examines the integration of computer vision with machine learning to address key challenges in obstacle detection, path planning, terrain classification, and real-time decision-making. We evaluate several state-of-the-art architectures including end-to-end learning systems and hybrid models that combine classical robotics algorithms with deep learning components. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach achieves 87% accuracy in terrain classification and reduces navigation errors by 42% compared to traditional methods. The study also addresses critical limitations including generalization to novel environments, computational efficiency for edge deployment, and robustness against visual perception challenges such as varying lighting conditions. This work contributes to advancing UGV autonomy in applications ranging from search and rescue operations to agricultural automation and last-mile delivery systems.

Generation of the NIR spectral Band for Satellite Images with Convolutional Neural Networks

This study presents a novel approach for generating Near-Infrared (NIR) spectral bands for satellite imagery using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). NIR data is crucial for numerous remote sensing applications including vegetation monitoring, land cover classification, and environmental assessment, yet many satellite platforms lack dedicated NIR sensors. We propose a deep learning framework that accurately synthesizes NIR bands from visible spectrum (RGB) satellite imagery. Our model employs a U-Net architecture with residual connections to learn the complex relationships between visible and NIR wavelengths across diverse landscapes and atmospheric conditions. Training on a dataset of 5,000 paired RGB-NIR image patches from Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8 satellites, our network achieves a mean absolute error of 0.023 and structural similarity index of 0.91 compared to ground truth NIR bands. Ablation studies demonstrate the importance of multi-scale feature extraction and the contribution of each visible band to NIR prediction accuracy. The generated NIR bands successfully reproduce vegetation indices (NDVI) with a correlation coefficient of 0.94 against indices calculated from actual NIR data. This approach enables the extension of NIR capabilities to satellite platforms with limited spectral resolution, potentially enhancing applications in agriculture, forestry, and environmental monitoring without requiring hardware modifications.

Machine Learning Classifications of Coronary Artery Disease

This study investigates the application of machine learning (ML) algorithms for the classification and risk stratification of coronary artery disease (CAD). We developed and evaluated multiple ML models using a comprehensive dataset of 5,842 patients with clinical, demographic, laboratory, and imaging features. Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, Gradient Boosting, and Deep Neural Networks were compared for their predictive accuracy in CAD diagnosis and severity classification. Our optimized ensemble model achieved 89.3% accuracy, 91.2% sensitivity, and 87.6% specificity in identifying significant coronary stenosis, outperforming traditional risk assessment tools (AUROC 0.92 vs. 0.78). Feature importance analysis revealed novel predictive markers beyond conventional risk factors, with particular significance in non-invasive biomarkers. The integration of ML-derived risk scores with clinical decision pathways reduced unnecessary invasive procedures by 27% in the validation cohort while maintaining diagnostic sensitivity. This research demonstrates the potential of ML approaches to enhance CAD diagnosis, optimize patient management, and improve resource allocation in cardiovascular care. Further prospective validation is warranted to establish these models in clinical practice.

A Robust Loss for Point Cloud Registration

Point cloud registration is a fundamental task in computer vision and robotics, involving the alignment of two or more 3D point sets to a common coordinate system. Despite significant advances in this field, existing registration methods often struggle with real-world challenges such as noise, outliers, and partial overlaps. In this paper, we propose a novel robust loss function specifically designed to address these limitations in point cloud registration. Our loss function dynamically adapts to the characteristics of the input data by automatically identifying and downweighting the influence of outliers during the optimization process. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on hard thresholding or manual parameter tuning, our method incorporates a learnable robustness parameter that adjusts the loss sensitivity based on the registration context. Through extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, including KITTI, ModelNet40, and Stanford 3D scans, we demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of registration accuracy, convergence speed, and robustness to outliers. The proposed loss function can be seamlessly integrated into existing registration frameworks, providing substantial improvements without introducing computational overhead. Our code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available to facilitate future research in this area.

Multi-resolution Networks For Flexible Irregular Time Series Modeling (Multi-FIT)

Time series data in real-world applications often exhibit irregularity in sampling rates, missing values, and varying temporal patterns across different timescales. This paper introduces Multi-FIT, a novel neural network architecture designed to handle the complexities of irregular time series modeling through a multi-resolution approach. Our framework decomposes temporal dynamics into different frequency bands using adaptive wavelet transformations while simultaneously learning representations at multiple time scales. Multi-FIT employs a hierarchical structure of temporal convolutional networks with specialized attention mechanisms that can flexibly accommodate irregular sampling intervals without requiring data imputation or resampling. Experiments on healthcare monitoring, financial forecasting, and environmental sensing datasets demonstrate that Multi-FIT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 15-22% improvement in prediction accuracy and 30% reduction in computational complexity. The model's interpretable multi-resolution structure also provides insights into which temporal scales contribute most significantly to predictive performance. Our approach offers a robust framework for modeling complex time series data while maintaining computational efficiency and interpretability.

Plugin Procedure in Segmentation and Application to Hyperspectral Image Segmentation

This paper presents a novel "plugin" procedure for image segmentation that enhances existing algorithms by incorporating specialized pre-processing and post-processing steps tailored to hyperspectral imagery. The proposed framework addresses the unique challenges posed by the high dimensionality and spectral complexity of hyperspectral data. Our method first applies dimensionality reduction techniques and spectral unmixing to extract meaningful features, then employs a modular segmentation approach where conventional algorithms can be "plugged in" as the core segmentation engine. The procedure is further refined through an adaptive boundary optimization process that leverages spectral gradient information specific to hyperspectral data. Experimental results on multiple hyperspectral datasets demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to standard approaches, with average increases of 15-20% in F1-score and Intersection over Union (IoU) metrics. The plugin nature of our framework offers flexibility for different application contexts while maintaining computational efficiency. This work contributes to advancing hyperspectral image analysis by providing a generalizable segmentation enhancement strategy that exploits the rich spectral information inherent in such imagery.

GaussiGAN: Controllable Image Synthesis with 3D Gaussians from Unposed Silhouettes

We present GaussiGAN, a novel generative framework that leverages 3D Gaussian Splatting for controllable image synthesis from unposed silhouettes. Unlike traditional methods that require camera poses or 3D supervision, our approach learns to reconstruct 3D representations from only 2D silhouettes with unknown viewpoints. GaussiGAN employs a two-stage architecture: first, a pose estimation network infers camera parameters from input silhouettes; second, a 3D-aware generator optimizes Gaussian primitives to create a volumetric representation consistent with the estimated viewpoint. By disentangling geometry and appearance, our method enables fine-grained control over generated outputs, allowing for view synthesis, shape manipulation, and texture editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GaussiGAN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in reconstruction quality and rendering speed while maintaining editability. Our approach bridges the gap between 2D generative models and explicit 3D representations, offering a promising direction for controllable content creation from limited supervision.

Selective Network Discovery via Deep Reinforcement Learning on Embedded Spaces

This paper introduces a novel approach to selective network discovery using deep reinforcement learning techniques operating on embedded spaces. Traditional network discovery methods often suffer from inefficiency and high computational costs when applied to large-scale complex networks. We propose a framework that leverages deep reinforcement learning to intelligently explore and identify critical network structures by operating on low-dimensional embeddings of network topologies. Our agent learns to navigate embedded network representations, making sequential decisions about which nodes or connections to examine next, thereby discovering important network components with minimal exploration overhead. We demonstrate that by combining graph embedding techniques with a carefully designed reward structure, our approach significantly outperforms conventional sampling and traversal algorithms, reducing the number of queries needed to discover key network properties by up to 65%. Experiments on social, biological, and technological networks show that our method maintains high discovery accuracy while substantially reducing computational requirements. This work represents an important step toward scalable and efficient analysis of massive real-world networks where complete exploration is prohibitively expensive.

Time Series Data Imputation: A Survey on Deep Learning Approaches

Missing data presents a significant challenge in time series analysis across various domains including healthcare, finance, and environmental monitoring. This survey provides a comprehensive review of deep learning approaches for time series data imputation. We systematically categorize and analyze state-of-the-art methods, examining architectures ranging from recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) to more recent innovations such as temporal convolutional networks (TCNs), attention mechanisms, and transformer-based models. The survey explores how these approaches handle different missing data patterns—missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), and missing not at random (MNAR)—while considering both univariate and multivariate time series scenarios. We evaluate these methods according to their imputation accuracy, computational efficiency, scalability, and ability to capture temporal dependencies and uncertainty. Additionally, we discuss domain-specific adaptations, highlight current research gaps, and identify promising directions for future work, including integrating physical constraints, developing self-supervised learning strategies, and addressing real-time imputation challenges. This survey serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand and implement effective deep learning solutions for time series imputation problems.

Analysis of Network Lasso for Semi-Supervised Regression

This paper presents a theoretical analysis of the Network Lasso (NetLasso) algorithm in the context of semi-supervised regression problems. We study how graph-based regularization through the NetLasso framework can effectively leverage the underlying data manifold structure when labeled samples are scarce. Our analysis establishes non-asymptotic error bounds that explicitly characterize the interplay between the graph construction, the number of labeled samples, and the smoothness of the target function with respect to the graph topology. We prove that under suitable conditions on the graph Laplacian and signal smoothness, NetLasso achieves significantly better generalization performance compared to supervised methods that ignore unlabeled data. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate our theoretical findings, demonstrating that NetLasso can effectively propagate label information across the graph while being robust to noise and maintaining computational efficiency. Our results provide practical guidance for parameter selection and graph construction in semi-supervised regression applications.

Fine-grained Generalization Analysis of Structured Output Prediction

This paper presents a novel theoretical framework for analyzing the generalization capabilities of structured output prediction models. Unlike traditional approaches that focus on average-case error bounds, we develop fine-grained analysis techniques that account for the internal structure and dependencies within complex output spaces. Our framework introduces structure-aware complexity measures that better characterize the learning difficulty across different regions of the output space. Through both theoretical results and empirical validation, we demonstrate that our fine-grained analysis provides tighter generalization bounds than existing methods, particularly for problems with heterogeneous output structures. We establish connections between structural properties of the output space and sample complexity, revealing that certain structural patterns require fewer examples to learn than previously thought. Our results have practical implications for model selection and training strategies in applications such as sequence labeling, image segmentation, and graph prediction tasks, where understanding the relationship between output structure and generalization is crucial for developing more efficient learning algorithms.

Hyperparameter-free and Explainable Whole Graph Embedding

Graph embedding techniques have gained significant attention for their ability to represent complex graph structures in low-dimensional vector spaces, enabling various downstream machine learning tasks. However, existing methods often require extensive hyperparameter tuning and produce embeddings that lack interpretability. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for whole graph embedding that addresses these limitations. Our approach eliminates the need for hyperparameter optimization by leveraging an adaptive mechanism that automatically determines optimal embedding configurations based on the intrinsic properties of the input graph. Furthermore, we incorporate an explainability module that provides transparent insights into how structural graph features contribute to the final embedding. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our hyperparameter-free method achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art techniques while offering clear explanations of the embedding process. The proposed approach significantly reduces the computational overhead associated with hyperparameter tuning and enhances trust in graph-based machine learning systems through its interpretable nature. Our work represents an important step toward making graph embedding techniques more accessible and trustworthy for real-world applications.

Context-Aware Generative Adversarial Privacy

This paper introduces Context-Aware Generative Adversarial Privacy (CAGAP), a novel framework for privacy preservation in data sharing that dynamically adapts to contextual factors. Building upon traditional Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), our approach incorporates contextual awareness to balance utility preservation with privacy protection based on situational requirements. We formulate privacy as a constrained minimax game between a privatizer and an adversary, where the privatizer generates privacy-preserving representations while the adversary attempts to infer sensitive information. Unlike static privacy mechanisms, CAGAP continuously evaluates contextual variables—including user preferences, data sensitivity, application requirements, and environmental factors—to optimize the privacy-utility tradeoff. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that CAGAP outperforms state-of-the-art privacy mechanisms, achieving up to 40% improvement in utility preservation while maintaining equivalent privacy guarantees. Our theoretical analysis provides formal privacy bounds that account for contextual variations. These results suggest that context-aware approaches represent a promising direction for developing adaptive privacy solutions for emerging data-sharing ecosystems.

A Scale Mixture Perspective of Multiplicative Noise in Neural Networks

This paper presents a novel theoretical framework for understanding multiplicative noise regularization techniques in neural networks through the lens of scale mixtures. We demonstrate that popular approaches such as Dropout and DropConnect can be reinterpreted as implicitly imposing scale mixture priors on network parameters, providing new insights into their regularization effects. Our analysis shows that these methods induce adaptive shrinkage that depends on both the parameter magnitudes and the network architecture. We develop a unified mathematical formulation that connects various noise injection strategies and reveals their relationship to Bayesian inference procedures. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we show that this perspective enables more principled noise distribution design, leading to improved generalization performance and uncertainty estimation. Additionally, we derive theoretical bounds on the regularization strength as a function of noise parameters, offering practical guidance for hyperparameter selection. Our scale mixture framework extends naturally to modern architectures and provides a coherent explanation for the empirical success of multiplicative noise techniques in deep learning.

Towards Self-Explainable Graph Neural Network

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in various graph-based learning tasks, yet their inherent complexity often renders them opaque "black boxes," limiting their applicability in domains requiring transparency and accountability. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for Self-Explainable Graph Neural Networks (SE-GNN) that integrates interpretability directly into the model architecture rather than relying on post-hoc explanation methods. SE-GNN employs a dual-branch architecture: a prediction branch that optimizes task performance and an explanation branch that generates human-understandable rationales for the model's decisions. These branches are jointly trained with a consistency regularization mechanism that ensures alignment between predictions and their corresponding explanations. Through extensive experiments on node classification, graph classification, and link prediction tasks across multiple real-world datasets, we demonstrate that SE-GNN achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art GNN models while providing faithful, concise explanations. Our qualitative analysis reveals that the generated explanations identify meaningful subgraph structures and node relationships that substantiate the model's predictions. SE-GNN represents a significant step toward trustworthy graph-based deep learning systems that maintain high performance while offering intrinsic interpretability.

Remembering for the Right Reasons: Explanations Reduce Catastrophic Forgetting

Catastrophic forgetting remains a significant challenge in continual learning, where neural networks tend to abruptly lose performance on previously learned tasks when trained on new data. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that leverages explanations to mitigate this problem. Our method, Explanation-Guided Continual Learning (EGCL), incorporates model explanations as an additional regularization mechanism during the learning process. By preserving not only the output predictions but also the reasoning patterns that led to those predictions, EGCL encourages models to remember for the right reasons. Through extensive experiments on image classification and natural language understanding benchmarks, we demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces forgetting compared to traditional regularization methods. Our results show that EGCL achieves up to 27% higher average accuracy on previously learned tasks while maintaining competitive performance on new tasks. Further analysis reveals that explanation-guided learning promotes more stable feature representations across task boundaries and improves knowledge transfer between related tasks. This work provides new insights into the role of explanations in continual learning and offers a promising direction for developing more robust lifelong learning systems.

Adaptive Label Smoothing To Regularize Large-Scale Graph Training

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in various graph-based learning tasks, yet they often struggle with overfitting when trained on large-scale graph datasets. In this paper, we introduce Adaptive Label Smoothing (ALS), a novel regularization technique specifically designed for graph-based deep learning models. Unlike traditional label smoothing which applies uniform regularization, ALS dynamically adjusts the smoothing intensity based on local graph properties including node degree, clustering coefficient, and feature similarity. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including OGB, SNAP, and real-world knowledge graphs, we demonstrate that ALS significantly improves model generalization, achieving up to 4.2% performance gain on node classification tasks and 3.7% on link prediction compared to standard training approaches. Our theoretical analysis reveals that ALS effectively mitigates overconfidence in predictions by creating an implicit regularization effect proportional to graph structural complexity. Furthermore, ALS shows particular effectiveness in handling graphs with heterogeneous degree distributions and noisy labels. The proposed method is computationally efficient, adding minimal overhead to the training process while being compatible with various GNN architectures including GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE.

A realistic approach to generate masked faces applied on two novel masked face recognition data sets

The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted significant challenges in facial recognition systems when subjects wear masks, necessitating the development of robust masked face recognition (MFR) algorithms. This paper presents a realistic approach to generate synthetic masked face images that accurately simulate various mask types, positions, and occlusion patterns. Unlike previous methods that rely on simple geometric overlays, our approach incorporates depth information, mask deformation, and material properties to create photorealistic masked face renderings. We introduce two novel datasets: MFR-Natural, containing 10,000 pairs of real unmasked and masked face images captured under controlled conditions, and MFR-Synthetic, comprising 50,000 synthetically generated masked faces derived from public face datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our synthetic data closely resembles real masked faces in terms of visual quality and recognition performance. Models trained on our synthetic data show significantly improved performance on real-world masked face recognition tasks, achieving 94.7% verification accuracy compared to 82.3% for models trained on conventional synthetic approaches. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive benchmark of state-of-the-art face recognition algorithms on our datasets, establishing new baselines for the MFR research community. Our approach offers a scalable solution to the data scarcity problem in masked face recognition research.

Mutual Information Maximization for Robust Plannable Representations

This paper introduces a novel approach to learning robust plannable representations for reinforcement learning through mutual information maximization. We address a fundamental challenge in model-based reinforcement learning: creating state representations that capture relevant environmental dynamics while being amenable to effective planning. Our method leverages mutual information principles to learn representations that maximize the information shared between current states, actions, and future states, while remaining invariant to task-irrelevant distractions. By optimizing this information-theoretic objective, we create compressed state embeddings that retain precisely the information needed for accurate transition modeling and planning. Extensive experiments across diverse environments, including visual-based continuous control tasks and partially observable settings, demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing representation learning methods. The learned representations show improved sample efficiency, better generalization to novel scenarios, and enhanced robustness to observational noise. Furthermore, we provide theoretical guarantees on the planning optimality of our representations. These results highlight the potential of information-theoretic approaches for creating robust representations that enable efficient planning in complex reinforcement learning problems.

NeuRoRA: Neural Robust Rotation Averaging

Rotation averaging is a fundamental problem in computer vision that involves estimating a set of absolute orientations from relative orientation measurements. This paper introduces NeuRoRA, a novel neural network-based approach for robust rotation averaging that effectively handles real-world challenges such as outliers and noise in rotation measurements. Unlike traditional optimization-based methods that can be sensitive to initialization and prone to local minima, our approach leverages the representational power of deep neural networks to learn robust features directly from noisy relative rotation data. NeuRoRA employs a graph neural network architecture that naturally encodes the view-graph structure of the problem while incorporating rotation-specific inductive biases. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that NeuRoRA achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly in scenarios with high outlier ratios and noise levels. Our method not only improves accuracy but also offers significant computational advantages over iterative optimization approaches. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the robustness properties of our network design. NeuRoRA represents an important step toward more reliable camera pose estimation in structure-from-motion pipelines and multi-view reconstruction systems.

Handling Variable-Dimensional Time Series with Graph Neural Networks

Time series data with varying dimensions present significant challenges for traditional analysis methods, particularly when the number of variables differs across samples or changes dynamically over time. This paper introduces a novel framework leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to effectively process and analyze variable-dimensional time series data. We represent time series as dynamic graphs where nodes correspond to variables and edges capture their temporal and inter-variable relationships. This approach naturally accommodates varying dimensions without requiring padding or dimension reduction techniques that may lose critical information. Our method constructs adaptive adjacency matrices that evolve with the changing variable sets, enabling the GNN to maintain contextual understanding despite dimensional variations. Experiments on healthcare monitoring, financial markets, and IoT sensor networks demonstrate that our approach outperforms conventional methods by 15-27% on prediction tasks and 18-32% on anomaly detection. Furthermore, the model exhibits strong generalization capabilities when handling previously unseen variable combinations. This work provides a flexible and robust solution for real-world applications where the dimensionality of time series cannot be standardized, opening new avenues for time series analysis in dynamic environments.

Cloud-based Image Classification Service Is Not Robust To Simple Transformations: A Forgotten Battlefield

Despite significant advancements in deep learning-based image classification, the robustness of commercial cloud-based image classification services remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we systematically evaluate the resilience of leading cloud vision APIs against simple image transformations that should not impede classification performance. Our experiments reveal concerning vulnerabilities: basic operations such as rotation, cropping, brightness adjustments, and compression significantly degrade classification accuracy across all tested platforms. Even minor transformations that preserve human recognition capabilities cause dramatic performance drops of up to 40%. We demonstrate that these vulnerabilities could be exploited by adversaries to bypass content moderation systems or manipulate recommendation algorithms through trivial image modifications. More concerning, we find that ensemble approaches combining multiple cloud services offer minimal robustness improvements, suggesting fundamental limitations in current deployment architectures. Our findings highlight a critical gap between research advances in adversarial robustness and practical implementation in commercial systems, calling for renewed attention to this forgotten battlefield in the machine learning security landscape.
