We provide recommendations for service providers and users to address these vulnerabilities and propose evaluation protocols for benchmarking robustness in real-world deployment scenarios.

Dense xUnit Networks

This paper introduces Dense xUnit Networks, a novel deep learning architecture that combines the strengths of DenseNets and the exponential linear unit (xUnit) activation function. Our approach creates densely connected blocks where each layer receives feature maps from all preceding layers, while employing xUnit activations to enhance gradient flow and representation capability. The dense connectivity pattern alleviates the vanishing gradient problem by providing direct paths for information propagation, while xUnit activations offer improved handling of negative inputs compared to traditional ReLU-based networks. We demonstrate that Dense xUnit Networks require fewer parameters while achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. Experimental results show that our architecture reduces training time by up to 30% while improving classification accuracy by 2-3% compared to baseline models. Furthermore, we observe enhanced feature reuse and improved robustness to overfitting, making Dense xUnit Networks particularly effective for tasks with limited training data. This work contributes a powerful and efficient architecture to the deep learning community with broad applications in computer vision tasks.

Partial Optimal Transport with Applications on Positive-Unlabeled Learning

This paper introduces a novel framework that leverages partial optimal transport (POT) theory to address the fundamental challenges in positive-unlabeled (PU) learning. PU learning, where only a subset of positive examples is labeled while the remaining data is unlabeled, presents significant difficulties in accurately estimating class distributions and decision boundaries. We formulate the PU learning problem as a partial transport problem, where the goal is to find an optimal coupling between the labeled positive distribution and a subset of the unlabeled distribution. Our approach extends traditional optimal transport by allowing for partial matching, which naturally accommodates the scenario where unlabeled data contains both positive and negative examples. We derive theoretical guarantees for our method, establishing convergence rates and error bounds that depend on the proportion of positive examples in the unlabeled data. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our POT-based framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art PU learning methods, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled positive examples and class imbalance. The proposed approach not only improves classification accuracy but also provides interpretable transport maps that offer insights into the structure of the underlying data distributions. Our work bridges the gap between optimal transport theory and weakly supervised learning, opening new avenues for addressing learning problems with partial information.

Learnability for the Information Bottleneck

This paper investigates the theoretical foundations of learnability within the Information Bottleneck (IB) framework, a principled approach for extracting relevant information from input data with respect to target variables. We establish formal connections between the IB objective and generalization capabilities of learning algorithms by analyzing the trade-off between compression and prediction. Our work introduces a novel learnability criterion for IB-based representations that characterizes when a compressed representation retains sufficient information to guarantee learning success. We prove several key theoretical results, including upper and lower bounds on sample complexity for learning optimal IB representations, convergence guarantees for practical IB algorithms, and necessary conditions for learnability in the IB setting. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our learnability analysis provides practical insights for model selection and regularization in deep neural networks. These findings bridge information theory and statistical learning theory, offering a more comprehensive understanding of representation learning through the lens of the Information Bottleneck principle.

A Scene Perception System for Visually Impaired Based on Object Detection and Classification Using Multi-Modal DCNN

This paper presents a novel scene perception system designed to assist visually impaired individuals in navigating and understanding their surroundings. Our approach leverages a multi-modal Deep Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN) architecture that integrates RGB imagery with depth information to achieve robust object detection and classification in diverse environments. The proposed system processes real-time video input from a wearable camera setup and converts detected objects into audio feedback, providing users with spatial awareness of their surroundings. We introduce a custom dataset containing 15,000 annotated images across various indoor and outdoor scenarios specifically tailored for assistive technology applications. Experimental results demonstrate that our multi-modal approach achieves 93.7% mean Average Precision (mAP) for object detection and 91.2% accuracy for classification, outperforming single-modality baseline models by 8.3% and 6.5% respectively. User studies with 27 visually impaired participants show significant improvements in navigation efficiency and obstacle avoidance compared to traditional mobility aids. The system operates at 18 frames per second on portable hardware, making it practical for real-world deployment. Our work contributes to the growing field of assistive technologies by demonstrating how deep learning approaches can enhance independence and quality of life for visually impaired individuals.

Finding Failures in High-Fidelity Simulation using Adaptive Stress Testing and the Backward Algorithm

This paper presents a novel approach to identifying critical failure scenarios in high-fidelity simulations by combining Adaptive Stress Testing (AST) with the Backward Algorithm. While traditional simulation testing often struggles to discover rare but consequential failures, our method efficiently searches the vast state space to find the most probable failure trajectories. We formulate the problem as a Markov decision process and employ reinforcement learning techniques to guide the search toward system failures. The Backward Algorithm enhances this process by working retrospectively from failure states to identify the most likely paths leading to these outcomes. We demonstrate our approach on three high-fidelity simulation environments: an aircraft collision avoidance system, an autonomous vehicle navigation scenario, and a robotic surgical assistant. Results show that our method discovers failure scenarios 2-3 orders of magnitude more efficiently than Monte Carlo methods and identifies previously unknown vulnerabilities in all three domains. Furthermore, the probabilistic nature of our approach provides valuable insights into the likelihood of different failure modes, enabling system designers to prioritize safety improvements. This work contributes a powerful framework for safety validation of complex autonomous systems before deployment in safety-critical environments.

Investigating Code-Mixed Modern Standard Arabic-Egyptian to English Machine Translation

This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the challenges and opportunities of machine translation for code-mixed text combining Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and Egyptian Arabic (EA) into English. Code-mixing, the alternation between two or more languages within a single utterance, is a common linguistic phenomenon in Arabic-speaking communities but poses significant challenges for current machine translation systems. We collected a diverse corpus of naturally occurring MSA-EA code-mixed texts from social media, online forums, and news comments, comprising 10,000 sentences with varying degrees of code-mixing. We evaluated several state-of-the-art neural machine translation architectures, including transformer-based models and those specifically designed for code-mixed input. Our experiments reveal that models pre-trained on monolingual MSA and EA separately, then fine-tuned on code-mixed data, outperform models trained directly on code-mixed content. We introduce a novel attention mechanism that dynamically identifies the language variety of each token and applies appropriate processing, improving translation quality by 4.2 BLEU points over baseline approaches. Error analysis indicates that dialectal expressions, inconsistent orthography, and structural ambiguities remain the most challenging aspects of code-mixed translation. These findings provide important insights for developing more robust translation systems for Arabic language varieties and other code-mixed language pairs.

RL Unplugged: A Suite of Benchmarks for Offline Reinforcement Learning

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) offers the promise of learning effective policies from pre-collected datasets without environment interaction, addressing key limitations in traditional online RL approaches. However, progress in this field has been hindered by the lack of standardized benchmarks specifically designed for the offline setting. In this paper, we introduce RL Unplugged, a comprehensive suite of benchmarks for offline RL spanning diverse domains including control tasks, arcade games, and real-world scenarios. Each benchmark provides fixed datasets of varying quality to evaluate algorithm performance under realistic conditions where data may be suboptimal or incomplete. We establish baseline performances using several state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms and demonstrate significant challenges that remain unsolved, particularly in terms of generalization from limited data and effective uncertainty estimation. Our benchmarks enable consistent evaluation protocols that facilitate reproducible research and highlight the gap between current methods and the potential of offline RL. RL Unplugged aims to accelerate progress in this important area by providing researchers with a standardized way to measure advancement in offline reinforcement learning algorithms.

Distributional Offline Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning with Neural Physics-Informed PDEs (SciPhy RL for DOCTR-L)

This paper introduces a novel approach to offline continuous-time reinforcement learning that leverages distributional perspectives through physics-informed neural networks. Traditional reinforcement learning methods typically operate in discrete time steps, which can limit their applicability to real-world physical systems that evolve continuously. We present SciPhy RL, a framework that formulates the continuous-time Bellman equation as a partial differential equation (PDE) and employs physics-informed neural networks to learn distributional value functions from offline data. By capturing full return distributions rather than merely expected values, our method provides uncertainty quantification and risk-sensitive decision-making capabilities critical for safety-critical applications. We demonstrate that incorporating scientific machine learning principles into the reinforcement learning paradigm enables more sample-efficient learning and better generalization in continuous domains with complex dynamics. Experimental results across several challenging control tasks show that SciPhy RL outperforms state-of-the-art discrete-time approaches, particularly in scenarios with limited or biased offline data. Furthermore, we provide theoretical convergence guarantees under mild assumptions about the system dynamics and reward structures. This work bridges the gap between scientific computing and reinforcement learning, opening new avenues for applying RL to complex continuous-time systems in fields such as robotics, autonomous vehicles, and industrial process control.

Multi-Level Adaptive Region of Interest and Graph Learning for Facial Action Unit Recognition

Facial Action Unit (AU) recognition plays a crucial role in understanding human emotions and non-verbal communication. However, existing approaches often struggle with capturing the subtle facial muscle movements and the complex spatial relationships between facial regions. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that combines multi-level adaptive Region of Interest (ROI) learning with dynamic graph construction for more accurate AU recognition. Our approach first employs a hierarchical attention mechanism to identify and focus on the most discriminative facial regions at different granularities, from coarse facial components to fine-grained muscle movements. These adaptive ROIs are then integrated into a graph learning module that dynamically constructs facial topology graphs to model both local and global dependencies between facial regions. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets DISFA and BP4D demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving average F1 scores of 62.8% and 65.3% respectively. Ablation studies further confirm the effectiveness of both the multi-level ROI adaptation and the dynamic graph learning components. The proposed framework not only advances AU recognition performance but also provides interpretable attention maps that align with anatomical knowledge of facial muscle actions, making it valuable for applications in affective computing, human-computer interaction, and psychological assessment.

Training face verification models from generated face identity data

Face verification systems have traditionally relied on large-scale datasets of real human faces, raising significant privacy concerns and ethical challenges regarding consent and data usage. This paper investigates the potential of using synthetically generated face identity data to train robust face verification models. We leverage state-of-the-art generative adversarial networks (GANs) to create a diverse dataset of 500,000 photorealistic synthetic identities, each with multiple images exhibiting variations in pose, lighting, and expression. Our methodology involves a two-stage approach: first generating high-fidelity synthetic face identities, then training deep convolutional neural networks on this synthetic data using a triplet loss function to learn discriminative embeddings. Experimental results demonstrate that models trained exclusively on our synthetic dataset achieve verification accuracy within 2.3% of those trained on real face data when evaluated on standard benchmarks including LFW, IJB-C, and MegaFace. Furthermore, we observe that fine-tuning these synthetic-trained models with a small amount of real data (10% of a typical training set) surpasses the performance of models trained entirely on real data. This work presents a promising direction for developing privacy-preserving face verification systems while reducing dependence on large collections of real human face data.

Curiosity Driven Exploration of Learned Disentangled Goal Spaces

This paper introduces a novel approach to reinforcement learning that combines curiosity-driven exploration with disentangled representation learning for more efficient goal-oriented learning. We present a framework that automatically discovers and disentangles meaningful factors of variation in the environment, creating a structured goal space that facilitates exploration. By learning disentangled latent representations of states, our agent can generate goals that systematically vary along semantically meaningful dimensions. We propose a curiosity mechanism that prioritizes goals in unexplored regions of this disentangled space, effectively guiding the agent toward informative experiences. Our experiments across diverse environments, including manipulation tasks and navigation problems, demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms previous goal exploration methods in sample efficiency, generalization capabilities, and transfer learning scenarios. The disentangled nature of the learned goal space also provides interpretable representations that enable more effective human oversight and intervention. This work represents an important step toward autonomous agents that can effectively explore complex environments through the lens of structured, meaningful goal representations.

RegionViT: Regional-to-Local Attention for Vision Transformers

Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated impressive performance on various computer vision tasks, but their computational complexity grows quadratically with image size due to global self-attention mechanisms. This paper introduces RegionViT, a novel hierarchical vision transformer architecture that efficiently processes visual information by incorporating both regional and local attention mechanisms. Our approach divides input images into non-overlapping regions and applies self-attention at two scales: first at a regional level to capture broader contextual relationships, then at a local level to preserve fine-grained details. This dual-attention strategy significantly reduces computational complexity while maintaining representational power. RegionViT incorporates a regional-to-local attention propagation mechanism that enables effective information flow across different scales. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that RegionViT outperforms previous vision transformer architectures and convolutional neural networks with comparable parameter counts. Our model achieves state-of-the-art results on ImageNet classification while requiring substantially fewer FLOPs than competing approaches, making it suitable for deployment across various computational environments.

3D Shape Classification Using Collaborative Representation based Projections

This paper presents a novel approach to 3D shape classification using Collaborative Representation based Projections (CRP). While traditional methods for 3D shape analysis often rely on handcrafted features or complex neural network architectures, our proposed framework leverages the power of collaborative representation to create discriminative projections that enhance classification performance. We extract multi-view depth maps from 3D models and employ a collaborative coding scheme that represents each test sample as a linear combination of all training samples under an ℓ2-norm regularization constraint. The resulting collaborative coefficients are then utilized to construct projection matrices that map the original feature space into a more discriminative subspace. Our extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including ModelNet40, ShapeNetCore, and SHREC'17 demonstrate that the proposed CRP method achieves state-of-the-art classification accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. Furthermore, we show that our approach is robust to noise, partial occlusions, and variations in shape resolution. The proposed method bridges the gap between representation-based approaches and projection learning, offering a promising direction for efficient 3D shape analysis in various applications including computer vision, robotics, and medical imaging.

MIA-Prognosis: A Deep Learning Framework to Predict Therapy Response

Accurate prediction of treatment response remains a critical challenge in personalized medicine. In this study, we introduce MIA-Prognosis, a novel deep learning framework designed to forecast patient responses to therapeutic interventions across multiple disease domains. Our model integrates multi-modal data including imaging, molecular profiles, clinical parameters, and longitudinal patient records to generate individualized treatment response predictions. Using a transformer-based architecture with attention mechanisms, MIA-Prognosis effectively captures complex interactions between patient-specific factors and treatment modalities. The framework was evaluated on diverse cohorts spanning oncology, neurology, and immunology, achieving significant improvements in prediction accuracy (AUC 0.87, 95% CI: 0.84-0.90) compared to conventional methods. Additionally, MIA-Prognosis provides interpretable visualizations of feature importance, enabling clinicians to understand the basis for predictions. External validation across three independent datasets demonstrated robust generalizability. Our findings suggest that MIA-Prognosis could serve as a valuable clinical decision support tool, potentially enabling more precise therapeutic selections and improved patient outcomes through treatment personalization.

Dilated Convolutions in Neural Networks for Left Atrial Segmentation in 3D Gadolinium Enhanced-MRI

Accurate segmentation of the left atrium in 3D Gadolinium Enhanced-MRI (GE-MRI) is crucial for treatment planning and risk assessment of cardiovascular diseases, particularly atrial fibrillation. However, this task remains challenging due to the complex morphology of the left atrium and the variable image quality of cardiac MRI. In this study, we propose a novel deep learning framework that leverages dilated convolutions to effectively capture multi-scale contextual information while maintaining computational efficiency. Our architecture incorporates a series of dilated convolutional layers with systematically increasing dilation rates, enabling the network to expand its receptive field without increasing the number of parameters or reducing spatial resolution. We evaluated our approach on a dataset of 100 3D GE-MRI scans, achieving a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.92 and a Hausdorff distance of 7.3 mm, outperforming conventional CNN architectures and state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Ablation studies confirm that the dilated convolution strategy significantly contributes to improved boundary delineation, particularly in regions with low contrast and around the pulmonary vein insertions. The proposed method demonstrates robust performance across varying image qualities and anatomical variations, presenting a promising approach for clinical applications requiring precise left atrial segmentation.

RUM: network Representation learning throUgh Multi-level structural information preservation

Network representation learning (NRL) has emerged as a powerful approach for capturing the complex relationships and structural properties inherent in graph data. In this paper, we introduce RUM, a novel framework for network representation learning that focuses on preserving multi-level structural information. Unlike existing methods that primarily focus on local neighborhood structures or single-scale topological features, RUM simultaneously captures and integrates structural information across multiple levels of granularity—from microscopic node-level interactions to mesoscopic community structures and macroscopic global network properties. Our approach employs a hierarchical encoding mechanism that learns representations by optimizing an objective function designed to preserve structural fidelity at each level while ensuring coherence across levels. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that RUM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various downstream tasks including node classification, link prediction, and community detection. Further analysis reveals that the multi-level representations learned by RUM are particularly effective in heterogeneous networks and networks with complex hierarchical structures. The proposed framework provides a principled and scalable solution for learning comprehensive network embeddings that can effectively capture the inherent multi-scale nature of real-world networks.

MAFF-Net: Filter False Positive for 3D Vehicle Detection with Multi-modal Adaptive Feature Fusion

This paper introduces MAFF-Net, a novel framework for 3D vehicle detection that effectively addresses the persistent challenge of false positive predictions in autonomous driving perception systems. Our approach leverages multi-modal data fusion, combining LiDAR point clouds and camera images through an adaptive feature fusion mechanism that dynamically adjusts the contribution of each modality based on context and data quality. Unlike existing methods that apply rigid fusion strategies, MAFF-Net employs attention-based modules to evaluate feature reliability and selectively emphasize the most informative signals while suppressing noisy or ambiguous inputs. We introduce a False Positive Filtering (FPF) module that specifically targets and eliminates erroneous detections by learning distinctive patterns of true and false predictions across modalities. Extensive experiments on the KITTI and nuScenes datasets demonstrate that MAFF-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance, reducing false positive rates by 18.7% while improving average precision by 3.2% for 3D vehicle detection compared to existing methods. Our ablation studies confirm that the adaptive fusion mechanism significantly outperforms fixed fusion strategies, particularly in challenging scenarios with occlusion, varying illumination, and sparse point clouds. MAFF-Net offers a robust solution for safety-critical autonomous driving applications where detection reliability is paramount.

Polarized Self-Attention: Towards High-quality Pixel-wise Regression

This paper introduces Polarized Self-Attention (PSA), a novel attention mechanism designed to enhance pixel-wise regression tasks in computer vision. While conventional self-attention mechanisms excel at modeling long-range dependencies, they often struggle with precise localization required for high-quality pixel-level predictions. Our proposed PSA addresses this limitation by decomposing the attention operation into two complementary components: a global branch that captures contextual information across the entire feature map, and a local branch that preserves fine-grained spatial details. This polarized design enables the network to simultaneously reason about global context while maintaining sensitivity to local structures. Through extensive experiments on challenging pixel-wise regression tasks including depth estimation, surface normal prediction, and optical flow estimation, we demonstrate that PSA consistently outperforms standard attention mechanisms and state-of-the-art approaches. Notably, our method achieves significant improvements in boundary preservation and structural coherence, leading to more accurate and visually appealing results. The proposed PSA module is lightweight, end-to-end trainable, and can be readily integrated into existing architectures to boost performance on various dense prediction tasks.

Taming GANs with Lookahead-Minmax

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generating realistic data across various domains, yet their training process remains notoriously unstable and sensitive to hyperparameter choices. In this paper, we introduce Lookahead-Minmax, a novel optimization framework designed to stabilize GAN training dynamics. Our approach extends the traditional minimax optimization by incorporating a lookahead mechanism that anticipates future adversarial responses, effectively dampening oscillations and preventing mode collapse. Through theoretical analysis, we establish convergence guarantees for our method under mild conditions and demonstrate its ability to navigate saddle points more efficiently than standard approaches. Extensive empirical evaluations across multiple GAN architectures (DCGAN, StyleGAN2, BigGAN) and benchmark datasets show that Lookahead-Minmax consistently improves Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores by 15-30% while reducing training time by up to 40%. Furthermore, our method exhibits remarkable robustness to hyperparameter choices, making GAN training more accessible and reliable. Our work provides both theoretical insights into minimax optimization dynamics and practical advances in stabilizing GAN training.

Learnable Sampling 3D Convolution for Video Enhancement and Action Recognition

This paper introduces Learnable Sampling 3D Convolution (LS3D), a novel neural network architecture designed to address the challenges of spatiotemporal feature extraction in video processing tasks. Unlike traditional 3D convolution operations that use fixed sampling patterns, LS3D dynamically learns optimal sampling locations across both spatial and temporal dimensions, enabling more efficient and effective video representation learning. Our approach incorporates deformable sampling mechanisms that adapt to motion patterns and content variations within video sequences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LS3D on two critical video understanding tasks: video enhancement and action recognition. For video enhancement, LS3D achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks, showing significant improvements in PSNR, SSIM, and perceptual quality metrics while requiring fewer computational resources than existing methods. In action recognition experiments across UCF-101, HMDB-51, and Kinetics datasets, our approach outperforms conventional 3D CNNs and transformer-based methods, particularly for actions with complex temporal dynamics. Ablation studies confirm that the learnable sampling strategy effectively captures motion cues and contextual information critical for both low-level enhancement and high-level semantic understanding tasks. The proposed LS3D represents a versatile and efficient architecture for video understanding that bridges the gap between representation quality and computational efficiency.

Learning Invariant Color Features for Person Re-Identification

Person re-identification (re-ID) systems face significant challenges due to color variations caused by different lighting conditions, camera settings, and viewing angles. This paper introduces a novel approach for learning color-invariant features that remain stable across diverse environmental conditions while preserving discriminative information essential for accurate person matching. Our method employs a dual-stream architecture that simultaneously processes original RGB images and their color-normalized counterparts, learning to extract features that are robust to illumination changes. We propose a Color Invariance Loss (CIL) that explicitly encourages feature consistency across different color transformations of the same identity. Extensive experiments on standard re-ID benchmarks including Market-1501, DukeMTMC-reID, and MSMT17 demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in cross-dataset scenarios where lighting conditions vary substantially. Ablation studies confirm that our learned color-invariant features maintain discriminative power while exhibiting enhanced robustness to color variations. The proposed method offers a practical solution to the color inconsistency problem in real-world surveillance systems without requiring additional computational resources during inference.

R-FCN-3000 at 30fps: Decoupling Detection and Classification

This paper presents R-FCN-3000, a novel object detection framework capable of recognizing 3,000 object categories at 30 frames per second. We address the fundamental speed-accuracy trade-off in large-scale object detection by decoupling the detection and classification stages of the detection pipeline. Our approach first employs a category-agnostic region proposal network to identify class-independent object candidates, followed by a lightweight classifier that efficiently categorizes these proposals across the large label space. This decoupling strategy significantly reduces computational complexity compared to conventional approaches that integrate classification within the detection process. Extensive experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that R-FCN-3000 achieves comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art methods while offering a 3-5× speed improvement. The framework maintains real-time performance even as the number of object categories scales to thousands, with minimal accuracy degradation. Our approach opens new possibilities for deploying large-scale object detection systems in resource-constrained environments and real-time applications such as autonomous driving and robotics.

Who is More Ready to Get Back in Shape?

This study investigates the psychological and behavioral factors that predict successful reengagement with fitness routines after periods of inactivity. Using a mixed-methods approach, we surveyed 487 adults (ages 25-65) who expressed intentions to "get back in shape" and followed their progress over a six-month period. Our findings reveal that readiness to successfully resume fitness activities was more strongly associated with psychological variables than demographic factors. Specifically, individuals who demonstrated high levels of intrinsic motivation, realistic goal-setting, and established implementation intentions were 3.2 times more likely to maintain consistent exercise habits after three months. Additionally, those with strong social support systems and who incorporated exercise into existing routines showed significantly higher adherence rates than participants relying primarily on willpower or external motivators. These results suggest that effective fitness reengagement strategies should focus on cultivating intrinsic motivation and practical implementation planning rather than emphasizing idealized outcomes. Our findings contribute to understanding the psychological mechanisms underlying successful behavioral change in fitness contexts and offer practical implications for health practitioners designing interventions for individuals returning to exercise.

Visual Evaluation of Generative Adversarial Networks for Time Series Data

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have shown remarkable success in generating realistic images, but their application to time series data remains challenging to evaluate effectively. This paper presents a novel visual evaluation framework specifically designed for assessing the quality of GAN-generated time series data. We introduce a suite of visualization techniques that enable researchers and practitioners to intuitively compare statistical properties, temporal dependencies, and domain-specific characteristics between real and synthetic time series. Our approach combines traditional statistical metrics with interactive visual analytics to reveal subtle differences in frequency components, autocorrelation structures, and distributional properties that may be missed by purely quantitative evaluation methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through case studies across multiple domains including financial markets, healthcare monitoring, and industrial sensor data. Results show that our visual evaluation approach can identify model shortcomings that quantitative metrics alone fail to detect, while providing actionable insights for GAN architecture improvements. This work bridges the gap between machine learning evaluation and visual analytics, offering a comprehensive toolkit for assessing and improving generative models for time series data.

Fast and Robust Multiple ColorChecker Detection using Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

This paper presents a novel approach for the automatic detection of multiple ColorChecker charts in images using deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). ColorChecker charts are essential tools for color calibration in photography, computer vision, and image processing applications, but their automatic detection remains challenging due to varying lighting conditions, occlusions, and perspective distortions. Our method employs a two-stage detection framework: first, a region proposal network identifies potential ColorChecker locations, followed by a classification and regression network that precisely localizes and identifies individual color patches. We introduce a specialized architecture with attention mechanisms that effectively captures the distinctive spatial arrangement of color patches in standard charts. The proposed approach achieves 97.8% detection accuracy on our diverse benchmark dataset, significantly outperforming traditional computer vision methods and previous deep learning approaches. Furthermore, our implementation processes high-resolution images at 15 frames per second on standard GPU hardware, making it suitable for real-time applications. Extensive experiments demonstrate the robustness of our method across various lighting conditions, partial occlusions, and multiple chart scenarios. The code and dataset are made publicly available to facilitate further research in this domain.

WaterGAN: Unsupervised Generative Network to Enable Real-time Color Correction of Monocular Underwater Images

Underwater imaging presents unique challenges due to light attenuation and scattering effects that significantly degrade image quality, hampering both human interpretation and computer vision tasks. This paper introduces WaterGAN, a novel unsupervised generative adversarial network designed to address the color distortion problem in underwater imagery without requiring paired training data. Our approach learns the complex light absorption and scattering models that characterize underwater environments by training on unpaired above-water and underwater image sets. WaterGAN consists of two key components: a physics-informed generator that models wavelength-dependent attenuation, and a discriminator architecture that enforces perceptual realism. Unlike previous methods that require manual parameter tuning or paired training examples, our framework automatically learns to restore natural colors and contrast from degraded underwater inputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that WaterGAN outperforms state-of-the-art underwater image enhancement techniques across multiple metrics while maintaining computational efficiency that enables real-time processing at 25+ frames per second on standard hardware. We further validate our approach through ablation studies and real-world deployment on autonomous underwater vehicles, showing improved performance in downstream computer vision tasks including object detection and segmentation. The proposed method represents a significant advancement in making underwater computer vision systems more robust across varying water conditions without specialized hardware requirements.

A Novel Semi-Supervised Data-Driven Method for Chiller Fault Diagnosis with Unlabeled Data

This paper presents a novel semi-supervised learning approach for chiller fault diagnosis that effectively leverages both labeled and unlabeled operational data. Chillers, as critical components in HVAC systems, require robust fault detection mechanisms to ensure energy efficiency and system reliability. Traditional supervised fault diagnosis methods demand large amounts of labeled fault data, which is often expensive and impractical to obtain in real-world settings. Our proposed method addresses this limitation by incorporating unlabeled data into the learning process, significantly reducing the dependency on labeled samples. The approach combines a manifold regularization framework with deep learning techniques to extract meaningful features from sensor measurements and operational parameters. Experimental validation conducted on a 90-ton centrifugal chiller test bed demonstrates that our method achieves 92.7% fault classification accuracy with only 30% of the labeled data required by conventional supervised approaches. Further analysis reveals improved performance across seven common chiller fault types, with particularly notable improvements in detecting subtle faults such as refrigerant leakage and condenser fouling. The method's ability to continuously adapt using streaming unlabeled data makes it particularly suitable for practical deployment in building management systems, offering a promising solution for enhancing chiller reliability and energy performance.

Model-Free Reinforcement Learning: from Clipped Pseudo-Regret to Sample Complexity

This paper establishes a novel theoretical connection between clipped pseudo-regret and sample complexity in model-free reinforcement learning (RL). We develop a unified analysis framework that bridges these two fundamental performance metrics, which have traditionally been studied separately in the RL literature. Our approach introduces a clipping technique for pseudo-regret that effectively handles the exploration-exploitation tradeoff in environments with potentially unbounded rewards. We prove that algorithms with sublinear clipped pseudo-regret guarantees can be transformed into PAC-optimal learners with tight sample complexity bounds. The framework is applied to both tabular and function approximation settings, demonstrating that several popular model-free algorithms—including Q-learning, SARSA, and deep Q-networks with appropriate modifications—achieve optimal sample complexity under mild assumptions. Empirical evaluations across diverse environments validate our theoretical findings and show that the clipped pseudo-regret metric better predicts practical performance than traditional cumulative regret. Our results provide new insights into the fundamental limits of model-free RL and offer practical guidance for algorithm design and analysis.

Sentiment and Emotion Classification of Epidemic Related Bilingual data from Social Media

This study investigates sentiment and emotion classification of epidemic-related content across bilingual social media data during public health crises. We collected and analyzed a large corpus of tweets and posts in English and Spanish related to COVID-19 and other recent epidemics. Using a hybrid approach combining transformer-based language models and traditional machine learning techniques, we developed a classification framework capable of identifying six distinct emotional categories (fear, anger, sadness, hope, relief, and neutral) alongside binary sentiment polarity. Our models achieved F1-scores of 0.83 for sentiment classification and 0.76 for emotion detection across both languages, outperforming previous monolingual approaches. Cross-lingual analysis revealed significant differences in emotional expression patterns between language communities during epidemic events. Additionally, we observed temporal shifts in sentiment that corresponded with key epidemic milestones. This research contributes a robust bilingual classification system and annotated dataset for epidemic-related social media content, providing valuable tools for public health communication strategies and real-time monitoring of public emotional responses during health emergencies.

Streaming Graph Neural Networks via Continual Learning

This paper presents a novel framework for adapting Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to streaming graph data through continual learning techniques. As real-world graph-structured data often evolves over time with the addition of new nodes, edges, and features, traditional static GNN approaches suffer from performance degradation when confronted with distribution shifts. Our proposed method, Streaming-GNN, leverages principles from continual learning to enable efficient adaptation to evolving graph structures without catastrophic forgetting of previously learned patterns. We introduce a dual-memory architecture that maintains representations of both historical graph structures and emerging topological patterns, coupled with a selective experience replay mechanism that prioritizes structurally significant subgraphs. Extensive experiments on dynamic citation networks, evolving social graphs, and temporal knowledge graphs demonstrate that Streaming-GNN outperforms static retraining approaches by 15-20% in predictive accuracy while requiring only 30% of the computational resources. Furthermore, our approach effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting, maintaining performance on historical subgraphs while adapting to newly observed structures. These results highlight the potential of continual learning strategies for maintaining high-performing GNN models in streaming graph environments common to recommendation systems, fraud detection, and social network analysis.

SGE Net: Video Object Detection with Squeezed GRU and Information Entropy Map

Video object detection remains challenging due to motion blur, occlusion, and the computational demands of processing sequential frames. In this paper, we propose SGE Net, a novel framework that integrates a Squeezed Gated Recurrent Unit (SGRU) and Information Entropy Map to enhance detection accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. The SGRU module compresses temporal information from consecutive frames into a lightweight representation, significantly reducing parameter count compared to traditional GRU architectures while preserving essential motion features. Our Information Entropy Map dynamically quantifies uncertainty in feature representations, allowing the network to focus computational resources on regions with high information value. Extensive experiments on standard video object detection benchmarks, including ImageNet VID and YouTube-BoundingBoxes, demonstrate that SGE Net achieves state-of-the-art performance with 15% fewer parameters and 23% reduction in inference time compared to existing methods. Ablation studies confirm that both the SGRU and entropy mapping components contribute substantially to detection performance, particularly for objects under challenging conditions such as fast motion and partial occlusion. Our approach provides an efficient solution for real-time video object detection applications without compromising accuracy.

AirRL: A Reinforcement Learning Approach to Urban Air Quality Inference

Urban air quality monitoring is crucial for public health policy and environmental management, yet traditional monitoring networks suffer from limited spatial coverage due to the high costs of deploying and maintaining sensor infrastructure. This paper introduces AirRL, a novel reinforcement learning framework for accurate, high-resolution air quality inference in urban environments. Our approach formulates air quality inference as a sequential decision-making problem, where an agent learns to optimally combine sparse ground-truth measurements with heterogeneous data sources including satellite imagery, traffic patterns, meteorological conditions, and land use information. The framework employs a Deep Q-Network architecture that adaptively weights these diverse inputs based on temporal and spatial contexts, effectively capturing complex pollution dynamics. Experiments conducted across three major metropolitan areas demonstrate that AirRL outperforms conventional interpolation methods and state-of-the-art machine learning approaches, reducing inference error by 27% while providing interpretable confidence metrics. Furthermore, AirRL shows remarkable robustness to sensor network sparsity, maintaining accuracy even when 40% of monitoring stations are unavailable. These results suggest that reinforcement learning offers a promising approach for environmental sensing applications where ground truth is sparse and expensive to obtain, potentially enabling more cost-effective air quality monitoring systems for urban centers worldwide.

Learning Joint Representations of Videos and Sentences with Web Image Search

This paper presents a novel approach for learning joint representations of videos and natural language sentences by leveraging web image search as an intermediary semantic bridge. Existing methods for video-text matching often struggle with the semantic gap between the visual dynamics of videos and the linguistic structures of textual descriptions. We address this challenge by introducing a framework that utilizes freely available web images as a connecting medium between these modalities. Our approach first maps both videos and sentences to a shared image-based semantic space by querying web image search engines with key concepts extracted from each modality. We then develop a triple-branch neural architecture that learns embeddings where semantically related videos and sentences are positioned closer together. Extensive experiments on standard video-text retrieval benchmarks, including MSR-VTT, MSVD, and ActivityNet Captions, demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by significant margins (improving R@1 by 4.7% on MSR-VTT). Further ablation studies confirm that web image search provides valuable contextual information that bridges the visual-linguistic divide. Our framework offers a scalable and effective solution for cross-modal understanding without requiring additional manual annotations.

Geometry Guided Adversarial Facial Expression Synthesis

This paper introduces a novel approach for synthesizing realistic facial expressions through a geometry-guided adversarial framework. Current facial expression synthesis methods often struggle to maintain identity preservation while generating diverse emotional expressions, particularly when geometric facial features undergo significant transformations. We propose a Geometry Guided Generative Adversarial Network (GG-GAN) that explicitly incorporates facial landmark information as a structural prior to guide the synthesis process. Our framework consists of two main components: a geometry encoder that extracts and manipulates facial landmark configurations, and an expression generator that transforms neutral faces to target expressions while preserving identity-specific features. By disentangling geometry from appearance, our method achieves fine-grained control over expression intensity and style. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of expression accuracy, identity preservation, and visual quality. Additionally, we show that our synthesized data can effectively augment training sets for facial expression recognition systems, improving their robustness to pose variations and partial occlusions. The proposed method has promising applications in animation, human-computer interaction, and data augmentation for affective computing.

Extraction of Key-frames of Endoscopic Videos by using Depth Information

This paper presents a novel approach for key-frame extraction from endoscopic videos by leveraging depth information. Endoscopic procedures generate extensive video data, making efficient summarization crucial for clinical documentation, education, and computer-assisted interventions. Our method addresses the limitations of traditional intensity-based extraction techniques by incorporating depth as a discriminative feature. We propose a two-stage framework that first estimates depth maps from monocular endoscopic images using a deep learning model trained on synthetic and real endoscopic data. Subsequently, we employ a depth-aware clustering algorithm that identifies frames with significant depth variations, representing distinct anatomical structures and clinical events. Experimental evaluation on a diverse dataset of 50 endoscopic videos across multiple procedures demonstrates that our approach achieves 87% precision and 83% recall in extracting clinically relevant key-frames, outperforming conventional methods by 18%. Additionally, a user study with 15 endoscopists confirms that our depth-based summaries better preserve diagnostic information while reducing redundancy by 65%. This work contributes to more efficient endoscopic video analysis and has potential applications in clinical documentation systems and computer-assisted intervention platforms.

Delving into Variance Transmission and Normalization: Shift of Average Gradient Makes the Network Collapse

This paper investigates the critical role of variance transmission and normalization in deep neural networks, with a particular focus on understanding network collapse phenomena. Through theoretical analysis and empirical validation, we demonstrate that the shift in average gradient magnitude across layers serves as a key indicator of impending network collapse. Our findings reveal that when the variance of activations becomes improperly scaled during forward propagation, it triggers a cascading effect that manifests as a systematic shift in gradient magnitudes during backpropagation. This shift ultimately leads to either vanishing or exploding gradients, causing network performance to deteriorate rapidly. We formalize this relationship mathematically, deriving a variance transmission equation that predicts collapse conditions across various network architectures. Additionally, we propose a novel normalization technique that specifically targets and regulates this average gradient shift, demonstrating significant improvements in training stability and convergence speed across multiple benchmark datasets. Our work provides both theoretical insights into the mechanics of network collapse and practical solutions for building more robust deep learning systems.

Reinforcement Learning for Decision-Making and Control in Power Systems: Tutorial, Review, and Vision

This paper presents a comprehensive examination of reinforcement learning (RL) applications in power systems, serving as both a tutorial for newcomers and a state-of-the-art review for researchers in the field. We begin by introducing fundamental RL concepts and methodologies particularly relevant to power system challenges, including Markov Decision Processes, value-based methods, policy optimization, and deep reinforcement learning approaches. The review systematically categorizes and analyzes existing RL implementations across critical power system domains including grid stability control, energy management, demand response, electricity markets, and microgrid optimization. We identify common patterns in problem formulation, highlighting how researchers have addressed the unique challenges of continuous state spaces, partial observability, and safety constraints inherent in power systems. Furthermore, we discuss the gap between simulation-based results and practical deployment, examining benchmarks and real-world implementations. The paper concludes with a forward-looking vision outlining promising research directions, including hybrid physics-informed RL models, multi-agent frameworks for distributed control, and transferable policies for power system resilience. This work aims to accelerate the adoption of RL techniques in power systems by providing both theoretical foundations and practical insights for implementation.

Q-learning with Uniformly Bounded Variance: Large Discounting Is Not a Barrier to Fast Learning

This paper challenges the conventional wisdom that large discount factors inherently slow down the convergence of Q-learning algorithms in reinforcement learning. We establish that Q-learning can achieve fast convergence rates with a uniformly bounded variance, even as the discount factor approaches one. Our analysis reveals that the primary barrier to efficient learning is not the discount factor itself, but rather the variance in the estimators. We introduce a novel variance-controlled Q-learning algorithm that maintains consistent performance across different discount regimes by adaptively adjusting its exploration strategy and update mechanisms. Through theoretical analysis, we prove that our approach achieves an O(1/√T) convergence rate independent of the discount factor, contradicting previous lower bounds that suggested an unavoidable Ω(1/(1-γ)) dependency. Extensive experiments on benchmark environments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms traditional Q-learning variants when dealing with long-horizon problems requiring large discount factors. These findings have important implications for tackling complex sequential decision-making problems where long-term rewards must be effectively balanced with learning efficiency.

Abstract: Graph Decoupling Attention Markov Networks for Semi-supervised Graph Node Classification

This paper introduces Graph Decoupling Attention Markov Networks (GDAMN), a novel framework for semi-supervised node classification in graph-structured data. We address the fundamental limitations of existing graph neural networks which often struggle with oversmoothing, heterophily, and the entanglement of feature and structural information. GDAMN explicitly decouples the learning of feature-based and structure-based representations through a dual-stream architecture, each utilizing specialized attention mechanisms to capture different aspects of node relationships. Our framework incorporates a Markov network component that models higher-order dependencies while maintaining computational efficiency. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that GDAMN effectively mitigates the oversmoothing problem by maintaining distinct feature spaces across network layers. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that GDAMN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with particularly significant improvements on heterophilous graphs where traditional message-passing approaches falter. Our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the decoupling mechanism and attention-guided message passing. The proposed approach offers a principled solution to semi-supervised node classification that balances local feature preservation with global structural awareness.

Simultaneously Color-Depth Super-Resolution with Conditional Generative Adversarial Network

This paper presents a novel approach to simultaneously enhance the resolution of both color and depth information in RGB-D images using conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs). While traditional super-resolution methods typically address color and depth enhancement separately, our framework processes both modalities in a unified architecture, leveraging the complementary information between them. We propose a dual-stream conditional GAN that captures cross-modal relationships while preserving the unique characteristics of each modality. Our network integrates specialized feature extraction paths for RGB and depth data with cross-modal attention mechanisms to facilitate information exchange. Extensive experiments on multiple RGB-D datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art single-modality super-resolution methods and existing joint approaches, achieving improvements of up to 2.3dB in PSNR for color images and 1.8dB for depth maps. The qualitative results show significantly enhanced edge preservation and structural coherence between modalities. Furthermore, our method demonstrates robust performance even with challenging inputs such as noisy depth maps and varying lighting conditions, making it applicable to real-world RGB-D sensing applications including robotics, augmented reality, and 3D reconstruction.

A Review of Deep Learning Methods for Irregularly Sampled Medical Time Series Data

Medical time series data presents unique challenges for deep learning applications due to its irregular sampling patterns, missing values, and variable-length observations. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of state-of-the-art deep learning approaches for handling irregularly sampled medical time series data. We examine various architectural innovations including recurrent neural networks with specialized gating mechanisms, attention-based models, neural ordinary differential equations (Neural ODEs), and transformer-based approaches that have been adapted for the medical domain. The review categorizes methods based on their underlying mathematical frameworks: interpolation-based techniques, models that directly incorporate time intervals, and continuous-time approaches. We evaluate these methods across diverse clinical applications including mortality prediction, disease progression modeling, early diagnosis, and treatment response forecasting. Our analysis reveals that while significant progress has been made in handling temporal irregularities, challenges remain in model interpretability, data heterogeneity, and generalizability across different clinical settings. We conclude by identifying promising research directions and emerging paradigms that may further advance the field of deep learning for irregular medical time series analysis.

Combinational Q-Learning for Dou Di Zhu

This paper presents Combinational Q-Learning (CQL), a novel reinforcement learning approach designed to address the unique challenges of the popular Chinese card game Dou Di Zhu. Unlike traditional card games, Dou Di Zhu features a vast action space with combinatorial play patterns and incomplete information, making it particularly challenging for AI systems. Our proposed CQL algorithm extends traditional Q-learning by decomposing the complex action selection process into a two-stage approach: first evaluating card combinations, then selecting optimal plays based on these evaluations. We introduce a hierarchical value function that captures both the immediate utility of card combinations and their strategic potential in varying game contexts. Experimental results demonstrate that CQL significantly outperforms baseline methods, including deep Q-networks and Monte Carlo approaches, achieving a 68% win rate against skilled human players. Additionally, our algorithm exhibits improved sample efficiency and interpretability compared to existing methods. The combinatorial approach developed in this work has potential applications beyond Dou Di Zhu to other complex games and decision-making problems with large, structured action spaces.

Temporally coherent video anonymization through GAN inpainting

This paper presents a novel approach to video anonymization that preserves temporal coherence while effectively protecting privacy. We introduce a framework that leverages generative adversarial networks (GANs) to inpaint regions containing privacy-sensitive information, such as faces and identifying features, with realistic alternatives that maintain consistency across video frames. Unlike traditional anonymization techniques that rely on blurring or pixelation, our method generates visually plausible content that preserves the natural appearance and flow of the video. We address the critical challenge of temporal coherence by incorporating a recurrent architecture that conditions each frame's inpainting on previous frames, minimizing flickering and inconsistencies across the sequence. Extensive experiments on diverse video datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves superior anonymization performance while maintaining high visual quality and temporal stability. Quantitative evaluations show that our method successfully prevents re-identification by state-of-the-art recognition systems while scoring significantly higher on perceptual quality metrics compared to conventional anonymization techniques. The proposed framework offers a promising solution for privacy protection in various applications including surveillance, healthcare, and social media platforms.

BRepNet: A topological message passing system for solid models

This paper introduces BRepNet, a novel neural network architecture designed specifically for processing boundary representation (B-rep) solid models. Unlike previous approaches that rely on voxelization or point cloud conversions, BRepNet operates directly on the topological structure of B-rep models, preserving their exact geometric and topological information. Our system implements a message passing framework that propagates information across the hierarchical elements of B-reps (faces, edges, and vertices) through their adjacency relationships. We demonstrate that this topological message passing approach enables the network to effectively capture both local geometric features and global structural relationships within solid models. Experiments on several benchmark datasets show that BRepNet significantly outperforms existing methods in classification, segmentation, and feature detection tasks, with improvements of 12-18% in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, BRepNet exhibits better generalization to complex industrial models and requires less computational resources than voxel-based approaches. These results suggest that topology-aware neural networks can bridge the gap between geometric deep learning and CAD/CAM applications, opening new possibilities for AI-assisted engineering design and manufacturing.

The Lipschitz Constant of Self-Attention

This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the Lipschitz properties of self-attention mechanisms, a fundamental component in modern transformer-based architectures. We derive tight upper bounds on the Lipschitz constant of self-attention layers under various normalization schemes and attention patterns. Our theoretical results demonstrate that standard self-attention implementations have unbounded Lipschitz constants, potentially explaining the instability observed in certain transformer training regimes. We introduce a novel regularization technique that constrains the Lipschitz behavior of self-attention while preserving its expressive capacity. Through extensive experiments on language modeling, machine translation, and image classification tasks, we show that Lipschitz-constrained self-attention leads to models with improved robustness to input perturbations, better generalization on out-of-distribution data, and enhanced convergence properties during training. Our findings provide new theoretical insights into the stability of transformer networks and offer practical methods to control their sensitivity to input variations without sacrificing performance.

OGB-LSC: A Large-Scale Challenge for Machine Learning on Graphs

Graph-based machine learning has demonstrated remarkable success across diverse domains, yet significant challenges persist in developing scalable methods for real-world graph datasets. In this paper, we introduce the Open Graph Benchmark Large-Scale Challenge (OGB-LSC), a comprehensive benchmark designed to accelerate progress in large-scale graph machine learning. OGB-LSC features carefully curated graph datasets that are orders of magnitude larger than existing benchmarks, encompassing millions of nodes and billions of edges drawn from critical application domains. The benchmark includes three fundamental tasks: node prediction on massive academic graphs, link prediction on large-scale knowledge graphs, and graph prediction for molecular property forecasting across millions of compounds. For each task, we provide standardized dataset splits, evaluation metrics, and baseline implementations to ensure fair comparison. Our extensive experiments with state-of-the-art graph neural networks reveal significant performance gaps between current methods and ideal solutions, highlighting numerous opportunities for algorithmic innovation. OGB-LSC not only establishes new challenges for the graph machine learning community but also provides a rigorous framework to measure progress on genuinely large-scale graph problems that better reflect real-world applications.

Planning with Learned Object Importance in Large Problem Instances using Graph Neural Networks

This paper presents a novel approach to automated planning in large-scale problem instances by incorporating learned object importance through Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Traditional planning methods often struggle with scalability when confronted with numerous objects and complex relationships. We introduce a framework that learns to identify and prioritize critical objects within a planning domain, effectively reducing the search space while maintaining solution quality. Our approach represents planning problems as graphs where nodes correspond to objects and edges capture their relationships, allowing GNNs to learn meaningful object embeddings that correlate with their importance to optimal plan construction. By training on smaller problem instances with known solutions, our model generalizes to significantly larger instances, where it guides heuristic search algorithms by focusing computational resources on high-importance object interactions. Experimental results across diverse planning domains demonstrate that our approach achieves up to 3x speedup compared to state-of-the-art planners while finding solutions of comparable quality. The method shows particular promise in logistics, manufacturing, and robotic task planning scenarios where hundreds of objects must be considered. Our work bridges machine learning and classical planning, offering a scalable approach to solving previously intractable planning problems.

Adaptive Neural Network Classifier for Decoding MEG Signals

This study presents a novel adaptive neural network architecture for real-time classification of magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. MEG data present unique challenges for decoding neural activity due to their high dimensionality, low signal-to-noise ratio, and non-stationarity across sessions and subjects. We introduce a self-adjusting classifier that combines convolutional and recurrent neural network components with an attention mechanism that dynamically adapts to individual variations in brain activity patterns. The proposed model incorporates a transfer learning framework that allows for rapid calibration with minimal training data when applied to new subjects. In experimental validation using a motor imagery paradigm with 24 participants, our adaptive classifier achieved 89.3% accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art fixed architecture approaches by 11.7%. Notably, the system maintained robust performance despite inter-session variability, with accuracy degradation of only 4.2% compared to 15.8% for conventional methods. The computational efficiency of our approach also enables real-time implementation in brain-computer interface applications. These results demonstrate the potential of adaptive neural network architectures to address the challenges of MEG signal decoding and advance neurofeedback and neuroprosthetic technologies.

Pattern Detection in the Activation Space for Identifying Synthesized Content

The proliferation of AI-generated content poses significant challenges to information integrity and security across digital platforms. This paper introduces a novel approach for detecting synthesized content by analyzing patterns in the neural network activation space rather than focusing solely on surface-level features. We demonstrate that AI-generated text, images, and audio exhibit distinctive activation signatures when processed through detection models, even when such content successfully mimics human-created work at the perceptual level. Our method leverages a multi-dimensional representation of intermediate layer activations to identify statistical regularities unique to synthesized content. Through extensive experimentation with content generated by various state-of-the-art models (including GPT-4, DALL-E 3, and WaveNet derivatives), we achieve detection accuracy of 94.3% across diverse content types while maintaining robustness against adversarial manipulations. The approach demonstrates particular strength in identifying content that has undergone multiple transformations or partial synthesis. We provide theoretical analysis connecting these activation patterns to the generative processes that produce them, offering insights into why AI-generated content contains subtle but detectable fingerprints. This work contributes a fundamental advancement in synthesized content detection that operates independently of specific generative architectures, suggesting promising applications for digital forensics, media authentication, and online trust systems.

GSVNet: Guided Spatially-Varying Convolution for Fast Semantic Segmentation on Video

This paper introduces GSVNet, a novel neural network architecture designed for real-time semantic segmentation in video sequences. Our approach leverages the temporal coherence inherent in videos through a guided spatially-varying convolution mechanism that dynamically adapts filter weights based on both spatial and temporal contexts. Unlike conventional approaches that process each frame independently or rely on computationally expensive optical flow estimation, GSVNet employs a lightweight guidance network that predicts pixel-specific convolution parameters, allowing for adaptive processing that accounts for motion and appearance changes across frames. Experimental results on standard video segmentation benchmarks, including Cityscapes and KITTI, demonstrate that GSVNet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while reducing computational costs by 35% compared to frame-by-frame approaches. Our method maintains robust performance even under challenging conditions such as motion blur, occlusions, and varying lighting conditions, operating at 28 frames per second on a single GPU. The proposed spatially-varying convolution mechanism provides an efficient alternative to traditional temporal modeling techniques, opening new possibilities for real-time video understanding applications including autonomous driving, augmented reality, and video surveillance.

Context-Aware Single-Shot Detector

Object detection remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision, particularly in complex scenes where contextual information is crucial for accurate identification. This paper introduces the Context-Aware Single-Shot Detector (CASSD), a novel architecture that enhances traditional single-shot detection frameworks by explicitly modeling contextual relationships between objects and their surroundings. Our approach incorporates a dual-stream feature extraction pathway: one focused on object-specific features and another dedicated to capturing broader scene context. We propose a Context Integration Module (CIM) that dynamically fuses these complementary information streams at multiple scales, enabling more robust detection across varying object sizes and scene complexities. Extensive experiments on COCO and PASCAL VOC benchmarks demonstrate that CASSD achieves significant improvements over baseline single-shot detectors, with particularly notable gains in detecting small objects and objects in cluttered environments. Our method maintains competitive inference speeds while reducing false positives by 12% and improving mean Average Precision (mAP) by 3.5% compared to state-of-the-art single-shot approaches. Code and pre-trained models are made publicly available to facilitate further research.

How Generative Adversarial Networks and Their Variants Work: An Overview

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have emerged as one of the most powerful frameworks for generative modeling in machine learning. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the fundamental principles behind GANs and their notable variants developed since their introduction in 2014. We examine the core adversarial training mechanism where generator and discriminator networks compete in a minimax game, leading to the generation of increasingly realistic synthetic data. The paper systematically reviews architectural innovations including DCGANs, Progressive GANs, and StyleGANs, as well as training stabilization techniques such as Wasserstein GANs and Spectral Normalization. We also explore conditional variants that enable controlled generation and specialized applications across domains including image synthesis, text-to-image translation, and medical imaging. Additionally, we discuss persistent challenges in GAN training including mode collapse, convergence instability, and evaluation metrics. This overview serves as both an introduction for newcomers to the field and a structured reference for researchers navigating the rapidly expanding landscape of GAN architectures and applications.

FeatherNets: Convolutional Neural Networks as Light as Feather for Face Anti-spoofing

Face anti-spoofing systems are critical for securing facial recognition technologies against presentation attacks, but deploying robust solutions on resource-constrained devices remains challenging. In this paper, we present FeatherNets, a family of extremely lightweight convolutional neural networks designed specifically for face anti-spoofing. Our approach dramatically reduces computational complexity while maintaining high detection accuracy across diverse attack scenarios. The proposed architecture leverages depth-wise separable convolutions, efficient channel attention mechanisms, and a novel feature fusion strategy to achieve state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer parameters than existing solutions. Experimental results on public benchmarks including OULU-NPU, CASIA-MFSD, and Replay-Attack demonstrate that FeatherNets achieve comparable or superior performance to much larger models while requiring only 0.35M parameters and 80M FLOPs, enabling real-time inference even on low-power edge devices. We further analyze the robustness of our models across different lighting conditions, presentation attack types, and cross-dataset scenarios. FeatherNets represent a significant advancement toward practical, deployable face anti-spoofing solutions for mobile and IoT applications.

Region Refinement Network for Salient Object Detection

Salient object detection (SOD) aims to identify and segment the most visually distinctive objects in an image. Despite significant progress in recent years, existing methods still struggle with accurately delineating object boundaries and handling complex scenes with multiple salient objects. In this paper, we propose a Region Refinement Network (RRNet) that addresses these challenges through a novel hierarchical refinement approach. Our network consists of three main components: (1) a feature extraction backbone that captures multi-scale contextual information, (2) a region proposal module that generates coarse salient object candidates, and (3) a region refinement module that progressively enhances boundary details and spatial coherence. The refinement process incorporates both local and global context through an attention mechanism that dynamically weighs feature contributions based on their relevance to saliency prediction. Extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets (DUTS, ECSSD, HKU-IS, PASCAL-S, and DUT-OMRON) demonstrate that our RRNet achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly in boundary accuracy and complex scene handling. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each component in our proposed architecture. Our approach not only advances the field of salient object detection but also provides insights for other pixel-level prediction tasks requiring precise boundary localization.

Recent Ice Trends in Swiss Mountain Lakes: 20-year Analysis of MODIS Imagery

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of ice cover dynamics in Swiss mountain lakes over the past two decades (2000-2020) using Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) satellite imagery. We analyzed temporal trends in ice phenology, including freeze-up dates, break-up dates, and ice duration for 25 high-altitude lakes across the Swiss Alps. The MODIS data, with its 250-500m spatial resolution and daily temporal coverage, was processed using a semi-automated classification algorithm to determine ice presence and extent.
