This paper presents a novel framework for real-time pedestrian detection and tracking in autonomous driving systems through efficient sensor fusion of camera and LiDAR data. While existing approaches often prioritize either detection accuracy or computational efficiency, our framework achieves both by implementing a cascaded architecture that strategically combines the complementary strengths of these sensor modalities. We propose a two-stage fusion methodology: an early fusion component that aligns and preprocesses raw sensor data, followed by a late fusion mechanism that integrates deep learning-based visual features with spatial point cloud information. Our approach demonstrates robust performance under challenging environmental conditions, including low light, occlusions, and adverse weather. Experimental validation on public datasets shows that our framework achieves 94.3% detection accuracy with a processing rate of 24 frames per second on standard automotive hardware platforms, representing a 17% improvement in accuracy and 35% reduction in computational overhead compared to single-sensor systems. Additionally, we introduce a lightweight tracking algorithm that maintains pedestrian identity across frames with 91.8% consistency. This research contributes to safer autonomous driving systems by enhancing pedestrian detection reliability while meeting the real-time processing requirements essential for practical deployment.

Label Refinement Network for Coarse-to-Fine Semantic Segmentation

This paper presents a novel Label Refinement Network (LRN) architecture that addresses the challenge of coarse-to-fine semantic segmentation in computer vision. Conventional semantic segmentation methods often struggle with precise boundary delineation and fine-grained detail preservation, particularly in complex scenes. Our proposed LRN employs a hierarchical refinement approach that progressively enhances segmentation masks from coarse predictions to fine-detailed outputs. The network consists of a main segmentation backbone that generates initial coarse predictions, followed by multiple refinement modules that iteratively refine boundary regions and detailed structures. We introduce a boundary-aware loss function that places greater emphasis on challenging boundary pixels, guiding the network to focus on regions requiring precise delineation. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and ADE20K demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particular improvements in boundary accuracy (+3.2% in boundary F-score) and fine structure preservation. The LRN architecture proves especially effective for classes with complex shapes and thin structures, while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time applications. Our ablation studies verify the contribution of each component in the refinement process, highlighting the effectiveness of our coarse-to-fine segmentation paradigm.

Hcore-Init: Neural Network Initialization based on Graph Degeneracy

Proper weight initialization is crucial for training deep neural networks efficiently. In this paper, we introduce Hcore-Init, a novel initialization method that leverages graph degeneracy concepts to establish more effective initial weights. By representing neural networks as directed graphs and applying k-core decomposition algorithms, our approach identifies hierarchical structures within the network architecture that inform the initialization process. Unlike traditional methods that rely solely on layer dimensions, Hcore-Init considers the topological properties of the network to determine appropriate scaling factors for weights. Through extensive experiments on various architectures including CNNs, ResNets, and Transformers, we demonstrate that Hcore-Init consistently outperforms standard initialization techniques such as Xavier, He, and Orthogonal initialization, achieving faster convergence and improved final performance. Our theoretical analysis shows that Hcore-Init helps maintain stable gradient flow during backpropagation by balancing the variance of activations across different network components based on their degeneracy values. This work establishes a promising connection between graph theory and neural network optimization, opening new avenues for architecture-aware initialization strategies.

ShapeConv: Shape-aware Convolutional Layer for Indoor RGB-D Semantic Segmentation

Indoor RGB-D semantic segmentation remains challenging due to the complex spatial relationships and varying geometric structures present in indoor environments. This paper introduces ShapeConv, a novel shape-aware convolutional layer specifically designed to enhance semantic segmentation performance for indoor RGB-D data. Unlike conventional convolutional operations that treat RGB and depth information as separate or simply concatenated channels, ShapeConv explicitly models the geometric relationships between pixels by incorporating local shape priors derived from depth information into the convolutional operation. Our approach dynamically adjusts convolutional kernels based on the underlying 3D structure, allowing the network to better distinguish between objects with similar appearance but different geometric properties. We propose a dual-stream architecture where ShapeConv layers process RGB features guided by depth-derived shape descriptors, enabling more effective feature extraction that respects physical boundaries and spatial continuity. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including NYUv2, SUN RGB-D, and ScanNet, demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, with particular improvements in challenging scenarios involving occlusions, varying lighting conditions, and objects with similar textures. ShapeConv introduces minimal computational overhead while significantly improving segmentation accuracy, making it a practical solution for real-world indoor scene understanding applications.

Interactive Illumination Invariance

This paper presents a novel framework for achieving illumination invariance in interactive visual systems. Our approach addresses the persistent challenge of maintaining consistent visual recognition and tracking under varying lighting conditions, a critical issue in applications ranging from augmented reality to computer vision-based interfaces. We introduce a real-time adaptive algorithm that dynamically compensates for illumination changes while preserving essential visual features. The system combines multi-scale representation with user interaction feedback loops to continuously refine illumination models. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, with our approach achieving 94% recognition accuracy under extreme lighting variations compared to 67% for baseline techniques. The framework's low computational overhead (averaging 12ms per frame on consumer hardware) enables its integration into interactive applications without noticeable latency. We validate our approach through comprehensive user studies across diverse environments, showing that interactive illumination invariance substantially enhances the robustness and usability of vision-based interactive systems.

Integrating Human Gaze into Attention for Egocentric Activity Recognition

This paper presents a novel approach to egocentric activity recognition by integrating human gaze data into attention mechanisms of deep learning architectures. While traditional egocentric vision systems rely solely on visual features from wearable cameras, they often struggle to identify relevant regions in cluttered first-person views. Our method leverages the natural human visual attention process by incorporating eye-tracking data as a supervisory signal for attention modules in convolutional-recurrent neural networks. We introduce a Gaze-Guided Attention Network (GGAN) that fuses implicit visual attention with explicit gaze fixation points to better focus on task-relevant objects and actions. Experiments on three public egocentric activity datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 4.7% in activity recognition accuracy. Further analysis reveals that the integration of gaze significantly improves performance in scenarios with complex hand-object interactions and dynamic backgrounds. Our work highlights the complementary nature of computational attention and human gaze for understanding egocentric activities, with potential applications in augmented reality, assistive technologies, and human-robot interaction.

Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery: Applications and Techniques

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into drug discovery processes represents a paradigm shift in pharmaceutical research and development. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of current AI applications and techniques revolutionizing the drug discovery pipeline. We examine how machine learning algorithms, deep neural networks, and natural language processing tools are accelerating target identification, lead optimization, and ADMET prediction while substantially reducing time and costs associated with traditional discovery methods. The review highlights successful case studies where AI has facilitated the discovery of novel therapeutic candidates across diverse disease areas, including previously intractable targets. Additionally, we analyze emerging techniques such as generative models for de novo molecular design, reinforcement learning for multi-parameter optimization, and knowledge graph approaches for drug repurposing. Despite promising advances, significant challenges remain, including data quality issues, model interpretability concerns, and regulatory considerations. We conclude by outlining future research directions and emphasizing the potential of hybrid approaches combining AI with experimental validation to transform the pharmaceutical landscape and address unmet medical needs more efficiently.

Anderson Acceleration for Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces Anderson Acceleration (AA) as an effective method to enhance the convergence properties of reinforcement learning algorithms. We demonstrate that AA, a well-established technique from numerical analysis for accelerating fixed-point iterations, can be seamlessly integrated with standard reinforcement learning methods such as Q-learning and policy gradient approaches. Our theoretical analysis reveals that AA reduces the spectral radius of the iteration operator, leading to faster convergence rates while maintaining solution quality. Empirical evaluations across various benchmark environments show that AA-enhanced algorithms consistently achieve better sample efficiency, requiring 20-40% fewer interactions to reach performance thresholds compared to their non-accelerated counterparts. The method is particularly effective in environments with sparse rewards or long temporal dependencies. Additionally, we provide practical guidelines for hyperparameter selection and demonstrate that AA introduces minimal computational overhead while being compatible with existing deep reinforcement learning architectures. Our results suggest that Anderson Acceleration represents a promising approach for improving the efficiency of reinforcement learning algorithms in both tabular and function approximation settings.

Local Label Propagation for Large-Scale Semi-Supervised Learning

Semi-supervised learning addresses the common challenge of leveraging limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data to improve model performance. However, traditional label propagation methods face significant computational and memory constraints when applied to large-scale datasets. In this paper, we propose Local Label Propagation (LLP), a novel algorithm that enables efficient semi-supervised learning on massive datasets by operating within localized neighborhoods of the feature space. Our approach constructs sparse similarity graphs using approximate nearest neighbor techniques and performs label diffusion within these constrained regions, dramatically reducing computational complexity from O(n²) to O(n log n) while maintaining competitive accuracy. Experimental results across diverse large-scale benchmarks demonstrate that LLP outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods in both efficiency and effectiveness, achieving up to 12% improvement in classification accuracy with orders of magnitude faster runtime. Furthermore, LLP exhibits robust performance even with extremely limited labeled examples (as low as 0.1% of the dataset). Our method provides a practical solution for applying semi-supervised learning to real-world problems involving millions of samples where existing approaches become computationally prohibitive.

Revisiting Causality Inference in Memory-less Transition Networks

This paper reexamines fundamental approaches to causality inference in memory-less transition networks, where state transitions depend solely on the current state rather than historical information. We identify critical limitations in existing methodologies that often conflate correlation with causation in these simplified network structures. By leveraging recent advances in counterfactual analysis and do-calculus, we propose a novel framework that distinguishes genuine causal relationships from spurious associations in memory-less systems. Our approach introduces a time-indexed intervention method that exploits the memory-less property to identify minimal causal structures without requiring extensive historical data. Through extensive simulations on synthetic networks and validation on three real-world datasets from communication networks, gene regulatory systems, and financial transaction graphs, we demonstrate that our method achieves a 37% improvement in causal identification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, we establish theoretical bounds on the minimum observation requirements for reliable causal inference in memory-less transition networks. These findings have significant implications for causal discovery in Markovian systems where intervention experiments are costly or infeasible.

End-to-End Semi-Supervised Object Detection with Soft Teacher

Semi-supervised learning has shown great promise in reducing the annotation burden for object detection tasks, yet many existing approaches rely on complex multi-stage pipelines that are difficult to optimize. In this paper, we present Soft Teacher, a simple yet effective end-to-end semi-supervised object detection framework that seamlessly integrates teacher-student mutual learning into a single training pipeline. Our approach leverages a teacher model to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, while employing two key innovations: (1) a soft pseudo-label mechanism that retains the probabilistic distribution of classification and regression targets, preserving valuable uncertainty information typically lost in hard label assignments; and (2) a confidence-based pseudo-label filtering strategy that dynamically selects high-quality pseudo-boxes to mitigate confirmation bias. Through extensive experiments on the COCO dataset under various low-annotation regimes (1%, 5%, and 10%), we demonstrate that Soft Teacher consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods by significant margins, achieving up to 6.2% absolute improvement in mAP. Furthermore, our method exhibits strong performance even when trained with just 1% of labeled data, matching the accuracy of fully-supervised models that use 10× more annotations. This work establishes a new benchmark for semi-supervised object detection and provides insights into effectively leveraging unlabeled data for detection tasks.

Autobahn: Automorphism-based Graph Neural Nets

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning on non-Euclidean data, but many existing architectures struggle to capture the complex symmetries inherent in graph structures. In this paper, we introduce Autobahn, a novel GNN framework that explicitly leverages graph automorphisms to enhance representation learning. Autobahn incorporates automorphism detection and utilization within its message-passing mechanism, enabling the network to recognize and preserve structural symmetries during feature aggregation. Our approach extends beyond the limitations of traditional GNNs by identifying structurally equivalent nodes and enforcing consistent representations across automorphic subgraphs. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets spanning molecular property prediction, social network analysis, and protein function classification, we demonstrate that Autobahn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art GNN architectures. Our model achieves an average improvement of 8.3% in classification accuracy and 12.7% in regression tasks while maintaining computational efficiency. Theoretical analysis confirms that Autobahn achieves greater expressive power than message-passing neural networks bounded by the Weisfeiler-Lehman isomorphism test. These results establish Autobahn as a powerful advancement in graph representation learning, particularly for applications where structural symmetries play a crucial role.

A New Framework for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning -- Centralized Training and Exploration with Decentralized Execution via Policy Distillation

This paper introduces a novel framework for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) that addresses the fundamental challenge of balancing centralized coordination with decentralized execution. Our approach, Centralized Training and Exploration with Decentralized Execution via Policy Distillation (CTED), leverages the strengths of centralized learning while maintaining the practical benefits of decentralized operation during deployment. We first train a centralized policy with full observability that effectively captures joint action dynamics and resolves coordination issues. This centralized policy then guides exploration for individual agent policies through a policy distillation mechanism, transferring the strategic knowledge to decentralized agents that operate with local observations only. Experimental results across various multi-agent environments, including cooperative navigation, predator-prey scenarios, and StarCraft II micromanagement tasks, demonstrate that CTED significantly outperforms existing MARL approaches. Our framework shows particular strength in scenarios requiring sophisticated coordination and communication, achieving up to 45% performance improvement over state-of-the-art baselines while reducing sample complexity by approximately 30%. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights into the convergence properties of our distillation process and analyze the trade-offs between centralized and decentralized paradigms. CTED offers a promising direction for developing MARL systems that can effectively handle complex real-world applications requiring coordinated behavior from independent agents.

Safe Exploration in Finite Markov Decision Processes with Gaussian Processes

This paper addresses the challenge of safe exploration in finite Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), where an agent must learn to maximize rewards while respecting safety constraints. We propose a novel approach that combines the sample efficiency of Gaussian Processes (GPs) with rigorous safety guarantees for reinforcement learning in unknown environments. Our method constructs confidence bounds on both the reward function and the probability of visiting unsafe states, allowing the agent to systematically explore the safe region of the state space while avoiding potentially catastrophic outcomes. We formulate the safe exploration problem as a constrained optimization task and develop an algorithm that adaptively refines its policy based on collected data. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that our approach achieves sublinear regret while maintaining safety constraints with high probability. Empirical evaluations on benchmark domains show that our method successfully balances exploration and safety, outperforming existing safe reinforcement learning approaches in terms of cumulative reward without violating constraints. These results highlight the effectiveness of Gaussian Processes for uncertainty quantification in safety-critical reinforcement learning tasks.

Adversarial Generation of Training Examples: Applications to Moving Vehicle License Plate Recognition

This paper presents a novel approach to addressing the challenge of limited training data in automated license plate recognition (ALPR) systems for moving vehicles. We introduce an adversarial framework for generating synthetic training examples that significantly improves recognition accuracy under challenging real-world conditions. Our method employs a generative adversarial network (GAN) architecture specifically designed to create realistic license plate images that incorporate various degradation factors encountered in moving vehicle scenarios, including motion blur, varying illumination, and perspective distortion. Through extensive experimentation on multiple public datasets, we demonstrate that augmenting training data with our adversarially generated examples reduces character recognition error rates by 27% compared to conventional data augmentation techniques. Furthermore, our approach shows particular efficacy in challenging scenarios such as high-speed vehicles and adverse weather conditions, where recognition accuracy improved by up to 35%. The proposed method requires minimal additional computational resources during inference and can be readily integrated into existing ALPR systems. Our work provides valuable insights into leveraging adversarial techniques for improving computer vision systems in domains with limited training data and challenging imaging conditions.

DCNN-GAN: Reconstructing Realistic Image from fMRI

This paper introduces DCNN-GAN, a novel framework for reconstructing naturalistic visual stimuli from functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data. While previous approaches to visual reconstruction from brain activity have shown promise, they often produce blurry or distorted images that lack fine-grained details. Our proposed architecture combines deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) with generative adversarial networks (GANs) to overcome these limitations. The DCNN component extracts hierarchical representations from fMRI data, capturing both low-level visual features and high-level semantic content, while the GAN framework ensures the generation of sharp, realistic images through adversarial training. We evaluated our model on a dataset of fMRI recordings from participants viewing natural scenes, achieving significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics (SSIM, PSNR) and human perceptual evaluations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DCNN-GAN can reconstruct fine details such as textures, edges, and complex object boundaries that were previously unattainable. These results represent an important step toward more accurate neural decoding and could enable applications in neuroscience, brain-computer interfaces, and clinical settings for patients with communication disorders.

Towards Best Practice in Explaining Neural Network Decisions with LRP

As deep neural networks become increasingly prevalent in critical decision-making systems, the need for transparency and interpretability has emerged as a significant concern. Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) has established itself as a promising technique for explaining neural network decisions by attributing relevance scores to input features. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for best practices in applying LRP across diverse neural architectures and domains. We systematically evaluate various LRP rule configurations on benchmark datasets and real-world applications, identifying key factors that influence explanation quality. Our findings reveal that explanation fidelity depends significantly on network architecture, data characteristics, and specific propagation rules. We propose a novel adaptive LRP approach that dynamically selects appropriate rules based on layer types and network depth, demonstrating superior performance compared to static implementations. Additionally, we establish quantitative metrics for evaluating explanation quality and introduce guidelines for domain-specific LRP applications. This work contributes to the standardization of explanation methods, enabling more reliable and consistent interpretability of neural network decisions in practice, particularly for high-stakes applications where understanding model behavior is crucial.

Unsupervised Learning of Foreground Object Detection

This paper presents a novel approach to foreground object detection that operates in a fully unsupervised manner, eliminating the need for labeled training data. Our method leverages the inherent motion and appearance patterns in video sequences to automatically distinguish foreground objects from background elements. We introduce a two-stream architecture that combines temporal consistency analysis with spatial feature extraction, allowing the model to learn discriminative representations without human annotation. The framework employs contrastive learning to maximize the mutual information between corresponding regions across frames while minimizing it between unrelated regions. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our unsupervised approach achieves competitive performance compared to supervised methods, with only a marginal decrease in accuracy (3-5%) while completely eliminating annotation costs. Our method shows particular robustness in dynamic environments and with moving cameras, where traditional background subtraction techniques often fail. Furthermore, we show that our model can effectively transfer to novel domains without additional training, making it suitable for real-world applications where labeled data is scarce or unavailable. This work represents a significant step toward practical, annotation-free object detection systems.

Smooth PARAFAC Decomposition for Tensor Completion

This paper presents a novel approach to tensor completion through a smooth PARAFAC decomposition framework. Tensor completion, the problem of recovering missing entries in multi-dimensional arrays, has gained significant attention due to its applications in signal processing, computer vision, and data mining. While traditional methods often rely on low-rank assumptions, they frequently struggle with highly incomplete or noisy tensors. Our proposed method integrates smoothness constraints into the PARAFAC (Parallel Factor Analysis) decomposition, effectively regularizing the factor matrices to preserve local structural information. By exploiting the inherent smoothness in many real-world tensor data, our approach achieves more accurate reconstructions, particularly when dealing with limited observations. We develop an efficient alternating optimization algorithm with theoretical convergence guarantees and analyze its computational complexity. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our smooth PARAFAC decomposition consistently outperforms state-of-the-art tensor completion methods, especially in challenging scenarios with high missing rates. The proposed framework offers a promising direction for tensor analysis with incomplete observations in various domains.

Grid Partitioned Attention: Efficient Transformer Approximation with Inductive Bias for High Resolution Detail Generation

Transformer models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generative tasks, but their quadratic computational complexity with respect to sequence length poses significant challenges for high-resolution content generation. In this paper, we introduce Grid Partitioned Attention (GPA), a novel attention mechanism that approximates full self-attention while maintaining linear computational complexity. GPA incorporates an inductive bias by partitioning the attention space into a grid structure, allowing tokens to attend primarily to spatially proximate regions while preserving pathways for global information flow. Our approach dynamically balances local and global attention patterns through learnable parameters that adapt to different generative contexts. Experimental results across multiple domains—including image generation, video synthesis, and 3D modeling—demonstrate that GPA achieves comparable quality to full attention models while reducing memory requirements by up to 85% and inference time by 73%. Notably, GPA excels at preserving fine-grained details in high-resolution outputs (1024×1024 and beyond) where traditional transformers struggle due to memory constraints. This efficiency enables the practical deployment of transformer-based generative models in resource-constrained environments while maintaining the high-fidelity detail generation critical for real-world applications.

Sparse-MLP: A Fully-MLP Architecture with Conditional Computation

This paper introduces Sparse-MLP, a novel neural network architecture that leverages only multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with conditional computation to achieve competitive performance while maintaining computational efficiency. Unlike traditional architectures that rely on convolutions or attention mechanisms, Sparse-MLP dynamically activates only a subset of neurons based on input patterns, enabling sparse computation paths through the network. We formulate a differentiable routing mechanism that learns to selectively engage MLP components during both training and inference, effectively creating input-dependent computational graphs. Our experiments demonstrate that Sparse-MLP achieves comparable accuracy to more complex architectures across image classification, object detection, and natural language processing tasks, while requiring significantly fewer FLOPs during inference. The architecture scales efficiently to larger models and datasets, with sparsity increasing proportionally to model size. Additionally, we show that the learned sparse patterns provide interpretable insights into the model's decision-making process. Sparse-MLP represents a promising direction for building simpler yet powerful neural architectures that balance performance and computational requirements through learned conditional computation.

EVOQUER: Enhancing Temporal Grounding with Video-Pivoted BackQuery Generation

Temporal grounding in videos—the task of localizing specific moments based on natural language queries—remains challenging due to the semantic gap between textual descriptions and visual content. This paper introduces EVOQUER (Enhancing Video-based Temporal grOunding with QUEry Refinement), a novel framework that addresses this challenge through a video-pivoted back-query generation approach. Unlike traditional methods that directly match queries to video segments, EVOQUER implements a bidirectional reasoning mechanism that generates refined queries from video content and then uses these "back-queries" to enhance temporal grounding performance. Our approach leverages a transformer-based architecture to extract rich spatio-temporal features from videos and generate semantically aligned textual descriptions that serve as intermediate representations. These back-queries effectively bridge the modality gap by providing video-grounded language that better corresponds to visual content. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including ActivityNet Captions, Charades-STA, and TACoS demonstrate that EVOQUER significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improving grounding accuracy by 4.2-6.8% across different metrics. Ablation studies confirm that our video-pivoted back-query generation contributes substantially to the performance gains. The proposed approach not only enhances temporal grounding precision but also provides interpretable insights into the model's decision-making process, representing an important advancement in multimodal video understanding.

Feature Importance Ranking for Deep Learning

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable performance across various domains, but their black-box nature often limits interpretability. This paper introduces a novel framework for ranking feature importance in deep neural networks to address this challenge. Our approach combines gradient-based attribution methods with statistical significance testing to produce robust, model-agnostic feature importance rankings. We propose a hierarchical importance scoring mechanism that evaluates features at both local and global levels, accounting for complex feature interactions that traditional methods often overlook. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing feature importance techniques, maintaining ranking stability across model retraining and hyperparameter variations. Furthermore, we show that selectively training on highly-ranked features yields models with comparable performance to those trained on complete feature sets, while using significantly fewer inputs. Our approach provides practitioners with valuable insights into model decision-making processes, facilitating model debugging, feature selection, and responsible AI deployment in critical domains where interpretability is essential.

Using Scene Graph Context to Improve Image Generation

This paper introduces a novel approach to image generation that leverages scene graph representations to enhance the quality and semantic coherence of generated images. Scene graphs, which explicitly model objects and their relationships in a structured format, provide rich contextual information that traditional image generation models often fail to capture. Our method incorporates scene graph context into a deep generative framework through a two-stage architecture: first encoding the scene graph into a contextualized representation, then using this representation to guide the image synthesis process. We demonstrate that this approach leads to significant improvements in both visual quality and semantic fidelity of generated images, particularly for complex scenes with multiple objects and interactions. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in generating images that accurately reflect specified object relationships and spatial arrangements. Furthermore, we show that the structured nature of scene graphs enables fine-grained control over the generation process, allowing users to manipulate specific elements of the scene while maintaining overall coherence. Our work highlights the importance of incorporating explicit relational context in image generation systems and opens new avenues for controllable and interpretable image synthesis.

Self-Supervised Multi-View Learning via Auto-Encoding 3D Transformations

This paper presents a novel self-supervised learning approach for multi-view representation learning that leverages the inherent 3D structure of visual scenes. Our method, which we call 3D-TransformAE, learns meaningful visual representations by auto-encoding geometric transformations between different views of the same 3D object or scene. Unlike previous approaches that rely on contrastive learning or view reconstruction, we explicitly model the 3D transformation space and train the network to predict the relative pose and perspective changes across views. By formulating this as an auto-encoding problem, our framework learns to disentangle viewpoint variations from object identity, resulting in more robust and generalizable representations. We evaluate 3D-TransformAE on several benchmark datasets including ShapeNet, ModelNet40, and real-world multi-view datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art self-supervised methods on downstream tasks such as object recognition, pose estimation, and few-shot learning. Furthermore, we show that our approach requires significantly fewer views during training while achieving better data efficiency and transferability to novel domains. Our results suggest that explicitly modeling 3D transformations provides a strong inductive bias for learning meaningful visual representations without human supervision.

Abstract

This paper presents a novel semi-supervised dimensionality reduction framework for hyperspectral imagery called Joint and Progressive Subspace Analysis with Spatial-Spectral Manifold Alignment (JPSA). The proposed method addresses the challenges of high dimensionality and limited labeled samples in hyperspectral image analysis by effectively integrating spatial-spectral information and manifold structure preservation. JPSA operates through a joint learning architecture that simultaneously optimizes a supervised subspace learning module guided by limited labeled samples and an unsupervised subspace learning component that captures the intrinsic data structure from abundant unlabeled samples. A progressive learning strategy is implemented to iteratively refine the subspace projection, allowing for gradual improvement of feature representation. The key innovation of JPSA lies in its spatial-spectral manifold alignment mechanism, which ensures that the learned low-dimensional representation preserves both the spatial coherence and spectral characteristics inherent in hyperspectral data. Extensive experiments on three benchmark hyperspectral datasets demonstrate that JPSA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art dimensionality reduction methods, particularly in scenarios with extremely limited labeled samples. The proposed approach not only enhances classification accuracy but also improves computational efficiency for subsequent hyperspectral image analysis tasks, making it particularly valuable for practical remote sensing applications.

GAN-Based Interactive Reinforcement Learning from Demonstration and Human Evaluative Feedback

This paper presents a novel approach that integrates Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) with interactive reinforcement learning to enable efficient learning from both demonstrations and human evaluative feedback. Our framework addresses the significant challenge of sample inefficiency in traditional reinforcement learning by leveraging human expertise in two complementary ways: through expert demonstrations that provide initial guidance and real-time evaluative feedback that refines agent behavior. The GAN architecture serves a dual purpose—the generator learns to mimic expert demonstrations while the discriminator evaluates the quality of generated actions, gradually aligning with human preferences through interactive feedback sessions. Experimental results across various domains demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms both standalone imitation learning and conventional reinforcement learning methods, reducing the required number of environment interactions by up to 70% while achieving superior task performance. The framework shows particular promise in tasks with sparse rewards and complex action spaces, where pure exploration strategies typically struggle. Additionally, we analyze the impact of different feedback mechanisms on learning efficiency and propose guidelines for effective human-agent interaction protocols. This work contributes to the growing field of human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning by providing a scalable approach that efficiently combines the complementary strengths of demonstration data and evaluative feedback.

A Short Review on Data Modelling for Vector Fields

This paper presents a comprehensive review of contemporary approaches to data modelling for vector fields, an increasingly important area at the intersection of computational mathematics, physics, and data science. We examine the evolution of vector field modelling techniques from traditional analytical methods to modern data-driven approaches. The review categorizes methodologies into three primary frameworks: basis function expansions, deep learning architectures, and hybrid physics-informed models. We analyze how these approaches address the inherent challenges of vector field representation, including preservation of divergence and curl properties, multi-scale phenomena, and boundary condition enforcement. Special attention is given to recent advances in neural network architectures specifically designed for vector field approximation, including vector-valued neural networks and equivariant models that respect underlying physical symmetries. The paper also discusses applications across diverse domains including fluid dynamics, electromagnetic field analysis, and geophysical modelling, highlighting how domain-specific constraints can be incorporated into modelling frameworks. Finally, we identify promising research directions and outstanding challenges in the field, particularly regarding computational efficiency, physical consistency, and uncertainty quantification in vector field modelling.

Inner and Inter Label Propagation: Salient Object Detection in the Wild

Salient object detection (SOD) remains challenging in unconstrained environments due to complex backgrounds, varying illumination conditions, and multiple objects with different scales. In this paper, we propose a novel framework called Inner and Inter Label Propagation (IILP) that addresses these challenges by effectively leveraging both inner-image and inter-image contextual information. Our approach consists of two complementary propagation mechanisms: (1) Inner Label Propagation, which explores relationships between pixels within the same image to enhance boundary details and spatial coherence, and (2) Inter Label Propagation, which transfers knowledge across similar image regions in the training set to improve robustness to variations. The IILP framework integrates these mechanisms through a dual-stream architecture with cross-attention modules that dynamically balance local and global contextual cues. Extensive experiments on five challenging benchmarks (DUTS-TE, DUT-OMRON, ECSSD, HKU-IS, and PASCAL-S) demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving improvements of 2.1% in mean F-measure and 1.8% in mean E-measure. Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of each component, and qualitative results showcase our method's superior performance in challenging scenarios with complex backgrounds, multiple objects, and varying lighting conditions. The proposed IILP framework provides a new perspective for SOD in unconstrained environments.

Learning to Separate: Detecting Heavily-Occluded Objects in Urban Scenes

Object detection in urban environments presents significant challenges due to frequent occlusions, particularly in crowded scenes where objects overlap substantially. This paper introduces a novel framework for detecting heavily-occluded objects in urban settings by learning to separate overlapping object instances. Our approach, which we call OcclusionNet, combines instance-aware feature disentanglement with an occlusion reasoning module that explicitly models the relationships between overlapping objects. We propose a new occlusion-aware loss function that guides the network to focus on discriminative features even when only small portions of objects are visible. Extensive experiments on challenging urban datasets, including Cityscapes and our newly collected Urban Occlusion Dataset (UOD), demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art detectors on heavily-occluded instances (improving average precision by 8.2% on objects with >70% occlusion) while maintaining competitive performance on non-occluded objects. Qualitative results show that OcclusionNet successfully identifies objects even when only 15-20% of their surface is visible, making it particularly valuable for autonomous driving and urban surveillance applications where reliable detection of partially-visible objects is critical for safety.

Graph and Temporal Convolutional Networks for 3D Multi-person Pose Estimation in Monocular Videos

This paper presents a novel approach for 3D multi-person pose estimation from monocular videos by leveraging both spatial and temporal information through a combination of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) and temporal convolutional networks (TCNs). While significant progress has been made in single-person 3D pose estimation, multi-person scenarios remain challenging due to occlusions, depth ambiguities, and complex interactions. Our method addresses these challenges by first detecting and tracking 2D human keypoints across video frames, then utilizing a two-stream network architecture to reconstruct accurate 3D poses. The spatial stream employs GCNs to model the structural relationships between human joints, while the temporal stream uses TCNs to capture motion dynamics and ensure temporal consistency. We propose a cross-attention mechanism that effectively integrates these complementary features, enabling robust pose estimation even in crowded scenes. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks including MuPoTS-3D and JTA demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 15% improvement in 3D pose accuracy while maintaining real-time performance. Additionally, we contribute a new annotated dataset to facilitate research in challenging multi-person scenarios with complex interactions. Our code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available to the research community.

Diagnostics in Semantic Segmentation

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for diagnosing and evaluating semantic segmentation models. While recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved semantic segmentation performance, systematic approaches to analyze failure modes and model behavior remain underdeveloped. We introduce a suite of diagnostic tools that provide insights beyond traditional metrics like mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and pixel accuracy. Our framework examines model performance across multiple dimensions: boundary precision, small object detection, class confusion patterns, texture versus shape bias, and robustness to various image perturbations. Through extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including PASCAL VOC, Cityscapes, and ADE20K, we identify common failure patterns across different architectures (CNNs, Transformers) and training paradigms. Our analysis reveals that contemporary models still struggle with object boundaries, rare classes, and semantically similar categories despite high overall accuracy. We demonstrate how these diagnostics can guide targeted model improvements, resulting in architectures with more balanced performance across challenging cases. The proposed diagnostic toolkit facilitates better model selection, more nuanced comparison between approaches, and clearer directions for future research in semantic segmentation.

Are Powerful Graph Neural Nets Necessary? A Dissection on Graph Classification

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as the dominant paradigm for graph classification tasks, with increasingly complex architectures being proposed to overcome the theoretical limitations of message-passing frameworks. However, the practical necessity of such powerful models remains questionable. In this work, we present a systematic dissection of graph classification methods, comparing state-of-the-art GNN architectures against simpler alternatives across diverse benchmark datasets. Our analysis reveals several surprising findings: (1) many benchmark datasets contain structural artifacts that allow even basic models to achieve competitive performance; (2) simple architectural modifications to standard GNNs often match or exceed the performance of theoretically more expressive models; and (3) the gap between complex and simple models narrows significantly when controlling for hyperparameter optimization and training procedures. Through ablation studies and interpretability analyses, we identify key factors that contribute to model performance beyond expressive power, including feature preprocessing, pooling mechanisms, and inductive biases. Our findings challenge the prevailing assumption that more powerful GNNs are necessary for effective graph classification, suggesting that researchers should carefully evaluate model complexity against practical performance gains and computational costs.

RGL-NET: A Recurrent Graph Learning Framework for Progressive Part Assembly

This paper introduces RGL-NET, a novel recurrent graph learning framework designed for progressive part assembly tasks. The framework addresses the complex challenge of assembling multi-part objects by leveraging graph-based representations to model both the geometric and relational properties of individual components. RGL-NET employs a recurrent architecture that iteratively refines assembly decisions by maintaining a dynamic memory of part relationships and assembly state. Our approach integrates graph neural networks with recurrent mechanisms to capture both spatial relationships and sequential dependencies in the assembly process. Through extensive experiments on diverse assembly datasets, we demonstrate that RGL-NET outperforms existing methods by achieving higher assembly accuracy while requiring fewer correction steps. The framework shows particular strength in handling complex assemblies with numerous interdependent parts and ambiguous connection points. Additionally, we present a new benchmark dataset for evaluating progressive assembly performance across various object categories. Our results indicate that RGL-NET's ability to learn from partial assemblies and predict optimal next steps makes it particularly suitable for robotic assembly applications and computer-aided design systems.

An Empirical Study of Graph-Based Approaches for Semi-Supervised Time Series Classification

Time series classification remains a challenging problem, particularly in scenarios where labeled data is scarce. This paper presents a comprehensive empirical study of graph-based approaches for semi-supervised time series classification, where we leverage both labeled and unlabeled data to improve classification performance. We investigate various graph construction methods specifically tailored for time series data, including dynamic time warping-based similarity graphs, visibility graphs, and recurrence networks. Through extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets from domains such as healthcare, finance, and industrial monitoring, we evaluate the effectiveness of different graph-based label propagation algorithms and assess their robustness to varying ratios of labeled to unlabeled data. Our findings reveal that graph-based semi-supervised learning can significantly outperform traditional supervised approaches when labeled instances are limited, with performance improvements of up to 27% in classification accuracy. We also identify key factors influencing the success of these methods, including time series characteristics, choice of similarity measure, and graph sparsification techniques. This study provides practical guidelines for researchers and practitioners seeking to apply graph-based semi-supervised learning to time series classification problems with limited labeled data.

Deep Learning-Based Automated Image Segmentation for Concrete Petrographic Analysis

This study presents a novel deep learning framework for automated image segmentation in concrete petrographic analysis. Petrographic examination of concrete microstructure is critical for quality assessment and durability prediction, but traditional manual methods are time-consuming and subject to operator variability. Our approach employs convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to accurately identify and segment key concrete constituents including aggregates, cement paste, air voids, and microcracks from thin-section microscopy images. The proposed model was trained on a diverse dataset of 5,000 annotated petrographic images representing various concrete mixtures and deterioration conditions. Performance evaluation demonstrated segmentation accuracy of 94.3%, significantly outperforming traditional threshold-based techniques (76.8%) and conventional machine learning methods (85.2%). The system successfully quantified phase distributions, void characteristics, and crack patterns, enabling rapid assessment of concrete quality parameters. This automated approach reduces analysis time from hours to minutes while maintaining high reliability, providing a powerful tool for both research and practical applications in concrete durability assessment and failure analysis. The framework's ability to process large image datasets efficiently opens new possibilities for comprehensive microstructural characterization of concrete materials.

Reflective Decoding Network for Image Captioning

This paper introduces the Reflective Decoding Network (RDN), a novel architecture for image captioning that enhances caption generation through an iterative refinement process. Unlike conventional encoder-decoder frameworks that generate captions in a single pass, our proposed RDN incorporates a reflection mechanism that allows the model to review and refine its outputs multiple times before producing the final caption. The network consists of a visual encoder that extracts rich semantic features from images, coupled with a reflective decoder that generates initial captions and then iteratively refines them by attending to both visual features and previous caption versions. Through this reflective process, the model addresses limitations in semantic relevance and descriptive accuracy found in traditional approaches. Extensive experiments on MS COCO and Flickr30K datasets demonstrate that RDN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across standard evaluation metrics, with particularly significant improvements in CIDEr and SPICE scores. Human evaluations further confirm that captions generated by our approach are more descriptive, accurate, and naturally aligned with human perception. Our ablation studies highlight the contribution of each component in the reflection mechanism, providing insights for future research in image captioning.

Domain-adversarial neural networks to address the appearance variability of histopathology images

Histopathology image analysis is crucial for cancer diagnosis and prognosis, but suffers from significant appearance variability due to differences in staining protocols, scanner types, and tissue preparation across laboratories. This variability poses a major challenge for developing robust deep learning models that can generalize across different medical centers. In this study, we propose a domain-adversarial neural network (DANN) approach to address this challenge. Our method simultaneously optimizes a feature extractor network to perform the primary histopathology classification task while making the extracted features invariant to the source domain through adversarial training. We evaluated our approach on multi-center datasets comprising H&E-stained tissue images from breast, colon, and prostate cancer specimens. The DANN model demonstrated significantly improved cross-domain generalization compared to conventional convolutional neural networks, achieving an average increase of 12.3% in accuracy when tested on unseen domains. Furthermore, t-SNE visualization of the learned feature space confirmed effective domain-invariant representations. Our findings suggest that domain-adversarial training offers a promising solution for developing robust histopathology image analysis systems that can maintain consistent performance across varying laboratory conditions without requiring explicit domain adaptation or normalization techniques.

Bidirectional Modeling and Analysis of Brain Aging with Normalizing Flows

This study introduces a novel approach to modeling and analyzing brain aging through bidirectional normalizing flows, addressing limitations in current unidirectional models. We present a framework that simultaneously captures both forward (young-to-old) and reverse (old-to-young) aging trajectories in neuroimaging data, providing a comprehensive characterization of age-related brain changes. Using T1-weighted MRI scans from 11,729 subjects across the lifespan (ages 18-90), our invertible neural network architecture learns a diffeomorphic mapping between age groups while preserving anatomical plausibility. The bidirectional model demonstrates superior performance in age prediction (MAE of 2.8 years) compared to unidirectional approaches and reveals asymmetric patterns in aging trajectories, suggesting that brain aging is not simply a time-reversed process of development. Our analysis identifies distinct neuroanatomical regions with varying rates of age-related change and resilience, with particular emphasis on volumetric changes in the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and white matter integrity. The model's ability to generate synthetic brain images at arbitrary ages provides a valuable tool for longitudinal studies and early detection of neurodegenerative conditions. This work contributes to our understanding of normal brain aging processes and establishes a foundation for distinguishing pathological from healthy aging trajectories.

Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge

Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a powerful technique for transferring knowledge from complex teacher models to more compact student networks, yet the fundamental question of what constitutes "knowledge" in this process remains inadequately formalized. This paper introduces a novel framework for quantifying and characterizing the knowledge transferred during distillation. We propose a mathematical formulation that decomposes knowledge into structural, relational, and decision boundary components, allowing us to measure knowledge transfer efficiency across different architectures and domains. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, we demonstrate that our quantification metrics strongly correlate with distillation performance. Our analysis reveals that effective knowledge transfer depends not merely on matching logits or feature representations, but on preserving specific knowledge types that vary by task complexity and model architecture. By identifying which knowledge components contribute most significantly to performance, we provide theoretical insights that explain previously observed empirical phenomena in KD and offer practical guidelines for designing more effective distillation strategies. Our framework advances the understanding of knowledge distillation beyond its black-box application, establishing a foundation for more principled approaches to model compression.

GNN-FiLM: Graph Neural Networks with Feature-wise Linear Modulation

In this paper, we introduce GNN-FiLM, a novel architecture that enhances graph neural networks by incorporating Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM). While graph neural networks have demonstrated remarkable performance in various graph-based tasks, they often struggle with capturing complex feature interactions across nodes and effectively conditioning on global graph properties. Our proposed GNN-FiLM framework addresses these limitations by dynamically modulating the feature representations at each layer through affine transformations conditioned on graph-level context. This approach enables more expressive feature transformations and adaptive computation based on graph characteristics. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets spanning node classification, graph classification, and link prediction tasks, we demonstrate that GNN-FiLM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art GNN architectures. Our ablation studies reveal that the feature-wise modulation mechanism significantly improves the model's capacity to capture long-range dependencies and complex structural patterns. Furthermore, we provide theoretical analysis showing that GNN-FiLM enhances the representational power of standard message-passing neural networks. These results establish GNN-FiLM as an effective and flexible enhancement to the graph neural network paradigm.

Visual Translation Embedding Network for Visual Relation Detection

Visual relation detection is a crucial task for image understanding, requiring models to identify not only objects but also the relationships between them. In this paper, we present the Visual Translation Embedding Network (VTransE), a novel framework that formulates visual relationships as translations in a semantic embedding space. Our key insight is that relationships between objects can be represented as translation vectors between object embeddings, similar to how word embeddings capture semantic relationships in natural language processing. The VTransE model first detects objects in an image and then learns to map the visual features of subject and object entities into a common embedding space where relationship predicates are modeled as translation operations. This approach effectively captures the compositional nature of visual relationships while maintaining computational efficiency. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including Visual Genome and VRD, we demonstrate that our translation embedding framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in zero-shot scenarios where relationships were not seen during training. Our model achieves significant improvements in recall and mean average precision while requiring fewer parameters than competing approaches. The results suggest that translation embeddings provide a powerful representation for modeling the rich semantic structure of visual relationships in complex scenes.

MiniVLM: A Smaller and Faster Vision-Language Model

This paper introduces MiniVLM, a compact and efficient vision-language model designed to address the computational challenges associated with deploying large-scale multimodal systems. While recent vision-language models have achieved impressive performance on various tasks, their substantial computational requirements and parameter counts limit practical applications. MiniVLM employs a novel architecture that significantly reduces model size while maintaining competitive performance across standard vision-language benchmarks. Through careful design choices including a lightweight vision encoder, an efficient cross-modal fusion mechanism, and knowledge distillation techniques, our model achieves a 75% reduction in parameters and 3.5× inference speedup compared to similarly performing models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MiniVLM performs competitively on visual question answering, image captioning, and visual reasoning tasks despite its compact size. Notably, MiniVLM achieves 92% of the performance of models 4× its size on the VQAv2 benchmark. Our work demonstrates that effective vision-language models need not be resource-intensive, opening possibilities for deployment in resource-constrained environments and real-time applications.

A Disentangled Recognition and Nonlinear Dynamics Model for Unsupervised Learning

We present a novel framework for unsupervised learning that integrates disentangled representation learning with nonlinear dynamics modeling. Our approach addresses a fundamental challenge in representation learning: discovering interpretable latent variables that capture both the static and temporal structure of complex, high-dimensional data without supervision. The proposed model consists of two complementary components: a recognition model that maps observations to disentangled latent representations, and a dynamics model that captures the nonlinear evolution of these latent variables over time. By enforcing disentanglement through information-theoretic constraints and modeling dynamics with a flexible nonparametric approach, our framework can identify interpretable factors of variation while accurately predicting temporal evolution. We evaluate our method on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing approaches in terms of representation quality, predictive accuracy, and generalization to unseen data. Our results show that the learned representations effectively separate content from dynamics, enabling applications in video prediction, anomaly detection, and controllable generation. This work provides a promising direction for unsupervised learning systems that can understand and model complex real-world phenomena without labeled data.

Data Science for Motion and Time Analysis with Modern Motion Sensor Data

This study explores the intersection of data science methodologies and motion sensor technologies for advanced motion and time analysis. With the proliferation of high-fidelity motion sensors in wearable devices, smartphones, and industrial equipment, unprecedented volumes of kinematic data are now available for analysis. We present a comprehensive framework for processing, analyzing, and extracting meaningful insights from modern motion sensor data streams. Our approach combines signal processing techniques, machine learning algorithms, and statistical methods to address challenges including noise reduction, feature extraction, activity recognition, and temporal pattern detection. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through case studies spanning healthcare applications (gait analysis, fall detection), athletic performance optimization, industrial process monitoring, and human-computer interaction. Results indicate that our integrated data science approach achieves 87% accuracy in complex motion classification tasks and enables the detection of subtle motion anomalies that traditional methods overlook. This research contributes to the growing field of motion analytics by establishing scalable methodologies for transforming raw sensor data into actionable knowledge, with significant implications for health monitoring, performance optimization, and process automation.

Less is More: Accelerating Faster Neural Networks Straight from JPEG

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable performance in computer vision tasks but often require significant computational resources, limiting their deployment on resource-constrained devices. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages the inherent compression properties of JPEG to accelerate neural network inference. Rather than decompressing JPEG images fully before processing, we present a framework that operates directly on the compressed representation, significantly reducing computational overhead. Our method exploits the discrete cosine transform coefficients and quantization structures within JPEG files to construct lightweight network architectures that require fewer operations while maintaining competitive accuracy. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves up to 3.5× speedup with only marginal accuracy loss (0.8-1.2%) compared to conventional models operating on fully decompressed images. For mobile and edge devices, our method reduces memory requirements by 47% and energy consumption by 38% on average. This "less is more" paradigm challenges the standard input preprocessing pipeline and opens new avenues for efficient deep learning in resource-limited environments.

One-Stage Inpainting with Bilateral Attention and Pyramid Filling Block

Image inpainting, the task of filling missing or damaged regions in images with plausible content, remains challenging due to the complexity of generating both structurally coherent and visually realistic results. In this paper, we present a novel one-stage inpainting approach that combines Bilateral Attention and Pyramid Filling Block architectures to address these challenges. Unlike previous two-stage methods that separate structure reconstruction and texture generation, our unified framework simultaneously handles both aspects, reducing computational overhead while maintaining high-quality results. The Bilateral Attention mechanism effectively captures both local and non-local dependencies across image features, enabling the network to reference relevant contextual information from undamaged regions. Meanwhile, our Pyramid Filling Block leverages multi-scale feature extraction to progressively reconstruct missing content from coarse to fine details, ensuring structural consistency and texture fidelity. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both quantitative metrics and visual quality, particularly for large and irregular holes. Our model achieves this superior performance with significantly reduced inference time, making it suitable for real-time applications. The code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available.

Domain Adaptation from Synthesis to Reality in Single-model Detector for Video Smoke Detection

This paper addresses the critical challenge of domain adaptation in video smoke detection systems, specifically the gap between synthetic training data and real-world application environments. While synthetic smoke data offers advantages in controlled generation and annotation, detectors trained solely on such data often underperform when deployed in real-world scenarios due to domain shift. We propose a single-model detection framework that effectively bridges this synthesis-to-reality gap through a novel domain adaptation approach. Our method incorporates adversarial feature alignment at multiple scales combined with a self-supervised consistency regularization mechanism that leverages the temporal nature of smoke dynamics. Experiments conducted on diverse real-world smoke video datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms traditional methods trained exclusively on synthetic data, achieving a 14.7% improvement in mean Average Precision (mAP) and reducing false alarm rates by 23.5%. Additionally, our single-model architecture maintains computational efficiency suitable for real-time applications. The proposed approach enables more reliable smoke detection systems that can be deployed in safety-critical environments without requiring extensive real-world training data, potentially improving early fire detection capabilities across various domains.

Anatomy of Domain Shift Impact on U-Net Layers in MRI Segmentation

Domain shift remains a significant challenge in medical image segmentation, particularly for deep learning models deployed across varied MRI acquisition protocols and scanners. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of how domain shift affects individual layers within U-Net architectures, the de facto standard for medical image segmentation tasks. We systematically investigate the propagation of domain-induced perturbations through the network by analyzing feature activations, gradient flows, and representational changes across different U-Net layers when exposed to out-of-distribution MRI data. Our experiments, conducted on multi-institutional brain MRI datasets with varying acquisition parameters, reveal that domain shifts disproportionately impact different network components: early encoder layers exhibit heightened sensitivity to scanner-specific noise patterns, while deeper layers demonstrate vulnerability to semantic distribution shifts. We quantify these effects through novel layer-specific metrics and propose targeted regularization strategies for different network sections to enhance cross-domain generalization. Our findings provide valuable insights into the mechanics of domain adaptation for medical image segmentation and suggest architectural modifications that can improve U-Net robustness when deployed in heterogeneous clinical environments.

Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Discrete-Continuous Hybrid Action Spaces

This paper addresses the challenge of applying deep reinforcement learning to multi-agent systems with hybrid action spaces, where agents must simultaneously make both discrete and continuous action decisions. While significant progress has been made in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for purely discrete or purely continuous domains, hybrid action spaces remain underexplored despite their prevalence in real-world applications such as robotics, autonomous vehicles, and resource allocation systems. We propose a novel framework, Hybrid-Action Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (HA-MADDPG), that extends MADDPG to effectively handle hybrid action spaces through a specialized neural network architecture that processes discrete and continuous actions in parallel branches while maintaining their interdependencies. Our approach incorporates a hybrid critic design that evaluates joint hybrid actions and a customized exploration strategy that balances discrete action selection with continuous action refinement. Extensive experiments across diverse multi-agent environments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing approaches adapted to hybrid spaces, achieving 15-30% higher cumulative rewards while exhibiting more stable learning dynamics. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees under certain conditions and demonstrate the scalability of our approach to systems with up to 10 agents. The results highlight the potential of our framework to address previously intractable multi-agent decision problems with mixed action requirements.

Topographic VAEs learn Equivariant Capsules

We present Topographic Variational Autoencoders (TopoVAEs), a novel architecture that combines the generative capabilities of VAEs with the representational power of capsule networks. Our approach leverages topographic organization principles to learn latent representations that naturally capture equivariant transformations of visual entities. Unlike traditional capsule networks that require explicit routing mechanisms, TopoVAEs employ a self-organizing latent space where spatially adjacent capsules encode related transformations of the same underlying features. Through extensive experiments on image datasets, we demonstrate that our model successfully disentangles object identity from transformations such as rotation, scale, and position. The equivariant properties of these learned capsules emerge naturally from the topographic constraint, without explicit supervision on transformation parameters. Our results show that TopoVAEs outperform standard VAEs and capsule networks on reconstruction fidelity, interpretability of latent manipulations, and downstream tasks requiring equivariant representations. This work bridges the gap between generative modeling and equivariant representation learning, offering new insights into building models that capture the compositional nature of visual data.

Learning Deep Analysis Dictionaries -- Part II: Convolutional Dictionaries

This paper extends our previous work on learning analysis dictionaries to the convolutional setting, introducing a framework for deep convolutional analysis operators. While synthesis convolutional dictionaries have been extensively studied, the analysis perspective offers distinct advantages in signal representation and processing. We develop a theoretical foundation for convolutional analysis dictionaries and propose an efficient learning algorithm that exploits the inherent structure of these operators. Our approach leverages the translation invariance property of convolutions to significantly reduce computational complexity while maintaining representational power. Experimental results on image restoration, classification, and compression tasks demonstrate that deep convolutional analysis dictionaries outperform their synthesis counterparts, particularly when dealing with structured signals and limited training data. We provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence of our learning algorithm and analyze the relationship between the depth of the dictionary and its representational capacity. This work bridges the gap between traditional analysis operators and modern deep convolutional architectures, offering new insights into the design of efficient signal representations.

DNN2LR: Interpretation-inspired Feature Crossing for Real-world Tabular Data

Despite the remarkable success of deep neural networks (DNNs) in various domains, linear models like logistic regression (LR) remain prevalent in industry applications involving tabular data due to their interpretability and robustness. However, linear models often underperform compared to DNNs because they cannot capture complex feature interactions automatically. In this paper, we propose DNN2LR, a novel framework that leverages the representation power of DNNs to enhance linear models through interpretation-inspired feature crossing. Our approach first trains a DNN on tabular data and then systematically extracts meaningful feature interactions using interpretability techniques. These interactions are transformed into explicit feature crossings that augment the original feature space, enabling a linear model to capture non-linear relationships. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate that our DNN2LR framework significantly improves the performance of linear models, closing the gap with DNNs while maintaining full interpretability. Furthermore, we show that the feature crossings identified by our method align with domain knowledge, providing valuable insights for practitioners. DNN2LR offers a practical solution for industries that require both high predictive performance and model transparency when working with tabular data.

Camera-trap Images Segmentation Using Multi-Layer Robust Principal Component Analysis

This study presents a novel approach to wildlife image segmentation in camera-trap data using a multi-layer robust principal component analysis (ML-RPCA) framework. Camera traps generate vast quantities of images essential for ecological monitoring, but automated processing remains challenging due to environmental variability, poor lighting conditions, and partial occlusions. Our proposed ML-RPCA method addresses these challenges by decomposing camera-trap images into multiple layers representing foreground objects (wildlife), background elements, and noise components. Unlike traditional segmentation techniques that rely heavily on supervised learning with extensive labeled datasets, our approach leverages the mathematical properties of RPCA to separate moving objects from static backgrounds while requiring minimal training data. Experimental results on diverse camera-trap datasets demonstrate that ML-RPCA achieves superior segmentation accuracy (average IoU of 0.87) compared to conventional methods, particularly in challenging low-light conditions and with partially occluded subjects. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of our algorithm makes it suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments. This work contributes to advancing automated wildlife monitoring systems by improving the accuracy and reliability of animal detection and identification in camera-trap imagery.

Unsupervised Speech Representation Learning Using WaveNet Autoencoders

This paper introduces a novel approach to learning speech representations without supervision using WaveNet-based autoencoder architectures.
