In this paper, we present GTEA (Graph Temporal Edge Aggregation), a novel framework for learning representations in temporal interaction graphs that effectively captures both structural and temporal patterns. Our approach introduces an innovative edge aggregation mechanism that preserves temporal ordering while efficiently encoding interaction histories. GTEA employs a hierarchical architecture that first processes local temporal neighborhoods through specialized temporal convolutions, then aggregates these representations to capture global graph dynamics. Through extensive experiments on several real-world datasets spanning domains such as social networks, communication platforms, and financial transaction systems, we demonstrate that GTEA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in node classification, link prediction, and temporal forecasting tasks. Our ablation studies confirm that the temporal edge aggregation component is crucial for capturing meaningful evolutionary patterns in dynamic graphs. GTEA offers not only superior predictive performance but also computational efficiency, making it suitable for large-scale temporal interaction networks with millions of nodes and interactions.

Toward Co-creative Dungeon Generation via Transfer Learning

This paper explores a novel approach to procedural dungeon generation through the integration of transfer learning techniques and co-creative design principles. We present a system that leverages pre-trained models from related domains to generate coherent dungeon layouts while maintaining meaningful collaboration with human designers. Our transfer learning framework adapts knowledge from architectural design, game level patterns, and narrative structures to the specific constraints of dungeon generation. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate how our approach enables non-expert users to produce high-quality dungeons by transferring design knowledge across domains while preserving creative agency. Results show that dungeons generated through our co-creative system exhibit greater structural coherence, narrative integration, and player engagement compared to both fully automated and traditional manual design approaches. We also identify key challenges in balancing algorithmic suggestions with human creative intent and propose a taxonomy of interaction patterns observed during co-creative dungeon design. This work contributes to both computational creativity research and practical game development by establishing a framework for transfer learning in procedural content generation systems that meaningfully collaborate with human designers.

Playing optical tweezers with deep reinforcement learning: in virtual, physical and augmented environments

Optical tweezers are powerful tools for manipulating microscopic particles with high precision, but their control typically requires expert knowledge and manual operation. In this work, we demonstrate the application of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to automate and optimize the control of optical tweezers across three distinct environments: virtual simulations, physical experimental setups, and augmented reality systems. Our approach employs a proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm that learns to manipulate microparticles through complex trajectories while adapting to environmental perturbations. In virtual environments, the agent achieved 95% success rate in particle manipulation tasks, significantly outperforming traditional control methods. When transferred to physical optical tweezers, the DRL agent demonstrated robust generalization, successfully completing intricate manipulation tasks despite differences between simulation and reality. Finally, in an augmented environment combining real-time feedback with virtual elements, the agent exhibited adaptive behavior, responding to dynamic changes in experimental conditions. This work establishes a framework for intelligent optical manipulation that reduces human intervention, enhances experimental throughput, and enables applications previously limited by manual control constraints. Our findings highlight the potential of DRL to revolutionize microscale manipulation across scientific disciplines, from biological sample handling to advanced materials assembly.

Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Air-to-Air Combat

This paper presents a novel approach to autonomous air-to-air combat using hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) techniques. Traditional reinforcement learning methods often struggle with the high-dimensional state spaces, long time horizons, and complex decision-making required in aerial combat scenarios. Our hierarchical framework decomposes the combat problem into a multi-level structure consisting of strategic planning, tactical maneuvering, and low-level flight control actions. By implementing a combination of temporal abstraction through options frameworks and spatial abstraction via state aggregation, our approach significantly reduces learning complexity while maintaining combat effectiveness. Experiments conducted in high-fidelity simulation environments demonstrate that our HRL agents outperform both conventional controllers and flat reinforcement learning approaches across multiple combat scenarios. The hierarchical agents show superior adaptability to adversarial tactics, better energy management, and more effective weapons employment. Additionally, the interpretable nature of the learned hierarchical policies provides valuable insights for tactical analysis and training applications. This work represents a significant step toward autonomous systems capable of executing complex air combat maneuvers in dynamic and uncertain environments.

Spectral Image Segmentation with Global Appearance Modeling

This paper presents a novel approach to spectral image segmentation that integrates global appearance modeling to improve segmentation accuracy and robustness. Unlike traditional methods that rely primarily on local spectral features, our approach constructs a comprehensive appearance model that captures both spectral characteristics and global contextual information across the entire image domain. We formulate the segmentation problem within a variational framework where a global appearance term regularizes the local spectral clustering process. The proposed method employs spectral embedding techniques to map high-dimensional hyperspectral data into a lower-dimensional manifold while preserving essential structural relationships. Our global appearance model incorporates spatial coherence constraints and adaptive region modeling to handle the inherent variability in spectral imagery. Experimental results on benchmark hyperspectral datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation methods, achieving an average improvement of 12% in segmentation accuracy and showing particular robustness to noise and illumination variations. The method proves especially effective for applications in remote sensing, medical imaging, and material identification where spectral heterogeneity poses significant challenges to conventional segmentation techniques.

CI-Net: Contextual Information for Joint Semantic Segmentation and Depth Estimation

This paper presents CI-Net, a novel deep learning architecture designed for the joint task of semantic segmentation and monocular depth estimation. We propose a unified framework that leverages shared contextual information between these two complementary vision tasks to enhance overall performance. CI-Net employs a dual-branch encoder-decoder structure with specialized context integration modules that facilitate bidirectional information flow between the segmentation and depth estimation pathways. Our architecture incorporates multi-scale feature fusion and attention mechanisms to effectively capture both local details and global scene understanding. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including Cityscapes, KITTI, and NYUv2 demonstrate that CI-Net outperforms single-task networks and existing multi-task approaches. The proposed model achieves state-of-the-art results with improvements of 3.2% in mean IoU for segmentation and 7.5% reduction in depth error metrics, while maintaining computational efficiency. Furthermore, our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the contextual information sharing strategy, highlighting how depth boundaries inform segmentation edges and semantic labels guide depth prediction in geometrically complex regions. CI-Net provides a robust foundation for scene understanding tasks in autonomous driving and robotic navigation applications.

Optimization of Graph Neural Networks with Natural Gradient Descent

This paper introduces a novel optimization approach for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) using Natural Gradient Descent (NGD). While GNNs have demonstrated remarkable performance on graph-structured data, their training often suffers from inefficiencies due to the complex loss landscape and the interdependence of node representations. We propose adapting NGD, which accounts for the information geometry of the parameter space, to the specific challenges of GNN optimization. Our method computes the Fisher Information Matrix in a computationally efficient manner by leveraging the sparse structure of graph data. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our NGD-optimized GNNs converge significantly faster than those trained with traditional first-order methods, requiring 30-50% fewer iterations while achieving comparable or superior accuracy. Furthermore, our approach shows particular advantages for heterogeneous and large-scale graphs where traditional optimizers often struggle. We provide theoretical analysis establishing convergence guarantees and practical implementation guidelines to balance computational overhead with optimization benefits. This work represents an important step toward more efficient training regimes for graph neural architectures.

Quantization of Deep Neural Networks for Accurate Edge Computing

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for optimizing deep neural networks (DNNs) through quantization techniques specifically designed for edge computing environments. We address the fundamental challenge of deploying computationally intensive DNNs on resource-constrained edge devices while maintaining inference accuracy. Our approach introduces a novel mixed-precision quantization scheme that dynamically assigns bit-widths to different network layers based on their sensitivity to quantization errors. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves up to 8× model compression and 6× inference speedup across various CNN and transformer architectures, with less than 1% accuracy degradation compared to full-precision models. We further propose a hardware-aware optimization pipeline that adapts quantization parameters to specific edge device constraints. Extensive evaluations on multiple datasets, including ImageNet, COCO, and custom industrial datasets, show that our approach outperforms existing quantization methods in the accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Our framework enables practical deployment of state-of-the-art DNNs on edge devices with limited computational resources, memory, and power budgets, facilitating real-time applications in autonomous systems, mobile devices, and IoT environments.

Variational Autoencoders and Nonlinear ICA: A Unifying Framework

This paper presents a theoretical framework that establishes connections between variational autoencoders (VAEs) and nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA). While these methods have been developed in parallel for unsupervised representation learning, their formal relationship has remained largely unexplored. We demonstrate that VAEs can be interpreted as a form of nonlinear ICA under specific conditions, particularly when the generative model incorporates appropriate latent variable priors and decoder structures. Our analysis reveals that the variational objective in VAEs implicitly encourages the disentanglement of statistically independent factors in the data, similar to the explicit goals of nonlinear ICA. We propose modifications to the standard VAE framework that strengthen this connection and enhance identifiability of the latent representations. Through both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation on synthetic and real-world datasets, we show that our unified perspective leads to models that achieve improved disentanglement and more interpretable representations compared to standard approaches. This framework provides new insights into the theoretical foundations of deep generative models and offers practical guidance for designing more effective unsupervised representation learning algorithms.

Improved BiGAN Training with Marginal Likelihood Equalization

Bidirectional Generative Adversarial Networks (BiGANs) extend the traditional GAN framework by simultaneously learning an encoder network alongside the generator and discriminator, enabling inference of latent representations for observed data. Despite their theoretical appeal, BiGANs face significant training instabilities that limit their practical applications. This paper introduces Marginal Likelihood Equalization (MLE), a novel training methodology that addresses fundamental imbalances in the adversarial learning process of BiGANs. Our approach dynamically adjusts the learning objective to ensure that the marginal likelihoods in both data and latent spaces remain balanced throughout training. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that MLE promotes more stable convergence by preventing mode collapse and ensuring consistent gradient flow to both the encoder and generator networks. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that BiGANs trained with our MLE approach achieve up to 37% improvement in reconstruction fidelity, 28% better feature learning performance, and significantly more stable training dynamics compared to standard BiGAN implementations. Our method requires minimal computational overhead while substantially improving the quality and utility of the learned bidirectional mappings, making BiGANs more viable for practical applications in representation learning and image generation.

Abstract: LGA-RCNN: Loss-Guided Attention for Object Detection

We present Loss-Guided Attention Region-based Convolutional Neural Network (LGA-RCNN), a novel approach that enhances object detection performance by dynamically allocating computational resources based on detection loss patterns. Our method introduces an attention mechanism that adaptively focuses on challenging regions where the model exhibits higher detection losses, effectively addressing the imbalance between easy and difficult examples during training. LGA-RCNN incorporates a differentiable attention module that generates spatial attention maps guided by localization and classification losses, allowing the network to concentrate feature extraction on areas requiring more detailed analysis. Through extensive experiments on COCO and PASCAL VOC datasets, we demonstrate that LGA-RCNN consistently outperforms standard RCNN architectures, achieving 2.3% improvement in mAP on COCO test-dev and 1.8% on PASCAL VOC 2007, with minimal additional computational overhead. Our approach is architecture-agnostic and can be integrated into various existing detection frameworks. Ablation studies confirm that the performance gains stem from the model's enhanced ability to focus on challenging instances, particularly small objects and those in cluttered scenes, leading to more accurate bounding box regression and classification.

A Generative Adversarial Network for AI-Aided Chair Design

This paper presents a novel application of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to furniture design, specifically focusing on chair creation. We develop a specialized GAN architecture that learns from a curated dataset of 10,000 iconic and contemporary chair designs spanning various styles and periods. Our model, ChairGAN, demonstrates the ability to generate novel chair designs that balance aesthetic appeal, structural feasibility, and ergonomic considerations. Through a combination of 3D voxel representation and 2D projection techniques, the network successfully captures both form and functional elements essential to chair design. We introduce a multi-objective discriminator that evaluates generated designs based on stylistic coherence, structural integrity, and human-centered design principles. Evaluation through both computational metrics and expert assessment from professional furniture designers indicates that 73% of generated designs were deemed both novel and potentially manufacturable. This research demonstrates how adversarial generative techniques can serve as creative tools that augment rather than replace human designers, opening new pathways for human-AI collaborative design processes in furniture and potentially broader industrial design applications.

Return-Based Contrastive Representation Learning for Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces a novel approach to representation learning in reinforcement learning (RL) that leverages contrastive learning guided by return signals. While traditional RL algorithms often struggle with high-dimensional observation spaces, our method, Return-Based Contrastive Representation Learning (RBCRL), learns state embeddings that effectively capture the value-relevant structure of the environment. We propose a contrastive objective that pulls together state representations with similar expected returns while pushing apart those with divergent return profiles. This approach creates a latent space where proximity corresponds to similarity in potential future rewards, facilitating more efficient value function approximation and policy learning. Through extensive experiments across diverse environments, including complex visual domains, we demonstrate that RBCRL significantly outperforms existing representation learning techniques in sample efficiency, stability, and final performance. Our method shows particular strength in tasks requiring long-horizon reasoning and sparse reward settings. Additionally, we provide theoretical analysis establishing connections between our contrastive objective and value function approximation error bounds. RBCRL offers a principled approach to integrating return-based signals into representation learning, addressing a fundamental challenge in scaling reinforcement learning to complex environments.

Counterfactual Attention Learning for Fine-Grained Visual Categorization and Re-identification

Fine-grained visual categorization (FGVC) and person re-identification (re-ID) remain challenging tasks due to subtle inter-class differences and significant intra-class variations. While attention mechanisms have improved feature representation in these domains, they often focus on visually prominent regions rather than discriminative features that are crucial for accurate classification. In this paper, we propose Counterfactual Attention Learning (CAL), a novel framework that enhances attention mechanisms by leveraging counterfactual reasoning to identify truly discriminative regions. CAL generates counterfactual attention maps by asking "what if" questions about feature importance, comparing original predictions with outcomes when certain visual regions are modified. This approach enables the model to distinguish between features that are merely correlated with class labels and those that are causally related to correct identification. Through extensive experiments on standard FGVC benchmarks (CUB-200-2011, Stanford Cars, and FGVC-Aircraft) and person re-ID datasets (Market-1501 and DukeMTMC-reID), our method demonstrates consistent performance improvements over state-of-the-art approaches. Qualitative visualizations further confirm that CAL successfully focuses on subtle discriminative features while ignoring misleading background contexts. Our work provides new insights into attention mechanism design through the lens of causal inference, offering a promising direction for fine-grained visual recognition tasks.

House Price Prediction using Satellite Imagery

This study explores the application of deep learning techniques to predict residential property values using satellite imagery. Traditional house price prediction models rely heavily on structured data such as square footage, number of bedrooms, and neighborhood statistics. Our research introduces a novel approach that leverages visual features extracted from high-resolution satellite images to enhance prediction accuracy. We developed a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture that processes aerial imagery of properties and their surroundings to identify visual indicators correlated with market value. The model was trained on a dataset of 15,000 properties across diverse urban and suburban regions, combining satellite imagery with traditional property attributes. Results demonstrate that the integration of visual features from satellite imagery improved prediction accuracy by 17% compared to conventional models using only structured data. Our approach particularly excelled in capturing neighborhood characteristics, environmental amenities, and property condition factors that are difficult to quantify in traditional datasets. This research highlights the potential of computer vision techniques to transform real estate valuation by incorporating rich visual information that reflects the complex factors influencing property values in the modern market.

Mitigating the Impact of Adversarial Attacks in Very Deep Networks

Deep neural networks have demonstrated remarkable performance across various domains, but their vulnerability to adversarial attacks remains a significant security concern. This paper investigates defensive strategies specifically tailored for very deep network architectures, where the complexity of feature propagation creates unique vulnerabilities and opportunities for defense. We propose a multi-faceted approach combining gradient masking, feature distillation, and adaptive regularization techniques that progressively strengthen with network depth. Our method, Deep Adversarial Resilience Training (DART), demonstrates robustness improvements of up to 37% against state-of-the-art attacks including PGD, C&W, and AutoAttack when evaluated on ResNet-152 and DenseNet-201 architectures. Unlike previous approaches that suffer from transferability vulnerabilities, DART maintains defensive integrity across black-box scenarios without compromising clean accuracy beyond 2.3%. Through extensive empirical evaluation on ImageNet and specialized security datasets, we identify critical depth thresholds where networks become particularly susceptible to adversarial manipulation, and demonstrate how targeted intervention at these layers significantly enhances overall network resilience. Our findings provide new theoretical insights into the relationship between network depth and adversarial vulnerability, while offering practical defensive strategies for deployment in security-critical applications.

Learning Disentangled Representations via Mutual Information Estimation

Disentangled representation learning aims to identify and separate the underlying explanatory factors in data, enabling more interpretable, generalizable, and robust machine learning models. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for learning such representations by leveraging mutual information estimation techniques. Our approach explicitly maximizes the mutual information between specific dimensions of the latent representation and known factors of variation, while minimizing the redundancy between different latent dimensions. We introduce a scalable estimator for these information-theoretic objectives and demonstrate how it can be integrated into various deep learning architectures. Experimental results across synthetic and real-world datasets show that our method successfully disentangles complex factors of variation without requiring explicit supervision of all factors. Compared to existing approaches, our framework achieves superior disentanglement scores while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the connection between mutual information maximization and disentanglement, establishing bounds on the expected disentanglement performance. Our approach advances the state of the art in unsupervised and semi-supervised disentangled representation learning, with promising applications in data generation, domain adaptation, and interpretable machine learning.

Imputation-Free Learning from Incomplete Observations

Missing data presents a significant challenge in machine learning applications across diverse domains. Traditional approaches often rely on imputation techniques to fill in missing values before model training, which can introduce bias and uncertainty into the learning process. This paper introduces a novel imputation-free framework for learning directly from incomplete observations. Our approach embeds the missingness pattern into the learning architecture, allowing models to extract meaningful representations from partially observed data without requiring explicit value replacement. We formulate a theoretically grounded objective function that accounts for the missing data mechanism while preserving the underlying data distribution. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets with various missingness patterns (MCAR, MAR, and MNAR) demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art imputation-based approaches across classification, regression, and clustering tasks. Further analysis reveals that our framework exhibits enhanced robustness to high missingness rates and provides natural uncertainty quantification. These results suggest that direct learning from incomplete data offers a promising alternative to the conventional impute-then-learn paradigm, particularly in scenarios where accurate imputation is challenging.

Learning Binary Decision Trees by Argmin Differentiation

Binary decision trees remain fundamental models in machine learning due to their interpretability and effectiveness. However, optimizing tree structures presents significant challenges as the learning process involves discrete optimization problems that are not amenable to standard gradient-based methods. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to decision tree learning through argmin differentiation, which enables efficient gradient-based optimization of tree parameters. Our method reformulates the tree construction process as a continuous optimization problem by representing splitting decisions as differentiable argmin operations. By leveraging recent advances in implicit differentiation, we derive analytical gradients that flow through the discrete tree structure, allowing end-to-end optimization with standard gradient descent algorithms. Experimental results across diverse classification and regression tasks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms traditional greedy tree induction methods while maintaining the interpretability of the resulting models. Additionally, our method exhibits faster convergence and greater robustness to noisy data compared to existing approaches. This work bridges the gap between the interpretability of decision trees and the optimization efficiency of differentiable models, opening new avenues for incorporating decision trees into deep learning frameworks.

Adversarial Variational Optimization of Non-Differentiable Simulators

We present a novel approach for optimizing parameters of non-differentiable simulators using adversarial variational techniques. Complex simulation systems are prevalent across scientific domains, but their non-differentiable nature poses significant challenges for traditional gradient-based optimization methods. Our framework, Adversarial Variational Optimization (AVO), circumvents this limitation by combining variational inference with adversarial learning principles. We introduce a surrogate loss function learned through a discriminator network that distinguishes between observed data and simulator outputs, enabling gradient-based optimization without requiring differentiability of the underlying simulator. The approach employs a variational approximation of the posterior distribution over simulator parameters, which is iteratively refined through adversarial training. Experimental results across diverse domains—including particle physics, computational fluid dynamics, and financial modeling—demonstrate that our method achieves superior parameter recovery compared to established techniques such as Approximate Bayesian Computation and Bayesian Optimization. AVO shows particular strength in high-dimensional parameter spaces and with computationally expensive simulators. This work provides a general-purpose methodology for scientific machine learning applications where simulator gradients are unavailable, substantially expanding the applicability of gradient-based optimization to previously intractable simulation-based inference problems.

An Unsupervised Approach towards Varying Human Skin Tone Using Generative Adversarial Networks

This paper presents a novel unsupervised approach for realistic skin tone variation in human images using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). While existing methods for skin tone manipulation often require extensive labeled data or produce unrealistic results that fail to preserve identity features, our framework addresses these limitations through an unsupervised learning paradigm. We introduce a specialized GAN architecture that disentangles skin tone features from other facial attributes, enabling targeted manipulation while maintaining facial identity, texture details, and lighting consistency. Our method incorporates a tone-specific latent space mapping and adaptive color transfer mechanisms guided by a perceptual consistency loss. Extensive evaluations on diverse datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing supervised and unsupervised techniques in terms of photorealism, identity preservation, and skin tone diversity. The proposed method achieves a 37% improvement in identity preservation metrics while successfully generating a continuous spectrum of natural skin tones. This work has significant implications for applications in computer vision, digital media, and promoting representation diversity in visual content.

EiGLasso for Scalable Sparse Kronecker-Sum Inverse Covariance Estimation

This paper introduces EiGLasso (Eigenvalue-based Graphical Lasso), a novel algorithm for estimating sparse Kronecker-sum structured inverse covariance matrices from high-dimensional data. While traditional graphical models struggle with computational and statistical challenges in high dimensions, our approach leverages the eigenvalue decomposition of sample covariance matrices to significantly reduce computational complexity. We model the precision matrix as a Kronecker-sum of sparse component matrices, enabling efficient representation of complex dependencies while maintaining interpretability. EiGLasso employs an alternating optimization framework with a specialized proximal gradient method that exploits the eigenstructure, achieving provable convergence guarantees with O(p³) complexity rather than the O(p⁴) of standard methods, where p is the dimension. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets from neuroimaging and genomics, we demonstrate that EiGLasso outperforms existing methods in estimation accuracy, computational efficiency, and scalability to dimensions exceeding 10,000 variables. Furthermore, we establish theoretical consistency properties under mild conditions. Our approach enables practical graphical modeling for previously intractable high-dimensional problems while preserving structural interpretability.

Deep Learning Convolutional Networks for Multiphoton Microscopy Vasculature Segmentation

This study presents a novel deep learning approach for automated segmentation of cerebral vasculature in multiphoton microscopy (MPM) images. Accurate delineation of vascular networks remains challenging due to complex vessel morphology, imaging artifacts, and variable contrast. We developed and evaluated several convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, including a modified U-Net with residual connections, to address these challenges. Our method was trained on a diverse dataset of 3D MPM images from murine brain tissue with corresponding expert manual annotations. The proposed network achieves a Dice coefficient of 0.91 and Jaccard index of 0.87, outperforming traditional segmentation methods and previous deep learning approaches. We demonstrate the model's robustness across varying imaging conditions and vessel calibers, with particular improvements in detecting small capillaries. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the computational requirements and introduce a publicly available dataset and code repository to facilitate further research. This automated segmentation framework enables more efficient quantitative analysis of vascular morphology and may enhance our understanding of neurovascular coupling in both healthy and pathological conditions.

To Trust Or Not To Trust A Classifier

Machine learning classifiers are increasingly deployed in critical decision-making contexts, yet their trustworthiness remains a significant concern. This paper presents a framework for evaluating when a classifier's predictions should be trusted. We introduce a trust score metric that measures the agreement between a classifier's prediction and the nearest class distributions in feature space. Our approach provides a principled alternative to confidence scores, which can be misleading when models are miscalibrated. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our trust scores reliably identify classification errors across various domains and model architectures. Furthermore, we show that selectively deferring high-stakes decisions when trust scores are low leads to improved overall performance. The proposed methodology enables practitioners to better understand model limitations, detect potential failure modes, and determine when human intervention is necessary. Our findings suggest that trustworthiness assessment should be an essential component of responsible machine learning deployment, particularly in high-risk applications where incorrect predictions can have serious consequences.

Deep-learning based discovery of partial differential equations in integral form from sparse and noisy data

This paper presents a novel deep learning framework for the automated discovery of partial differential equations (PDEs) in their integral form from sparse and noisy measurement data. While traditional data-driven discovery methods focus on differential forms that require high-quality spatial and temporal derivatives, our approach leverages the integral formulation of PDEs, which demonstrates enhanced robustness to noise and data sparsity. We introduce a specialized neural network architecture that incorporates physics-informed constraints and conservation principles to identify the underlying governing equations. The framework employs a two-stage process: first, learning continuous field representations from discrete measurements through physics-guided interpolation, and second, discovering the symbolic structure of the integral equations through a sparse regression technique coupled with a custom loss function. Through comprehensive testing on synthetic datasets from fluid dynamics, heat transfer, and wave propagation phenomena, our method successfully recovers the correct governing equations even when data is corrupted with up to 20% noise and sampled at irregular spatial intervals. Comparative analysis demonstrates that our integral-based approach significantly outperforms differential-based methods under challenging data conditions. This work extends the capabilities of scientific machine learning for equation discovery in real-world scenarios where measurement data is inherently limited and imperfect.

Vehicle Local Position Estimation System

This paper presents a novel approach to vehicle local position estimation that integrates multiple sensor modalities to achieve robust and accurate positioning in diverse driving environments. The proposed system addresses the limitations of conventional GPS-based positioning by implementing a sensor fusion framework that combines inertial measurement units (IMUs), wheel odometry, visual odometry, and LiDAR data. Through an extended Kalman filter architecture, the system dynamically weights sensor inputs based on their estimated reliability, enabling continuous position tracking even during GPS signal degradation or loss in challenging environments such as urban canyons, tunnels, and parking structures. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves positional accuracy within 0.5 meters in 95% of test scenarios, significantly outperforming traditional positioning methods. The system's real-time processing capabilities and fault-tolerant design make it particularly suitable for advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and autonomous driving applications. This research contributes to the ongoing development of reliable vehicle localization technologies essential for next-generation intelligent transportation systems.

ReGenMorph: Visibly Realistic GAN Generated Face Morphing Attacks by Attack Re-generation

Face morphing attacks pose a significant threat to facial recognition systems by creating synthetic images that can match multiple identities simultaneously. While GAN-based morphing techniques have advanced rapidly, they often produce artifacts that can be detected by both automated systems and human observers. In this paper, we present ReGenMorph, a novel approach that addresses the visible quality limitations of GAN-generated face morphs through a specialized attack re-generation pipeline. Our method employs a two-stage process: first generating initial morphs using StyleGAN-based architecture, then applying a targeted refinement procedure that preserves biometric characteristics while enhancing visual realism. Experimental results demonstrate that ReGenMorph produces morphing attacks that are significantly more difficult to detect visually compared to previous GAN-based approaches, achieving a 37% reduction in detection rates by human examiners and a 42% decrease in automated detection accuracy. Simultaneously, ReGenMorph maintains high attack success rates of 89% against commercial facial recognition systems. Our comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets and recognition systems establishes ReGenMorph as an important advancement in understanding morphing vulnerabilities, highlighting the need for more robust countermeasures against increasingly realistic synthetic identity attacks.

Comparing seven methods for state-of-health time series prediction for the lithium-ion battery packs of forklifts

This study presents a comprehensive comparison of seven distinct methods for predicting the state-of-health (SOH) time series of lithium-ion battery packs used in industrial forklifts. Accurate SOH prediction is crucial for optimizing battery maintenance schedules, preventing unexpected downtime, and extending battery lifespan in commercial fleet operations. We evaluated traditional statistical approaches (ARIMA, exponential smoothing), machine learning methods (Random Forest, Support Vector Regression, XGBoost), and deep learning techniques (LSTM and Transformer networks) on operational data collected from a fleet of 50 electric forklifts over a 24-month period. Performance metrics included RMSE, MAE, prediction horizon accuracy, and computational efficiency. Results demonstrate that while deep learning approaches achieved the highest prediction accuracy for long-term forecasting (LSTM: RMSE=1.87%, MAE=1.42%), the XGBoost model provided the best balance between accuracy (RMSE=2.13%, MAE=1.89%) and computational efficiency for medium-term predictions. The transformer-based model exhibited superior performance in capturing degradation pattern changes during rapid capacity fade periods. Our findings provide practical guidelines for selecting appropriate SOH prediction methods based on specific operational requirements in industrial forklift applications, with potential implications for other electric vehicle battery management systems.

Fader Networks: Manipulating Images by Sliding Attributes

This paper introduces Fader Networks, a novel approach for image manipulation that enables continuous attribute editing through simple slider controls. Our framework leverages an encoder-decoder architecture with adversarial training to disentangle identity information from specific visual attributes such as age, gender, or facial expressions. Unlike previous methods that require paired training data or complex optimization procedures, Fader Networks learn to separate content from attribute information during training, allowing for smooth interpolation along desired attribute dimensions at inference time. We demonstrate that by simply adjusting slider values, users can manipulate images to enhance, reduce, or neutralize specific attributes while preserving identity and structural integrity. Extensive experiments on facial datasets show that our approach produces high-quality transformations that are both realistic and accurately reflect the target attributes. Additionally, we show the generalizability of our method to other domains beyond faces. Fader Networks provide an intuitive and effective solution for semantic image editing that maintains the coherence of the original image while allowing fine-grained control over visual attributes.

Faster Bounding Box Annotation for Object Detection in Indoor Scenes

Object detection in indoor environments remains a challenging task that requires large amounts of annotated data to achieve high performance. However, the manual annotation of bounding boxes is time-consuming and expensive, creating a bottleneck in the development of accurate detection systems. This paper presents a novel semi-automated annotation framework that significantly reduces the time required for bounding box annotation in indoor scene datasets. Our approach combines an initial automated detection phase using a pre-trained model with an efficient human-in-the-loop verification and correction mechanism. We introduce a clustering-based proposal method that leverages spatial and visual cues specific to indoor environments, reducing annotation time by 62% compared to traditional manual annotation. Experiments conducted on three indoor scene datasets demonstrate that our approach not only accelerates the annotation process but also maintains annotation quality comparable to fully manual methods. Additionally, object detectors trained on our efficiently annotated data achieve performance within 1.5% mAP of those trained on traditionally annotated datasets, while requiring only 38% of the annotation time. This work addresses a critical need in the computer vision community by providing a practical solution to scale up high-quality annotations for indoor scene understanding.

SalProp: Salient Object Proposals via Aggregated Edge Cues

This paper presents SalProp, a novel approach for generating high-quality salient object proposals through the aggregation of edge-based visual cues. Unlike traditional object proposal methods that generate thousands of candidate regions, our approach focuses on producing a compact set of proposals that effectively capture salient objects in images. SalProp leverages the complementary strengths of boundary detection and saliency estimation by integrating multiple edge signals including intensity gradients, texture discontinuities, and learned contour features. We introduce an adaptive edge aggregation framework that assigns weights to different edge cues based on their reliability in various image contexts. The aggregated edge map is then used to guide a hierarchical segmentation process that generates object proposals with precise boundaries. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets (PASCAL VOC, MS COCO, and ECSSD) demonstrate that SalProp achieves state-of-the-art performance, producing significantly fewer proposals while maintaining higher recall rates for salient objects. Our method achieves an 87.3% recall with just 100 proposals on the ECSSD dataset, outperforming competing methods that require 5-10 times more proposals to achieve comparable recall. SalProp's efficiency makes it particularly suitable for applications requiring real-time object localization such as robotics and augmented reality.

Learning to Relate from Captions and Bounding Boxes

Understanding the complex relationships between objects in visual scenes is a fundamental challenge in computer vision and multimodal learning. In this paper, we present a novel approach that leverages the complementary information from image captions and bounding box annotations to learn rich visual relationship representations. Our method integrates textual cues from natural language descriptions with spatial information from bounding boxes to identify and characterize relationships between entities in images. We introduce a dual-stream architecture that processes linguistic and visual inputs separately before fusing them through a cross-modal attention mechanism. This approach enables the model to ground textual relationship descriptions in visual data while maintaining spatial awareness. Experiments on standard visual relationship detection benchmarks demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods that rely solely on either captions or bounding boxes. Furthermore, we show that our model can generalize to recognize novel relationships by transferring knowledge between seen and unseen object pairs. Our work provides insights into how language supervision can enhance spatial reasoning in visual scenes and opens new directions for weakly supervised relationship learning.

Learning overcomplete, low coherence dictionaries with linear inference

This paper introduces a novel approach for learning overcomplete dictionaries that enable efficient linear inference while maintaining low coherence between dictionary elements. Traditional sparse coding methods often require computationally expensive iterative optimization for inference, limiting their practical application in real-time systems. We propose a framework that jointly optimizes for dictionary representational power and inference efficiency by directly incorporating linear approximation constraints during the dictionary learning process. Our method enforces low mutual coherence among dictionary atoms while preserving the overcomplete nature of the representation, resulting in dictionaries that balance expressivity with computational efficiency. Theoretical analysis establishes guarantees on the recovery error when using simple linear inference methods with the learned dictionaries. Extensive empirical evaluation on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates that our approach achieves comparable reconstruction quality to traditional sparse coding techniques while reducing inference time by orders of magnitude. The proposed method shows particular promise for applications requiring real-time signal processing, such as image denoising, compressive sensing, and feature extraction for large-scale machine learning systems.

ACFNet: Adaptively-Cooperative Fusion Network for RGB-D Salient Object Detection

RGB-D salient object detection (SOD) has attracted significant attention due to its ability to leverage complementary information from both RGB and depth modalities. However, existing methods often struggle with effectively fusing cross-modal features, particularly when dealing with low-quality depth maps or complex scenes. In this paper, we propose ACFNet, an Adaptively-Cooperative Fusion Network that dynamically integrates RGB and depth information through a novel fusion mechanism. Our approach introduces three key components: (1) a dual-stream feature extraction backbone that captures modality-specific representations, (2) an adaptive fusion module that dynamically weights modal contributions based on their reliability, and (3) a cooperative refinement strategy that enables bidirectional information flow between modalities. Extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that ACFNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 2.3% in F-measure and 1.8% in MAE. Our model shows particular robustness in challenging scenarios with low-quality depth maps or complex backgrounds. Furthermore, ablation studies verify the effectiveness of each proposed component. The code will be made publicly available to facilitate future research.

Adversarial Symmetric GANs: Bridging Adversarial Samples and Adversarial Networks

This paper introduces Adversarial Symmetric GANs (AS-GANs), a novel framework that establishes a theoretical and practical connection between adversarial examples and generative adversarial networks. While both domains leverage adversarial optimization, they have largely developed as separate research areas. Our approach demonstrates that the generation of adversarial samples can be reformulated as a specialized GAN training process with symmetrical constraints. We present a unified mathematical framework that models both phenomena through a common lens of adversarial optimization, revealing that adversarial examples represent a special case of the more general GAN formulation when specific symmetry conditions are imposed. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets show that AS-GANs not only generate high-quality synthetic samples but also provide enhanced robustness against adversarial attacks, improving classification accuracy by 18% on adversarially perturbed inputs compared to baseline models. Furthermore, our framework enables novel transfer learning capabilities between the two domains, allowing defensive strategies developed for one to be effectively adapted to the other. These findings provide new theoretical insights while offering practical benefits for both generative modeling and adversarial robustness.

Dynamics Generalization via Information Bottleneck in Deep Reinforcement Learning

Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have demonstrated impressive performance in complex decision-making tasks, but often struggle with generalization to novel environments with different dynamics. This paper introduces a novel information bottleneck (IB) approach to dynamics generalization in RL. Our method, which we call Dynamics-IB, constrains the information flow between environmental observations and the agent's internal representations to extract only the most task-relevant features while discarding spurious correlations that hinder generalization. We formalize this approach through an IB objective that balances task performance against representation compression, encouraging the agent to learn invariant features across dynamics variations. Through extensive experiments across continuous control tasks with varying dynamics parameters, we demonstrate that Dynamics-IB significantly outperforms standard RL approaches and existing generalization methods. Our analysis reveals that the learned representations effectively capture the underlying causal structure of the tasks while remaining robust to distributional shifts in environment dynamics. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights connecting the IB principle to generalization bounds in RL. These results suggest that information-theoretic constraints can serve as a powerful inductive bias for learning dynamics-invariant policies in reinforcement learning.

Predicting Rigid Body Dynamics using Dual Quaternion Recurrent Neural Networks with Quaternion Attention

This paper presents a novel approach for predicting rigid body dynamics by leveraging dual quaternion representations within a recurrent neural network architecture enhanced with quaternion attention mechanisms. Rigid body motion prediction remains challenging due to the complex coupling between rotational and translational dynamics. Our framework, Dual Quaternion Recurrent Neural Networks (DQ-RNN), addresses these challenges by representing rigid body states as dual quaternions, which elegantly unify rotation and translation in a single mathematical structure. We further enhance the model with a quaternion attention mechanism that effectively captures the geometric relationships between temporal states. Experiments conducted on synthetic datasets and real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, reducing prediction error by 27% compared to conventional methods that treat rotation and translation separately. The model exhibits improved long-term stability and preserves essential physical properties such as conservation of angular momentum. Additionally, we show that our approach transfers effectively to unseen dynamic scenarios, making it suitable for applications in robotic control, physical simulation, and computer graphics where accurate rigid body motion prediction is essential.

Application of Machine Learning to Accidents Detection at Directional Drilling

This study explores the implementation of machine learning (ML) techniques for early detection and prediction of accidents in directional drilling operations. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset from multiple drilling sites, we developed and validated several ML models including random forests, support vector machines, and deep neural networks to identify precursory patterns leading to drilling accidents. The models were trained on historical operational data encompassing drilling parameters, geological formations, equipment status, and historical incident reports. Our best-performing model achieved 87% accuracy in predicting potential accidents with a 30-minute lead time, allowing for preventive intervention. Feature importance analysis revealed that sudden changes in torque, abnormal mud pressure, and specific vibration patterns were the most significant indicators of impending accidents. Implementation of this predictive system in a pilot program reduced accident rates by 43% and associated downtime by 38%. These findings demonstrate that ML-based monitoring systems can significantly enhance safety protocols in directional drilling operations while reducing operational costs and environmental risks. The methodology presented offers a scalable framework that can be adapted to various drilling environments and integrated with existing monitoring systems.

VAE/WGAN-Based Image Representation Learning For Pose-Preserving Seamless Identity Replacement In Facial Images

This paper introduces a novel approach to facial identity replacement that preserves pose and expression while seamlessly transferring identity attributes. Our method leverages a hybrid architecture combining Variational Autoencoders (VAE) and Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks (WGAN) to learn disentangled facial representations that separately encode identity and non-identity features. By decomposing facial images into identity-specific and identity-independent components, our framework enables precise manipulation of identity while maintaining the original pose, expression, and environmental conditions. We propose a specialized latent space organization that enforces orthogonality between identity and non-identity representations, alongside a custom loss function that balances reconstruction fidelity with identity transfer accuracy. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and user studies, achieving more natural and artifact-free identity replacements across diverse facial poses and lighting conditions. The proposed technique has significant applications in privacy protection, entertainment, and digital content creation while addressing ethical considerations through built-in safeguards against misuse.

Orderly Disorder in Point Cloud Domain

This paper explores the paradoxical concept of "orderly disorder" within point cloud data representations. We investigate how seemingly chaotic point distributions can exhibit underlying structural patterns that are essential for robust 3D understanding. Our work demonstrates that controlled stochasticity in point cloud sampling and organization can enhance model generalization and feature extraction in deep learning architectures. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we introduce a novel framework that leverages this ordered randomness to improve performance in classification, segmentation, and object detection tasks. Results show that our approach outperforms conventional deterministic point cloud processing methods by 7.3% on average while requiring 18% less computational resources. Furthermore, we establish theoretical foundations explaining why certain forms of structured disorder provide optimal trade-offs between information preservation and model robustness. This research provides new insights into the fundamental nature of point cloud representations and offers practical guidelines for designing more effective point-based deep learning systems.

Bayesian Image Segmentation by Potts Prior and Loopy Belief Propagation

This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation using a Bayesian framework that combines the Potts model as a prior distribution with loopy belief propagation (LBP) for inference. The Potts model, a generalization of the Ising model to multiple states, effectively captures the spatial coherence of image segments by encouraging neighboring pixels to share the same label. We formulate image segmentation as a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation problem and develop an efficient approximate inference scheme using LBP to overcome the computational intractability of exact inference. Our method addresses the limitations of traditional segmentation approaches by incorporating uncertainty quantification through the Bayesian paradigm. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods while providing principled uncertainty estimates. Furthermore, we analyze the convergence properties of LBP in this context and propose practical modifications to improve its stability and efficiency. The proposed framework is flexible and can be extended to incorporate various likelihood models for different imaging modalities, making it applicable to a wide range of segmentation tasks.

Transfer Learning using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations

This paper explores the application of Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) to transfer learning tasks. We present a novel framework that leverages the continuous-depth nature of Neural ODEs to facilitate more effective knowledge transfer between source and target domains. Unlike traditional neural networks with discrete layers, Neural ODEs represent the evolution of hidden states as a continuous flow, offering unique advantages for transfer learning scenarios. Our approach adapts the ODE dynamics learned from source domains to new target domains with minimal architectural modifications. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our Neural ODE-based transfer learning method achieves superior performance compared to conventional transfer learning techniques, particularly when target data is limited. We observe a 12% improvement in convergence speed and a 7% increase in accuracy on challenging domain adaptation tasks. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into why the continuous representation of Neural ODEs enables more natural knowledge transfer across domains. This work opens new directions for transfer learning by exploiting the mathematical properties of differential equations in deep learning architectures.

Label-similarity Curriculum Learning

This paper introduces Label-similarity Curriculum Learning (LCL), a novel approach that leverages the semantic relationships between class labels to improve deep neural network training. Unlike traditional curriculum learning methods that focus solely on sample difficulty, LCL incorporates the inherent similarity structure among labels to create a more effective learning progression. We propose a dual-phase curriculum where networks first learn to distinguish between semantically distant classes before gradually tackling more challenging distinctions between similar classes. Our method automatically constructs this curriculum by computing label embeddings from both knowledge bases and data-driven sources, then using these embeddings to schedule training examples. Extensive experiments on image classification benchmarks (CIFAR-100, ImageNet) and fine-grained classification tasks demonstrate that LCL consistently outperforms standard training and other curriculum learning approaches. The results show improved generalization performance, faster convergence, and enhanced robustness to label noise. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into why exploiting label similarity structures benefits the optimization landscape of deep neural networks. Our approach requires minimal computational overhead and can be easily integrated into existing training pipelines.

Aerial Spectral Super-Resolution using Conditional Adversarial Networks

This paper presents a novel approach to spectral super-resolution of aerial imagery using conditional adversarial networks. While traditional methods for enhancing the spectral resolution of remote sensing data often suffer from spectral distortion and limited generalization capabilities, our proposed framework leverages the power of conditional GANs to generate high spectral resolution imagery from lower resolution inputs. We introduce a custom architecture that combines a generator network optimized for preserving spatial details with a discriminator designed to enforce spectral fidelity. Our method is evaluated on diverse aerial datasets including multispectral and hyperspectral imagery acquired from both satellite and UAV platforms. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art spectral enhancement techniques by achieving up to 45% improvement in spectral accuracy while maintaining spatial coherence. The model shows robust performance across varying imaging conditions and geographical regions, making it particularly valuable for environmental monitoring, precision agriculture, and urban planning applications where detailed spectral information is crucial. Additionally, we provide an analysis of the computational efficiency of our approach, making it suitable for operational remote sensing workflows.

Scene Gated Social Graph: Pedestrian Trajectory Prediction Based on Dynamic Social Graphs and Scene Constraints

Accurately predicting pedestrian trajectories in crowded environments remains a significant challenge in computer vision and autonomous systems. This paper introduces the Scene Gated Social Graph (SGSG), a novel framework that integrates dynamic social interactions with physical scene constraints to improve trajectory prediction. Our approach models pedestrian movement as a time-evolving graph structure where connections between individuals are dynamically established based on their spatiotemporal relationships and potential interactions. Unlike previous methods that treat social dynamics uniformly, SGSG employs a scene-gated mechanism that modulates social influence based on environmental context, recognizing that physical constraints (buildings, roads, obstacles) significantly shape human navigation decisions. Through extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets including ETH/UCY and Stanford Drone, we demonstrate that SGSG achieves state-of-the-art performance, reducing average displacement error by 17% compared to existing methods. Our ablation studies confirm that the integration of scene-aware gating with dynamic social graphs significantly enhances prediction accuracy, particularly in complex environments with multiple obstacles and dense crowds. The proposed approach offers valuable insights for developing more robust pedestrian prediction systems for autonomous vehicles, social robots, and intelligent surveillance systems.

Self-Supervised Monocular 3D Face Reconstruction by Occlusion-Aware Multi-view Geometry Consistency

This paper presents a novel self-supervised approach for monocular 3D face reconstruction that addresses the fundamental challenge of partial face occlusions without requiring ground truth 3D face data or explicit occlusion annotations. Our key innovation is an occlusion-aware multi-view geometry consistency framework that leverages the geometric relationships between different viewpoints of the same face to provide supervision signals. The proposed method introduces an adaptive visibility mask that automatically identifies occluded facial regions, enabling the network to focus learning on reliable visible areas. By enforcing cross-view consistency only on mutually visible facial regions across synthetic viewpoints, our approach effectively handles occlusions during both training and inference. We further incorporate a differentiable rendering module with a landmark consistency loss to ensure accurate alignment between the reconstructed 3D face model and input images. Extensive experiments on challenging benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing self-supervised approaches, achieving comparable results to fully supervised methods while maintaining robustness to various types of occlusions. Our approach advances the field by eliminating the need for expensive 3D annotations or occlusion labels, making high-quality 3D face reconstruction more accessible for real-world applications.

Perturbation Analysis of Learning Algorithms: A Unifying Perspective on Generation of Adversarial Examples

This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding adversarial examples through the lens of perturbation analysis. While deep learning models have achieved remarkable performance across various domains, their vulnerability to carefully crafted perturbations remains a significant security concern. We develop a unified mathematical formulation that characterizes how small input perturbations propagate through learning algorithms to influence their outputs. By examining the functional sensitivity of different model architectures, we establish theoretical bounds on the minimum perturbation required to induce misclassification. Our analysis reveals that adversarial vulnerability stems from fundamental properties of high-dimensional optimization rather than specific architectural choices. We demonstrate that this framework can unify seemingly disparate adversarial attack methods, showing they are special cases of our general perturbation theory. Experimental validation across convolutional, recurrent, and transformer architectures confirms our theoretical predictions about vulnerability patterns. Furthermore, we leverage our analysis to develop more robust training procedures that explicitly account for worst-case perturbation directions. This work provides both theoretical insights into the nature of adversarial examples and practical guidance for developing more secure machine learning systems.

Deep Model Compression Via Two-Stage Deep Reinforcement Learning

This paper presents a novel approach to deep neural network compression using a two-stage deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework. As deep learning models continue to grow in size and complexity, their deployment on resource-constrained devices becomes increasingly challenging. Our method addresses this limitation by automatically learning compression policies that significantly reduce model size while maintaining performance. The proposed framework consists of two sequential DRL agents: the first agent determines the optimal compression ratios for different network layers, while the second agent fine-tunes the specific compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and low-rank factorization) for each layer based on its structural characteristics. Experiments conducted on benchmark datasets including ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and PASCAL VOC demonstrate that our approach achieves compression rates of up to 15× with negligible accuracy loss (<1%) compared to state-of-the-art methods. For ResNet-50, our method reduces model size from 98MB to 7.2MB while maintaining 75.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet. The two-stage design enables more efficient exploration of the compression policy space and demonstrates superior transferability across different network architectures. Our approach represents a significant step toward enabling deployment of sophisticated deep learning models on edge devices with limited computational resources.

HTTP2vec: Embedding of HTTP Requests for Detection of Anomalous Traffic

This paper introduces HTTP2vec, a novel approach for detecting anomalous web traffic through the embedding of HTTP requests. As web applications become increasingly prevalent targets for cyberattacks, traditional signature-based detection methods struggle to identify sophisticated and previously unseen threats. Our method leverages natural language processing techniques to transform HTTP requests into dense vector representations that capture semantic relationships between different elements of web traffic. By learning these embeddings in an unsupervised manner from large volumes of legitimate traffic, HTTP2vec creates a comprehensive model of normal behavior that can identify anomalies without requiring labeled attack data. We evaluate our approach on multiple real-world datasets containing various attack types, including SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and command injection attacks. Experimental results demonstrate that HTTP2vec outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving 96.3% detection accuracy with a false positive rate of only 0.7%. Furthermore, our approach shows robust performance against adversarial evasion techniques and maintains detection capabilities even for zero-day attacks. The embedding-based nature of HTTP2vec also provides interpretable results, allowing security analysts to understand the nature of detected anomalies. This work represents a significant advancement in applying machine learning techniques to web security and offers a practical solution for protecting modern web applications.

Meticulous Object Segmentation

This paper presents a novel approach to object segmentation that achieves unprecedented precision in boundary delineation. Our method, termed Meticulous Object Segmentation (MOS), addresses the persistent challenge of accurate object boundary detection in complex visual scenes. We introduce a hierarchical feature extraction framework that combines multi-scale contextual information with fine-grained boundary refinement techniques. The proposed architecture employs a dual-stream attention mechanism that simultaneously processes global semantic cues and local edge features, allowing for precise separation of foreground objects from challenging backgrounds. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including COCO, ADE20K, and Cityscapes, demonstrate that MOS outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins, particularly in scenarios involving intricate object boundaries, occlusions, and varying lighting conditions. Our approach reduces boundary localization error by 18% compared to previous methods while maintaining competitive inference speeds. These results highlight the potential of MOS for applications requiring precise object delineation, such as medical image analysis, autonomous driving, and augmented reality.

Efficient Bayesian Optimization using Multiscale Graph Correlation

Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful framework for optimizing expensive black-box functions, but faces significant computational challenges when scaling to high-dimensional spaces or large evaluation budgets. This paper introduces a novel approach called Multiscale Graph Correlation (MGC) for enhancing the efficiency of Bayesian optimization. Our method leverages graph-theoretic representations of the function domain at multiple scales to capture complex correlations between input variables that standard BO approaches may miss. By constructing a hierarchical graph structure that adaptively refines based on observed function evaluations, MGC enables more efficient exploration of the search space while maintaining strong theoretical convergence guarantees. We derive regret bounds that demonstrate improved scaling properties compared to conventional BO methods and empirically validate our approach on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter tuning tasks, and real-world engineering design problems. Results show that MGC significantly reduces the number of function evaluations required to find near-optimal solutions, particularly in high-dimensional settings with complex variable interactions. Our method maintains computational tractability even as the dimensionality and evaluation budget increase, addressing a key limitation of traditional Bayesian optimization approaches.

Double-Linear Thompson Sampling for Context-Attentive Bandits

This paper introduces Double-Linear Thompson Sampling (DLTS), a novel algorithm designed for context-attentive bandit problems where the relevance of contextual features varies across different actions. Traditional contextual bandit approaches often assume uniform feature importance across all arms, leading to suboptimal performance in real-world scenarios where feature relevance is heterogeneous. DLTS addresses this limitation by maintaining two separate linear models for each arm: one capturing the reward prediction and another modeling the context attention weights. Our approach employs Thompson sampling to balance exploration and exploitation while adaptively learning which contextual features matter for each action. Through theoretical analysis, we establish regret bounds that improve upon existing methods when the underlying reward structure exhibits context-attention patterns. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that DLTS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art contextual bandit algorithms, particularly in environments with sparse or varying feature relevance. The proposed method shows promising applications in recommendation systems, online advertising, and clinical trials where context-dependent decision making is essential.

Triple Memory Networks: a Brain-Inspired Method for Continual Learning

Continual learning remains a significant challenge for artificial neural networks, which typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning new tasks sequentially. In this paper, we introduce Triple Memory Networks (TMN), a novel brain-inspired architecture that addresses this limitation by mimicking key memory mechanisms observed in human cognition. Drawing on neuroscientific evidence of complementary learning systems, our approach integrates three distinct memory components: a fast-encoding episodic memory that captures task-specific experiences, a semantic memory that consolidates generalizable knowledge across tasks, and a procedural memory that maintains task-specific skills. These components interact through a dynamic consolidation process that selectively transfers information between memory systems while preserving previously acquired knowledge. Extensive experiments across multiple continual learning benchmarks, including Split-MNIST, Permuted-MNIST, and CORe50, demonstrate that TMN significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of both forward knowledge transfer and backward forgetting resistance. Our analysis reveals that the triple memory architecture enables more efficient parameter utilization and exhibits emergent properties such as improved robustness to distribution shifts. These results suggest that incorporating brain-inspired memory mechanisms provides a promising direction for advancing continual learning systems.

Latent Complete Row Space Recovery for Multi-view Subspace Clustering

This paper addresses the challenging problem of multi-view subspace clustering, where data from multiple views or sources must be effectively integrated to discover the underlying cluster structure. We propose a novel approach called Latent Complete Row Space Recovery (LCRSR), which focuses on recovering a comprehensive latent representation that preserves the complete row space information across all views. Unlike existing methods that often suffer from information loss during view fusion, our approach constructs a unified representation by explicitly modeling the complementary information within the row spaces of different views. LCRSR employs a joint optimization framework that simultaneously learns view-specific self-representation matrices and a consensus latent space that captures the complete clustering structure. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that our method effectively preserves the block-diagonal structure essential for accurate subspace clustering. Extensive experiments on benchmark multi-view datasets show that LCRSR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios with corrupted or incomplete views. The proposed approach exhibits robust performance across various data types including images, documents, and videos, validating its effectiveness in real-world multi-view clustering applications.

Pyramidal Edge-maps and Attention based Guided Thermal Super-resolution

This paper presents a novel approach to thermal image super-resolution using pyramidal edge-maps and attention mechanisms guided by visible spectrum information. Thermal imaging, while valuable for numerous applications including surveillance, medical diagnostics, and autonomous systems, often suffers from limited spatial resolution due to hardware constraints. We propose a deep learning framework that leverages the complementary high-frequency details present in visible images to enhance the resolution of corresponding thermal imagery. Our method introduces a pyramidal edge-map extraction module that captures multi-scale structural information from visible images, which is then integrated into the thermal super-resolution process through a custom attention mechanism. This attention-based guidance allows the network to selectively transfer relevant structural details while preserving the thermal characteristics of the original image. Extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art thermal super-resolution methods, achieving improvements of up to 2.3dB in PSNR and 0.08 in SSIM for 4× upscaling tasks. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of both the pyramidal edge-map representation and the attention guidance mechanism. The proposed method maintains thermal fidelity while substantially enhancing fine details, making it particularly suitable for applications requiring both high spatial resolution and accurate thermal information.

Evaluation of Spectral Learning for the Identification of Hidden Markov Models
