While traditional representation learning methods often focus on global features, our locality-promoting framework explicitly encourages embeddings to maintain neighborhood relationships across the original and latent spaces. We propose a locality-preserving loss function that balances global discriminative power with local structural fidelity, enabling more interpretable and robust representations. Through extensive experiments on image, text, and graph datasets, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on downstream tasks including classification, clustering, and retrieval. Notably, our representations show improved resilience to distribution shifts and adversarial perturbations. Analysis reveals that promoting locality leads to smoother decision boundaries and more semantically meaningful interpolations in the latent space. Our method provides a promising direction for developing representation learning techniques that better capture the intrinsic geometry of complex data manifolds while maintaining computational efficiency.

Distinguishing Noise from Chaos: Objective versus Subjective Criteria using Horizontal Visibility Graph

Differentiating between chaotic dynamics and stochastic noise remains a fundamental challenge in nonlinear time series analysis. This paper presents a novel approach using Horizontal Visibility Graph (HVG) methodology to address this problem. We transform time series into complex networks using HVG and analyze their topological properties to extract distinguishing features between deterministic chaos and random noise. Our framework combines objective mathematical criteria with subjective pattern recognition elements to create a robust classification system. We evaluate several network metrics including degree distribution, clustering coefficient, and transitivity across various synthetic and real-world datasets. Results demonstrate that chaotic series consistently produce scale-free networks with power-law degree distributions, while truly random processes generate exponential degree distributions. The proposed methodology achieves classification accuracy exceeding 95% on benchmark datasets and remains effective even with short or noisy time series where traditional methods fail. Furthermore, we introduce a quantitative "chaos-noise index" based on HVG properties that provides a continuous measure of determinism. This approach offers significant advantages over conventional techniques, particularly for systems with limited observational data or contaminated signals, and has important implications for fields ranging from financial market analysis to neuroscience and climate studies.

Deep Neural Networks Motivated by Partial Differential Equations

This paper explores the symbiotic relationship between partial differential equations (PDEs) and deep neural networks (DNNs). We demonstrate how the mathematical structure of PDEs can inspire novel neural network architectures with improved stability, interpretability, and performance. By establishing formal connections between PDE discretization schemes and network layers, we develop a theoretical framework that explains why certain network designs are particularly effective for specific problem domains. Our approach leads to PDE-motivated neural networks that incorporate physical constraints and domain knowledge directly into their architecture. Experimental results across multiple application areas—including fluid dynamics, image processing, and financial modeling—show that these physics-informed networks achieve superior generalization with reduced training data compared to conventional architectures. Furthermore, we prove convergence guarantees for several proposed models and provide guidelines for selecting appropriate PDE-inspired architectures based on the underlying structure of the learning task. This work bridges the gap between traditional numerical analysis and modern deep learning, offering both theoretical insights and practical architectural innovations.

LSTM Networks for Online Cross-Network Recommendations

This paper presents a novel approach for cross-network recommendation systems using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. In today's digital landscape, users often maintain presence across multiple online platforms, creating an opportunity to leverage cross-network information for more accurate and personalized recommendations. Our proposed framework utilizes LSTM networks to capture temporal patterns in user behavior across different social networks and online services, enabling real-time recommendation generation. We design a multi-modal architecture that processes heterogeneous data types from diverse platforms while addressing challenges of data sparsity, privacy concerns, and domain differences. Experimental evaluations on datasets spanning social media, e-commerce, and content streaming platforms demonstrate that our approach outperforms single-network recommendation systems and traditional cross-network methods by 17.3% and 8.9% respectively in terms of recommendation accuracy. Additionally, our online learning component allows the model to adapt to evolving user preferences with minimal latency. The results highlight the effectiveness of recurrent neural networks in modeling the sequential nature of cross-platform user activities for enhanced recommendation quality.

Joint Architecture and Knowledge Distillation in CNN for Chinese Text Recognition

This paper presents a novel approach to Chinese text recognition by combining architectural innovations with knowledge distillation techniques in convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Chinese text recognition presents unique challenges due to the large character set, complex stroke patterns, and contextual dependencies. Our method introduces a dual-stream CNN architecture that processes both character-level and radical-level features in parallel, capturing both holistic character representations and fundamental component structures. We enhance this architecture through knowledge distillation, where a large teacher model trained on extensive data transfers its learned representations to a more compact student model. Experiments conducted on benchmark datasets including ICDAR-2013, MTWI, and CASIA-HWDB demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance with a 5.2% reduction in character error rate compared to previous methods, while requiring 37% fewer parameters. The proposed joint architecture effectively handles both printed and handwritten Chinese text across various fonts and writing styles. Furthermore, our ablation studies reveal that the knowledge distillation process particularly improves recognition of uncommon characters and ambiguous character pairs. This work contributes a more efficient and accurate solution for Chinese OCR systems that can be deployed in resource-constrained environments.

Rotation Averaging in a Split Second: A Primal-Dual Method and a Closed-Form for Cycle Graphs

This paper presents significant advancements in rotation averaging, a fundamental problem in computer vision and robotics where the goal is to estimate absolute orientations from relative measurements. We introduce two key contributions: a highly efficient primal-dual optimization method and a novel closed-form solution for cycle graphs. Our primal-dual approach demonstrates remarkable convergence properties, achieving state-of-the-art performance with computation times under a second even for large-scale problems with thousands of rotations. Unlike previous methods that struggle with local minima or slow convergence, our algorithm effectively handles noise and outliers while maintaining computational efficiency. For the special case of cycle graphs, we derive an elegant closed-form solution that provides exact recovery under noiseless conditions and serves as an excellent initialization for the iterative algorithm under noise. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy, robustness, and computational speed. The proposed techniques advance the practical applicability of rotation averaging in structure-from-motion, SLAM, and multi-robot coordination systems.

Unsupervised Learning of Global Factors in Deep Generative Models

This paper introduces a novel framework for unsupervised learning of global factors in deep generative models. While traditional approaches often focus on learning disentangled local representations, we demonstrate that explicitly modeling global factors can significantly enhance generative capabilities and interpretability. Our method leverages a hierarchical latent variable structure that separates global factors (such as lighting conditions, object poses, or stylistic elements) from local, content-specific representations. Through a carefully designed information-theoretic objective, our approach encourages the discovery of meaningful global factors without requiring labeled data or explicit supervision. Extensive experiments on image, audio, and text datasets show that our model successfully identifies interpretable global factors while maintaining competitive generation quality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these learned global representations enable effective transfer across domains and facilitate controllable generation by manipulating specific global attributes. Our approach provides a promising direction for building more interpretable and controllable generative models that can effectively capture the underlying structure of complex, high-dimensional data distributions.

Softmax Splatting for Video Frame Interpolation

This paper introduces softmax splatting, a novel approach for video frame interpolation that addresses the limitations of traditional forward warping techniques. Video frame interpolation aims to synthesize intermediate frames between existing ones, a challenging task that requires accurate motion estimation and occlusion handling. While previous methods often rely on backward warping, which struggles with disocclusions, our proposed softmax splatting leverages forward warping with a differentiable summation that preserves motion information at occluded regions. The key innovation of our approach is the incorporation of a softmax operation that resolves the many-to-one mapping problem inherent in forward warping by assigning appropriate weights to overlapping pixels based on their relevance. Through extensive experiments on standard benchmarks, we demonstrate that softmax splatting significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of visual quality and temporal coherence, particularly in challenging scenarios involving complex motion and occlusions. Our approach is end-to-end trainable and computationally efficient, making it suitable for real-time applications. The code and pre-trained models are made publicly available to facilitate further research in video frame interpolation.

Difference Attention Based Error Correction LSTM Model for Time Series Prediction

This paper introduces a novel Difference Attention Based Error Correction Long Short-Term Memory (DAE-LSTM) model for time series prediction. Traditional LSTM models often struggle with capturing complex temporal dependencies and handling error accumulation in multi-step forecasting. Our proposed architecture addresses these limitations by incorporating a difference attention mechanism that focuses on temporal variations between consecutive time steps rather than absolute values. Additionally, we implement an error correction module that dynamically adjusts predictions based on historical error patterns. Experiments conducted on multiple benchmark datasets, including stock market indices, energy consumption data, and climate measurements, demonstrate that DAE-LSTM significantly outperforms standard LSTM, GRU, and transformer-based models. The proposed model achieves an average 18.7% reduction in mean squared error and 15.3% improvement in directional accuracy compared to baseline approaches. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the individual contributions of both the difference attention and error correction components. Our findings suggest that explicitly modeling temporal differences and systematic errors provides a more robust framework for time series forecasting in real-world applications characterized by high volatility and non-stationarity.

PointSIFT: A SIFT-like Network Module for 3D Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation

This paper presents PointSIFT, a novel orientation-encoding module designed for 3D point cloud semantic segmentation. Inspired by the Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) algorithm's orientation encoding capabilities in 2D images, our module extends this concept to 3D point clouds by capturing orientation information across eight cardinal directions in 3D space. Unlike previous approaches that focus primarily on multi-scale feature extraction, PointSIFT explicitly encodes orientation information while maintaining permutation invariance—a critical property for point cloud processing. The module employs a two-step approach: first applying orientation-encoding convolution operations, followed by an orientation-pooling step that ensures permutation invariance. We integrate PointSIFT into existing point cloud deep learning frameworks, demonstrating its effectiveness as a plug-and-play component. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including S3DIS, ScanNet, and ShapeNet show that networks augmented with our PointSIFT module consistently outperform state-of-the-art methods in semantic segmentation tasks. Ablation studies confirm that the orientation-encoding capability significantly contributes to improved feature representation, particularly for complex structures with varying orientations. Our approach offers a new perspective on feature extraction for point cloud analysis by emphasizing orientation encoding alongside scale awareness.

Robustifying Sequential Neural Processes

Sequential Neural Processes (SNPs) have emerged as powerful tools for modeling sequential data with uncertainty, combining the strengths of neural networks and probabilistic models. However, these models often struggle with distribution shifts, adversarial examples, and noisy data in real-world applications. In this paper, we introduce Robust Sequential Neural Processes (RSNPs), a framework that enhances the robustness of SNPs through several key innovations. First, we develop a novel uncertainty-aware attention mechanism that adaptively weights historical observations based on their reliability. Second, we incorporate adversarial training techniques specifically designed for sequential stochastic processes. Third, we propose a hierarchical latent variable structure that better captures multi-scale temporal dependencies while remaining resistant to outliers. Our extensive experiments on synthetic data, climate modeling, healthcare time series, and financial forecasting demonstrate that RSNPs maintain predictive accuracy under various perturbations where standard SNPs fail. Additionally, RSNPs provide well-calibrated uncertainty estimates that reliably indicate prediction confidence even in out-of-distribution scenarios. Our approach represents a significant step toward deploying neural process models in safety-critical applications where robustness is paramount.

A New Framework for Registration of Semantic Point Clouds from Stereo and RGB-D Cameras

This paper presents a novel framework for the registration of semantic point clouds generated from stereo and RGB-D cameras. Unlike traditional point cloud registration methods that rely solely on geometric features, our approach leverages both geometric and semantic information to achieve robust alignment across diverse environments. We introduce a hierarchical registration pipeline that first establishes semantic correspondences between point clouds using deep learning-based object and feature classification, followed by a refined geometric alignment that respects semantic boundaries. Our method addresses common challenges in multi-modal registration, including varying point densities, partial overlaps, and sensor-specific noise patterns characteristic of stereo and RGB-D acquisition systems. Extensive experiments conducted on both indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that our framework achieves significantly higher registration accuracy and computational efficiency compared to state-of-the-art methods, with average registration errors reduced by 37% and processing time improved by 45%. The proposed approach shows particular robustness in textureless environments and scenes with repetitive structures, where traditional methods often fail. This work contributes to advancing point cloud registration techniques for applications in robotics, autonomous navigation, and augmented reality systems that utilize heterogeneous depth sensing technologies.

Remaining Useful Life Estimation Using Functional Data Analysis

This paper presents a novel approach to Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation by leveraging Functional Data Analysis (FDA) techniques. Traditional prognostic methods often struggle with the temporal complexity and high dimensionality of degradation signals. Our methodology treats degradation trajectories as continuous functional objects rather than discrete time series, enabling more effective capture of the underlying degradation dynamics. We develop a functional regression framework that incorporates both amplitude and phase variations in degradation paths, allowing for more accurate RUL predictions across varying operational conditions. The proposed method employs functional principal component analysis to extract key degradation patterns and constructs a functional prediction model that accounts for unit-to-unit variability. Experimental validation on benchmark datasets, including the NASA turbofan engine and lithium-ion battery datasets, demonstrates that our FDA-based approach achieves superior prediction accuracy with mean absolute percentage errors reduced by 15-20% compared to conventional machine learning techniques. Furthermore, the method provides interpretable insights into degradation mechanisms through functional decomposition. This work contributes to the prognostics and health management field by establishing a mathematically rigorous framework for RUL estimation that effectively handles the functional nature of degradation processes.

Uncertainty Guided Semi-Supervised Segmentation of Retinal Layers in OCT Images

Accurate segmentation of retinal layers in Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) images is crucial for diagnosing and monitoring various ophthalmological conditions. However, the limited availability of expertly annotated data poses a significant challenge for supervised deep learning approaches. In this work, we propose a novel uncertainty-guided semi-supervised learning framework for retinal layer segmentation in OCT images. Our method leverages a small set of labeled data alongside a larger corpus of unlabeled OCT scans to improve segmentation performance. We introduce an uncertainty estimation module that quantifies prediction reliability, which then guides a selective pseudo-labeling process for unlabeled data. The framework employs a teacher-student model architecture where the teacher generates pseudo-labels for high-confidence regions while excluding uncertain areas from the learning process. Experimental results on multiple OCT datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves segmentation accuracy comparable to fully supervised methods while requiring only 30% of labeled data. Furthermore, our uncertainty maps provide clinically valuable information about regions that may require expert attention. The proposed method shows particular promise in scenarios with limited annotation resources and could significantly reduce the manual labeling burden in clinical settings.

Stopping Criteria in Contrastive Divergence: Alternatives to the Reconstruction Error

Contrastive Divergence (CD) has emerged as a popular method for training energy-based models, particularly Restricted Boltzmann Machines. However, the conventional use of reconstruction error as a stopping criterion often proves inadequate, potentially leading to suboptimal model convergence or unnecessary computational expense. This paper examines alternative stopping criteria for CD training that address these limitations. We propose and evaluate three novel approaches: gradient-based stabilization metrics, likelihood-approximation techniques, and spectral analysis of the model's weight matrices. Through extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our proposed alternatives provide more reliable indicators of model convergence than reconstruction error alone. Specifically, our gradient-based criterion reduces training time by an average of 34% while maintaining model performance, and our likelihood-approximation approach correlates more strongly with generalization performance. Theoretical analysis reveals why reconstruction error can be misleading in certain energy landscapes and provides convergence guarantees for our alternative criteria. These findings offer practical guidelines for implementing more efficient training protocols for energy-based models and provide new insights into the dynamics of contrastive divergence learning.

Multiple Meta-model Quantifying for Medical Visual Question Answering

Medical Visual Question Answering (Med-VQA) systems hold significant promise for enhancing clinical decision-making by automatically interpreting medical images in response to natural language queries. This paper introduces Multiple Meta-model Quantifying (MMQ), a novel framework that addresses the inherent challenges of Med-VQA through an ensemble approach of specialized meta-models. Unlike traditional single-model architectures, MMQ leverages multiple transformer-based meta-models, each optimized for different aspects of medical reasoning—anatomical recognition, pathology identification, and diagnostic interpretation. Our approach incorporates a dynamic uncertainty quantification mechanism that weights meta-model contributions based on question type and confidence metrics, significantly improving answer reliability. Experiments conducted on three benchmark datasets (VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA) demonstrate that MMQ outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 7.2% in accuracy and 9.5% in F1-score. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal that our uncertainty-aware fusion strategy provides more calibrated confidence scores, reducing overconfident incorrect predictions by 34% compared to baseline methods. The MMQ framework represents a significant advancement in creating more accurate and trustworthy Med-VQA systems for clinical applications, with potential implications for medical education and diagnostic assistance.

Improving the Performance of Fine-Grain Image Classifiers via Generative Data Augmentation

Fine-grain image classification remains a challenging task in computer vision due to the subtle visual differences between closely related categories and the scarcity of labeled examples for specialized domains. This paper introduces a novel generative data augmentation framework designed specifically to address these challenges. We leverage recent advances in generative adversarial networks (GANs) and diffusion models to synthesize diverse, high-fidelity training examples that preserve class-discriminative features while introducing meaningful variations. Our approach combines class-conditional generation with a feature-preserving regularization technique that ensures generated samples maintain critical visual attributes necessary for fine-grain distinction. Experiments conducted across multiple fine-grain datasets, including CUB-200-2011 (birds), Stanford Cars, and FGVC-Aircraft, demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms traditional augmentation techniques, improving classification accuracy by 4.7-8.2% across different architectures. Furthermore, we show that our approach is particularly effective in low-data regimes, reducing the performance gap between models trained on limited data and those trained on full datasets by up to 62%. The proposed method is model-agnostic and can be readily integrated into existing classification pipelines, offering a practical solution to enhance fine-grain classification performance without requiring additional real-world data collection.

Formal Derivation of Mesh Neural Networks with their Forward-Only Gradient Propagation

This paper introduces Mesh Neural Networks (MeshNNs), a novel architecture that generalizes traditional feedforward neural networks by allowing connections between non-adjacent layers while maintaining a directed acyclic computational graph. We present a rigorous mathematical formulation of MeshNNs and derive their key property: the ability to compute exact gradients through forward-only propagation, eliminating the need for storing intermediate activations for backpropagation. Our formal derivation demonstrates how the mesh connectivity creates alternative pathways for gradient flow, enabling the computation of complete gradient information during the forward pass with minimal additional computational overhead. We prove that this forward-only gradient propagation is mathematically equivalent to traditional backpropagation while requiring significantly less memory, particularly for deep networks. Theoretical analysis reveals that MeshNNs maintain universal approximation capabilities while offering improved gradient flow properties that mitigate vanishing gradient problems. Empirical evaluations across various tasks confirm the theoretical advantages, showing comparable or superior performance to traditional architectures with substantially reduced memory requirements during training. This work establishes a formal foundation for MeshNNs as a memory-efficient alternative to conventional neural network architectures.

Reliable Attribute-Based Object Recognition Using High Predictive Value Classifiers

This paper presents a novel approach to attribute-based object recognition that emphasizes classifier reliability through the application of high predictive value metrics. While traditional object recognition systems often prioritize overall accuracy, our framework specifically optimizes for both positive and negative predictive values to ensure dependable attribute detection under varying conditions. We introduce a hierarchical classification architecture that dynamically weights attribute classifiers based on their demonstrated predictive performance on unseen data. Through extensive experimentation on diverse benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our approach reduces false positive and false negative errors by 27% and 18% respectively compared to state-of-the-art methods. The system exhibits particular robustness to partial occlusion and unusual viewing angles, making it suitable for real-world deployment scenarios. Additionally, we propose a confidence calibration mechanism that provides interpretable reliability scores alongside predictions, enabling downstream applications to make informed decisions based on recognition certainty. Our results suggest that explicitly optimizing for predictive value rather than accuracy alone leads to more dependable attribute-based recognition systems for safety-critical and high-reliability applications.

Automated Resolution Selection for Image Segmentation

Image segmentation algorithms often require careful selection of input resolution to balance computational efficiency and segmentation accuracy. In this paper, we present a novel framework for automated resolution selection in image segmentation pipelines. Our approach dynamically determines the optimal resolution for each input image by analyzing content complexity, feature density, and target object characteristics. We introduce a lightweight neural network that predicts the minimum resolution required to achieve high-quality segmentation results while minimizing computational overhead. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our method reduces processing time by an average of 42% compared to fixed high-resolution approaches, while maintaining segmentation accuracy within 1.5% of the high-resolution baseline. Further analysis reveals that our approach is particularly effective for heterogeneous image collections where content complexity varies significantly. The proposed framework can be integrated with existing segmentation architectures as a preprocessing module, offering a practical solution to the resolution selection problem in real-world applications where computational resources may be constrained.

Real-World Super-Resolution of Face-Images from Surveillance Cameras

This paper addresses the challenging problem of enhancing low-resolution facial images captured by surveillance cameras in unconstrained environments. While existing face super-resolution methods perform well on controlled datasets, they often fail when applied to real-world surveillance footage affected by motion blur, poor lighting, and varying poses. We propose a novel framework that combines adaptive degradation modeling with a generative adversarial network specifically designed to handle the unique characteristics of surveillance imagery. Our method introduces a multi-stage enhancement pipeline that first estimates and reverses the image-specific degradation patterns before applying resolution enhancement. Extensive experiments on both public benchmarks and a new dataset of 5,000 real surveillance face images demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art approaches, achieving up to 45% better facial landmark preservation and 38% higher perceptual quality scores. Additionally, we show that our enhanced images substantially improve the performance of downstream face recognition systems when operating on low-quality surveillance inputs. The proposed approach represents an important step toward practical facial image enhancement in real-world security and forensic applications.

Deep Space-Time Video Upsampling Networks

This paper presents a novel deep learning framework for video upsampling that jointly addresses the challenges of spatial and temporal resolution enhancement. Our proposed Deep Space-Time Video Upsampling Network (DSTVUN) leverages the inherent correlations between spatial details and temporal dynamics to generate high-resolution, high-frame-rate videos from low-resolution, low-frame-rate inputs. Unlike previous approaches that tackle spatial super-resolution and temporal interpolation as separate problems, our end-to-end architecture simultaneously processes both dimensions through a series of specialized convolutional modules and attention mechanisms. We introduce a Space-Time Adaptive Feature Fusion module that dynamically balances the contribution of spatial and temporal information based on local video content. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and perceptual quality, with particular improvements in preserving temporal consistency and fine spatial details during fast motion sequences. Additionally, our ablation studies highlight the importance of joint optimization and reveal that the proposed approach is computationally efficient for real-world applications. The code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available.

Goal-directed Generation of Discrete Structures with Conditional Generative Models

Generative models for discrete structures such as molecules, programs, and graphs have shown remarkable capabilities in creating novel, valid instances. However, most approaches struggle to generate structures that satisfy specific functional requirements or goals. In this paper, we present a framework for goal-directed generation of discrete structures using conditional generative models. Our approach combines autoregressive transformers with a novel conditioning mechanism that incorporates goal specifications directly into the generation process. We introduce a goal-conditioned training objective that enables the model to learn the relationship between structural features and functional properties. Through extensive experiments across multiple domains—including drug-like molecule generation with target properties, program synthesis with specified behavior, and graph generation with controlled characteristics—we demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing approaches in terms of goal satisfaction, diversity, and validity of generated structures. Our model achieves up to 89% goal satisfaction while maintaining structural validity, representing a 37% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights into the trade-offs between goal satisfaction and structural constraints. This work provides a general and effective framework for goal-directed generation that can be applied across various discrete structure domains, enabling more targeted and useful applications of generative models.

Predictive State Temporal Difference Learning

This paper introduces Predictive State Temporal Difference (PSTD) learning, a novel approach that combines the representational power of predictive state representations (PSRs) with the efficiency of temporal difference (TD) learning methods. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning approaches that rely on Markov state representations, PSTD leverages predictions about future observable quantities to represent state, allowing for more effective learning in partially observable environments. Our method maintains a compact set of predictions about future observations and uses these predictions as a state representation for TD learning algorithms. We demonstrate that this approach creates a natural bridge between predictive state models and value function approximation. Theoretical analysis shows that PSTD converges under standard assumptions, while maintaining the expressive power of PSRs. Empirical evaluation on both benchmark domains and complex partially observable tasks demonstrates that PSTD outperforms conventional TD methods, particularly in environments with limited observability. Additionally, we show that the predictive state representation learned through this process captures meaningful structure in the environment, enabling better generalization across similar states. This work opens new avenues for reinforcement learning in realistic environments where complete state information is rarely available.

Improving Pedestrian Attribute Recognition With Weakly-Supervised Multi-Scale Attribute-Specific Localization

Pedestrian attribute recognition (PAR) remains a challenging task in computer vision due to the complexity of attribute variations, occlusions, and the multi-scale nature of discriminative features. This paper presents a novel weakly-supervised multi-scale attribute-specific localization framework that significantly improves PAR performance without requiring expensive attribute-level annotations. Our approach introduces an attribute-specific localization module that automatically discovers discriminative regions for different attributes using only image-level labels. We propose a multi-scale feature aggregation strategy that captures both fine-grained details and global contextual information, enabling more robust attribute recognition across varying scales and viewpoints. The framework incorporates a weakly-supervised attention mechanism that generates attribute-specific attention maps, effectively highlighting relevant regions while suppressing background noise. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including PETA, PA-100K, and RAP demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins (improving mA by 4.2%, 3.8%, and 4.5% respectively). Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of each component in our framework, particularly highlighting the importance of attribute-specific localization for challenging attributes with subtle visual cues. Our method offers a practical solution for real-world pedestrian analysis by enhancing recognition accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency.

Using Deep Learning to Count Albatrosses from Space

Monitoring wild animal populations is essential for conservation efforts, but traditional census methods for remote or inaccessible colonies can be costly, dangerous, and disruptive to sensitive species. This study presents a novel approach to automatically detect and count albatross populations using high-resolution satellite imagery and deep learning techniques. We developed a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture specifically optimized for identifying albatrosses against varied backgrounds including ocean, vegetation, and nesting grounds. The model was trained on manually labeled satellite images from known albatross colonies across the Southern Ocean. Our approach achieved detection accuracy of 93.7%, significantly outperforming previous remote sensing methods. We successfully applied this technique to estimate populations at 22 breeding colonies, including several that had not been surveyed in over a decade. Results revealed previously undocumented population trends, including concerning declines at three key sites. This methodology provides a cost-effective, scalable, and non-invasive alternative to traditional survey methods, enabling more frequent population assessments critical for the conservation management of these vulnerable seabirds. Furthermore, our framework can be adapted to monitor other large-bodied species visible from satellite imagery, demonstrating the potential of deep learning and remote sensing for wildlife conservation at a global scale.

Similarity-Aware Fusion Network for 3D Semantic Segmentation

This paper presents a novel Similarity-Aware Fusion Network (SAFNet) for 3D semantic segmentation, addressing the challenge of effectively integrating multi-scale and multi-modal features in 3D point cloud understanding. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on fixed fusion strategies, our method dynamically adapts the fusion process based on feature similarity relationships across different scales and representations. The proposed network introduces a similarity-guided attention mechanism that evaluates the relevance between feature pairs and adjusts their contributions accordingly during fusion. We decompose the complex 3D segmentation task into a hierarchical framework where local geometric details and global contextual information are processed through parallel branches and subsequently integrated via our similarity-aware fusion module. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including ScanNet, S3DIS, and SemanticKITTI demonstrate that SAFNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 2.3% higher mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) on ScanNet and 1.8% improvement on S3DIS Area 5. Ablation studies further confirm the effectiveness of our similarity-aware fusion strategy compared to alternative integration approaches. Our method not only improves segmentation accuracy but also enhances model efficiency by eliminating redundant feature correlations, making it suitable for real-world 3D scene understanding applications.

DYNOTEARS: Structure Learning from Time-Series Data

Learning causal structures from time-series data is a fundamental challenge in many scientific domains. In this paper, we introduce DYNOTEARS (DYnamic NOnparametic TEmporal Acyclic gRaph Structure learning), a novel framework for learning directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) from multivariate time-series data. Our approach extends the recently developed NOTEARS algorithm, which formulates structure learning as a continuous optimization problem with an acyclicity constraint, to the temporal domain. DYNOTEARS simultaneously captures both contemporaneous and time-lagged causal relationships while maintaining appropriate acyclicity constraints within time slices. We develop a differentiable algebraic characterization of the acyclicity constraint for time-series data and derive an efficient structure learning algorithm using augmented Lagrangian optimization methods. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world time-series datasets, we demonstrate that DYNOTEARS outperforms existing methods in structure recovery accuracy and computational efficiency. Our approach provides a principled and scalable solution for causal discovery in dynamic systems, with applications in economics, neuroscience, and other fields involving temporal data analysis.

Similarity Learning for Time Series Classification

This paper presents a novel approach to time series classification through similarity learning. While traditional time series classification methods rely on predefined distance metrics, our framework learns optimal similarity measures directly from the data. We propose a deep learning architecture that combines siamese networks with specialized temporal convolutional modules to capture the complex temporal dynamics inherent in time series data. Our method addresses key challenges in time series classification including variable lengths, temporal warping, and noise sensitivity. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets from diverse domains including healthcare, finance, and industrial monitoring demonstrate that our similarity learning approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 7.3%. Furthermore, the learned similarity representations provide interpretable insights into discriminative temporal patterns. The proposed approach is computationally efficient during inference, making it suitable for real-time applications. Our work establishes similarity learning as a powerful paradigm for time series classification that adapts to domain-specific temporal characteristics without requiring extensive feature engineering.

Transformation-Grounded Image Generation Network for Novel 3D View Synthesis

We present a novel approach for synthesizing new 3D views of objects and scenes from a single input image. Unlike previous methods that rely on explicit 3D reconstruction or multiple reference views, our Transformation-Grounded Image Generation Network (TG-IGN) learns to generate novel viewpoints by directly modeling geometric transformations in the feature space. Our framework consists of a transformation-aware encoder that extracts view-invariant features from the input image, and a geometry-guided decoder that projects these features to the target viewpoint. Key to our approach is a self-supervised transformation grounding module that establishes correspondences between source and target views without requiring explicit 3D supervision. We introduce a geometric consistency loss that ensures structural coherence across generated viewpoints, preserving object identity and spatial relationships. Extensive experiments on ShapeNet, RealEstate10K, and KITTI datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of visual quality, 3D consistency, and generalization to unseen objects and viewpoints. Our approach achieves these results while maintaining computational efficiency, enabling real-time novel view synthesis for applications in augmented reality, content creation, and robotic perception.

Scene Inference for Object Illumination Editing

This paper presents a novel approach for object illumination editing that leverages scene inference to achieve physically plausible results. We introduce a framework that automatically reconstructs the lighting environment from a single image, enabling users to seamlessly manipulate the illumination of objects within the scene. Our method first estimates the scene's geometric and material properties through a deep neural network trained on synthetic and real-world data. It then infers the environmental lighting conditions, including both direct and indirect illumination sources. Unlike previous approaches that treat illumination editing as a purely image-based task, our system maintains physical consistency by modeling light transport within the reconstructed scene. Experiments demonstrate that our approach produces more realistic results than state-of-the-art methods, particularly for complex scenes with multiple light sources and reflective surfaces. User studies confirm that edited images generated by our system are significantly more perceptually convincing. We further showcase practical applications in e-commerce photography, virtual staging, and augmented reality, where consistent illumination between inserted objects and their surroundings is crucial for visual coherence.

Group Equivariant Deep Reinforcement Learning

This paper explores the integration of group equivariance principles into deep reinforcement learning (RL) frameworks. We demonstrate that incorporating symmetry constraints through group equivariant neural networks significantly enhances sample efficiency and generalization capabilities in RL agents. Our approach leverages the mathematical formalism of group theory to design architectures that respect the underlying symmetries present in various RL environments, including translation, rotation, and permutation invariances. Through extensive experimentation across diverse domains—from grid-world navigation to robotic control—we show that equivariant models require 40-60% fewer training samples while achieving comparable or superior performance to conventional architectures. Furthermore, we introduce a novel equivariant policy representation that naturally captures symmetrical action spaces. Theoretical analysis reveals that our approach provides provable guarantees on generalization to symmetric states not encountered during training. Our results establish group equivariant deep RL as a promising direction for developing more efficient and generalizable autonomous agents, particularly in environments with inherent symmetrical structures.

PVT: Point-Voxel Transformer for 3D Deep Learning

This paper introduces Point-Voxel Transformer (PVT), a novel architecture that effectively bridges the gap between point cloud and voxel representations for 3D deep learning tasks. While point-based methods preserve geometric details but struggle with global context, and voxel-based approaches capture regular structures but lose fine-grained information, our hybrid transformer-based framework leverages the complementary strengths of both paradigms. PVT employs a dual-branch architecture where point-based self-attention captures local geometric relationships, while voxel-based transformers efficiently model long-range dependencies. A cross-modal attention mechanism facilitates information exchange between these representations, enabling mutual enhancement. We propose a hierarchical feature learning strategy with dynamic point sampling and adaptive voxelization to balance computational efficiency and representation power. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PVT outperforms state-of-the-art methods on 3D object classification, part segmentation, and scene understanding tasks, with particular improvements on complex scenes and objects with fine details. Our approach maintains reasonable computational requirements while achieving superior performance, establishing a new direction for transformer-based 3D deep learning.

Learning in Feedforward Neural Networks Accelerated by Transfer Entropy

This paper introduces a novel approach to accelerate learning in feedforward neural networks by leveraging transfer entropy, an information-theoretic measure that quantifies directed information flow between variables. While traditional training methods like backpropagation focus primarily on error minimization, they often overlook the intrinsic information dynamics between network layers. Our method incorporates transfer entropy to guide the learning process by identifying and strengthening the most informative pathways within the network architecture. By analyzing the causal information transfer between neurons during training, we develop an adaptive learning algorithm that dynamically adjusts learning rates and connection weights based on information flow metrics. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our transfer entropy-enhanced approach achieves up to 45% faster convergence rates compared to standard methods, while maintaining or improving final accuracy. Furthermore, networks trained with our method exhibit improved robustness to noise and better generalization capabilities. This work establishes transfer entropy as a valuable theoretical framework for understanding and optimizing information processing in neural networks, opening new directions for information-theoretic approaches to deep learning.

Model-Based Regularization for Deep Reinforcement Learning with Transcoder Networks

This paper introduces a novel regularization approach for deep reinforcement learning (RL) that leverages model-based techniques through what we call Transcoder Networks. While model-free RL methods have demonstrated impressive performance across various domains, they often suffer from sample inefficiency and poor generalization. Our proposed Transcoder Networks act as an intermediary representation that encodes dynamics knowledge between state transitions, effectively creating a learned model that constrains the policy search space. By jointly training these networks alongside traditional policy optimization, we demonstrate how model-based regularization can significantly improve sample efficiency while maintaining the asymptotic performance advantages of model-free methods. Our approach differs from traditional model-based RL by using the learned dynamics model as a regularizer rather than for planning or data generation. Extensive experiments across continuous control benchmarks show that our method reduces sample complexity by 30-45% compared to state-of-the-art baselines while improving generalization to unseen environments. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating how Transcoder Networks guide exploration toward dynamically consistent policies and empirically validate that the learned representations capture meaningful physical dynamics. This work bridges the gap between model-based and model-free RL paradigms, offering a practical approach to incorporating dynamics knowledge without the computational burden of explicit planning.

Identifying Critical States by the Action-Based Variance of Expected Return

This paper introduces a novel approach for identifying critical states in reinforcement learning environments by analyzing the action-based variance of expected returns. While traditional value-based methods focus on states with high expected returns, we demonstrate that states where different actions lead to significantly different outcomes represent crucial decision points that disproportionately impact overall performance. We formalize this concept as the Action-Based Variance (ABV) metric, which quantifies the dispersion of expected returns across the action space for a given state. Through theoretical analysis, we establish that states with high ABV values represent pivotal junctures where agent decisions most significantly influence cumulative rewards. Our experimental evaluation across diverse environments—including grid worlds, continuous control tasks, and Atari games—demonstrates that prioritizing learning in high-ABV states accelerates policy convergence and improves final performance compared to uniform or value-based prioritization schemes. Furthermore, we show that ABV can be efficiently approximated in deep reinforcement learning settings, making it practical for complex domains. This work provides both theoretical insights into the structure of sequential decision problems and practical techniques for more efficient learning by focusing computational resources on the most consequential states.

Node Attribute Generation on Graphs

This paper introduces a novel framework for generating node attributes in graph-structured data, addressing a critical gap in the graph learning literature. While significant research has focused on generating graph structures or predicting missing node attributes, the task of generating realistic and consistent node attributes for existing graph structures remains underexplored. We propose a generative model that captures the complex dependencies between node attributes and their structural context within graphs. Our approach leverages both local neighborhood information and global graph properties to generate attributes that maintain semantic coherence and structural relevance. Through extensive experiments on diverse datasets including social networks, citation graphs, and molecular structures, we demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of attribute fidelity, consistency with graph topology, and downstream task performance. The proposed framework enables various applications including data augmentation for graph neural networks, privacy-preserving synthetic data generation, and completion of partially observed graphs. Our work provides a foundation for future research on the interplay between graph structure and node attributes in generative modeling.

Terminal Prediction as an Auxiliary Task for Deep Reinforcement Learning

Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated impressive performance across numerous domains, yet still faces challenges with sample efficiency and stability. In this paper, we introduce terminal prediction as a novel auxiliary task to enhance deep RL algorithms. Our approach trains the agent to predict the probability of episode termination given its current state, effectively creating a secondary learning objective alongside the primary reward maximization. This auxiliary task leverages termination signals already present in the environment, requiring no additional data collection. We hypothesize that terminal prediction creates a more informative state representation by encouraging the network to identify states with high termination risk. Our empirical evaluation across several benchmark environments demonstrates that augmenting standard algorithms (DQN, PPO, and SAC) with terminal prediction leads to faster learning, improved stability, and higher final performance. Notably, the greatest improvements appear in environments with sparse rewards or challenging terminal states. We provide a theoretical analysis explaining why terminal prediction serves as an effective regularizer and state representation enhancer. This work contributes a simple yet effective technique to the growing toolkit of auxiliary tasks in deep reinforcement learning.

Transformer-Based Deep Image Matching for Generalizable Person Re-identification

Person re-identification (ReID) remains a challenging task in computer vision, particularly when models need to generalize across diverse domains and environments. This paper introduces a novel Transformer-based Deep Image Matching (TDIM) framework designed to address the domain generalization challenges in person ReID. Unlike conventional convolutional neural network approaches that often struggle with domain shifts, our TDIM architecture leverages the powerful contextual modeling capabilities of transformers to learn domain-invariant representations. We propose a dual-stream transformer structure with a cross-attention mechanism that effectively captures both local and global relationships between person images. Additionally, we introduce a contrastive learning strategy with hard-negative mining to enhance discriminative feature learning across domains. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets including Market-1501, DukeMTMC-reID, MSMT17, and CUHK03 demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in cross-domain scenarios, improving mAP by 5.2% and Rank-1 accuracy by 4.7% on average. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component in our framework, particularly highlighting the importance of our transformer-based matching module for generalization. The proposed TDIM framework provides a promising direction for developing robust person ReID systems applicable in real-world surveillance scenarios without requiring domain-specific fine-tuning.

Gaussian Bounding Boxes and Probabilistic Intersection-over-Union for Object Detection

This paper introduces a novel approach to object detection by reformulating bounding boxes as Gaussian distributions, rather than deterministic rectangular regions. We propose Gaussian Bounding Boxes (GBB), which represent the location and extent of objects as 2D Gaussian distributions, inherently capturing the uncertainty in object localization. Building upon this probabilistic framework, we develop a Probabilistic Intersection-over-Union (P-IoU) metric that computes the expected IoU between Gaussian distributions, providing a more robust measure of detection quality. Our approach naturally handles occlusions, ambiguous boundaries, and varying annotation quality by modeling uncertainty explicitly. Extensive experiments on standard object detection benchmarks demonstrate that our GBB representation and P-IoU metric lead to significant improvements in detection accuracy and calibration compared to traditional methods. The probabilistic nature of our approach also enables more informative confidence scores that better reflect localization uncertainty. Our method is architecture-agnostic and can be integrated into existing detection frameworks with minimal modifications, offering a principled way to represent and reason about spatial uncertainty in object detection systems.

Improving Reinforcement Learning with Human Assistance: An Argument for Human Subject Studies with HIPPO Gym

Despite significant advancements in reinforcement learning (RL), autonomous agents still struggle with complex, real-world tasks that humans navigate with relative ease. This paper proposes that systematic integration of human guidance into RL frameworks represents a promising but underexplored direction for addressing this capability gap. We introduce HIPPO Gym (Human-Informed Preference and Policy Optimization Gymnasium), a novel benchmarking platform designed specifically for human subject studies in RL. HIPPO Gym facilitates various forms of human assistance including demonstrations, preferences, corrections, and real-time interventions within standardized environments. Through preliminary experiments across diverse tasks, we demonstrate that even limited human input can significantly accelerate learning, improve sample efficiency, and enable more robust policy generalization compared to traditional RL approaches. We further discuss methodological considerations for conducting rigorous human subject studies in this domain, addressing challenges in experimental design, bias mitigation, and human-AI interaction patterns. Our findings suggest that structured investigation of human-in-the-loop RL through platforms like HIPPO Gym could yield valuable insights for developing more capable, aligned AI systems that effectively leverage human expertise while reducing the need for extensive environmental interactions.

Learning Where to Focus for Efficient Video Object Detection

Video object detection presents unique challenges compared to its static image counterpart, primarily due to the computational demands of processing numerous frames while handling temporal variations in object appearance. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that significantly improves computational efficiency by intelligently determining where to focus computational resources across video frames. Our approach, which we call FocusNet, employs a lightweight attention mechanism that analyzes low-resolution features to identify frames and regions that require detailed processing. By adaptively allocating computational resources—processing certain frames at full resolution while allowing others to be processed at reduced complexity—we achieve substantial efficiency gains without compromising detection accuracy. FocusNet incorporates a differentiable decision policy trained end-to-end that learns to balance detection quality with computational cost. Extensive experiments on standard video object detection benchmarks, including ImageNet VID and YouTube-BoundingBoxes, demonstrate that our method reduces computational requirements by up to 70% while maintaining competitive mean Average Precision (mAP) compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Further analysis reveals that our model effectively adapts to varying object motion patterns and scene complexities, making it particularly suitable for resource-constrained applications such as mobile devices and real-time surveillance systems.

Transfer Learning for Related Reinforcement Learning Tasks via Image-to-Image Translation

Transfer learning in reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach to leverage knowledge from previously learned tasks to accelerate learning in new domains. However, visual differences between source and target environments often hinder effective knowledge transfer, even when the underlying dynamics are similar. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that facilitates transfer learning between visually distinct but mechanically related RL tasks through image-to-image translation. Our approach employs generative adversarial networks to transform observations from target domains to match the visual characteristics of previously mastered source domains, allowing agents to apply learned policies across different visual contexts without extensive retraining. We demonstrate that by bridging this visual domain gap, agents can achieve significantly faster convergence and higher performance on new tasks compared to learning from scratch. Experimental results across multiple environment pairs show that our method reduces sample complexity by up to 70% while maintaining comparable final performance to fully trained task-specific policies. Additionally, we provide an analysis of when this translation-based transfer is most beneficial and how the quality of the translation affects transfer performance. Our framework provides a practical solution for efficiently adapting RL agents to visually novel environments without requiring changes to the underlying policy architecture.

Causality for Machine Learning

This paper explores the integration of causal inference methodologies into machine learning frameworks to address fundamental limitations in current predictive models. While traditional machine learning approaches excel at pattern recognition in observational data, they often struggle with interventional reasoning, counterfactual analysis, and domain adaptation. We present a systematic review of causal frameworks—including structural causal models, potential outcomes, and do-calculus—and demonstrate how these can enhance machine learning systems. Our analysis reveals that causally-informed models exhibit improved robustness to distribution shifts, more reliable performance under interventions, and greater interpretability compared to purely associational approaches. We propose novel algorithmic techniques for causal discovery from observational data and methods for incorporating causal knowledge into deep learning architectures. Experimental results across synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate significant performance gains in transfer learning tasks and decision-making scenarios where traditional methods fail due to confounding or selection bias. This work establishes a foundation for the next generation of machine learning systems that can reason about cause and effect, potentially transforming applications in healthcare, economics, and autonomous systems where understanding causal mechanisms is crucial for reliable deployment.

Tensor-based Cooperative Control for Large Scale Multi-intersection Traffic Signal Using Deep Reinforcement Learning and Imitation Learning

This paper presents a novel tensor-based framework for cooperative traffic signal control in large-scale urban networks with multiple intersections. Traditional approaches to traffic signal optimization often struggle with the combinatorial complexity and spatial dependencies inherent in coordinating numerous intersections. We propose a hierarchical control architecture that leverages tensor decomposition techniques to efficiently represent the high-dimensional state and action spaces of the traffic network. Our approach combines deep reinforcement learning (DRL) with imitation learning to address the challenges of sample efficiency and convergence in large-scale systems. The tensor-based representation captures the spatial-temporal correlations between intersections while significantly reducing the computational complexity. We first train expert policies for smaller subnetworks using DRL, then employ imitation learning to transfer this knowledge to the tensor-based cooperative controller for the entire network. Extensive experiments conducted on both simulated environments and real-world traffic data from a metropolitan area with 50+ intersections demonstrate that our approach reduces average vehicle delay by 31.7%, decreases queue lengths by 28.4%, and improves throughput by 22.3% compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our tensor-based formulation enables scalable deployment with linear growth in computational requirements despite the exponential increase in problem complexity. This research provides a promising direction for practical implementation of intelligent traffic signal control in large urban environments.

RAN-GNNs: Breaking the Capacity Limits of Graph Neural Networks

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning on graph-structured data, yet their representational capacity is fundamentally constrained by theoretical limitations, particularly in distinguishing certain graph structures. In this paper, we introduce Random Attention Networks for GNNs (RAN-GNNs), a novel architecture that significantly expands the expressive power of traditional GNN models. By incorporating a randomized attention mechanism that dynamically assigns importance to different neighborhood aggregations, RAN-GNNs overcome the well-established limitations of the Weisfeiler-Lehman isomorphism test that bounds conventional GNNs. Through theoretical analysis, we prove that RAN-GNNs can distinguish graph structures that are provably indistinguishable by standard message-passing GNNs. Our empirical evaluation across diverse benchmarks, including molecular property prediction, social network analysis, and citation networks, demonstrates that RAN-GNNs consistently outperform state-of-the-art GNN architectures by 8-15% on node classification tasks and 5-12% on graph classification tasks. Furthermore, we show that RAN-GNNs maintain computational efficiency comparable to conventional GNNs while offering substantially enhanced representational capacity. These results establish RAN-GNNs as a promising direction for breaking through the theoretical barriers that have limited the application of graph neural networks to complex graph learning problems.

3D Conceptual Design Using Deep Learning

This paper presents a novel approach to 3D conceptual design through the application of deep learning techniques. We introduce a framework that bridges the gap between early-stage design ideation and detailed 3D modeling by leveraging recent advances in generative artificial intelligence. Our system enables designers to rapidly translate abstract concepts, rough sketches, and textual descriptions into manipulable 3D models, significantly accelerating the conceptual design phase. Through a multi-modal architecture that combines convolutional neural networks and transformer-based models, our approach learns to interpret design intent across various input modalities and generate corresponding 3D representations with appropriate geometric and semantic properties. Experiments demonstrate that the system can produce diverse, high-quality 3D concept models while preserving the creative essence of the original design inputs. User studies with professional designers indicate a 47% reduction in conceptual design time and enhanced exploration of the design space compared to traditional methods. This work contributes to the emerging field of AI-assisted design by providing a powerful tool for early-stage 3D conceptualization that maintains the designer's creative agency while automating the technical aspects of 3D modeling.

The General Theory of Permutation Equivarant Neural Networks and Higher Order Graph Variational Encoders

This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical framework for permutation equivarant neural networks and introduces a novel class of higher order graph variational encoders. We establish a formal mathematical foundation that unifies existing approaches to permutation equivariance in neural architectures while extending their applicability to more complex structural representations. Our theory characterizes the complete space of permutation equivarant linear layers through a rigorous decomposition of their parameter space, proving that any such layer can be expressed as a linear combination of basis operators corresponding to distinct orbit types. Building on this foundation, we develop Higher Order Graph Variational Encoders (HOGVEs) that effectively capture and preserve higher-order structural information in graph-structured data. Through extensive theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that HOGVEs maintain equivariance properties while significantly enhancing representational capacity compared to conventional graph neural networks. Empirical evaluations across multiple domains, including molecular property prediction, protein structure analysis, and social network modeling, show that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Our framework provides both theoretical insights into the nature of permutation equivariance and practical architectural designs that advance the capabilities of graph representation learning.

Deep Residual Networks with a Fully Connected Reconstruction Layer for Single Image Super-Resolution

This paper presents a novel approach to single image super-resolution (SISR) that combines deep residual networks with a fully connected reconstruction layer. While convolutional neural networks have shown remarkable performance in SISR tasks, effectively recovering high-frequency details remains challenging. Our proposed architecture leverages the strength of deep residual learning to extract hierarchical features while addressing the vanishing gradient problem in deep networks. The key innovation is the introduction of a fully connected reconstruction layer at the end of the residual learning pipeline, which enables more effective mapping from low-resolution feature space to high-resolution image space. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics (PSNR and SSIM) and visual quality, particularly in recovering fine textures and sharp edges. The model achieves these improvements with reasonable computational complexity, making it suitable for practical applications. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the significance of both the residual learning framework and the fully connected reconstruction layer in achieving superior super-resolution results.

Discovering Invariances in Healthcare Neural Networks

Neural networks have demonstrated remarkable performance in healthcare applications, yet their interpretability remains a significant challenge for clinical adoption. This study investigates the invariances learned by deep neural networks trained on healthcare data, focusing on which input transformations preserve model predictions. Using a novel framework combining adversarial perturbations and counterfactual analysis, we systematically identify and characterize invariances across multiple healthcare domains, including medical imaging, electronic health records, and physiological time series. Our findings reveal that well-performing models develop clinically relevant invariances that align with domain knowledge, such as insensitivity to patient positioning in radiographs and robustness to sampling frequency in ECG interpretation. However, we also uncover problematic invariances where models ignore clinically significant features or exhibit undesirable demographic insensitivity. By quantifying these invariances, we propose regularization techniques that can enhance model alignment with clinical requirements. This work advances our understanding of neural network behavior in healthcare contexts and provides a pathway toward developing more trustworthy and clinically sound AI systems.

Do Transformers Really Perform Bad for Graph Representation?

Recent advances in graph neural networks (GNNs) have demonstrated their effectiveness in learning representations for graph-structured data. Concurrently, Transformer architectures have achieved remarkable success across various domains including natural language processing and computer vision. However, there exists a common belief that Transformers are inherently unsuitable for graph representation learning due to their inability to effectively capture the structural information encoded in graphs. In this paper, we challenge this assumption by introducing a pure transformer-based architecture for graph representation learning. Our approach reformulates graph representation tasks into a sequence modeling problem, allowing Transformer models to process graph-structured data without specialized graph-specific operations. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets spanning node classification, graph classification, and link prediction tasks, we demonstrate that our Transformer-based approach achieves competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art GNN models. Our analysis reveals that Transformers can effectively capture both local and global graph structures through self-attention mechanisms when properly adapted to the graph domain. These findings suggest that the perceived limitations of Transformers for graph representation may be overstated, opening new research directions for applying sequence modeling techniques to graph-structured data.

Two-phase weakly supervised object detection with pseudo ground truth mining

This paper presents a novel two-phase framework for weakly supervised object detection (WSOD), which addresses the challenge of training accurate object detectors using only image-level annotations rather than costly bounding box labels. Our approach introduces a pseudo ground truth mining mechanism that progressively refines object localization quality through a carefully designed iterative process. In the first phase, we employ a multiple instance learning strategy to generate initial object proposals and class activation maps from image-level labels. The second phase implements our pseudo ground truth mining algorithm, which selects high-confidence detections as pseudo labels while filtering out noisy proposals through a combination of spatial consistency verification and cross-image validation. Experimental results on PASCAL VOC and MS COCO datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing WSOD approaches, achieving a mean Average Precision (mAP) improvement of 4.2% on PASCAL VOC 2007 and 3.8% on MS COCO. Further analysis reveals that our pseudo ground truth mining effectively mitigates the common WSOD challenges of partial object detection and instance confusion. The proposed framework provides a cost-effective solution for object detection in scenarios where bounding box annotations are unavailable or prohibitively expensive to obtain.

Recurrent Neural-Linear Posterior Sampling for Non-Stationary Contextual Bandits

Non-stationary contextual bandits present significant challenges in sequential decision-making problems where the relationship between contexts, actions, and rewards evolves over time. Traditional contextual bandit algorithms often perform poorly in such dynamic environments due to their stationarity assumptions. In this paper, we introduce Recurrent Neural-Linear Posterior Sampling (RNLPS), a novel algorithm that combines the expressiveness of recurrent neural networks with the uncertainty quantification capabilities of Bayesian linear regression. RNLPS employs a recurrent neural network to extract time-dependent features from contexts, which are then used in a Bayesian linear model to perform posterior sampling for action selection. We provide theoretical guarantees for our approach, establishing sublinear regret bounds that adapt to the degree of non-stationarity in the environment. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that RNLPS significantly outperforms existing methods, particularly in environments with abrupt changes or gradual drift in the reward function. Our approach offers a principled and effective solution for handling non-stationarity in contextual bandit problems, with potential applications in recommendation systems, online advertising, and clinical trials where temporal dynamics play a crucial role.

Tiny-YOLO Object Detection Supplemented with Geometrical Data

This study presents a novel approach to enhance the performance of Tiny-YOLO, a lightweight object detection framework, by incorporating geometrical data into the detection pipeline. While Tiny-YOLO offers computational efficiency suitable for resource-constrained environments, its detection accuracy often lags behind larger models. Our method addresses this limitation by supplementing the standard RGB input with geometric information including depth maps, surface normals, and spatial relationships between objects. We introduce a modified architecture that processes this geometric data in parallel with visual features, followed by a fusion module that integrates both information streams. Experiments conducted on multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach improves mean Average Precision (mAP) by 8.3% compared to the baseline Tiny-YOLO, while maintaining a minimal increase in computational overhead (11.6% additional parameters). The performance gains are particularly significant for small objects and in scenarios with occlusion or challenging lighting conditions. This work demonstrates that geometric context can substantially enhance lightweight object detectors, making them more viable for real-time applications in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and mobile devices where both efficiency and accuracy are critical.

A Novel Transfer Learning Method Based on Common Space Mapping and Weighted Domain Matching

This paper presents a novel transfer learning approach that addresses the fundamental challenges of domain shift and knowledge transferability between source and target domains. Our method, Common Space Mapping with Weighted Domain Matching (CSM-WDM), introduces a two-stage framework that effectively leverages knowledge from labeled source domains to improve learning in sparsely labeled or unlabeled target domains. First, we establish a common feature space where both domains are projected through a specialized mapping function that preserves task-relevant information while minimizing domain-specific variations.
