Graph-LDA: Graph Structure Priors to Improve the Accuracy in Few-Shot Classification

Few-shot classification remains a challenging problem in machine learning, where models must generalize to new classes with very limited labeled examples. In this paper, we introduce Graph-LDA, a novel approach that leverages graph structure priors to enhance few-shot classification performance. Our method integrates graph-based relationships between samples with Linear Discriminant Analysis to create a more robust feature space for classification tasks. By encoding relational inductive biases through graph structures, Graph-LDA effectively captures the underlying manifold of the data, allowing for better generalization from sparse examples. We formulate a principled optimization framework that jointly learns class-discriminative features while respecting the topological constraints imposed by the graph prior. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and CUB demonstrate that Graph-LDA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods, with particularly significant improvements in the challenging 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios. Our approach not only improves classification accuracy but also exhibits greater stability across different domains and enhanced robustness to distribution shifts. These results highlight the effectiveness of incorporating structural priors in addressing the fundamental challenge of data scarcity in few-shot learning tasks.

Learning Universal Graph Neural Network Embeddings With Aid Of Transfer Learning

This paper introduces a novel framework for developing universal graph neural network (GNN) embeddings through the strategic application of transfer learning techniques. We address the fundamental challenge of creating graph representations that generalize effectively across diverse domains and tasks without requiring task-specific retraining. Our approach leverages pre-trained GNN models from data-rich source domains and adapts them to target domains with limited labeled data. By implementing a hierarchical transfer learning architecture, we demonstrate how knowledge can be effectively transferred at both the node and graph levels. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks—including molecular property prediction, social network analysis, and protein interaction networks—show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, reducing the embedding quality gap between specialized and universal models by up to 37%. Furthermore, our universal embeddings exhibit remarkable robustness to distribution shifts and require significantly fewer parameters compared to task-specific alternatives. This work provides important insights into the development of versatile graph representations that can serve as foundation models for a wide range of graph-based applications.

Short-term Demand Forecasting for Online Car-hailing Services using Recurrent Neural Networks

This study presents a novel approach to short-term demand forecasting for online car-hailing services using recurrent neural networks (RNNs). As ride-sharing platforms continue to transform urban transportation, accurate prediction of spatial-temporal demand patterns has become critical for optimizing resource allocation, reducing customer wait times, and maximizing service efficiency. We develop a deep learning framework that leverages the sequential modeling capabilities of RNNs to capture complex temporal dependencies in historical ride request data. Our model incorporates multiple features including time-of-day, day-of-week, weather conditions, and special events to enhance prediction accuracy. Using a comprehensive dataset from a major ride-hailing platform comprising over 3 million trips across six months, we evaluate various RNN architectures including LSTM and GRU networks. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms traditional time series forecasting methods and standard machine learning algorithms, achieving a 17.8% reduction in mean absolute error and a 22.3% improvement in prediction accuracy for 15-minute forecast horizons. The model shows particular strength in predicting demand surges during peak hours and special events. These findings provide valuable insights for ride-hailing companies seeking to implement data-driven strategies for fleet management and dynamic pricing.

From BoW to CNN: Two Decades of Texture Representation for Texture Classification

This paper presents a comprehensive survey of texture representation methods for texture classification developed over the past two decades, tracing the evolution from traditional Bag-of-Words (BoW) models to modern Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Texture analysis remains a fundamental problem in computer vision with applications spanning medical imaging, material recognition, scene understanding, and industrial inspection. We systematically categorize texture representation approaches into three main paradigms: statistical methods based on hand-crafted features, dictionary learning approaches including BoW and sparse coding, and deep learning techniques dominated by CNNs. For each paradigm, we analyze the key innovations, theoretical foundations, and practical implementations that marked significant advances in the field. Our experimental evaluation on benchmark datasets demonstrates the progressive improvement in classification accuracy across these generations of methods, with modern CNN architectures achieving state-of-the-art performance while offering insights into texture characteristics that traditional methods could not capture. We also discuss remaining challenges including the interpretability of deep features, performance on limited training data, and computational efficiency considerations. This survey provides both historical context and forward-looking perspectives on texture representation, serving as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in this evolving field.

Relation-aware Graph Attention Model With Adaptive Self-adversarial Training

This paper presents a novel approach to graph representation learning by introducing a Relation-aware Graph Attention Model with Adaptive Self-adversarial Training (RGAT-AST). Traditional graph neural networks often struggle to effectively capture complex relational patterns while maintaining computational efficiency. Our model addresses these limitations through two key innovations: (1) a relation-aware attention mechanism that dynamically weights the importance of different relation types and neighboring nodes, and (2) an adaptive self-adversarial training framework that automatically generates challenging negative samples to improve model robustness and generalization. Experimental evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that RGAT-AST consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across various graph-based tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. The performance improvements are particularly significant on heterogeneous graphs with complex relation structures. Further analysis reveals that our adaptive self-adversarial component effectively prevents overfitting and enhances the model's ability to learn discriminative features. The proposed approach not only advances the theoretical understanding of relation-aware graph representation learning but also provides a practical solution for real-world applications involving complex relational data.

Abstract

This paper addresses a novel class of multi-agent multi-armed bandit (MA-MAB) problems where agents face both option unavailability constraints and stochastic communication protocols. We consider a decentralized network of N agents attempting to identify optimal arms while operating under two practical constraints: (1) certain arms may be temporarily unavailable to specific agents, and (2) inter-agent communication occurs through a stochastic protocol with varying connectivity. We propose a decentralized policy that enables agents to make effective decisions despite these limitations by leveraging local observations and intermittent information sharing. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed algorithm achieves logarithmic regret with respect to time horizon T, with a regret bound of O(log T), while maintaining computational efficiency. The policy dynamically balances exploration, exploitation, and collaborative learning through a novel weighted consensus mechanism that accounts for communication uncertainties. Extensive simulations across various network topologies and unavailability patterns validate our theoretical guarantees and demonstrate the algorithm's robustness in practical scenarios. Our work extends the theoretical foundations of decentralized bandit algorithms while addressing key challenges in applications such as distributed resource allocation, multi-robot coordination, and wireless network optimization.

Self-Supervised Learning of Audio-Visual Objects from Video

This paper presents a novel self-supervised learning approach for discovering and modeling audio-visual objects in unconstrained video, without requiring manual annotations. Our method leverages the natural correspondence between visual and auditory signals to learn meaningful representations of objects that both appear in the visual stream and produce sounds. By employing a contrastive learning framework, we train our model to associate time-synchronized audio-visual pairs while discriminating against misaligned samples. The proposed architecture consists of dual-pathway encoders that extract modality-specific features, followed by cross-modal attention mechanisms that enable the discovery of spatial regions corresponding to sound sources. Through extensive experiments on diverse video datasets, we demonstrate that our approach successfully localizes audio-visual objects, separates multiple sound sources, and generates high-quality object-centric representations that transfer effectively to downstream tasks including audio-visual source separation, sound localization, and action recognition. Our results show significant improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods while requiring no labeled data, highlighting the potential of self-supervised multimodal learning for understanding the audio-visual world.

Towards Automated Melanoma Screening: Exploring Transfer Learning Schemes

Melanoma is one of the most aggressive forms of skin cancer, but early detection significantly improves patient outcomes. This study explores the application of transfer learning techniques to develop automated melanoma screening systems with improved diagnostic accuracy. We evaluated several pre-trained convolutional neural network architectures (including ResNet, DenseNet, and EfficientNet) fine-tuned on the ISIC 2020 dataset containing 33,126 dermoscopic images. Our experiments compared various transfer learning strategies, including feature extraction, fine-tuning, and progressive resizing, alongside data augmentation techniques to address class imbalance. The EfficientNet-B3 architecture with a two-stage fine-tuning approach achieved the best performance, with 92.8% accuracy, 91.3% sensitivity, and 93.4% specificity. We also employed Grad-CAM visualizations to enhance model interpretability, revealing the network's focus on clinically relevant lesion features. Our findings demonstrate that optimized transfer learning schemes can approach dermatologist-level diagnostic performance while requiring significantly less labeled training data, potentially enabling more accessible melanoma screening in resource-limited settings. Future work will focus on model robustness across diverse skin types and integration with mobile platforms for point-of-care applications.

Efficient Cross-Validation of Echo State Networks

Echo State Networks (ESNs) have emerged as powerful recurrent neural network models for time series prediction and temporal pattern recognition tasks, offering a balance between computational efficiency and modeling capability. However, the hyperparameter optimization process for ESNs often requires extensive cross-validation, which can be computationally expensive. This paper introduces a novel approach for efficient cross-validation of ESNs that significantly reduces computational overhead while maintaining model performance. By leveraging the inherent properties of reservoir computing, we develop a method that reuses pre-computed reservoir states across validation folds, eliminating redundant computations of the reservoir dynamics. Our approach further incorporates a strategic pruning technique to identify optimal hyperparameter regions early in the validation process. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method achieves up to 70% reduction in computational time compared to standard cross-validation techniques, with no statistically significant difference in model performance. This efficient cross-validation framework makes ESNs more practical for real-world applications with limited computational resources or time constraints, while providing robust hyperparameter selection.

RL STaR Platform: Reinforcement Learning for Simulation based Training of Robots

This paper introduces the Reinforcement Learning Simulation-based Training and Robotics (RL STaR) platform, a comprehensive framework designed to accelerate the development and deployment of reinforcement learning algorithms for robotic applications. The platform addresses key challenges in robot learning by providing a simulation environment that bridges the reality gap while enabling safe, efficient, and scalable training. RL STaR integrates high-fidelity physics simulation, parameterizable environments, and domain randomization techniques to facilitate robust policy learning that can successfully transfer to physical robots. Our experiments demonstrate that policies trained using RL STaR achieve up to 85% performance retention when deployed on real hardware across multiple robotic tasks, including manipulation, navigation, and human-robot interaction scenarios. The platform supports distributed training capabilities that reduce learning time by 76% compared to single-instance approaches. We provide benchmark results across various reinforcement learning algorithms and robot configurations, establishing RL STaR as a valuable resource for both research and industrial applications in robotic learning. The platform's modular architecture allows for easy extension to new robot models, environments, and learning algorithms, making it a versatile tool for advancing the field of robot learning.

Treant: Training Evasion-Aware Decision Trees

Decision trees are widely used in security-critical applications due to their interpretability and efficiency, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial evasion attacks. In this paper, we present Treant, a novel framework for training decision trees that are inherently robust against evasion attacks. Unlike post-hoc hardening approaches, Treant incorporates adversarial awareness directly into the tree construction process, optimizing split criteria to minimize adversarial risk. Our method introduces an evasion-aware information gain metric that accounts for potential feature manipulations within attacker capability constraints. Through extensive experiments on multiple security datasets, we demonstrate that Treant-trained trees maintain classification accuracy comparable to standard trees while significantly improving robustness against both white-box and black-box evasion attacks. Trees trained with our approach show 47% higher adversarial accuracy on average compared to traditional decision trees and outperform existing defense mechanisms including adversarial training and robust pruning techniques. Furthermore, we provide theoretical guarantees on the robustness properties of our trees and analyze the inherent trade-offs between model interpretability, standard accuracy, and adversarial robustness. Treant offers security practitioners a principled approach to deploying decision trees in adversarial environments without sacrificing the interpretability benefits that make these models valuable in security applications.

Cascade Attentive Dropout for Weakly Supervised Object Detection

Weakly supervised object detection (WSOD) aims to localize objects using only image-level annotations, significantly reducing labeling costs compared to fully supervised approaches. However, existing WSOD methods often suffer from incomplete object localization and tend to focus on the most discriminative parts rather than entire objects. In this paper, we propose Cascade Attentive Dropout (CAD), a novel framework that progressively refines object proposals through a multi-stage attention mechanism. Our approach introduces an attentive dropout strategy that systematically masks the most discriminative regions in a cascading manner, forcing the network to discover complementary object parts across multiple stages. By integrating these region-specific features hierarchically, CAD effectively addresses the partial activation problem common in WSOD. Extensive experiments on PASCAL VOC and MS COCO datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving significant improvements in detection accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. The cascade structure enables more complete object coverage and better discrimination between objects and background, particularly for challenging cases with occlusion or complex backgrounds. Our work provides new insights into leveraging weak supervision signals for robust object detection.

Federated Generative Privacy

This paper introduces Federated Generative Privacy (FGP), a novel framework that combines federated learning principles with generative models to enhance privacy preservation in distributed machine learning systems. We address the inherent tension between data utility and privacy protection by developing a decentralized approach where generative models are trained locally on user devices, sharing only synthetic data representations rather than raw data. Our framework leverages differential privacy guarantees while maintaining model performance through a hierarchical federated aggregation mechanism. Experimental results across multiple domains demonstrate that FGP significantly reduces privacy leakage risks compared to traditional federated learning approaches, while achieving comparable utility metrics. We further analyze the framework's resilience against reconstruction attacks and membership inference attacks. The proposed methodology offers a promising direction for privacy-preserving machine learning in sensitive applications such as healthcare, finance, and smart homes, where both data utility and strict privacy guarantees are essential requirements.

Don't Forget Your Teacher: A Corrective Reinforcement Learning Framework

This paper introduces a novel corrective reinforcement learning (CRL) framework that addresses the issue of catastrophic forgetting in reinforcement learning systems. While traditional reinforcement learning approaches often overwrite previously acquired knowledge when adapting to new environments or tasks, our framework preserves critical past experiences by maintaining a "teacher" model alongside the actively learning "student" model. The teacher provides corrective feedback when the student's policy deviates significantly from previously mastered behaviors. We formalize this approach through a constrained optimization problem that balances exploration of new behaviors with preservation of essential past knowledge. Empirical evaluations across diverse environments, including robotic manipulation tasks and complex game environments, demonstrate that our CRL framework achieves up to 45% better performance retention on previously learned tasks while maintaining comparable learning efficiency on new tasks. Furthermore, we provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence properties of our approach. Our results suggest that incorporating corrective teacher feedback offers a promising direction for developing reinforcement learning systems that can continuously learn without catastrophically forgetting crucial past experiences.

Symbolic Regression Methods for Reinforcement Learning

This paper explores the integration of symbolic regression techniques into reinforcement learning (RL) frameworks to enhance interpretability, sample efficiency, and generalization capabilities. While deep reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable success across various domains, the resulting policies often lack transparency and require substantial training data. We propose a novel approach that leverages symbolic regression to discover compact, human-readable mathematical expressions that represent value functions and policies in RL settings. Our method employs genetic programming to evolve these symbolic models while incorporating domain knowledge through carefully designed fitness functions. Experimental results across classic control problems, continuous control tasks, and partially observable environments demonstrate that our symbolic RL approach achieves competitive performance compared to neural network baselines while providing inherently interpretable solutions with significantly fewer parameters. Furthermore, we show that the discovered symbolic representations enable more effective transfer learning and better robustness to distribution shifts. This work contributes to the growing field of interpretable reinforcement learning and offers promising directions for applications where model transparency and data efficiency are paramount.

Generating Realistic Training Images Based on Tonality-Alignment Generative Adversarial Networks for Hand Pose Estimation

Hand pose estimation remains a challenging computer vision task due to the complexity of hand articulation and the difficulty in obtaining large-scale, diverse, and accurately annotated training datasets. This paper presents a novel approach to generate realistic synthetic hand images using Tonality-Alignment Generative Adversarial Networks (TA-GANs). Our method addresses two critical limitations in existing synthetic data generation: the domain gap between synthetic and real images, and the preservation of precise hand pose annotations during image generation. The proposed TA-GAN architecture incorporates a tonality-alignment module that matches the color distribution and lighting conditions of target real-world environments while maintaining structural and skeletal alignment with the original pose annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that training hand pose estimators on our synthetic dataset achieves performance improvements of 15.3% mean joint error reduction on common benchmarks compared to training on conventional synthetic data, and approaches the accuracy of models trained on real data. Furthermore, when combined with limited real training samples in a semi-supervised setting, our approach outperforms fully-supervised methods trained on larger real datasets. The proposed framework provides a scalable solution for generating virtually unlimited annotated training data for hand pose estimation, potentially extending to other pose estimation tasks.

Improving Single-Image Defocus Deblurring: How Dual-Pixel Images Help Through Multi-Task Learning

Single-image defocus deblurring remains a challenging computational photography problem due to the inherent ill-posed nature of recovering sharp details from blurred regions. This paper presents a novel approach that leverages dual-pixel (DP) sensor data through multi-task learning to significantly improve defocus deblurring performance. We demonstrate how the phase information embedded in DP images provides valuable cues about defocus blur that are absent in conventional single images. Our proposed architecture incorporates a multi-task learning framework that jointly optimizes for defocus map estimation and image deblurring, enabling the network to learn robust representations that generalize well across varying defocus conditions. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art single-image deblurring techniques by substantial margins, achieving up to 2.3dB improvement in PSNR and producing visually superior results with better preservation of fine details and textures. Furthermore, we provide insights into how the dual-pixel information specifically contributes to the deblurring process through detailed ablation studies. Our approach not only advances the field of computational defocus deblurring but also highlights the potential of sensor-level innovations when combined with deep learning techniques.

Feasible Actor-Critic: Constrained Reinforcement Learning for Ensuring Statewise Safety

This paper introduces Feasible Actor-Critic (FAC), a novel constrained reinforcement learning framework designed to ensure safety across the entire state space during policy optimization. Unlike conventional constrained RL approaches that focus on expectation-based constraints, our method enforces state-dependent safety constraints that must be satisfied for each visited state. We formulate the problem as a constrained Markov Decision Process with pointwise constraints and develop a primal-dual optimization approach that simultaneously learns a policy and a set of Lagrangian multipliers. FAC incorporates a feasibility layer that projects actions into the safe action space while maintaining policy performance. Our theoretical analysis establishes convergence guarantees under appropriate conditions and provides bounds on constraint violations during training. Extensive experiments on safety-critical control tasks, including autonomous driving simulations and robotic manipulation problems, demonstrate that FAC consistently outperforms existing methods in maintaining safety without significant performance degradation. Results show up to 95% reduction in safety violations compared to baseline approaches while achieving comparable or superior task performance. The proposed framework offers a promising direction for deploying reinforcement learning in real-world safety-critical applications where violation of constraints in any state could lead to catastrophic outcomes.

Video Face Manipulation Detection Through Ensemble of CNNs

This paper presents a novel approach to detecting manipulated facial content in videos using an ensemble of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). With the rapid advancement of deepfake technology and facial manipulation techniques, there is an urgent need for robust detection methods to identify synthetic media. Our proposed framework leverages the complementary strengths of multiple CNN architectures to improve detection accuracy across diverse manipulation techniques. We extract temporal and spatial features through a combination of frame-level analysis and sequence modeling, enabling the detection of subtle inconsistencies that single-model approaches often miss. The ensemble methodology employs a weighted voting mechanism that dynamically adjusts based on each model's confidence and historical performance on specific manipulation types. Experimental evaluation on multiple benchmark datasets, including FaceForensics++, Deepfake Detection Challenge, and Celeb-DF, demonstrates that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art single-model methods, achieving an average accuracy of 94.7% and showing particular robustness to unseen manipulation techniques. Furthermore, our system maintains real-time performance, processing videos at 18 frames per second on standard GPU hardware, making it suitable for practical deployment in social media and news verification pipelines.

Attention-based Fusion for Multi-source Human Image Generation

This paper presents a novel attention-based fusion framework for multi-source human image generation, addressing the limitations of existing methods that struggle to integrate information from multiple reference images. Our approach leverages a transformer-based architecture that dynamically attends to relevant features across diverse source images containing human subjects. By decomposing the generation process into structure, appearance, and detail components, our model effectively preserves identity characteristics while allowing flexible manipulation of pose, clothing, and contextual elements. We introduce a hierarchical cross-attention mechanism that selectively transfers information from source images to the target domain, enabling fine-grained control over which attributes are inherited from each reference. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of visual quality, identity preservation, and attribute transfer accuracy. Both qualitative and quantitative evaluations confirm the effectiveness of our attention-based fusion strategy for generating photorealistic human images that faithfully combine elements from multiple sources while maintaining coherence and natural appearance.

Modern Hopfield Networks for Few- and Zero-Shot Reaction Template Prediction

Reaction template prediction is a critical task in computational chemistry that facilitates retrosynthetic planning and reaction outcome prediction. However, traditional approaches typically require extensive training data and struggle with rare or novel reaction types. In this work, we introduce a novel framework leveraging Modern Hopfield Networks (MHNs) for few- and zero-shot reaction template prediction. MHNs, with their energy-based associative memory capabilities, offer significant advantages over traditional neural architectures in handling sparse data regimes. Our approach encodes molecular structures and reaction contexts into a continuous representation space where MHNs can efficiently retrieve relevant templates through pattern completion. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves 87.3% top-10 accuracy in few-shot settings (1-10 examples per template) on the USPTO dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art graph neural network approaches by 15.2%. More remarkably, in zero-shot scenarios involving completely novel reaction templates, our approach maintains 63.8% top-10 accuracy by leveraging chemical similarity principles encoded in the network's associative memory. This work represents a significant advancement in reaction prediction with limited data and offers promising directions for improving computational tools in synthetic chemistry.

Image Segmentation via Cellular Automata

This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation utilizing cellular automata (CA), a discrete computational model capable of exhibiting complex emergent behavior through simple local rules. We introduce a specialized CA framework that treats image pixels as individual cells whose states evolve according to transition rules based on local intensity variations, gradient information, and neighborhood configurations. Our method leverages the inherent parallelism and self-organizing properties of cellular automata to identify coherent regions within images while preserving important boundaries. The proposed algorithm demonstrates robust performance across various image types, including natural scenes, medical images, and textured surfaces. Experimental results show that our CA-based segmentation achieves competitive accuracy compared to traditional watershed algorithms and modern deep learning approaches, while requiring significantly less computational resources and no training data. Furthermore, the interpretable nature of the CA rules allows for intuitive parameter tuning to address specific segmentation challenges. We demonstrate the versatility of our approach through quantitative evaluation on standard benchmark datasets and qualitative analysis of segmentation quality in challenging scenarios featuring noise, illumination variations, and complex textures.

Semantic Adversarial Deep Learning

Deep learning systems have demonstrated remarkable performance across various domains but remain vulnerable to adversarial examples—inputs modified by imperceptible perturbations that cause misclassification. While numerous defense mechanisms have been proposed, they typically focus on statistical robustness without considering the semantic meaning of these perturbations. In this paper, we introduce Semantic Adversarial Deep Learning, a novel framework that bridges the gap between statistical robustness and semantic understanding in adversarial settings. Our approach incorporates semantic knowledge into both the generation and detection of adversarial examples, ensuring that defense mechanisms preserve the semantic integrity of inputs while improving resilience against attacks. Through extensive experiments across image classification, natural language processing, and autonomous driving scenarios, we demonstrate that semantically-informed models achieve significantly higher robustness against diverse adversarial attacks compared to traditional defenses, while maintaining high performance on benign inputs. Furthermore, we establish theoretical guarantees on the semantic consistency of our approach. Our work highlights the importance of semantic understanding in developing truly robust deep learning systems for safety-critical applications.

Generation of Synthetic Electronic Health Records Using a Federated GAN

Electronic health records (EHRs) are invaluable for healthcare research, but their use is often constrained by privacy regulations and data access limitations. This study presents a novel approach to generating high-quality synthetic EHRs through a federated generative adversarial network (FedGAN) framework. Our method enables healthcare institutions to collaboratively train robust generative models without sharing sensitive patient data. We implemented a multi-institutional FedGAN architecture where local GANs are trained on private EHR datasets, with only model parameters being exchanged with a central server for aggregation. Experimental evaluation across five healthcare systems demonstrated that our approach preserves statistical properties and complex relationships between clinical variables while maintaining patient privacy. The synthetic records generated by our FedGAN showed superior utility compared to centralized approaches, with 92% accuracy in preserving feature correlations and passing differential privacy guarantees with an ε value of 1.2. Furthermore, machine learning models trained on our synthetic data achieved performance within 3.5% of those trained on real data for common clinical prediction tasks. This work provides a practical solution to the data sharing challenges in healthcare while enabling broader access to representative EHR data for research and innovation.

Convolutional Transformer based Dual Discriminator Generative Adversarial Networks for Video Anomaly Detection

Video anomaly detection remains a challenging task in computer vision due to the complexity of defining and identifying abnormal events in diverse real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a novel framework, Convolutional Transformer based Dual Discriminator Generative Adversarial Networks (CT-D²GAN), which effectively combines the spatial feature extraction capabilities of convolutional neural networks with the temporal modeling strengths of transformers for unsupervised video anomaly detection. Our approach employs a dual discriminator architecture where the first discriminator focuses on frame-level appearance inconsistencies while the second evaluates temporal coherence across video sequences. The generator, enhanced with a convolutional transformer backbone, learns to reconstruct normal patterns in both spatial and temporal dimensions. By leveraging attention mechanisms from the transformer architecture, our model captures long-range dependencies critical for distinguishing subtle anomalous behaviors from normal activities. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including UCSD Ped2, CUHK Avenue, and ShanghaiTech demonstrate that CT-D²GAN achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing previous methods by 2.3%, 3.1%, and 2.7% in AUC respectively. Further ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our dual discriminator design and the convolutional transformer integration. The proposed framework offers a robust solution for real-world surveillance systems requiring minimal human supervision while maintaining high detection accuracy.

Compact Neural Representation Using Attentive Network Pruning

Deep neural networks have demonstrated remarkable performance across various domains but often at the cost of excessive computational complexity and memory requirements. This paper introduces Attentive Network Pruning (ANP), a novel approach that systematically reduces network parameters while preserving model accuracy. Unlike traditional pruning methods that rely on magnitude-based criteria, ANP leverages attention mechanisms to identify and retain the most salient neurons and connections based on their contribution to the network's decision-making process. Our method incorporates a learnable attention module that dynamically assigns importance scores to network components during training, enabling a more informed pruning strategy. Extensive experiments across image classification, natural language processing, and speech recognition tasks demonstrate that ANP achieves compression rates of up to 90% with negligible performance degradation compared to state-of-the-art pruning techniques. Furthermore, the resulting compact networks exhibit improved inference speed and reduced energy consumption on resource-constrained devices. We also provide theoretical insights into why attention-guided pruning preserves the representational capacity of deep networks. The proposed ANP framework offers a principled approach to developing efficient neural architectures for deployment in real-world applications with limited computational resources.

Mining Recurrent Concepts in Data Streams using the Discrete Fourier Transform

This paper introduces a novel approach for detecting and managing recurrent concepts in data stream mining using the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT). Data streams in real-world applications often exhibit concept drift where the underlying data distribution changes over time, with certain concepts reappearing periodically. We propose a framework that leverages the frequency-domain properties of the DFT to efficiently identify, store, and reuse recurring patterns in evolving data streams. Our method transforms concept representations into the frequency domain, enabling dimensionality reduction while preserving essential characteristics for concept matching. The approach includes: (1) a DFT-based concept signature mechanism that captures the fundamental properties of concepts with minimal storage requirements; (2) an adaptive concept matching algorithm that identifies similarities between current and historical concepts; and (3) a concept ensemble technique that leverages previously learned models when recurrent concepts are detected. Experimental evaluation on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates that our approach significantly reduces computational overhead and improves classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, particularly in environments with periodic concept recurrence. The results show that our DFT-based framework provides an effective solution for handling concept drift while maintaining high predictive performance in streaming environments with limited computational resources.

Atomic Convolutional Networks for Predicting Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity

Accurate prediction of protein-ligand binding affinity remains a central challenge in computational drug discovery. In this work, we present a novel deep learning architecture, Atomic Convolutional Networks (AtomNet), designed specifically to capture the complex atomic interactions that govern binding affinity. Our approach leverages 3D convolutional neural networks operating directly on atomic coordinates and properties, eliminating the need for hand-crafted descriptors. AtomNet incorporates specialized atomic feature extraction layers that account for different interaction types (electrostatic, hydrophobic, hydrogen bonding) while maintaining rotational and translational invariance. We trained our model on a diverse dataset of over 300,000 protein-ligand complexes with experimentally determined binding affinities. AtomNet significantly outperforms traditional scoring functions and other machine learning methods, achieving a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.82 and RMSE of 1.25 kcal/mol on our test set. Furthermore, we demonstrate AtomNet's ability to generalize across different protein families, including those absent from the training data. This work represents a substantial advancement in structure-based binding affinity prediction and offers promising applications in virtual screening and lead optimization for drug discovery.

AgeFlow: Conditional Age Progression and Regression with Normalizing Flows

This paper introduces AgeFlow, a novel framework for age progression and regression that leverages normalizing flows to model the complex distribution of facial appearance across different ages. Unlike previous approaches that often rely on generative adversarial networks (GANs) or encoder-decoder architectures, our method utilizes the bijective nature of normalizing flows to create a continuous and invertible mapping between age groups. AgeFlow explicitly models the aging process as a conditional transformation in the latent space, allowing for smooth and realistic transitions across any desired age range. Our approach maintains identity permanence while accurately capturing age-specific features such as skin texture, facial structure, and hair color changes. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including MORPH, CACD, and FG-NET demonstrate that AgeFlow outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of aging accuracy, identity preservation, and photorealism. Additionally, the invertible nature of our model enables both age progression and regression using a single trained network, providing a versatile tool for various applications including missing person identification, entertainment, and face recognition across age gaps.

Explainable Time Series Tweaking via Irreversible and Reversible Temporal Transformations

This paper introduces a novel framework for time series modification that preserves explanatory capabilities through carefully designed temporal transformations. We categorize these transformations into irreversible operations that fundamentally alter the data structure and reversible operations that maintain invertibility. Our approach addresses the critical challenge of modifying time series data for various downstream applications while ensuring that the transformations remain interpretable and justifiable. We formalize a mathematical framework that characterizes the information preservation properties of each transformation type and quantifies their impact on predictive model performance. Through extensive experiments on financial, healthcare, and IoT sensor datasets, we demonstrate that our proposed reversible transformations maintain up to 95% of the original predictive power while providing clear explanations for the modifications. The irreversible transformations, while more aggressive, still preserve critical temporal patterns identified through our proposed importance sampling technique. Our framework enables practitioners to make informed decisions about time series modifications with a clear understanding of the tradeoffs between data utility and transformation complexity. This work contributes to the growing field of explainable AI by extending interpretability concepts to the temporal domain.

Joint Demosaicing and Denoising with Perceptual Optimization on a Generative Adversarial Network

This paper presents a novel approach to simultaneously address the challenges of image demosaicing and denoising using a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework optimized for perceptual quality. Digital cameras typically capture images through a color filter array, requiring demosaicing to reconstruct full-color images, while sensor noise necessitates effective denoising strategies. Traditional pipeline approaches that handle these tasks sequentially often propagate and amplify artifacts. Our proposed end-to-end solution leverages a conditional GAN architecture that directly transforms mosaiced, noisy sensor data into clean, full-color images. The network incorporates perceptually-motivated loss functions that prioritize visual quality over purely statistical metrics, addressing limitations in previous methods that optimize for PSNR but produce over-smoothed results. Extensive experiments across multiple noise levels and camera sensors demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in perceptual quality metrics and human preference studies, while maintaining competitive performance in traditional error-based metrics. The model shows particular strength in preserving texture details and natural image statistics in challenging scenarios with limited light. Our unified approach not only improves computational efficiency compared to sequential processing but also establishes a new direction for camera image processing pipelines guided by perceptual optimization principles.

Fair Decisions Despite Imperfect Predictions

Decision-making algorithms increasingly influence critical domains including hiring, lending, and criminal justice, raising concerns about fairness when these systems rely on imperfect predictions. This paper addresses the fundamental challenge of making fair decisions in scenarios where predictive models exhibit varying accuracy across different demographic groups. We propose a novel framework that acknowledges the inevitability of prediction errors while establishing formal fairness guarantees for downstream decisions. Our approach introduces a calibration-based adjustment mechanism that compensates for group-specific prediction uncertainties without requiring perfect prediction parity. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that our method satisfies multiple fairness criteria including equalized opportunity and predictive parity while maintaining near-optimal utility. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets from employment, credit, and recidivism prediction domains show that our approach reduces disparity by 37-52% compared to standard methods, with minimal sacrifice in overall performance. These results suggest a promising path toward fair algorithmic decision-making even when underlying predictions remain imperfect, offering practical guidance for policymakers and system designers navigating the complex fairness-accuracy trade-off.

Privileged Zero-Shot AutoML

Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) has emerged as a promising approach to democratize machine learning by automating the process of model selection and hyperparameter optimization. However, traditional AutoML methods often require extensive computational resources for model search and validation, limiting their applicability in resource-constrained environments. In this paper, we introduce Privileged Zero-Shot AutoML (PZ-AutoML), a novel framework that leverages privileged information during training while requiring no task-specific adaptation at inference time. Our approach distills knowledge from a teacher model with access to privileged features into a student model that can rapidly adapt to new tasks without additional training or hyperparameter tuning. Through theoretical analysis, we establish generalization bounds for our method and demonstrate how it effectively transfers knowledge across the task distribution. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets show that PZ-AutoML achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art AutoML methods while reducing computational overhead by orders of magnitude. Furthermore, our approach exhibits remarkable robustness to distribution shifts between training and deployment environments. These results suggest that PZ-AutoML represents a significant step toward making sophisticated machine learning accessible in zero-shot scenarios where traditional AutoML approaches are computationally prohibitive.

Graph Barlow Twins: A self-supervised representation learning framework for graphs

Self-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for representation learning on graph-structured data without relying on manual labels. In this paper, we introduce Graph Barlow Twins (GBT), a novel self-supervised framework for learning node and graph representations that extends the Barlow Twins approach to the graph domain. Our method generates two augmented views of an input graph and trains a graph neural network encoder to produce representations that maximize the similarity between corresponding nodes while minimizing redundancy in the latent space. By employing a cross-correlation objective function on the embeddings, GBT encourages the network to capture essential structural and feature-based information while being robust to noise and perturbations. We theoretically analyze the properties of our approach and demonstrate its effectiveness across multiple downstream tasks including node classification, graph classification, and link prediction. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that GBT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised graph representation learning methods, with particular advantages in scenarios with limited labeled data. Our framework provides a versatile and computationally efficient solution for learning discriminative graph representations without human supervision.

Efficient Urban-scale Point Clouds Segmentation with BEV Projection

This paper introduces a novel approach for semantic segmentation of large-scale urban point clouds using Bird's Eye View (BEV) projection. While 3D point cloud segmentation is crucial for autonomous driving and urban planning, existing methods often struggle with computational efficiency when processing massive urban-scale datasets. Our method addresses this challenge by transforming the 3D segmentation problem into a 2D domain through BEV projection, significantly reducing computational complexity while preserving critical spatial information. We propose a two-stage architecture that first projects point clouds to a BEV representation, then applies an efficient 2D convolutional network with specialized height-aware features to maintain vertical context. Experiments on large-scale urban datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art 3D methods while reducing processing time by 78% and memory consumption by 65%. Additionally, our method shows robust performance on sparse regions and maintains consistent segmentation quality across varying point densities. The proposed framework enables real-time processing of urban-scale point clouds on standard hardware, making it particularly suitable for autonomous vehicle perception and large-scale urban modeling applications.

Deep Extrapolation for Attribute-Enhanced Generation

This paper introduces a novel framework for attribute-enhanced generation that enables models to extrapolate beyond the attribute distributions observed in training data. While existing generative models excel at interpolating within the boundaries of their training distribution, they often struggle when tasked with generating content that extends attribute values beyond these limits. Our proposed method, Deep Extrapolation for Attribute-Enhanced Generation (DEAEG), addresses this limitation by learning disentangled representations of attributes and content, followed by a specialized extrapolation mechanism that can systematically extend attribute values while maintaining semantic coherence. Through a series of experiments across multiple domains—including image generation, text-to-image synthesis, and language modeling—we demonstrate that DEAEG significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in generating high-quality content with attribute values that lie outside the training distribution. Quantitative evaluations show improvements of up to 37% in extrapolation accuracy while maintaining comparable quality metrics to baseline models. Our approach opens new possibilities for creative applications that require pushing the boundaries of generative capabilities beyond the constraints of training data distributions.

Unsupervised Learning of Depth and Ego-Motion from Cylindrical Panoramic Video

This paper presents a novel unsupervised learning framework for jointly estimating depth and ego-motion from cylindrical panoramic video sequences. Unlike conventional approaches that process perspective images, our method directly operates on 360° cylindrical panoramas, leveraging their comprehensive spatial information and unique geometric properties. We introduce a specialized network architecture that accounts for the continuous and warped nature of panoramic imagery, incorporating cylindrical projection constraints into both our depth estimation and pose prediction networks. By exploiting temporal consistency between consecutive panoramic frames, our approach learns to predict dense depth maps and camera motion without requiring ground truth supervision. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world panoramic datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques adapted from perspective imagery, achieving up to 18% improvement in depth accuracy and 15% in ego-motion estimation. Furthermore, we show that the holistic understanding of scene geometry provided by panoramic inputs enhances performance in challenging scenarios involving large camera motions and complex environments. Our approach opens new possibilities for 3D perception in applications such as virtual reality, autonomous navigation, and immersive environment mapping.

Pixel2Mesh: Generating 3D Mesh Models from Single RGB Images

We present Pixel2Mesh, a novel end-to-end deep learning framework that can generate 3D mesh models from single RGB images. Unlike existing approaches that typically produce voxel grids, point clouds, or implicit functions, our method directly generates triangular meshes, which are more efficient for rendering and storage. Starting with a coarse ellipsoid mesh, our network progressively deforms and refines it to match the target 3D shape visible in the input image. The framework employs a graph-based convolutional neural network that learns to leverage perceptual image features and geometric cues to predict vertex displacements while maintaining mesh regularity. Through extensive experiments on ShapeNet and real-world images, we demonstrate that Pixel2Mesh produces high-quality 3D meshes that capture both overall structure and fine-grained details, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in reconstruction accuracy and visual quality. Our approach bridges the gap between 2D perception and 3D shape modeling, enabling applications in augmented reality, computer graphics, and robotic perception from monocular images.

Deep Reinforcement Learning that Matters

Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have demonstrated remarkable success in solving complex tasks across various domains. However, despite these achievements, there remains significant inconsistency in evaluation methodology, reproducibility challenges, and limited understanding of the factors that critically influence performance. This paper presents a systematic investigation into the sensitivity of DRL algorithms to implementation choices, hyperparameter settings, and random seeds. Through extensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmark environments, we demonstrate that seemingly minor implementation details can dramatically impact learning outcomes, often overshadowing the differences between algorithms themselves. We identify key sources of variability including network initialization schemes, reward scaling, batch normalization, and optimizer selection. Our results highlight the need for more rigorous reporting standards, comprehensive ablation studies, and statistical significance testing in DRL research. By establishing a more thorough evaluation framework, we aim to enhance reproducibility and facilitate meaningful progress in the field. This work provides practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners to better understand when and why deep reinforcement learning matters.

Statistical mechanics of unsupervised feature learning in a restricted Boltzmann machine with binary synapses

This study investigates the statistical mechanics of unsupervised feature learning in restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) with binary synaptic weights. Using analytical techniques from statistical physics, we characterize the learning dynamics and representational capacity of these networks when constrained to binary (0/1) connections. We derive phase diagrams that reveal distinct learning regimes as functions of temperature, input sparsity, and hidden layer size. Our results demonstrate that despite severe weight quantization, binary-synapse RBMs can successfully extract meaningful features from complex datasets through unsupervised learning. We identify critical thresholds where learning performance transitions sharply, analogous to phase transitions in physical systems. Additionally, we provide theoretical bounds on memory capacity and feature detection capabilities, comparing them with experimental results on benchmark datasets. This work bridges machine learning and statistical mechanics, offering insights into the fundamental limits of learning with highly constrained neural architectures and suggesting hardware-efficient implementations for neuromorphic computing systems where binary synapses are particularly advantageous.

FD-GAN: Pose-guided Feature Distilling GAN for Robust Person Re-identification

Person re-identification (re-ID) remains challenging due to significant pose variations and occlusions in real-world surveillance scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Feature Distilling Generative Adversarial Network (FD-GAN) that leverages pose information to generate robust identity-preserving features for person re-ID. Our framework consists of two main components: a pose-guided image generator that synthesizes person images under different poses while preserving identity details, and a feature distilling mechanism that extracts identity-relevant features while filtering out pose variations. The generator employs an innovative attention mechanism to focus on identity-relevant regions, while the discriminator is designed to ensure both pose accuracy and identity consistency. Extensive experiments on Market-1501, DukeMTMC-reID, and CUHK03 datasets demonstrate that our FD-GAN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, especially in challenging scenarios with dramatic pose variations and partial occlusions. The proposed approach improves rank-1 accuracy by 5.3% on Market-1501 and 4.7% on DukeMTMC-reID compared to previous methods, proving the effectiveness of our feature distilling strategy for robust person re-identification.

Automatically Generating Codes from Graphical Screenshots Based on Deep Autocoder

This paper presents a novel approach for automatically converting graphical user interface (GUI) screenshots into functional code using an enhanced deep learning framework based on the Autocoder architecture. Our system, Deep Autocoder, employs a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract visual features from screenshots, followed by a transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture that generates corresponding code in multiple programming languages. We trained our model on a diverse dataset of 150,000 paired screenshot-code examples spanning web, mobile, and desktop applications. Experimental results demonstrate that Deep Autocoder achieves 87.3% accuracy in correctly identifying UI components and generates syntactically valid code for 92.1% of test cases. When compared to existing solutions, our approach shows a 23% improvement in code correctness and a 35% reduction in post-generation manual adjustments. Additionally, we introduce a component-aware attention mechanism that significantly enhances the model's ability to maintain structural relationships between visual elements and their code representations. This research advances the field of automated programming and offers practical applications in rapid prototyping, legacy system modernization, and accessibility enhancement.

Attention Routing Between Capsules

This paper introduces a novel attention-based routing mechanism for capsule networks that addresses the computational inefficiencies and performance limitations of traditional dynamic routing approaches. Our proposed attention routing leverages self-attention principles to dynamically determine the strength of connections between capsules in adjacent layers, enabling more effective part-whole relationships modeling. Unlike conventional routing algorithms that require multiple iterative steps, our method computes routing coefficients in a single forward pass, significantly reducing computational overhead while maintaining representational capacity. Extensive experiments on image classification benchmarks demonstrate that attention routing not only accelerates training and inference by up to 3× but also improves classification accuracy by 2.4% compared to dynamic routing. Further analysis reveals that our approach produces more stable and interpretable routing paths, with attention maps that clearly highlight relevant spatial relationships between lower and higher-level features. The proposed attention routing mechanism represents a promising direction for scaling capsule networks to more complex visual recognition tasks.

Troy: Give Attention to Saliency and for Saliency

Visual saliency detection is a fundamental task in computer vision that aims to identify the most visually distinctive regions in an image. In this paper, we present Troy, a novel attention-based framework that addresses both the utilization and generation of saliency information in a bidirectional manner. Our approach leverages a dual-stream architecture where saliency information guides the attention mechanism while simultaneously refining saliency predictions through attention feedback loops. Through extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that Troy achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing previous methods by an average of 3.2% in mean F-measure. The bidirectional attention mechanism proves particularly effective in challenging scenarios involving complex backgrounds and multiple salient objects. Additionally, our ablation studies reveal that the reciprocal relationship between attention and saliency significantly improves feature representation, leading to more precise saliency maps with clearer object boundaries and fewer false positives. The proposed framework not only advances saliency detection performance but also provides insights into the synergistic relationship between visual attention and saliency perception that could benefit other vision tasks.

Content-based Propagation of User Markings for Interactive Segmentation of Patterned Images

This paper presents a novel approach for interactive segmentation of patterned images through intelligent propagation of user markings. Patterned images—containing repetitive elements, textures, or structured motifs—present unique challenges for traditional segmentation algorithms, which often struggle to distinguish between visually similar regions that belong to different semantic objects. Our method leverages minimal user input in the form of sparse markings and propagates these annotations to similar content across the image based on pattern-aware feature representations. We introduce a dual-stream architecture that simultaneously analyzes both local texture characteristics and global pattern structures to identify visually coherent regions. The propagation mechanism employs a content-adaptive similarity metric that dynamically adjusts to the specific patterns present in each image. Experimental evaluation on diverse datasets of textiles, wallpapers, natural scenes with repetitive elements, and biological imagery demonstrates that our approach significantly reduces the required user interaction compared to existing methods while maintaining high segmentation accuracy. The results show particular effectiveness for challenging cases where patterns cross object boundaries or exhibit subtle variations. Our user studies further confirm that the proposed system enables more intuitive and efficient interactive segmentation of complex patterned images.

TNE: A Latent Model for Representation Learning on Networks

This paper introduces TNE (Topological Network Embedding), a novel latent variable model for learning low-dimensional representations of nodes in complex networks. Unlike previous approaches that primarily focus on preserving local structural properties, TNE explicitly models both local connectivity patterns and global topological features through a principled probabilistic framework. Our model employs a variational inference approach to learn embeddings that capture the inherent community structures while preserving higher-order network characteristics. We formulate network representation learning as a statistical inference problem, where node embeddings are treated as latent variables that generate the observed network topology. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that TNE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple downstream tasks, including link prediction, node classification, and community detection. The learned representations exhibit strong generalization capabilities, effectively capturing both microscopic and macroscopic network properties. Furthermore, our model provides interpretable embeddings that offer insights into the underlying generative processes of real-world networks. The theoretical guarantees and empirical results establish TNE as a powerful and flexible framework for network representation learning.

Object Detection in Videos by High Quality Object Linking

This paper presents a novel approach to object detection in videos through high quality object linking. While single-frame object detection has advanced significantly with deep learning techniques, accurately tracking and linking objects across video frames remains challenging due to occlusions, motion blur, and appearance variations. Our method addresses these limitations by introducing a two-stage framework that combines frame-level detection with temporal linking. First, we employ a state-of-the-art convolutional neural network to generate object proposals in individual frames. Then, we develop a high-quality linking algorithm that establishes object correspondences across frames by jointly modeling appearance similarity, motion consistency, and spatial-temporal relations. The linking process is formulated as an energy minimization problem that enforces consistency while handling detection gaps and identity switches. We evaluate our approach on multiple video object detection benchmarks, including ImageNet VID and YouTube-Objects, demonstrating significant improvements over frame-by-frame detection baselines and existing video object detection methods. Our approach achieves 4.3% higher mAP on ImageNet VID while maintaining real-time performance, proving particularly effective in challenging scenarios with fast motion and partial occlusions. The proposed method requires minimal additional computational overhead and can be integrated with various underlying detection architectures.

Non-Gaussianity of Stochastic Gradient Noise

This paper investigates the statistical properties of stochastic gradient noise in deep learning optimization, challenging the common assumption that this noise follows a Gaussian distribution. Through extensive empirical analysis across various neural network architectures and datasets, we demonstrate that stochastic gradient noise exhibits significant non-Gaussian characteristics, including heavy tails and asymmetric distributions. We quantify these deviations using statistical measures such as kurtosis, skewness, and Wasserstein distance from Gaussian references. Our theoretical analysis connects these non-Gaussian properties to the geometry of the loss landscape and batch sampling mechanisms. Furthermore, we show that accounting for this non-Gaussianity in optimization algorithms leads to improved convergence rates and generalization performance. These findings have important implications for the development of more accurate stochastic optimization theory and the design of more effective training algorithms that explicitly account for the true distributional properties of gradient noise.

How Hard is to Distinguish Graphs with Graph Neural Networks?

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning on graph-structured data, yet their expressive power remains constrained by fundamental limitations. This paper provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the discriminative capabilities of GNNs in distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs. We establish formal connections between GNN expressiveness and the Weisfeiler-Leman (WL) test, demonstrating that standard message-passing GNNs cannot exceed the discriminative power of the 1-WL algorithm. Through a complexity-theoretic lens, we characterize classes of graphs that are provably indistinguishable by conventional GNNs and quantify the computational hardness of graph discrimination tasks. Our analysis extends to recent architectural innovations designed to overcome these limitations, including higher-order GNNs and substructure-aware variants. Experimental results across synthetic and real-world graph classification benchmarks validate our theoretical findings, revealing practical scenarios where discrimination challenges arise. This work provides both theoretical foundations and practical insights into the fundamental question of graph distinguishability with GNNs, offering guidance for model selection and architectural design when facing challenging graph discrimination tasks.

Simple Interactive Image Segmentation using Label Propagation through kNN graphs

This paper presents a novel approach to interactive image segmentation that leverages label propagation through k-nearest neighbor (kNN) graphs. Our method simplifies the segmentation process by requiring minimal user input in the form of sparse foreground and background labels, which are then propagated throughout the image using a graph-based framework. We construct a kNN graph where each pixel is connected to its k nearest neighbors in a joint spatial-color feature space. The label propagation algorithm efficiently diffuses user annotations across this graph structure, respecting both color similarity and spatial proximity. We introduce an adaptive weighting scheme that dynamically adjusts the influence of spatial versus appearance features based on local image characteristics. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive segmentation accuracy compared to more complex methods while maintaining real-time performance. The simplicity of our framework makes it particularly suitable for mobile applications and interactive editing tools where computational resources may be limited. Furthermore, we show that our method is robust to variations in user input and can effectively handle objects with complex boundaries and texture variations.

Revisiting Unsupervised Meta-Learning: Amplifying or Compensating for the Characteristics of Few-Shot Tasks

Unsupervised meta-learning has emerged as a promising approach to overcome the data scarcity challenges in few-shot learning scenarios without requiring labeled data for meta-training. However, the fundamental mechanisms by which unsupervised meta-learning methods interact with the inherent characteristics of few-shot tasks remain underexplored. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis examining whether unsupervised meta-learning algorithms amplify or compensate for the distinctive properties of few-shot learning problems. Through extensive experiments across diverse domains and task distributions, we identify that current unsupervised meta-learning approaches primarily function as characteristic amplifiers when task distributions exhibit strong structural regularity, but transition to compensatory mechanisms when facing heterogeneous task environments. We propose a unified theoretical framework that explains these dual behaviors and introduce a novel adaptive meta-learning algorithm that dynamically balances amplification and compensation based on task characteristics. Our findings challenge several prevailing assumptions in the field and provide actionable insights for designing more effective unsupervised meta-learning systems that can better leverage the intrinsic properties of few-shot tasks.

Multi-Domain Image-to-Image Translation with Adaptive Inference Graph

Image-to-image translation across multiple domains remains a challenging task, particularly when maintaining consistency across diverse visual styles while preserving content integrity. In this paper, we present a novel framework for multi-domain image translation utilizing an Adaptive Inference Graph (AIG) that dynamically adjusts the translation pathway based on input and target domain characteristics. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on fixed translation networks or pairwise mappings, our method constructs a flexible computational graph that selectively activates domain-specific modules while sharing common feature representations. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including CelebA-HQ, Animal Faces, and Seasons, we demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance in terms of both translation quality and computational efficiency. Quantitative evaluations show improvements of 15% in FID scores and 12% in user preference studies compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our adaptive inference mechanism reduces computational overhead by 30% during inference while maintaining translation fidelity. The proposed approach enables effective many-to-many domain translations without requiring explicit pairwise mappings, making it particularly suitable for applications requiring flexible style transfer across multiple visual domains.

Ego2Hands: A Dataset for Egocentric Two-hand Segmentation and Detection

We present Ego2Hands, a large-scale dataset designed specifically for the segmentation and detection of both hands in egocentric vision. While hand analysis is crucial for understanding human-object interactions in first-person perspectives, existing datasets often fall short in capturing diverse, natural two-hand interactions with precise annotations. Ego2Hands contains over 180,000 frames of high-resolution RGB images collected from 30 participants performing various bimanual tasks across different environments, lighting conditions, and backgrounds. Each frame is meticulously annotated with pixel-level segmentation masks and bounding boxes for both hands, distinguishing between left and right hands even during complex interactions and occlusions. We benchmark several state-of-the-art segmentation and detection models on our dataset, establishing strong baselines while highlighting the unique challenges of egocentric two-hand analysis. Experimental results demonstrate that models trained on Ego2Hands significantly outperform those trained on existing datasets when evaluated on real-world egocentric hand tasks. We believe Ego2Hands will accelerate research in egocentric vision, human-computer interaction, and augmented reality applications that rely on accurate hand understanding.

Neural Optimization Kernel: Towards Robust Deep Learning

Despite significant advances in deep learning performance, modern neural networks remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, distribution shifts, and noisy data. This paper introduces the Neural Optimization Kernel (NOK), a novel framework that enhances the robustness of deep learning systems without sacrificing accuracy on clean data. NOK operates by adaptively modifying the optimization landscape during training through a learnable kernel that identifies and mitigates potentially harmful gradient directions. Our approach integrates theoretical insights from differential geometry and robust optimization to create a training methodology that promotes invariance to perturbations. Extensive experiments across image classification, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning tasks demonstrate that NOK-trained models consistently outperform state-of-the-art methods in robustness benchmarks, including adversarial attacks, common corruptions, and out-of-distribution scenarios. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence properties of NOK and analyze its computational efficiency. Our findings suggest that NOK represents a significant step toward developing inherently robust deep learning systems for real-world applications.

Deep Learning for Identifying Radiogenomic Associations in Breast Cancer

This study investigates the application of deep learning techniques to establish associations between radiological imaging features and genomic signatures in breast cancer. We developed a novel multi-modal deep learning framework that integrates mammographic and MRI imaging data with genomic sequencing information from 1,245 breast cancer patients. Our model employs convolutional neural networks to extract high-dimensional imaging features, which are then correlated with key genomic alterations including mutations in BRCA1/2, TP53, and PIK3CA genes, as well as molecular subtypes. Results demonstrate that specific imaging patterns can predict genomic characteristics with an AUC of 0.83, outperforming traditional radiomics approaches (AUC 0.71). Notably, we identified previously unreported associations between tumor margin characteristics on MRI and PIK3CA mutation status, and between parenchymal patterns on mammography and immune infiltration signatures. These radiogenomic associations may enable non-invasive tumor characterization, potentially reducing the need for invasive biopsies and facilitating personalized treatment planning. Our findings suggest that deep learning-based radiogenomics could serve as a valuable tool for precision oncology in breast cancer management.

An Actor-Critic Algorithm for Sequence Prediction

This paper introduces a novel actor-critic reinforcement learning framework designed specifically for sequence prediction tasks. Our approach combines the advantages of policy-based and value-based methods to address the challenges of sparse rewards and long-term dependencies inherent in sequential data. The actor network generates predictions while the critic network provides value estimates that guide the learning process, reducing variance and improving stability. We formulate sequence prediction as a Markov Decision Process and develop specialized training techniques to handle the structured output space.
