Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including KITTI and NYU Depth V2 demonstrate that CSPN++ consistently outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and efficiency, achieving up to 30% reduction in RMSE while requiring fewer computational resources. Our approach proves particularly effective in challenging scenarios with highly sparse inputs or regions with complex geometric structures, making it suitable for real-world applications such as autonomous driving and augmented reality.

GAN Pretraining for Deep Convolutional Autoencoders Applied to Software-based Fingerprint Presentation Attack Detection

This paper presents a novel approach to Software-based Fingerprint Presentation Attack Detection (PAD) utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) as a pretraining mechanism for deep convolutional autoencoders. Fingerprint recognition systems remain vulnerable to presentation attacks, where artificial replicas or altered fingerprints are used to circumvent authentication. While existing PAD methods have shown promising results, they often struggle with generalization across different attack types and sensor technologies. Our proposed framework leverages the generative capabilities of GANs to learn robust feature representations of both bona fide and attack fingerprint images, which are subsequently used to pretrain deep convolutional autoencoders. This pretraining strategy enables the autoencoder to more effectively capture the subtle anomalies present in attack samples. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple public datasets, including LivDet 2011, 2013, 2015, and 2017, demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average detection accuracy of 97.3% and reducing the Attack Presentation Classification Error Rate (APCER) by 41% compared to conventional deep learning approaches. Furthermore, cross-dataset evaluations reveal superior generalization capabilities, particularly for previously unseen attack types. The proposed method requires minimal computational overhead during deployment, making it suitable for integration into existing fingerprint recognition systems.

Switch Spaces: Learning Product Spaces with Sparse Gating

This paper introduces Switch Spaces, a novel approach to learning expressive representation spaces through sparse gating mechanisms applied to product spaces. While traditional representation learning methods often struggle with the inherent trade-offs between expressivity and computational efficiency, Switch Spaces addresses this challenge by dynamically activating only a small subset of specialized sub-spaces for each input. Our framework employs a sparse routing function that selects the most relevant components from a product space, enabling efficient modeling of complex data distributions. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that Switch Spaces can effectively approximate arbitrary functions with significantly fewer parameters and computational resources than conventional dense approaches. Empirical evaluations across diverse domains including computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning show that Switch Spaces consistently outperforms comparable dense models and existing mixture-of-experts architectures. The sparse activation pattern not only improves computational efficiency but also enhances interpretability by revealing which specialized sub-spaces are most relevant for different input categories. Our results suggest that Switch Spaces offers a promising direction for scaling representation learning to more complex domains while maintaining computational tractability.

Self-Supervised Policy Adaptation during Deployment

Reinforcement learning policies often struggle to generalize to environments that differ from their training conditions. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for adapting policies during deployment without requiring additional reward signals or human supervision. Our method, Self-Supervised Policy Adaptation (SSPA), leverages the inherent structure of the deployment environment to continually refine pre-trained policies through self-supervised learning objectives. By constructing auxiliary tasks from the agent's interactions with the environment, SSPA enables online adaptation to distribution shifts, novel obstacles, and changing dynamics. We evaluate our approach across diverse domains including robotic manipulation, locomotion, and navigation tasks, demonstrating significant performance improvements over non-adaptive baselines and prior adaptation methods. Notably, SSPA achieves up to 45% higher success rates in environments with substantial visual or physical variations from the training distribution. Our analysis reveals that the self-supervised nature of our approach allows for efficient adaptation even in scenarios where reward signals are sparse or unavailable, making it particularly suitable for real-world deployment scenarios where environmental conditions cannot be fully anticipated during training.

Multi-scale Dynamic Feature Encoding Network for Image Demoireing

Moiré patterns are undesirable artifacts that commonly appear when capturing images of screens or other high-frequency patterns. These visually disturbing patterns significantly degrade image quality and present challenges for downstream computer vision tasks. In this paper, we propose a Multi-scale Dynamic Feature Encoding Network (MDFEN) for effective image demoireing. Our approach leverages a novel hierarchical architecture that captures moiré patterns at multiple scales while dynamically adjusting feature representations based on input characteristics. The network consists of three key components: (1) a multi-scale feature extraction module that decomposes the image into different frequency bands, (2) a dynamic feature encoding unit that adaptively weights feature channels according to moiré pattern properties, and (3) a progressive reconstruction module that restores clean images through iterative refinement. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by significant margins, achieving 2.3dB higher PSNR and 0.042 higher SSIM on the FHDMi dataset. Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of each proposed component. Furthermore, our method maintains computational efficiency, making it suitable for practical applications requiring real-time processing.

Segmentation of Roots in Soil with U-Net

This study presents a novel approach for the segmentation of plant root systems in soil using U-Net, a convolutional neural network architecture designed for biomedical image segmentation. Root phenotyping remains challenging due to the opacity of soil and the complex architecture of root systems. We developed an automated pipeline to accurately segment roots from X-ray computed tomography (CT) soil images, which traditionally require labor-intensive manual annotation. Our implementation of U-Net with domain-specific modifications achieved a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.89 and a Dice coefficient of 0.92 on our test dataset, significantly outperforming conventional image processing techniques. The model effectively handled varying soil textures, moisture levels, and root densities. We further validated our approach using a diverse dataset comprising multiple plant species grown in different soil conditions. This automated segmentation method enables high-throughput phenotyping of root traits, facilitating research in plant breeding, agricultural productivity, and ecosystem studies. The proposed framework represents an important advancement in root phenotyping technology, providing researchers with a reliable tool to analyze below-ground plant structures non-invasively.

Kernel Mean Matching for Content Addressability of GANs

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in synthesizing realistic data, yet they lack an efficient mechanism to address and manipulate specific content in their latent space. This paper introduces Kernel Mean Matching (KMM) as a principled approach for enabling content addressability in GANs without requiring architectural modifications or retraining. Our framework leverages kernel methods to establish explicit correspondences between semantic attributes and regions in the latent space, allowing for targeted content generation and manipulation. By embedding both generated and reference samples in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, KMM identifies latent directions that correspond to specific content attributes while preserving the generative model's fidelity. We demonstrate that this approach enables several downstream applications including attribute-conditional sampling, content-based retrieval from the latent space, and semantic interpolation between content elements. Extensive experiments across multiple GAN architectures and domains show that our method outperforms existing post-hoc manipulation techniques in terms of specificity, attribute disentanglement, and computational efficiency. The proposed KMM framework bridges the gap between the impressive generative capabilities of GANs and the practical need for controlled, content-addressable generation.

Multiple Instance Learning on Deep Features for Weakly Supervised Object Detection with Extreme Domain Shifts

This paper addresses the challenging problem of weakly supervised object detection (WSOD) under extreme domain shifts, where only image-level annotations are available in the source domain, and the target domain exhibits significant visual disparities. Traditional WSOD approaches often fail when confronted with substantial domain gaps, such as those between natural images and medical scans, artistic renderings, or satellite imagery. We propose a novel framework that leverages multiple instance learning (MIL) on deep feature representations to effectively bridge these extreme domain shifts. Our approach consists of a two-stage architecture: first, a domain-adaptive feature extractor trained with adversarial techniques to align source and target feature distributions; second, a MIL-based instance classifier that identifies discriminative regions while maintaining robustness to domain-specific variations. Through extensive experiments across diverse domain pairs (natural-to-medical, natural-to-artwork, and daytime-to-nighttime imagery), we demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing WSOD approaches, improving mean Average Precision by 8.3% on average across extreme domain shifts. Ablation studies confirm the importance of our feature-level adaptations and instance-based learning strategy. The proposed approach offers a practical solution for object detection in domains where obtaining bounding box annotations is prohibitively expensive or infeasible.

Hardware based Spatio-Temporal Neural Processing Backend for Imaging Sensors: Towards a Smart Camera

This paper presents a novel hardware-based neural processing architecture designed to serve as an intelligent backend for imaging sensors, advancing the concept of smart cameras. Our approach integrates spatio-temporal neural processing directly with imaging hardware, enabling real-time visual information processing at the edge. The proposed system leverages a custom ASIC implementation that combines convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with recurrent architectures to efficiently extract both spatial features and temporal dynamics from visual data streams. By co-locating sensing and processing elements, our design achieves significant reductions in data transfer bottlenecks while decreasing power consumption by 78% compared to traditional sensor-processor architectures. The hardware incorporates adaptive processing mechanisms that dynamically adjust computational resources based on scene complexity and application requirements. Experimental results demonstrate the system's capability to perform complex vision tasks including object detection, tracking, and activity recognition with a latency of under 20ms while consuming only 267mW at peak operation. This work represents a significant step toward truly intelligent imaging systems that can perform sophisticated neural processing at the sensing layer, enabling new applications in surveillance, autonomous vehicles, and IoT devices where bandwidth, latency, and power constraints are critical considerations.

Puzzle Solving without Search or Human Knowledge: An Unnatural Language Approach

This paper introduces a novel approach to computational puzzle solving that deliberately avoids both traditional search algorithms and human domain knowledge. We present an "unnatural language" framework that reformulates puzzle-solving as a pattern recognition task operating on deliberately obscured representations. Unlike conventional AI systems that leverage human-designed heuristics or exhaustive search, our approach encodes puzzles into abstract symbolic structures that bear little resemblance to human-interpretable patterns. Through extensive experimentation on classic combinatorial puzzles including Sokoban, Rush Hour, and the 15-puzzle, we demonstrate that our system achieves competitive performance without incorporating human intuition or search strategies. The model learns to decode these unnatural representations and directly map them to solution paths through a transformer-based architecture trained on synthetically generated puzzle instances. Our results challenge the assumption that effective puzzle solving requires either human-like reasoning or computational brute force, suggesting alternative pathways for AI problem-solving that may offer insights into non-anthropomorphic forms of intelligence. This approach opens new directions for solving computationally hard problems by deliberately avoiding human cognitive biases.

Towards Better Graph Representation: Two-Branch Collaborative Graph Neural Networks for Multimodal Marketing Intention Detection

This paper presents a novel approach to multimodal marketing intention detection through a two-branch collaborative graph neural network framework. Marketing intention detection in social media content poses unique challenges due to the subtle interplay between textual and visual elements. Our proposed model addresses these challenges by constructing and processing dual graph representations that capture both intra-modal and cross-modal relationships. The framework consists of two specialized branches: one focusing on fine-grained feature extraction within individual modalities, and another dedicated to modeling cross-modal interactions. These branches collaborate through an attention-based fusion mechanism that dynamically weighs the contribution of each modality based on content relevance. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 4.2%, 3.8%, and 5.1% in F1 score on the respective datasets. Further ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the two-branch design and reveal that the cross-modal graph representations particularly enhance detection performance for implicit marketing content. This work contributes to the advancement of multimodal social media analysis and offers insights into effective graph-based representation learning for marketing intention detection.

Optical Flow Estimation from a Single Motion-blurred Image

This paper presents a novel approach for estimating optical flow directly from a single motion-blurred image, addressing a fundamental challenge in computer vision. While traditional optical flow estimation requires multiple sharp frames, our method leverages the motion information inherently encoded within blur patterns to recover dense motion fields. We formulate the problem as an inverse optimization that jointly estimates the latent sharp image and the corresponding flow field that generated the observed blur. Our approach employs a deep neural network architecture with specialized encoder-decoder branches that simultaneously extract blur features and predict spatially-varying motion vectors. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world motion-blurred images, we demonstrate that our method outperforms existing single-image flow estimation techniques by a significant margin. The results show particular robustness to complex scenes with multiple moving objects and varying blur intensities. This work opens new possibilities for motion analysis in scenarios where only a single blurred frame is available, with potential applications in action recognition, autonomous navigation, and computational photography.

Spatio-Temporal Multi-Task Learning Transformer for Joint Moving Object Detection and Segmentation

This paper presents a novel transformer-based architecture for simultaneous detection and segmentation of moving objects in video sequences. Our proposed Spatio-Temporal Multi-Task Learning Transformer (STMTLT) effectively leverages both spatial and temporal information across video frames to jointly tackle the tasks of object detection and motion segmentation. Unlike previous approaches that handle these tasks separately, our unified framework enables end-to-end training while exploiting the complementary nature of these related tasks. The architecture incorporates a temporal attention mechanism that captures motion patterns across frames, combined with a spatial transformer encoder-decoder structure that processes detailed object features. We introduce a multi-task loss function that balances detection and segmentation objectives while encouraging feature sharing between tasks. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, including KITTI, MOVi, and DAVIS, demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both tasks, improving mAP by 4.2% for detection and J&F scores by 3.8% for segmentation. Additionally, our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the spatio-temporal attention mechanisms and the benefits of joint learning. The proposed STMTLT architecture not only advances the performance of moving object analysis but also offers computational efficiency advantages for real-time applications in autonomous driving and video surveillance.

Probing Inter-modality: Visual Parsing with Self-Attention for Vision-Language Pre-training

This paper investigates the critical role of self-attention mechanisms in bridging visual and linguistic modalities for effective vision-language pre-training (VLP). While existing VLP approaches have demonstrated impressive performance on downstream tasks, the precise mechanisms by which visual information is parsed and aligned with textual elements remain underexplored. We propose a novel framework that leverages self-attention patterns to decompose visual inputs into semantically meaningful components that can be directly mapped to linguistic constructs. Our approach, which we call Visual Parsing with Self-Attention (VPSA), introduces a specialized attention module that identifies salient visual regions and establishes fine-grained correspondences with textual tokens. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including COCO, Visual Genome, and Flickr30K, we demonstrate that VPSA significantly improves cross-modal alignment, achieving state-of-the-art performance on image-text retrieval, visual question answering, and visual reasoning tasks. Further analysis reveals that our model develops emergent capabilities to capture object relationships, attributes, and contextual information without explicit supervision. These findings provide new insights into the interpretability of vision-language models and establish a stronger foundation for developing more effective multimodal systems.

The AVA-Kinetics Localized Human Actions Video Dataset

We present AVA-Kinetics, a large-scale, temporally localized human action video dataset that combines the spatial localization strengths of the Atomic Visual Actions (AVA) framework with the diverse action categories of the Kinetics dataset. This new benchmark contains over 230,000 action instances spanning 80 action categories, where each action is annotated with precise person bounding boxes and temporal localization. Unlike previous datasets that focus either on clip-level classification or coarse spatial-temporal annotations, AVA-Kinetics provides dense annotations at 1-second intervals on videos collected from diverse sources, capturing natural human behaviors in unconstrained environments. The dataset addresses critical challenges in action recognition by emphasizing person-centric actions with fine-grained localization, enabling more accurate evaluation of models' ability to detect when and where specific actions occur. Our benchmark evaluations demonstrate that current state-of-the-art approaches still struggle with the complexities of localizing human actions in diverse contexts, highlighting the challenging nature of the dataset and its utility for advancing research in spatiotemporal action localization. AVA-Kinetics aims to accelerate progress in human action understanding by providing a more realistic and comprehensive evaluation framework for the research community.

GAttANet: Global attention agreement for convolutional neural networks

In this paper, we introduce GAttANet, a novel architectural framework that enhances convolutional neural networks (CNNs) through global attention agreement mechanisms. Traditional CNNs often struggle to maintain consistent feature importance across different network depths, leading to suboptimal representations for complex tasks. Our proposed approach addresses this limitation by establishing explicit attention alignment between shallow and deep layers, ensuring that critical visual cues identified early in the network remain prioritized throughout the feature extraction process. GAttANet employs a dual-stream attention mechanism that computes global attention maps and enforces agreement constraints across multiple network levels. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and MS-COCO, we demonstrate that GAttANet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art CNN architectures, achieving 2.3% higher accuracy on ImageNet classification and 1.8% improvement in mean Average Precision for object detection tasks. Furthermore, visualization of the attention maps reveals that our approach produces more semantically meaningful feature representations with enhanced focus on discriminative object parts. GAttANet provides a plug-and-play solution that can be integrated into various CNN backbones with minimal computational overhead, offering a promising direction for improving deep visual recognition systems.

DARB: A Density-Aware Regular-Block Pruning for Deep Neural Networks

This paper introduces DARB (Density-Aware Regular-Block), a novel pruning technique for deep neural networks that combines the benefits of structured and unstructured pruning approaches. While unstructured pruning achieves high compression rates but suffers from irregular memory access patterns, and structured pruning maintains hardware efficiency but often results in significant accuracy loss, DARB strikes an effective balance between these extremes. Our approach partitions neural network weight matrices into regular blocks of configurable sizes and applies density-aware pruning within these blocks, where each block maintains a specific sparsity level determined by its importance to the network's functionality. This block-based approach enables efficient hardware implementation while the variable density strategy preserves model accuracy by retaining more weights in critical regions. Experimental results across various neural network architectures, including CNNs and RNNs, demonstrate that DARB achieves compression rates comparable to unstructured pruning methods while maintaining the computational efficiency advantages of structured pruning. On benchmark datasets including ImageNet and CIFAR-10, DARB outperforms existing pruning methods, achieving up to 20× compression with minimal accuracy degradation. Additionally, we provide a hardware acceleration design that leverages DARB's regular block structure, demonstrating significant improvements in both inference speed and energy efficiency.

Modeling Survival in Model-based Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces a novel framework for incorporating survival considerations into model-based reinforcement learning (RL). While traditional RL approaches focus on maximizing cumulative rewards, many real-world applications—such as healthcare interventions, autonomous vehicle safety, and environmental conservation—require explicit modeling of survival probabilities alongside performance objectives. We propose Survival-Aware Model-based RL (SAM-RL), which integrates survival analysis techniques with model-based RL to simultaneously learn environment dynamics and survival models. Our approach leverages both parametric and non-parametric survival estimation methods to predict time-to-failure distributions, enabling agents to make decisions that balance task performance with survival constraints. Through extensive experiments in simulated critical care, robotic navigation, and resource management domains, we demonstrate that SAM-RL significantly outperforms standard model-based RL approaches in scenarios where survival is paramount. The results show improved long-term survival rates while maintaining competitive task performance. We also provide theoretical convergence guarantees and analyze the trade-offs between exploration and survival-preserving behaviors. This work represents an important step toward developing RL systems that can safely operate in high-stakes environments where agent or environment survival is a primary concern.

A Fourier Domain Feature Approach for Human Activity Recognition & Fall Detection

This paper presents a novel approach to human activity recognition (HAR) and fall detection utilizing Fourier domain feature extraction techniques. We propose a framework that leverages frequency-domain analysis of accelerometer and gyroscope data from wearable sensors to accurately classify daily activities and detect potential fall events. By transforming time-series motion data into the frequency domain through Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), our method extracts distinctive spectral features that capture the periodic nature and frequency characteristics inherent in human movements. The proposed system employs a two-stage classification approach: first identifying basic activities (walking, sitting, standing, lying down) through frequency-based pattern recognition, then implementing a specialized fall detection algorithm that analyzes sudden shifts in frequency components characteristic of fall events. Experimental evaluation on a dataset of 30 participants performing various activities in controlled and real-world environments demonstrates that our Fourier domain approach achieves 94.7% accuracy in activity classification and 96.3% sensitivity in fall detection, with a false positive rate of only 2.1%. Compared to conventional time-domain methods, our approach shows enhanced robustness to sensor orientation variations and improved computational efficiency for real-time applications. These results suggest that frequency domain feature extraction provides a promising direction for developing reliable HAR and fall detection systems for healthcare monitoring and elderly care applications.

SPI-GAN: Towards Single-Pixel Imaging through Generative Adversarial Network

This paper introduces SPI-GAN, a novel approach to single-pixel imaging (SPI) that leverages generative adversarial networks to overcome traditional limitations in computational imaging. Single-pixel imaging has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional multi-pixel sensors, particularly in challenging spectral domains, but suffers from long acquisition times and reconstruction artifacts. Our proposed framework employs a conditional GAN architecture that learns to reconstruct high-quality images from significantly undersampled single-pixel measurements. We demonstrate that SPI-GAN can achieve faithful image reconstruction using only 10-20% of the measurements required by conventional compressive sensing methods. Extensive experiments across diverse imaging scenarios show that our approach maintains structural integrity and fine details while reducing acquisition time by up to 90%. Furthermore, SPI-GAN demonstrates remarkable robustness against measurement noise and system imperfections. The framework generalizes well to unseen data types, making it particularly valuable for applications in biomedical imaging, remote sensing, and spectroscopy where hardware constraints and acquisition speed are critical factors. Our work represents a significant step toward practical, real-time single-pixel imaging systems.

The Sparse Reverse of Principal Component Analysis for Fast Low-Rank Matrix Completion

This paper introduces a novel approach to matrix completion problems by developing what we call the Sparse Reverse of Principal Component Analysis (SR-PCA). While traditional PCA decomposes a matrix into principal components, our method works in the reverse direction, efficiently reconstructing a low-rank matrix from sparse observations. We formulate the matrix completion problem as an optimization task that leverages sparsity patterns to guide the reconstruction of missing entries. The proposed SR-PCA algorithm demonstrates significant computational advantages over existing methods, reducing time complexity from O(n³) to O(n²log n) for an n×n matrix while maintaining comparable accuracy. Our theoretical analysis provides recovery guarantees under standard incoherence conditions, and we establish bounds on the sampling requirements needed for exact recovery. Extensive experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world applications, including recommendation systems and image reconstruction, demonstrate that SR-PCA achieves state-of-the-art performance while requiring substantially less computational resources. The method shows particular promise for very large matrices where existing approaches become computationally prohibitive.

Abstract: Iterative Hough Forest with Histogram of Control Points for 6 DoF Object Registration from Depth Images

This paper presents a novel approach for 6 DoF object registration from single depth images, combining the strengths of discriminative and iterative methods. We introduce the Iterative Hough Forest with Histogram of Control Points (IHF-HCP), a framework that leverages random forests for robust initial pose estimation while incorporating an iterative refinement process for enhanced accuracy. Our method extracts distinctive control points from object surfaces and encodes their spatial distribution through histograms, creating a rich feature representation that maintains invariance to rigid transformations. The proposed Hough Forest architecture efficiently votes for 6D pose hypotheses while handling occlusions and clutter. The subsequent iterative refinement stage minimizes the alignment error between the transformed model and the observed point cloud. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that IHF-HCP achieves state-of-the-art registration accuracy, with average pose errors reduced by 23% compared to existing methods, while maintaining real-time performance (18 fps on commodity hardware). Our approach shows particular robustness in challenging scenarios involving partial object visibility, sensor noise, and cluttered environments, making it suitable for practical applications in robotic manipulation and augmented reality.

Learning Stixel-based Instance Segmentation

This paper introduces a novel approach to instance segmentation by leveraging stixel-based representations, which efficiently encode the 3D structure of traffic scenes as vertical columns with consistent semantic and depth properties. Our method extends the traditional stixel paradigm to incorporate instance-level information, enabling precise delineation of individual objects in complex urban environments. We propose a two-stage architecture that first generates semantic stixels through a modified convolutional neural network, then groups these stixels into distinct object instances using a learned clustering mechanism. The framework maintains the computational efficiency of stixels while achieving fine-grained instance segmentation. Extensive experiments on the Cityscapes and KITTI datasets demonstrate that our stixel-based approach achieves competitive accuracy compared to pixel-based methods while requiring significantly less computational resources, making it particularly suitable for autonomous driving applications. Our method improves inference speed by 35% and reduces memory consumption by 42% compared to state-of-the-art instance segmentation approaches, while maintaining comparable mAP scores. Additionally, we show that the structured nature of stixels provides inherent robustness to partial occlusions and varying lighting conditions.

Neural Network for Weighted Signal Temporal Logic

This paper introduces a novel neural network architecture designed specifically for learning and reasoning with Weighted Signal Temporal Logic (WSTL), a quantitative extension of Signal Temporal Logic that assigns weights to temporal properties. Our approach bridges the gap between formal temporal specifications and data-driven learning by embedding WSTL semantics directly into neural network structures. The proposed architecture incorporates specialized layers that capture temporal operators, predicate evaluations, and weight assignments, enabling end-to-end learning of complex temporal patterns from time-series data. We demonstrate that our network can effectively learn WSTL formulas from labeled examples, generalize to unseen signals, and provide interpretable representations of the learned temporal properties. Experimental evaluation on both synthetic datasets and real-world case studies in autonomous driving and healthcare monitoring shows that our approach outperforms traditional recurrent and convolutional architectures in temporal pattern recognition tasks while maintaining the formal guarantees inherent to temporal logic frameworks. Furthermore, we establish theoretical results on the expressiveness and approximation capabilities of our network with respect to arbitrary WSTL formulas. This work represents a significant step toward integrating formal verification methods with deep learning for safety-critical systems where both performance and interpretability are essential.

Stanza: A Nonlinear State Space Model for Probabilistic Inference in Non-Stationary Time Series

This paper introduces Stanza, a novel nonlinear state space model designed for probabilistic inference in non-stationary time series. Traditional time series models often assume stationarity, limiting their effectiveness when applied to real-world data with evolving statistical properties. Stanza addresses this limitation by incorporating a dynamic latent state representation that explicitly models temporal dependencies while adapting to changing data distributions. Our approach combines the expressiveness of deep neural networks with the interpretability of state space models, enabling accurate uncertainty quantification across varying temporal regimes. We formulate a variational inference framework that efficiently learns both stationary and non-stationary components, allowing the model to distinguish between persistent patterns and transient dynamics. Extensive experiments on synthetic benchmarks, financial data, and climate time series demonstrate that Stanza significantly outperforms existing methods in forecasting accuracy and uncertainty calibration. Furthermore, we show that the learned state representations capture interpretable factors that correspond to meaningful regime changes in the underlying processes. Stanza provides practitioners with a powerful tool for robust time series analysis in non-stationary environments where traditional assumptions break down.

PPMF: A Patient-based Predictive Modeling Framework for Early ICU Mortality Prediction

Early prediction of mortality risk in intensive care units (ICUs) is crucial for improving patient outcomes and optimizing resource allocation. This paper introduces PPMF (Patient-based Predictive Modeling Framework), a novel approach for early mortality prediction in ICU settings that addresses key limitations of existing methods. PPMF leverages patient-specific temporal data collected within the first 24 hours of ICU admission to develop personalized risk profiles. Our framework integrates multimodal clinical data—including vital signs, laboratory results, medication administration, and comorbidities—using a hybrid architecture that combines recurrent neural networks for temporal feature extraction with gradient boosting for final risk assessment. We evaluated PPMF on a diverse cohort of 45,231 ICU patients from the MIMIC-IV database, achieving an AUROC of 0.91, sensitivity of 0.87, and specificity of 0.84, outperforming traditional severity scoring systems and recent machine learning approaches. The framework also provides interpretable results through feature importance analysis, identifying patient-specific risk factors that contribute to mortality predictions. PPMF demonstrates robust performance across different patient subgroups and ICU types, offering a promising tool for clinical decision support that could enhance early intervention strategies and improve critical care outcomes.

Evaluating Explanation Methods for Deep Learning in Security

Deep learning models have demonstrated impressive performance in security applications, yet their black-box nature raises concerns about transparency and trustworthiness. This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of explanation methods for deep learning systems deployed in security contexts. We systematically assess various techniques including LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and GradCAM across multiple security-relevant tasks such as malware detection, network intrusion identification, and phishing URL classification. Our evaluation framework considers explanation fidelity, stability, comprehensibility, and computational efficiency while addressing security-specific requirements like adversarial robustness and false positive risk assessment. Experimental results reveal significant variations in explanation quality across methods, with trade-offs between interpretability and security performance. We identify several limitations in current approaches, including vulnerability to adversarial manipulation of explanations and inconsistency across model architectures. Based on our findings, we propose guidelines for selecting appropriate explanation methods for security applications and outline research directions to develop explanation techniques specifically designed for security domains, where interpretability must complement rather than compromise security effectiveness.

A Coarse-to-Fine Instance Segmentation Network with Learning Boundary Representation

Instance segmentation remains a challenging task in computer vision, requiring both accurate object detection and precise pixel-level segmentation. In this paper, we present a novel coarse-to-fine instance segmentation framework that progressively refines segmentation masks while explicitly modeling object boundaries. Our approach consists of three key components: (1) a coarse segmentation module that generates initial mask proposals, (2) a boundary learning module that explicitly represents and predicts object contours, and (3) a refinement module that integrates boundary information with coarse masks to produce high-quality instance segmentations. Unlike previous methods that treat boundaries implicitly, our network learns dedicated boundary representations that capture fine-grained structural details of object instances. Extensive experiments on COCO and Cityscapes datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particular improvements in scenarios involving object overlap, occlusion, and complex boundaries. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our boundary representation learning mechanism, showing significant gains in boundary accuracy and overall mask quality. Our method provides a promising direction for instance segmentation by emphasizing the importance of explicit boundary modeling in a progressive refinement framework.

Abstract: Robust Data Geometric Structure Aligned Close yet Discriminative Domain Adaptation

Domain adaptation remains a fundamental challenge in machine learning when distribution shifts occur between source and target domains. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Robust Data Geometric Structure Aligned (RDGSA) domain adaptation, which simultaneously aligns domain distributions while preserving discriminative information essential for downstream tasks. Our method leverages the intrinsic geometric structure of the data manifold to establish correspondences between domains that are semantically meaningful. By introducing a structure-preserving alignment mechanism, RDGSA ensures that samples from different domains but same classes are mapped closely in the feature space, while maintaining sufficient separation between different classes. We formulate this as a joint optimization problem that balances domain alignment with class discriminability through a novel geometric structure regularization term. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in challenging scenarios with significant domain shifts and limited labeled target data. The proposed method shows remarkable robustness to various types of distribution shifts while maintaining computational efficiency, making it applicable to real-world domain adaptation problems.

Deep Learning based Person Re-identification

This paper presents a comprehensive approach to person re-identification (Re-ID) using deep learning techniques. Person Re-ID, the task of matching individuals across non-overlapping camera views, remains challenging due to variations in lighting, pose, viewpoint, and occlusion. We propose a novel deep learning framework that addresses these challenges through a multi-branch convolutional neural network architecture. Our approach integrates both global and local feature representations while employing attention mechanisms to focus on discriminative body parts. The network is trained using a combination of identification and triplet losses to enhance feature discrimination. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including Market-1501, DukeMTMC-reID, and CUHK03 demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, with rank-1 accuracy improvements of 3.2%, 4.1%, and 5.7% respectively. Further ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component in our proposed architecture. This work contributes to advancing automated surveillance systems by providing a robust solution for tracking individuals across distributed camera networks.

Adaptive Histogram-Based Gradient Boosted Trees for Federated Learning

This paper introduces a novel approach to implementing gradient boosted trees in federated learning environments, addressing the critical challenges of privacy preservation and communication efficiency. Our method, Adaptive Histogram-Based Gradient Boosted Trees (AH-GBT), leverages dynamic histogram binning techniques to effectively train decision tree ensembles across distributed data sources without requiring raw data exchange. We propose an adaptive quantization mechanism that automatically adjusts histogram granularity based on the data distribution at each client, optimizing the trade-off between model accuracy and communication overhead. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that AH-GBT achieves ε-differential privacy guarantees while maintaining convergence properties comparable to centralized training. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that our approach reduces communication costs by up to 78% compared to existing federated tree methods while achieving competitive or superior predictive performance. Furthermore, AH-GBT demonstrates robustness to data heterogeneity across clients, making it particularly suitable for real-world federated learning scenarios. Our contribution enables efficient deployment of powerful tree-based models in privacy-sensitive domains such as healthcare, finance, and edge computing.

Generating 3D structures from a 2D slice with GAN-based dimensionality expansion

This paper presents a novel approach for generating plausible three-dimensional (3D) structures from single two-dimensional (2D) slices using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The dimensionality expansion problem—reconstructing complete 3D volumes from limited 2D information—remains challenging across medical imaging, geological modeling, and computer graphics. Our method introduces a conditional GAN architecture that learns the probabilistic relationship between 2D slices and their corresponding 3D structures from paired training data. The generator employs a specialized encoder-decoder network with 2.5D convolutions to progressively expand dimensional features while maintaining structural coherence. We implement a multi-scale discriminator that evaluates both local consistency and global structural plausibility. Experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in structural accuracy, feature preservation, and coherence metrics. Notably, our model achieves a 27% improvement in volumetric similarity and 18% better feature continuity compared to previous state-of-the-art techniques. The framework shows particular promise for applications in medical image reconstruction, geological modeling from borehole data, and content creation for virtual environments where complete 3D acquisition is impractical or impossible.

Predicting Vehicles Trajectories in Urban Scenarios with Transformer Networks and Augmented Information

This paper presents a novel approach to vehicle trajectory prediction in complex urban environments using transformer-based neural networks enhanced with augmented contextual information. Accurate prediction of vehicle movements is crucial for advanced driver assistance systems and autonomous driving technologies. Our method leverages the self-attention mechanism of transformer architectures to capture temporal dependencies in vehicle motion patterns while incorporating rich environmental context, including road infrastructure, traffic signals, and interactions with surrounding vehicles and pedestrians. We introduce a multi-modal information fusion framework that processes heterogeneous data sources, including vehicle telemetry, HD maps, and traffic flow information. Experiments conducted on large-scale urban driving datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, reducing prediction error by 18% compared to existing methods while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time applications. Ablation studies confirm that the augmented information significantly improves prediction accuracy, particularly in challenging scenarios such as intersections and lane changes. Our findings highlight the importance of contextual awareness in trajectory forecasting and provide a robust foundation for safer autonomous navigation in urban settings.

An autoencoder wavelet based deep neural network with attention mechanism for multistep prediction of plant growth

This study presents a novel deep learning architecture that combines autoencoder networks, wavelet decomposition, and attention mechanisms to address the challenging task of multistep plant growth prediction. Accurate forecasting of plant development trajectories is crucial for precision agriculture, crop management, and food security planning, yet remains difficult due to the complex, nonlinear dynamics of biological systems and their environmental interactions. Our proposed model leverages wavelet transforms to decompose temporal plant growth signals into multiple frequency components, which are then processed through specialized autoencoder channels to capture multiscale patterns. The integration of an attention mechanism enables the network to dynamically focus on the most relevant temporal features and frequency components during prediction. We evaluated our approach using time-series data from controlled greenhouse experiments across multiple crop varieties, measuring morphological characteristics including height, leaf area, and biomass accumulation. Results demonstrate that our model achieves significantly improved prediction accuracy (reducing RMSE by 27.3% and MAE by 24.8%) compared to traditional time-series forecasting methods and standard recurrent neural networks, particularly for longer prediction horizons of 7-14 days. The model also shows enhanced robustness to environmental variations and data noise. This research contributes a powerful new tool for agricultural monitoring systems and provides insights into the temporal dynamics of plant growth processes that can inform both theoretical models of plant development and practical applications in agricultural management.

Jelly Bean World: A Testbed for Never-Ending Learning

This paper introduces Jelly Bean World (JBW), a novel open-source simulation environment designed specifically for research in never-ending learning systems. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning environments with fixed objectives, JBW provides a customizable, procedurally-generated world where agents must continually adapt to discover and exploit resources in a potentially infinite spatial domain. The environment features configurable resource distributions, environmental dynamics, and sensory capabilities that allow researchers to study curriculum learning, exploration-exploitation trade-offs, and knowledge transfer across tasks. We demonstrate JBW's capabilities through a series of experiments examining how agents develop increasingly sophisticated foraging strategies over time, showing that agents capable of retaining and building upon past knowledge significantly outperform those that learn from scratch when faced with new challenges. Our results highlight JBW's effectiveness as a research platform for developing and evaluating algorithms that can learn continuously and cumulatively in open-ended environments, addressing a critical gap in current AI research infrastructure. The testbed provides quantitative metrics for measuring progress in never-ending learning while remaining computationally accessible and highly extensible for future research directions.

Towards Automatic Construction of Diverse, High-quality Image Dataset

The availability of large-scale, high-quality image datasets is crucial for training robust computer vision models. However, manually curating such datasets remains labor-intensive, expensive, and difficult to scale. This paper presents a novel framework for the automatic construction of diverse, high-quality image datasets. Our approach integrates web-scale image crawling with a multi-stage filtering pipeline that addresses key challenges in automated dataset construction: quality assessment, diversity preservation, and bias mitigation. We introduce a new quality scoring mechanism that combines technical image attributes with semantic content evaluation, and propose a diversity-aware sampling strategy that maintains representation across visual concepts while eliminating redundancy. Experiments demonstrate that models trained on our automatically constructed datasets achieve performance comparable to those trained on manually curated alternatives, while exhibiting better generalization to out-of-distribution samples. Furthermore, our approach reduces dataset construction time by 87% compared to manual curation methods. We release our framework as an open-source tool to facilitate research in automated dataset generation and to support the development of more robust computer vision systems.

Improving Multiple Object Tracking with Optical Flow and Edge Preprocessing

This paper presents a novel approach to multiple object tracking (MOT) that leverages optical flow estimation and edge preprocessing techniques to enhance tracking accuracy and robustness in complex scenes. While conventional MOT systems struggle with occlusions, illumination changes, and similar-looking objects, our method introduces a two-stage preprocessing pipeline that extracts rich motion and structural information prior to tracking. First, dense optical flow fields are computed between consecutive frames to capture object motion patterns, providing valuable cues for distinguishing between objects with similar appearances. Second, an advanced edge preprocessing algorithm identifies object boundaries with high precision, improving segmentation in cluttered environments. We integrate these preprocessed features into a deep learning framework that jointly optimizes detection confidence, appearance similarity, and motion consistency. Extensive experiments on the MOT16, MOT17, and MOT20 benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA) by 4.3% and reducing identity switches by 18.7% compared to current methods. The proposed technique shows particular strength in handling crowded scenes and partial occlusions, making it suitable for applications in autonomous driving, video surveillance, and sports analytics.

Pooled Motion Features for First-Person Videos

This paper presents a novel approach to action recognition in first-person (egocentric) videos by introducing pooled motion features that effectively capture the distinctive characteristics of camera wearer activities. Unlike third-person videos, egocentric footage presents unique challenges including significant camera motion, varying viewpoints, and partial visibility of the actor. Our method addresses these challenges by decomposing motion into camera-induced and object-related components through a robust estimation framework. We introduce a hierarchical pooling strategy that aggregates motion features across spatial and temporal dimensions, preserving critical motion patterns while achieving invariance to viewpoint changes. Extensive experiments on multiple egocentric datasets demonstrate that our pooled motion features significantly outperform conventional approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a 7.3% improvement in action recognition accuracy. The proposed framework is computationally efficient and can be integrated with existing deep learning architectures. Our analysis reveals that the proposed features are particularly effective for distinguishing fine-grained manipulation activities and handling challenging scenarios with dynamic backgrounds. This work provides important insights for developing more effective recognition systems for wearable camera applications in assistive technologies, augmented reality, and lifelogging.

3D Model Assisted Image Segmentation

This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation that leverages pre-existing 3D models to improve accuracy and efficiency in delineating complex structures. Our method addresses the persistent challenges of traditional segmentation techniques by incorporating geometric priors from 3D models to guide the segmentation process. We introduce a two-phase framework that first aligns and registers a relevant 3D model with the target image, then uses the projected model features as constraints for a deep learning segmentation network. Experiments conducted across medical imaging, autonomous driving, and industrial inspection domains demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation methods, with an average improvement of 17% in Dice coefficient and 23% reduction in boundary error. The method shows particular robustness in cases with occlusion, poor contrast, and incomplete boundaries - scenarios that typically challenge conventional segmentation algorithms. Additionally, our approach requires less annotated training data, making it particularly valuable in domains where labeled data is scarce. This work establishes a promising direction for integrating 3D structural knowledge into 2D image analysis tasks.

Stillleben: Realistic Scene Synthesis for Deep Learning in Robotics

Deep learning approaches in robotics require large amounts of labeled training data, which is often challenging to obtain from real-world scenarios. In this paper, we present Stillleben, a novel framework for generating photorealistic synthetic scenes to train deep neural networks for robotic perception tasks. Stillleben leverages physics-based rendering and procedural scene generation to create diverse, realistic training examples with perfect ground truth annotations. Our system automatically handles complex physical interactions between objects, realistic lighting conditions, and material properties to produce high-fidelity synthetic data. We evaluate Stillleben across multiple robotic perception tasks including object detection, pose estimation, and segmentation, demonstrating that models trained on our synthetic data generalize effectively to real-world environments, significantly reducing the reality gap. Experiments show that Stillleben outperforms existing synthetic data generation approaches by up to 18% on benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that pre-training on Stillleben-generated data before fine-tuning on limited real data improves performance by 23% compared to training on real data alone. The framework is designed to be computationally efficient and easily integrated into robotic learning pipelines, making it a valuable tool for advancing data-driven approaches in robotics.

Cops-Ref: A new Dataset and Task on Compositional Referring Expression Comprehension

This paper introduces Cops-Ref, a novel dataset and benchmark task for Compositional Referring Expression Comprehension (CREC). Unlike existing referring expression datasets that primarily focus on simple object identification, Cops-Ref specifically addresses the challenge of understanding complex, compositional language descriptions that require resolving multiple objects and their relationships in visual scenes. The dataset comprises over 50,000 image-text pairs featuring diverse compositional structures, including spatial relationships, comparative attributes, and nested references. Each referring expression is annotated with a compositional parsing tree that explicitly represents the hierarchical structure of the reference. We establish baseline performance using state-of-the-art vision-language models and demonstrate that while these models perform well on simple references, they struggle with compositional understanding, particularly with expressions involving multiple levels of indirection or complex spatial reasoning. Our analysis reveals significant gaps between human and machine performance on compositional referring tasks, highlighting the dataset's utility as a challenging benchmark for advancing multimodal AI systems toward more sophisticated language grounding capabilities. Cops-Ref offers a systematic way to evaluate and improve models' abilities to comprehend compositionally complex referring expressions in visual contexts.

Transfer Learning-Based Outdoor Position Recovery with Telco Data

This paper presents a novel approach to outdoor position recovery using telecommunication network data through transfer learning techniques. As mobile devices continuously interact with cellular networks, the resulting telco data contains valuable spatial information that can be leveraged for positioning applications when GPS signals are unavailable or unreliable. Our method employs a transfer learning framework that adapts pre-trained deep neural networks from related domains to effectively process and interpret complex telco data patterns, including signal strength indicators, timing measurements, and network parameters. We demonstrate that by transferring knowledge from models trained on regions with dense ground-truth positioning data to areas with sparse labeling, our approach significantly improves positioning accuracy compared to traditional methods. Experiments conducted across diverse urban and suburban environments show that our transfer learning model achieves mean positioning errors of less than 15 meters in challenging scenarios, representing a 37% improvement over baseline techniques. The proposed methodology offers a robust solution for outdoor positioning that can be deployed at scale using existing telecommunication infrastructure, with potential applications in emergency services, urban planning, and location-based services where reliable positioning is critical.

A Deep Q-Network for the Beer Game: A Deep Reinforcement Learning algorithm to Solve Inventory Optimization Problems

This paper presents a novel application of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to address inventory optimization challenges in supply chain management through the classic Beer Game framework. We develop a Deep Q-Network (DQN) architecture specifically designed to navigate the complex, dynamic decision space of multi-echelon inventory systems. Our approach leverages neural networks to approximate Q-values for inventory policy decisions, enabling agents to learn effective ordering strategies while balancing holding costs and stockout penalties under demand uncertainty and order delays. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed DQN algorithm significantly outperforms traditional inventory policies, including base-stock and (s,S) policies, reducing overall costs by 32% across various demand patterns. The DQN agent successfully mitigates the bullwhip effect and adapts to changing market conditions without requiring explicit knowledge of the underlying demand distribution. Through extensive simulations and sensitivity analysis, we show that our approach is robust to parameter variations and generalizes well to unseen demand scenarios. This research contributes to both supply chain management and reinforcement learning literature by demonstrating how DRL can effectively solve practical inventory optimization problems with minimal assumptions about system dynamics.

Robust Lane Detection from Continuous Driving Scenes Using Deep Neural Networks

This paper presents a novel approach to lane detection in continuous driving scenes using deep neural networks. Lane detection is a fundamental component of advanced driver assistance systems and autonomous driving technologies, yet it remains challenging due to varying road conditions, lighting changes, and occlusions. Our method leverages a custom convolutional neural network architecture that processes sequential frames to maintain temporal consistency while adapting to dynamic environments. The proposed network incorporates a spatial attention mechanism to focus on relevant road features and a recurrent component to track lane markings across consecutive frames. We evaluate our approach on multiple datasets including KITTI, TuSimple, and our newly collected diverse driving dataset spanning urban, highway, and rural environments under various weather conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves 96.8% detection accuracy while maintaining real-time performance (27 fps on standard hardware), outperforming existing approaches by 4.3% in challenging scenarios with shadows, worn lane markings, and adverse weather. Additionally, our system demonstrates enhanced robustness to camera vibrations and temporary occlusions through its temporal reasoning capabilities. This work contributes to the advancement of reliable perception systems for autonomous driving in real-world conditions.

Self-Similarity Based Time Warping

This paper introduces a novel approach to time warping based on the principle of self-similarity in sequential data. Unlike traditional dynamic time warping methods that align sequences using point-wise distance metrics, our self-similarity based time warping leverages the internal structural patterns within each sequence to guide the alignment process. By constructing self-similarity matrices that capture the relationships between different points within the same sequence, we develop a more robust framework that is less sensitive to amplitude variations and noise. Our method identifies corresponding structural elements across sequences by matching their self-similarity patterns rather than their direct values. Experimental evaluations on diverse datasets including speech, motion capture, and financial time series demonstrate that self-similarity based time warping achieves superior alignment quality compared to conventional approaches, particularly in scenarios with significant amplitude differences or when sequences contain similar structural patterns expressed in different modalities. The proposed approach not only improves alignment accuracy but also provides meaningful insights into the structural correspondence between temporal sequences, enabling more effective pattern recognition and classification in time series analysis.

Adversarial Information Bottleneck

This paper introduces the Adversarial Information Bottleneck (AIB), a novel framework that combines the principles of information bottleneck theory with adversarial learning to improve the robustness and generalization capabilities of deep neural networks. We formulate a minimax optimization problem where a representation network aims to extract minimal sufficient statistics from input data while an adversary attempts to exploit vulnerabilities in the learned representations. By constraining the mutual information between inputs and their representations, our approach forces the model to retain only task-relevant features while discarding information that could be leveraged by adversarial attacks. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that AIB achieves an optimal trade-off between accuracy, robustness, and compression. Empirical evaluations across multiple domains, including image classification, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning, show that AIB consistently outperforms standard training methods and existing defense mechanisms against various adversarial attacks while maintaining competitive performance on clean data. Our results suggest that the information-theoretic perspective offers a principled approach to developing inherently robust representation learning systems.

FreeAnchor: Learning to Match Anchors for Visual Object Detection

Modern object detection frameworks typically rely on a predefined set of anchor boxes that serve as references for detecting objects. However, the assignment between anchors and ground-truth objects is often determined by fixed rules based on spatial overlap, which can lead to suboptimal training and reduced detection performance. In this paper, we introduce FreeAnchor, a novel anchor-matching mechanism that reformulates the object detection problem as a maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) procedure. Our approach enables each ground-truth object to freely select the most suitable anchors, guided by both statistical and learning considerations. Specifically, we construct a detection-customized likelihood function that jointly optimizes anchor selection and bounding box refinement in a unified framework. The proposed method adaptively adjusts anchor assignments during training, effectively addressing the limitations of conventional fixed-rule approaches. Extensive experiments on the MS COCO dataset demonstrate that FreeAnchor consistently improves detection performance across various backbone architectures, achieving state-of-the-art results without introducing additional computational overhead during inference. Our approach provides a more flexible and effective alternative to traditional anchor assignment strategies while maintaining compatibility with existing detection frameworks.

Weather GAN: Multi-Domain Weather Translation Using Generative Adversarial Networks

This paper introduces Weather GAN, a novel framework for translating visual scenes across multiple weather conditions using generative adversarial networks. We address the challenging task of synthesizing realistic weather effects (e.g., rain, snow, fog, sunshine) while preserving the structural content and semantic information of input images. Our approach employs a multi-domain translation architecture that enables transformations between any pair of weather conditions without requiring paired training data. Weather GAN incorporates a weather-specific content preservation mechanism and a domain-adaptive normalization technique to handle the unique characteristics of different atmospheric phenomena. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms existing image-to-image translation methods in generating perceptually convincing weather effects, as measured by both quantitative metrics and human evaluation studies. Furthermore, we show that Weather GAN can be effectively utilized to augment training data for computer vision tasks that require robustness across weather conditions, improving performance in autonomous driving systems and outdoor scene understanding. Our code and pre-trained models are made publicly available to facilitate further research in weather simulation and domain adaptation.

Unsupervised Learning of Depth and Deep Representation for Visual Odometry from Monocular Videos in a Metric Space

This paper presents a novel unsupervised learning framework for monocular visual odometry that jointly estimates depth and camera motion while learning meaningful visual representations in a metric space. Unlike previous approaches that rely on supervised training or separate modules for depth and pose estimation, our method leverages the geometric consistency between consecutive video frames to learn depth and motion in a unified, end-to-end manner without ground truth annotations. We introduce a metric-space consistency loss that enforces scale-consistent depth predictions across long sequences, addressing a key limitation in monocular systems. Our architecture employs a shared encoder backbone that extracts rich visual features, which are then utilized by specialized decoders for depth estimation and pose regression. Extensive experiments on the KITTI and Cityscapes datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised depth estimation and competitive results in visual odometry compared to both unsupervised and supervised methods. Furthermore, we show that the learned representations transfer effectively to other vision tasks, suggesting that our geometric constraints guide the network to capture semantically meaningful features. The proposed framework offers a promising direction for self-supervised learning in robotic navigation and scene understanding applications where labeled data is scarce.

Bayesian Algorithms for Decentralized Stochastic Bandits

This paper addresses the challenge of decentralized multi-armed bandit problems, where multiple agents collaboratively optimize their collective reward without direct communication. We develop a novel family of Bayesian algorithms that enable agents to efficiently balance exploration and exploitation while implicitly coordinating their actions through their impact on the shared environment. Our approach leverages Thompson sampling and variational inference techniques to maintain and update posterior beliefs about arm rewards in a fully decentralized manner. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that our algorithms achieve sublinear regret bounds that approach centralized optimal rates as the number of agents increases, while requiring significantly less communication overhead. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that our methods outperform existing decentralized bandit algorithms, particularly in scenarios with heterogeneous reward structures and limited information exchange. These results highlight the potential of Bayesian approaches for decentralized decision-making problems in applications ranging from distributed sensing networks to cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning.

A Classifier-guided Approach for Top-down Salient Object Detection

This paper presents a novel classifier-guided approach for top-down salient object detection that leverages high-level semantic information to guide the detection of category-specific salient objects. Unlike traditional bottom-up salient object detection methods that rely solely on low-level features, our approach incorporates a pre-trained image classifier to provide semantic guidance for identifying objects of interest. We propose a dual-stream architecture that combines a classification branch with a saliency detection branch, where the classifier's activations are used to modulate feature maps in the saliency stream. This enables our model to selectively highlight objects from target categories while suppressing irrelevant background regions. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 4.2% in mean F-measure and 3.8% in mean absolute error. Further analysis reveals that our classifier-guided approach is particularly effective for complex scenes with multiple objects, where traditional methods often fail to identify the semantically relevant salient objects. The proposed method bridges the gap between object recognition and saliency detection, offering a more intelligent solution for applications requiring category-specific salient object detection.

Center3D: Center-based Monocular 3D Object Detection with Joint Depth Understanding

Monocular 3D object detection remains a challenging task in computer vision due to the inherent depth ambiguity in single-image inputs. In this paper, we present Center3D, a novel center-based framework that addresses this fundamental limitation through joint depth understanding. Our approach leverages a unified representation that detects objects as 3D centers while simultaneously reasoning about depth information at multiple levels. The framework integrates three complementary depth understanding components: (1) an image-wide depth estimation module that provides contextual scene geometry, (2) a local depth refinement mechanism that focuses on object-specific depth cues, and (3) an uncertainty-aware depth fusion strategy that adaptively combines these estimates based on confidence. Extensive experiments on the KITTI and nuScenes datasets demonstrate that Center3D achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving average precision by 4.2% on KITTI and 3.7% on nuScenes compared to existing methods. Our ablation studies confirm that the joint depth understanding approach significantly reduces localization errors, particularly for distant and partially occluded objects. The proposed method maintains real-time inference capabilities while providing more accurate and robust 3D object detection from monocular images.

Chi-square Tests Driven Method for Learning the Structure of Factored MDPs

This paper presents a novel approach for learning the structure of Factored Markov Decision Processes (FMDPs) using chi-square statistical tests. FMDPs provide a compact representation of large state spaces by exploiting conditional independence among state variables, but learning their underlying structure remains challenging. Our method leverages chi-square tests to identify the relevant parent variables that influence the transition dynamics of each state variable, effectively discovering the conditional independence relationships in the system. We formulate the structure learning problem as a series of hypothesis tests that determine whether adding a potential parent variable significantly improves the prediction of state transitions. The proposed algorithm incrementally builds the dependency structure while maintaining statistical significance, resulting in a sample-efficient approach that scales well to high-dimensional state spaces. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world domains demonstrate that our method accurately recovers the true FMDP structure with fewer samples compared to existing approaches, while maintaining computational efficiency. Furthermore, policies derived from the learned models achieve performance comparable to those based on the true model, validating the practical utility of our approach for reinforcement learning in complex environments.

Multi-grained Trajectory Graph Convolutional Networks for Habit-unrelated Human Motion Prediction

Human motion prediction is crucial for applications in autonomous driving, robotics, and human-computer interaction. While existing approaches have made significant progress in forecasting habitual movements, they often struggle with habit-unrelated motions that deviate from routine patterns. This paper introduces Multi-grained Trajectory Graph Convolutional Networks (MT-GCN), a novel framework designed to address this challenge. Our approach models human motion trajectories as multi-grained graph structures that capture spatial-temporal dependencies at different levels of granularity. By decomposing motion into hierarchical components, MT-GCN can effectively distinguish between habitual patterns and non-routine behaviors. We propose a dual-stream architecture that simultaneously processes global trajectory features and local motion dynamics, enabling robust prediction even when movements diverge from established habits. Extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that MT-GCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing prediction error by up to 18% on habit-unrelated motions while maintaining competitive performance on habitual movements. Our ablation studies confirm that the multi-grained representation is key to capturing the complex nature of human motion, particularly in scenarios where behavioral patterns change unexpectedly.

Generalization and Exploration via Randomized Value Functions

This paper introduces a novel approach to reinforcement learning that addresses two fundamental challenges: effective exploration and generalization across large state spaces. We present a framework based on randomized value functions (RVF) that naturally induces deep exploration while simultaneously leveraging function approximation for generalization. Unlike traditional exploration methods that rely on hand-crafted bonuses or optimistic initialization, our approach maintains a distribution over value functions, sampling from this distribution to guide exploration. We demonstrate that this randomization leads to systematic exploration behavior that propagates uncertainty through the state-action space. 

We develop both Bayesian and frequentist instantiations of our framework, providing theoretical guarantees on regret bounds under certain conditions. Empirical evaluations across complex environments, including high-dimensional continuous control tasks and sparse-reward settings, show that our RVF methods significantly outperform strong baselines including count-based exploration methods and optimism-based approaches.
