The results highlight how uncertainty-driven randomization enables agents to effectively balance exploration and exploitation while generalizing learned knowledge across similar states. Our work establishes randomized value functions as a principled and practical approach to the exploration-generalization challenge in reinforcement learning.

Learnable Online Graph Representations for 3D Multi-Object Tracking

Multi-object tracking (MOT) in 3D space remains a challenging problem in computer vision, particularly for autonomous vehicles and robotics applications. This paper introduces a novel approach to 3D MOT through learnable online graph representations that effectively model the complex spatial and temporal relationships between objects. Our method constructs dynamic graphs where nodes represent detected objects and edges capture their interactions across frames. We propose a Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture that learns to update these representations in an online manner, enabling robust tracking even in cluttered environments with occlusions and sparse detections. The framework incorporates both appearance and motion cues through specialized graph attention mechanisms that adaptively weight the importance of different features. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo Open datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA) by 3.2% and reducing identity switches by 24% compared to previous methods. Furthermore, our online processing achieves real-time performance (25 FPS), making it suitable for deployment in practical applications. Code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available.

Analyzing Perception-Distortion Tradeoff using Enhanced Perceptual Super-resolution Network

This paper investigates the fundamental tradeoff between perceptual quality and distortion metrics in image super-resolution (SR) tasks. We propose an Enhanced Perceptual Super-resolution Network (EPSRN) that effectively navigates this tradeoff by incorporating a novel adaptive perceptual loss function and a dual-branch architecture. Our approach enables flexible adjustment between reconstruction fidelity and perceptual realism without requiring separate model training. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that EPSRN achieves superior perceptual quality compared to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining competitive distortion metrics. We provide theoretical analysis of the perception-distortion boundary and empirically validate that our approach closely approximates the optimal tradeoff curve. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation protocol that better quantifies the balance between perceptual and distortion metrics. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the perception-distortion relationship in SR tasks and offer practical insights for developing SR systems that can be dynamically tuned according to specific application requirements.

Addressing Cold Start in Recommender Systems with Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks

The cold start problem remains a significant challenge in recommender systems, where new users or items with limited interaction history receive poor quality recommendations. This paper introduces a novel approach using Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks (HGNNs) to address this challenge. Our framework leverages both content features and the sparse interaction data available for cold-start entities by modeling the recommendation problem as a hierarchical graph structure. The proposed HGNN architecture operates at multiple levels of abstraction: a local level capturing immediate user-item interactions, and higher levels aggregating categorical, contextual, and semantic information. Through this hierarchical representation, our model can effectively transfer knowledge from warm entities to cold ones by exploiting shared attributes and structural patterns. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 18.7% improvement in recommendation accuracy for cold-start users and 15.3% for cold-start items. Furthermore, our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each hierarchical component and highlight the model's robustness to varying degrees of data sparsity. These results suggest that hierarchical graph representations provide a promising direction for mitigating the cold start problem in recommender systems.

Deep Double-Side Learning Ensemble Model for Few-Shot Parkinson Speech Recognition

This paper presents a novel Deep Double-Side Learning Ensemble (DDSLE) model for few-shot Parkinson's disease (PD) speech recognition. PD speech recognition remains challenging due to limited availability of labeled data and the heterogeneous manifestation of speech impairments across patients. Our DDSLE approach addresses these limitations through a dual-perspective architecture that simultaneously leverages acoustic-phonetic features and temporal speech patterns. The model employs a meta-learning framework with a double-sided feature extraction mechanism: one pathway captures dysarthria-related acoustic anomalies while the other extracts prosodic and temporal irregularities characteristic of parkinsonian speech. We introduce a cross-attention fusion module that dynamically weights feature importance based on speech sample characteristics. Experiments conducted on three PD speech datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves 87.3% classification accuracy with only 10 samples per class, outperforming state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods by 6.2%. The DDSLE model shows particular robustness in distinguishing early-stage PD patients from healthy controls, suggesting potential clinical utility for early diagnosis. Our findings indicate that double-sided feature learning combined with ensemble techniques significantly improves few-shot learning performance for automated PD speech assessment.

Retina U-Net: Embarrassingly Simple Exploitation of Segmentation Supervision for Medical Object Detection

Medical object detection often faces unique challenges including limited annotated data and the need for precise localization. In this paper, we present Retina U-Net, a novel architecture that seamlessly integrates the strengths of RetinaNet's object detection capabilities with U-Net's powerful semantic segmentation framework. Our approach exploits pixel-wise segmentation supervision to enhance object detection performance in medical imaging applications. Unlike previous methods that treat detection and segmentation as separate tasks, Retina U-Net employs a shared encoder backbone and leverages segmentation masks as an auxiliary supervisory signal during training, creating a powerful multi-task learning framework. We demonstrate that this embarrassingly simple modification leads to significant improvements in detection accuracy, particularly for small or partially occluded structures common in medical images. Extensive experiments on multiple medical imaging datasets, including chest X-rays and abdominal CT scans, show that Retina U-Net consistently outperforms state-of-the-art detection-only approaches, with particularly notable gains in scenarios with limited training data. Our findings suggest that incorporating segmentation supervision provides valuable complementary information that helps the network learn more robust and generalizable features for medical object detection tasks.

Attack to Fool and Explain Deep Networks

Despite the impressive performance of deep neural networks across various domains, concerns about their vulnerability to adversarial attacks and their inherent opacity remain significant challenges. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that simultaneously addresses both issues by developing an attack framework that not only fools deep networks but also provides explanatory insights into their decision-making processes. Our method, which we call Explanatory Adversarial Attacks (EAA), generates adversarial examples that cause misclassification while revealing critical weaknesses in the model's learned representations. By analyzing the patterns of successful attacks, we demonstrate how these adversarial examples can serve as a lens for understanding model behavior and identifying regions of feature space where the network is most vulnerable. Experiments across multiple architectures and datasets show that our approach achieves competitive attack success rates while providing interpretable explanations that highlight decision boundaries and feature importance. This work represents a significant step toward using adversarial methods not merely as a security concern but as a tool for enhancing model transparency and improving deep learning systems.

LiDAR Ground Filtering Algorithm for Urban Areas Using Scan Line Based Segmentation

This paper presents a novel approach for ground filtering in urban LiDAR point clouds using scan line based segmentation. Ground point classification remains a fundamental challenge in LiDAR data processing, particularly in complex urban environments with diverse structures and terrain variations. Our proposed algorithm leverages the inherent scan line pattern of LiDAR acquisitions to perform efficient segmentation prior to ground classification. The method initially organizes points into scan lines and analyzes elevation profiles to identify potential ground segments based on local geometric features. These segments are then refined through an adaptive region growing process that considers both slope and elevation constraints specific to urban morphology. Experimental results on diverse urban datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves an overall accuracy of 94.3% and F1-score of 0.92, outperforming traditional methods in areas with steep terrain, dense buildings, and vegetation. The algorithm shows particular robustness to discontinuities in the ground surface and requires minimal parameter tuning across different urban landscapes. This scan line segmentation strategy significantly reduces computational complexity while maintaining high classification accuracy, making it suitable for processing large-scale urban LiDAR datasets for applications in 3D city modeling, infrastructure planning, and autonomous navigation.

Adversarial Normalization for Multi-Domain Image Segmentation

Image segmentation across multiple domains remains challenging due to domain shifts in visual characteristics, acquisition protocols, and imaging modalities. We propose Adversarial Normalization (AdverseNorm), a novel approach that addresses domain discrepancies in segmentation networks through adversarial learning of domain-adaptive normalization parameters. Our method introduces a domain discriminator that competes with the segmentation network to encourage feature distributions that are both discriminative for segmentation and invariant across domains. Unlike previous approaches that focus on domain adaptation between source and target domains, AdverseNorm learns a unified representation space that accommodates multiple domains simultaneously. The framework comprises a domain-aware normalization module that dynamically adjusts feature statistics based on domain characteristics, while an adversarial training scheme ensures these normalized features remain domain-agnostic at higher network levels. Extensive experiments on diverse multi-domain datasets, including medical imaging (CT, MRI, ultrasound) and natural images, demonstrate that AdverseNorm significantly outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods, achieving 5-12% improvement in Dice coefficient and 8-15% reduction in Hausdorff distance across domains. Our approach enables robust segmentation performance without requiring domain-specific models or extensive data augmentation, making it particularly valuable for applications where annotation resources are limited across domains.

Fast Underwater Image Enhancement for Improved Visual Perception

Underwater imaging is plagued by unique degradation factors including light absorption, scattering, and color distortion, which significantly impair visual perception for both human operators and computer vision systems. This paper presents a novel approach for fast underwater image enhancement that addresses these challenges while maintaining real-time processing capabilities. Our method integrates a physics-based transmission map estimation with a lightweight deep learning architecture to simultaneously correct color distortion, enhance contrast, and reduce noise artifacts. Unlike previous approaches that prioritize either computational efficiency or restoration quality, our framework achieves both through an adaptive multi-scale fusion technique that selectively enhances features based on local content characteristics. Extensive experiments on diverse underwater datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics (PSNR, SSIM, UIQM) and processing speed (averaging 45 fps on standard hardware). Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that the enhanced images significantly improve the performance of downstream tasks including object detection, segmentation, and tracking in underwater environments. The proposed method's efficiency makes it particularly suitable for deployment on resource-constrained platforms such as autonomous underwater vehicles and diver monitoring systems.

Attention Aware Cost Volume Pyramid Based Multi-view Stereo Network for 3D Reconstruction

This paper presents a novel multi-view stereo (MVS) approach that leverages attention mechanisms within a cost volume pyramid framework to enhance 3D reconstruction accuracy and efficiency. Our method, dubbed Attention Aware Cost Volume Pyramid Network (AA-CVP-MVSNet), addresses the limitations of existing MVS techniques by introducing a hierarchical cost volume architecture augmented with spatial and channel attention modules. The proposed network intelligently focuses computational resources on the most informative regions and features across multiple resolution scales. By incorporating cross-view attention mechanisms, our approach effectively handles occlusions, textureless regions, and viewpoint variations that traditionally challenge MVS systems. We construct a coarse-to-fine pyramid structure that progressively refines depth estimates while maintaining global context through attention-guided feature propagation. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including DTU, Tanks and Temples, and ETH3D demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both reconstruction quality and computational efficiency. Ablation studies confirm the significant contribution of our attention modules in improving feature matching and depth estimation accuracy. The proposed approach represents an important advancement in learning-based MVS for high-fidelity 3D reconstruction from multi-view images.

TSPNet: Hierarchical Feature Learning via Temporal Semantic Pyramid for Sign Language Translation

Sign Language Translation (SLT) presents unique challenges due to the complex spatio-temporal nature of sign languages and their distinct grammatical structures compared to spoken languages. In this paper, we introduce TSPNet, a novel framework that employs a Temporal Semantic Pyramid architecture to capture hierarchical features across multiple temporal scales for improved SLT performance. Our approach addresses the limitations of existing methods that often struggle with long-range dependencies and contextual information in continuous sign language videos. TSPNet progressively builds semantic representations by analyzing sign language content at different temporal resolutions, enabling the model to simultaneously capture fine-grained hand movements and broader contextual patterns. Through extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets including PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily, TSPNet demonstrates state-of-the-art performance, achieving a 4.3% improvement in BLEU-4 scores compared to previous approaches. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our temporal pyramid structure, while qualitative analyses show enhanced handling of complex linguistic phenomena such as non-manual features and grammatical inflections. TSPNet represents a significant advancement in sign language translation technology with potential applications in improving communication accessibility for deaf and hard-of-hearing communities.

Self-grouping Convolutional Neural Networks

We introduce Self-grouping Convolutional Neural Networks (SG-CNNs), a novel architecture that dynamically organizes convolutional filters into specialized groups during training. Unlike traditional grouped convolutions with fixed, manually-defined filter assignments, SG-CNNs employ a differentiable grouping mechanism that allows the network to learn optimal filter clustering based on feature correlations and task requirements. This approach enables the network to discover meaningful feature hierarchies while simultaneously reducing computational complexity. Our experiments across multiple computer vision benchmarks demonstrate that SG-CNNs achieve comparable or superior accuracy to standard CNNs with significantly fewer parameters and FLOPs. The learned groupings reveal interpretable patterns, with filters in the same group often responding to semantically related features. SG-CNNs also exhibit improved robustness to overfitting on smaller datasets. This work provides new insights into the structural organization of deep convolutional networks and offers a promising direction for designing more efficient and adaptive neural architectures.

Discovering Traveling Companions using Autoencoders

This paper presents a novel approach to identifying traveling companions in mobility data using autoencoder neural networks. We address the challenge of distinguishing between individuals who are genuinely traveling together and those who coincidentally share similar trajectories. Our method employs a specialized autoencoder architecture that learns compressed representations of spatiotemporal movement patterns, enabling the detection of subtle behavioral correlations that indicate companion relationships. By training on a diverse dataset of GPS trajectories from urban environments, our model achieves 87% accuracy in companion identification, outperforming traditional clustering and rule-based approaches by 23%. We introduce a new metric, the Companion Coherence Index (CCI), which quantifies the strength of traveling relationships while accounting for contextual factors such as location density and time of day. Our approach demonstrates robust performance across varying movement speeds, sampling rates, and environmental conditions, making it applicable to diverse scenarios including tourism analytics, social relationship mining, and transportation planning. This work contributes to the growing field of mobility data analysis by providing a scalable, privacy-preserving framework for understanding group movement behavior.

Property Inference for Deep Neural Networks

This paper explores the vulnerability of deep neural networks (DNNs) to property inference attacks, where adversaries extract sensitive information about the training data or model architecture without direct access to them. We formulate a theoretical framework for characterizing these attacks and evaluate their effectiveness across various neural network architectures. Our experiments demonstrate that even when models are trained with privacy-preserving techniques, certain properties of the training data can still be inferred with high accuracy through careful analysis of model parameters or outputs. We investigate multiple defense strategies, including differential privacy, knowledge distillation, and architectural modifications, quantifying their effectiveness in preventing property leakage while maintaining model utility. Our findings reveal fundamental trade-offs between model performance, transparency, and privacy, with implications for the deployment of DNNs in privacy-sensitive applications. Finally, we propose a set of guidelines for practitioners to assess and mitigate property inference risks in their deep learning systems.

Anatomy-Aware Siamese Network: Exploiting Semantic Asymmetry for Accurate Pelvic Fracture Detection in X-ray Images

Pelvic fracture detection in X-ray images presents significant challenges due to the complex anatomical structure of the pelvis, subtle fracture patterns, and variable image quality. This paper introduces the Anatomy-Aware Siamese Network (AASN), a novel deep learning architecture that leverages the inherent bilateral symmetry of the pelvis to enhance fracture detection accuracy. Unlike conventional approaches that treat X-ray images as homogeneous data, our method explicitly models the semantic asymmetry between normal and fractured regions by using a Siamese network with shared weights but specialized attention mechanisms. The AASN incorporates an anatomical prior knowledge module that segments the pelvis into key regions, enabling region-specific feature extraction and comparison between corresponding bilateral structures. We evaluate our approach on a diverse dataset of 2,450 pelvic X-ray images from multiple clinical centers, demonstrating superior performance (92.7% sensitivity, 94.3% specificity) compared to state-of-the-art methods. Notably, AASN shows particular strength in detecting subtle non-displaced fractures that are frequently missed by radiologists and existing algorithms. Ablation studies confirm that the integration of anatomical knowledge and asymmetry-aware feature comparison significantly contributes to the model's effectiveness. This work represents an important advancement in computer-aided diagnosis for trauma assessment and has potential applications in emergency medicine settings where rapid and accurate fracture detection is critical.

Dynamic Zoom-in Network for Fast Object Detection in Large Images

Object detection in large high-resolution images presents significant computational challenges due to the extensive processing requirements and memory constraints. This paper introduces the Dynamic Zoom-in Network (DZNet), a novel two-stage detection framework that substantially reduces computation time while maintaining detection accuracy. DZNet first employs a lightweight global network operating on downsampled images to identify regions of interest (ROIs) containing potential objects. Then, a refined local network processes these selected regions at their original resolution, enabling precise object localization and classification. Our approach incorporates an adaptive zoom-in mechanism that dynamically adjusts the number and scale of regions to process based on image content complexity. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets, including aerial imagery, medical scans, and surveillance footage, demonstrate that DZNet achieves comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art detectors while reducing computation time by up to 75%. The framework is particularly effective for images with sparse object distributions or significant scale variations. Additionally, we propose a region proposal quality metric that further optimizes the trade-off between speed and accuracy. Our method addresses practical limitations of deploying object detection systems on large images, making it suitable for real-time applications with limited computational resources.

AlignMix: Improving representation by interpolating aligned features

We present AlignMix, a novel approach for improving representation learning through feature interpolation in deep neural networks. Unlike traditional data augmentation techniques that operate in the input space, our method works in the feature space by aligning and interpolating semantically meaningful representations. AlignMix first identifies corresponding features across samples using a cross-attention mechanism, then performs a controlled interpolation of these aligned features to generate new, coherent representations. Through extensive experiments on image classification benchmarks including ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and fine-grained datasets, we demonstrate that AlignMix consistently outperforms existing mixing-based regularization methods, improving top-1 accuracy by 1.2-2.5% across various network architectures. Further analysis reveals that representations learned with AlignMix exhibit better clustering of semantic concepts and improved robustness to distribution shifts. Our approach is architecture-agnostic, computationally efficient, and can be seamlessly integrated into existing training pipelines. The code is available at [project URL].

Exploiting Explanations for Model Inversion Attacks

As machine learning models are increasingly deployed in sensitive applications, the security implications of model explainability techniques warrant careful examination. This paper investigates how explanation methods, intended to increase transparency and trustworthiness, can paradoxically be exploited to conduct more effective model inversion attacks. We demonstrate that gradient-based and attention-based explanations provide adversaries with privileged information about feature importance and decision boundaries, facilitating the reconstruction of private training data. Through extensive experimentation on image, text, and tabular datasets, we show that explanation-guided inversion attacks achieve significantly higher fidelity reconstructions compared to traditional black-box approaches, while requiring fewer queries to the target model. We quantify this vulnerability across popular explanation techniques including LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and GradCAM, finding that models producing more interpretable explanations often leak more information about their training data. Finally, we propose defensive strategies including explanation obfuscation, selective disclosure, and adversarial regularization during training to mitigate these risks. Our findings highlight a fundamental tension between model transparency and privacy, suggesting that explanation systems must be designed with potential inversion attacks in mind.

Iterative Bounding MDPs: Learning Interpretable Policies via Non-Interpretable Methods

This paper introduces Iterative Bounding MDPs (IB-MDPs), a novel framework that bridges the gap between high-performing but opaque reinforcement learning policies and interpretable decision-making systems. While deep reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable performance across various domains, the resulting policies often lack transparency and interpretability, limiting their adoption in high-stakes applications. Our approach leverages the power of black-box optimization methods to iteratively discover simple, interpretable policy structures with performance guarantees. The IB-MDP framework alternates between (1) learning high-performing policies using unrestricted methods and (2) extracting interpretable policy bounds that provably constrain the solution space while maintaining near-optimal performance. Through theoretical analysis, we establish convergence properties and performance bounds for the iterative process. Empirical evaluations across diverse environments demonstrate that IB-MDPs can produce policies represented as small decision trees or sparse rule lists that achieve 90-95% of the performance of state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning approaches while maintaining human-interpretable structures. Our results suggest that interpretability need not come at a significant cost to performance, opening new possibilities for deploying reinforcement learning in domains requiring transparency and accountability.

Robustly Disentangled Causal Mechanisms: Validating Deep Representations for Interventional Robustness

Deep learning models excel at pattern recognition but often struggle when faced with interventions or distribution shifts not encountered during training. This paper introduces a framework for learning robustly disentangled causal representations that maintain their efficacy under interventional conditions. We formalize the notion of disentangled causal mechanisms in deep neural networks and propose a theoretical framework that connects representation learning with causal structure. Our approach leverages a novel regularization technique that encourages independence between latent factors while preserving causal relationships essential for downstream tasks. Through rigorous experiments across synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that models trained with our method significantly outperform state-of-the-art approaches when evaluated under various interventional scenarios. We provide theoretical guarantees on the identifiability of causal factors under specific conditions and validate our approach through ablation studies. Our results suggest that robust disentanglement of causal mechanisms enables more reliable deployment of deep learning systems in dynamic, real-world environments where interventions occur naturally. This work bridges the gap between the expressivity of deep representations and the interventional robustness demanded by high-stakes applications.

An Optical Biomimetic Eye with Interested Object Imaging

This paper presents a novel optical biomimetic eye system capable of selectively imaging objects of interest, mimicking the attentional mechanisms of biological vision. Our design incorporates a curved photoreceptor array on a hemispherical substrate that emulates the human retina's structure, combined with an adaptive optical system that can dynamically adjust its focal properties. Unlike conventional artificial vision systems that capture entire scenes with uniform resolution, our biomimetic eye implements a foveal-peripheral architecture that concentrates imaging resources on objects of interest while maintaining awareness of the surrounding environment. The system utilizes a machine learning algorithm to identify potentially relevant objects, which then triggers mechanical and optical adjustments to center and enhance the image of the selected target. Experimental results demonstrate that this selective imaging approach achieves superior resolution and detail capture of objects of interest while reducing computational load and power consumption compared to traditional wide-field high-resolution imaging. This biomimetic approach represents a significant advancement toward artificial vision systems that more efficiently process visual information by incorporating biologically-inspired attentional mechanisms, with potential applications in robotics, medical imaging, and autonomous vehicles.

Styleformer: Transformer based Generative Adversarial Networks with Style Vector

This paper introduces Styleformer, a novel architecture that combines the representational power of Transformers with the generative capabilities of GANs, integrated with an innovative style vector approach. Unlike traditional GAN architectures, Styleformer leverages self-attention mechanisms from Transformers to capture long-range dependencies in data while incorporating a disentangled style representation that enables fine-grained control over generated outputs. Our model employs a dual-pathway design: a Transformer-based generator that maps latent codes through multiple self-attention layers, and a style vector module that modulates features at different resolutions. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that Styleformer achieves state-of-the-art results in image synthesis quality, diversity, and style manipulation capabilities. The model exhibits improved training stability compared to conventional GANs and demonstrates remarkable disentanglement of style attributes. Furthermore, we show that the learned style space is highly interpretable and enables intuitive editing operations. Our approach bridges the gap between Transformer-based models and StyleGAN-like architectures, offering a powerful new paradigm for controllable generative modeling.

Predicting the Critical Number of Layers for Hierarchical Support Vector Regression

This study investigates the optimal architecture design for Hierarchical Support Vector Regression (HSVR) models by developing a theoretical framework to predict the critical number of layers required for optimal performance. While SVR has proven effective for complex regression tasks, determining the ideal hierarchical structure remains challenging. We formulate a mathematical model that relates dataset characteristics—including feature dimensionality, sample size, and underlying function complexity—to the optimal layer count in HSVR architectures. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our predictive framework accurately estimates the critical layer threshold beyond which performance improvements plateau or deteriorate. The results reveal that the critical number of layers follows a logarithmic relationship with the ratio of sample size to feature dimensionality, modified by a complexity factor derived from the target function's intrinsic properties. Our findings provide practical guidelines for HSVR implementation, potentially reducing computational costs by avoiding unnecessarily deep architectures while maintaining predictive accuracy. This work contributes to the theoretical understanding of hierarchical learning in kernel-based methods and offers an efficient approach to HSVR architecture optimization.

Poet: Product-oriented Video Captioner for E-commerce

This paper introduces Poet, a novel video captioning framework specifically designed for e-commerce applications. Unlike traditional video captioning systems that focus on general scene descriptions, Poet generates product-centric captions that highlight key selling points, specifications, and usage scenarios. Our approach integrates visual feature extraction with product metadata to create contextually relevant and persuasive descriptions optimized for online shopping environments. Through a multi-stage architecture, Poet first identifies salient product attributes from video frames, then synthesizes this information with category-specific language models trained on effective marketing copy. Experiments conducted across diverse product categories demonstrate that Poet outperforms general-purpose video captioners by 37% on our proposed Product Description Quality (PDQ) metric. User studies further confirm that Poet-generated captions significantly improve purchase intent and product understanding compared to baseline approaches. As e-commerce platforms increasingly incorporate video content into product listings, Poet offers a scalable solution for automatically generating compelling product descriptions that enhance the online shopping experience.

Deep Representation Learning For Multimodal Brain Networks

This paper presents a novel deep learning framework for representation learning across multimodal brain networks derived from different neuroimaging modalities. Brain connectivity analysis often involves multiple data types (e.g., functional MRI, diffusion MRI, EEG), each capturing distinct aspects of neural architecture and dynamics. Our approach leverages graph neural networks to extract complementary information from these heterogeneous brain networks while preserving their topological properties. We introduce a cross-modal contrastive learning strategy that aligns representations across modalities while maintaining modality-specific characteristics. Experiments on datasets spanning multiple neurological conditions demonstrate that our multimodal representations outperform single-modality approaches in downstream tasks including disease classification, cognitive score prediction, and brain state decoding. The learned embeddings reveal biologically meaningful patterns that correspond to known functional systems and highlight cross-modal relationships not evident in unimodal analyses. Our method provides a unified framework for integrating diverse brain connectivity data, offering new insights into the multiscale organization of brain networks and potential biomarkers for neurological and psychiatric disorders.

How many moments does MMD compare?

Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) is a widely used metric for comparing probability distributions based on their embeddings in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. While MMD is known to compare infinitely many moments when used with characteristic kernels, the relationship between specific kernel choices and the effective number of moments being compared remains poorly understood. This paper provides a theoretical analysis of MMD's moment-comparing properties across different kernel families. We prove that for translation-invariant kernels, MMD's sensitivity to distribution moments follows a pattern determined by the kernel's spectral properties. Our analysis reveals that common kernels like Gaussian RBF effectively prioritize lower-order moments, with sensitivity decreasing exponentially for higher-order moments. We introduce a novel kernel design framework that allows practitioners to explicitly control which moments receive emphasis during distribution comparison. Empirical evaluations on synthetic distributions and real-world applications in generative modeling demonstrate that tailoring moment sensitivity can significantly improve MMD's performance in specific distribution testing scenarios. Our findings provide new insights into MMD's behavior and offer practical guidance for kernel selection based on the statistical properties of the distributions being compared.

Unsupervised Deep Transfer Feature Learning for Medical Image Classification

Medical image classification remains a challenging task due to limited labeled data, high variability in image quality, and the specialized expertise required for annotation. This paper presents a novel unsupervised deep transfer feature learning framework that addresses these limitations by leveraging knowledge from large-scale natural image datasets while adapting to the unique characteristics of medical imaging. Our approach employs a two-stage architecture: first, we pre-train a deep convolutional neural network on diverse natural images, then develop a domain adaptation mechanism using contrastive learning and self-supervised feature distillation to bridge the domain gap between natural and medical images. The framework extracts meaningful representations without requiring labeled medical data, making it particularly valuable for rare conditions or newly emerging imaging modalities. Extensive experiments on multiple medical imaging datasets, including chest X-rays, dermatological images, and histopathology slides, demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional supervised transfer learning methods by 4-7% in classification accuracy while using only 10% of the labeled data. Furthermore, our feature visualization analysis reveals that the learned representations effectively capture clinically relevant patterns. The proposed method offers a promising solution for developing robust medical image classification systems in low-resource settings and has the potential to accelerate the deployment of AI-assisted diagnostic tools in clinical practice.

Variational Bayesian Inference for Hidden Markov Models With Multivariate Gaussian Output Distributions

This paper presents a novel variational Bayesian framework for inference in Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) with multivariate Gaussian output distributions. While HMMs are powerful tools for modeling sequential data, exact Bayesian inference is often intractable, particularly in high-dimensional settings with multivariate outputs. We develop a computationally efficient variational approximation that provides a principled approach to posterior inference while maintaining scalability. Our method employs a structured mean-field approximation that factorizes the posterior distribution while preserving key dependencies between model parameters. We derive closed-form update equations for the variational parameters and present an algorithm that guarantees convergence to a local optimum of the evidence lower bound. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach offers comparable accuracy to sampling-based methods while requiring significantly less computational resources. Additionally, we show how our framework naturally handles missing data and can be extended to incorporate prior knowledge. The proposed method enables robust uncertainty quantification in applications ranging from speech recognition to financial time series analysis, where multivariate Gaussian emissions are common. Our implementation is made publicly available to facilitate further research and applications.

Set2Graph: Learning Graphs From Sets

This paper introduces Set2Graph, a novel neural network framework designed to learn mappings from sets to graphs. Unlike traditional approaches that process sets into fixed-dimensional vectors, Set2Graph directly generates graph structures with variable numbers of nodes and edges from unordered input sets. Our framework addresses the fundamental challenge of transforming set-structured data into rich relational representations while maintaining permutation invariance of the input. 

We present a theoretical analysis demonstrating that Set2Graph can universally approximate continuous set-to-graph functions, and propose an architecture that efficiently learns pairwise and higher-order interactions between set elements. The model consists of a set-processing backbone followed by specialized decoder modules that predict graph adjacency information while preserving permutation equivariance throughout the computation.

Experimental evaluation across diverse domains—including social network inference, particle physics interactions, and protein structure prediction—demonstrates that Set2Graph significantly outperforms existing methods. Our approach shows particular strength in capturing complex relational patterns that emerge from set elements without requiring explicit graph inputs during training. The results highlight the effectiveness of our framework for tasks where the goal is to discover latent graph structures underlying set data.

Hierarchical Imitation and Reinforcement Learning

This paper presents a novel framework that integrates hierarchical imitation learning with reinforcement learning to address complex sequential decision-making problems. We introduce Hierarchical Imitation and Reinforcement Learning (HIRL), which leverages expert demonstrations to efficiently learn both high-level task decomposition and low-level control policies. Our approach decomposes complex tasks into a hierarchy of subtasks, enabling more effective learning through abstraction. By combining imitation learning at the higher levels of the hierarchy with reinforcement learning at the lower levels, HIRL effectively balances the benefits of demonstration-guided learning with autonomous policy optimization. Experimental results across several challenging domains demonstrate that our hierarchical approach significantly outperforms flat imitation learning and reinforcement learning methods in terms of sample efficiency, learning speed, and final performance. Additionally, we show that HIRL enables effective transfer learning, where policies learned for subtasks can be reused across different complex tasks. Our work provides a principled approach to scaling learning algorithms to solve increasingly complex sequential decision problems.

Optimal Transport for Multi-source Domain Adaptation under Target Shift

Domain adaptation remains a critical challenge in machine learning, particularly when knowledge must be transferred from multiple source domains to a target domain with distribution shift. This paper addresses the complex problem of multi-source domain adaptation under target shift—where the label distributions differ between source and target domains. We propose a novel framework that leverages optimal transport (OT) theory to align distributions across domains while explicitly accounting for shifts in target label proportions. Our approach introduces a joint optimization procedure that simultaneously learns domain-invariant feature representations and estimates target label distributions through an iterative transport plan refinement. We derive theoretical guarantees on the target error bounds and demonstrate how our method mitigates negative transfer from irrelevant source domains. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant improvements in classification accuracy under various target shift scenarios. The proposed method proves particularly effective when source domains exhibit high diversity or when the target shift is substantial, making it a robust solution for real-world applications where labeled target data is scarce and distribution shifts are common.

The Hessigheim 3D (H3D) Benchmark on Semantic Segmentation of High-Resolution 3D Point Clouds and Textured Meshes from UAV LiDAR and Multi-View-Stereo

This paper introduces the Hessigheim 3D (H3D) Benchmark, a novel dataset and evaluation framework for semantic segmentation of high-resolution 3D geospatial data. The benchmark features complementary data modalities captured via Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) platforms: dense LiDAR point clouds (>800 points/m²) and photorealistic textured meshes derived from Multi-View-Stereo (MVS) techniques. Covering a 0.4 km² semi-urban area in Hessigheim, Germany, the dataset includes detailed annotations across 11 semantic classes representing common urban elements such as buildings, vegetation, roads, and infrastructure. We establish standardized evaluation protocols and baseline results using state-of-the-art deep learning architectures for point cloud and mesh segmentation. Our experiments demonstrate the unique challenges of high-resolution 3D semantic segmentation and highlight the complementary nature of geometric and spectral information contained in the different modalities. The H3D Benchmark addresses a critical gap in existing 3D semantic segmentation datasets by providing multi-modal, high-resolution geospatial data with precise annotations, enabling researchers to develop and evaluate algorithms for applications in urban planning, digital twins, and environmental monitoring. The benchmark dataset, code, and evaluation server are made publicly available to foster further research in this domain.

Solid Texture Synthesis using Generative Adversarial Networks

This paper presents a novel approach to solid texture synthesis utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Unlike traditional methods that focus on 2D textures, our framework generates consistent volumetric textures that maintain coherence across arbitrary cutting planes. We propose a specialized 3D convolutional GAN architecture that learns to synthesize solid textures from a limited set of 2D exemplars without requiring volumetric training data. Our method incorporates a multi-slice discriminator that simultaneously evaluates texture quality along the three principal orthogonal planes, ensuring cross-sectional consistency. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach successfully generates high-quality solid textures for a wide range of material types, outperforming existing methods in both visual quality and spatial consistency. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation metric specifically designed for solid textures that quantifies both the fidelity to exemplar statistics and the coherence between orthogonal cross-sections. The generated solid textures can be directly applied in volumetric rendering, virtual material design, and computer-aided manufacturing applications, offering a significant advancement in the field of procedural content generation.

Integrating Transductive And Inductive Embeddings Improves Link Prediction Accuracy

Link prediction in graphs remains a fundamental challenge in network analysis with applications spanning recommendation systems, knowledge graph completion, and social network analysis. While transductive embedding methods excel at capturing global graph structure and inductive approaches generalize well to unseen nodes, each approach has inherent limitations when used in isolation. This paper introduces a novel hybrid framework that integrates transductive and inductive graph embeddings to enhance link prediction accuracy. Our approach leverages the complementary strengths of both paradigms: transductive methods provide rich representations of existing graph topology, while inductive techniques enable generalization to dynamic network environments. Through extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our integrated approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods using either paradigm alone, achieving an average improvement of 8.3% in AUC-ROC scores. Further analysis reveals that the performance gains are particularly significant in sparse regions of graphs and for newly emerging nodes. These findings suggest that combining embedding paradigms offers a promising direction for improving link prediction systems in evolving network environments.

Face Recognition: A Novel Multi-Level Taxonomy based Survey

This paper presents a comprehensive survey of face recognition technologies through the lens of a novel multi-level taxonomic framework. Despite decades of research and significant advancements, face recognition systems continue to face challenges in real-world scenarios involving variations in illumination, pose, aging, and occlusions. Our proposed taxonomy systematically categorizes face recognition approaches across four principal levels: preprocessing techniques, feature extraction methodologies, classification strategies, and application domains. At each level, we identify key subcategories and emerging trends, providing researchers with a structured understanding of the field's evolution from traditional geometric and appearance-based methods to contemporary deep learning architectures. Through extensive analysis of over 200 recent publications, we identify critical research gaps and highlight promising directions, particularly in addressing bias, privacy concerns, and adversarial robustness. This multi-level taxonomy not only serves as a valuable reference for understanding the current state of face recognition research but also provides a roadmap for future innovations in this rapidly evolving field.

AttentionGAN: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation using Attention-Guided Generative Adversarial Networks

Image-to-image translation has witnessed significant advancements through Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), yet existing approaches often struggle with preserving background details and maintaining structural integrity during translation. In this paper, we introduce AttentionGAN, a novel framework that integrates attention mechanisms into the unpaired image-to-image translation pipeline. Our approach generates attention masks that automatically identify discriminative regions to transform while preserving background elements. Unlike previous methods that process the entire image uniformly, AttentionGAN focuses computational resources on regions that require modification, resulting in more precise translations. We propose a dual attention mechanism: a foreground attention module that highlights target transformation areas and a background preservation module that maintains contextual consistency. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets including horse2zebra, summer2winter, and face attribute manipulation demonstrate that AttentionGAN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both qualitative visual fidelity and quantitative metrics. Our approach reduces artifacts, preserves background details, and maintains structural coherence without requiring additional supervision or paired training data.

Where To Look: Focus Regions for Visual Question Answering

Visual Question Answering (VQA) requires models to reason about both visual content and natural language questions. While recent approaches have achieved impressive performance on VQA benchmarks, they often lack the ability to effectively focus on image regions that are most relevant to answering the question. In this paper, we present a novel attention mechanism that learns to identify and attend to critical focus regions in images when answering visual questions. Our approach incorporates a hierarchical attention framework that first identifies candidate regions of interest and then refines attention weights based on question semantics. Through extensive experiments on the VQA, VQA 2.0, and COCO-QA datasets, we demonstrate that our focus region approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 3.2% absolute improvement on VQA 2.0. Qualitative visualizations of the attention maps reveal that our model successfully localizes relevant image regions even for complex questions requiring multi-step reasoning. Furthermore, our approach shows particular strength in questions demanding fine-grained spatial understanding and object relationship reasoning. The proposed focus region mechanism provides both improved performance and better model interpretability, offering insights into the reasoning process behind visual question answering.

Neural Discrete Representation Learning

We present a novel approach to unsupervised learning of discrete representations through a Vector Quantized-Variational AutoEncoder (VQ-VAE) framework. Unlike conventional VAEs that encode inputs as continuous latent variables, our model maps inputs to discrete latent representations, effectively functioning as a powerful neural discrete representation learning system. The VQ-VAE employs a vector quantization layer that discretizes the latent space by mapping encoder outputs to the nearest vectors in a learned codebook. This discretization process creates a more structured and interpretable latent space while maintaining gradient-based training through a straight-through estimator. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach successfully addresses posterior collapse issues common in traditional VAEs and produces high-quality reconstructions across various domains including images, speech, and video. The discrete nature of our representations proves particularly valuable for generative modeling, where we show that autoregressive models applied to our learned discrete space can generate coherent and diverse samples. Additionally, we demonstrate that these discrete representations capture meaningful semantic information that transfers well to downstream tasks, even with limited labeled data. The VQ-VAE framework provides a promising direction for learning useful discrete representations that bridge the gap between continuous deep learning approaches and symbolic reasoning systems.

Deep Sets for Generalization in RL

This paper introduces a novel approach to enhancing generalization capabilities in reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging Deep Sets, a permutation-invariant neural network architecture. We address the critical challenge of enabling RL agents to transfer knowledge across environments with varying numbers of entities while maintaining consistent performance. Our method represents environment states as sets of elements, allowing the network to process inputs of arbitrary cardinality while preserving relational information. Through extensive experiments across diverse domains including multi-agent systems, robotic manipulation tasks, and procedurally generated environments, we demonstrate that our Deep Sets-based architecture significantly outperforms conventional RL approaches in generalization scenarios. The results show improved sample efficiency during training and robust zero-shot transfer to previously unseen environment configurations with different numbers of objects or agents. Additionally, we provide theoretical analysis establishing the representational capacity of our approach for value function approximation in RL settings. This work opens promising directions for developing RL systems capable of generalizing across structurally varying environments without requiring environment-specific retraining.

Whitening and Coloring Batch Transform for GANs

This paper introduces a novel normalization technique called Whitening and Coloring Batch Transform (WCBT) specifically designed to enhance the training stability and generation quality of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Unlike conventional normalization methods such as Batch Normalization that only standardize features to zero mean and unit variance, WCBT performs a more comprehensive transformation by removing feature correlations through whitening and then applying a learnable coloring transformation. Our approach addresses the inherent training instabilities of GANs by ensuring that feature distributions are properly normalized across both spatial and channel dimensions. Through extensive experiments on multiple datasets including CIFAR-10, CelebA, and ImageNet, we demonstrate that WCBT significantly improves training convergence, mitigates mode collapse, and enhances the diversity and visual quality of generated samples. Quantitative evaluations using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score show that GAN architectures incorporating WCBT consistently outperform their counterparts using traditional normalization techniques. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into why whitening and coloring operations are particularly beneficial for adversarial training dynamics. Our method can be seamlessly integrated into existing GAN frameworks with minimal computational overhead, offering a practical solution to improve GAN performance across various applications.

Learning Sight from Sound: Ambient Sound Provides Supervision for Visual Learning

This paper explores how ambient sounds can serve as a natural form of supervision for visual learning systems. We demonstrate that the co-occurrence of visual and auditory information in the environment provides a rich signal that can be leveraged to learn meaningful visual representations without explicit human annotation. Our approach capitalizes on the inherent correspondence between what is seen and heard in everyday scenes, enabling models to learn visual features that are semantically meaningful and contextually relevant. Through a series of experiments, we show that networks trained using only ambient sound supervision can learn to recognize objects, scenes, and events with surprising effectiveness. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that representations learned from audio-visual correspondences transfer well to various downstream visual tasks, including object detection, scene classification, and action recognition. Our findings suggest that multimodal learning from naturally co-occurring sensory data offers a promising path toward more scalable and human-like visual learning systems that can understand the world through multiple sensory dimensions.

Physically Realizable Adversarial Examples for LiDAR Object Detection

LiDAR sensors are critical components in the perception systems of autonomous vehicles, enabling accurate object detection and distance measurement. However, the security vulnerabilities of LiDAR-based object detection algorithms remain underexplored. This paper presents the first systematic study of physically realizable adversarial examples targeting LiDAR detection systems. We demonstrate that carefully designed physical objects can manipulate the point cloud data to cause state-of-the-art LiDAR-based detection models to misclassify, mislocalize, or completely fail to detect objects. Our approach generates adversarial objects that are manufacturable in the real world and robust across various environmental conditions. Through extensive experiments in both simulated environments and real-world settings, we show that our attacks achieve success rates of over 80% against popular detection frameworks including PointPillars and PointRCNN. We analyze the transferability of these attacks across different models and propose practical countermeasures to enhance the robustness of LiDAR detection systems. Our findings highlight significant security implications for autonomous driving and other LiDAR-dependent applications, emphasizing the need for adversarially robust perception algorithms.

YAHPO Gym -- Design Criteria and a new Multifidelity Benchmark for Hyperparameter Optimization

Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is a critical component in developing effective machine learning systems, yet benchmarking HPO methods remains challenging due to the computational expense of training models repeatedly. In this paper, we introduce YAHPO Gym, a novel multifidelity benchmark suite designed specifically for HPO research. We establish key design criteria for HPO benchmarks, including reproducibility, diverse problem characteristics, computational efficiency, and realistic complexity. YAHPO Gym implements these criteria through surrogate models trained on extensive evaluations across multiple datasets, algorithms, and hyperparameter configurations. The benchmark supports multifidelity optimization by allowing evaluation at varying resource levels (e.g., number of iterations, sample sizes), enabling research on budget-aware optimization methods. Our empirical validation demonstrates that YAHPO Gym accurately captures the performance landscapes of original HPO problems while providing orders of magnitude faster evaluation. The benchmark includes diverse scenarios spanning classification, regression, and time series forecasting tasks, with varying dimensionality and optimization difficulty. YAHPO Gym provides a standardized, accessible platform for fair comparison of HPO methods, accelerating research in this important field while maintaining realistic challenges that transfer to practical applications.

Closed-form Continuous-Depth Models

This paper introduces a novel framework for continuous-depth neural networks that admits closed-form solutions. Unlike traditional discrete-layer architectures, our approach conceptualizes neural networks as continuous transformations along a depth dimension, allowing for precise mathematical characterization of information flow. We derive analytical expressions for these continuous-depth models by formulating them as solutions to carefully designed ordinary differential equations. Our closed-form representations enable direct analysis of model properties including expressivity, stability, and generalization bounds without relying on discretization approximations. Theoretical results demonstrate that these models achieve optimal trade-offs between computational complexity and representational power. Empirical evaluations across multiple domains show that our closed-form continuous-depth models not only match the performance of state-of-the-art discrete networks but also exhibit enhanced robustness to perturbations and improved sample efficiency. Furthermore, the analytical nature of our approach provides interpretability advantages and facilitates theoretical insights into deep learning phenomena that have previously remained elusive to formal analysis.

Everybody Sign Now: Translating Spoken Language to Photo Realistic Sign Language Video

This paper presents a novel end-to-end framework for translating spoken language into photo-realistic sign language video. Our approach bridges the communication gap between hearing and Deaf communities by generating natural-looking sign language content from text or speech input. We introduce a multi-stage architecture that first translates source language into a sign language gloss representation, then maps this intermediate representation to continuous 3D signing poses, and finally renders these poses into realistic video using a generative adversarial network. The system incorporates linguistic features specific to sign languages, including non-manual elements such as facial expressions and mouthing patterns. Extensive evaluations with native signers demonstrate that our approach produces significantly more accurate and natural signing compared to previous methods, achieving a mean opinion score of 4.2/5 for comprehensibility. Our model generalizes across different signing contexts and can be adapted to various sign languages with minimal additional training. We release our dataset of 250 hours of aligned spoken language and sign language video pairs to facilitate further research in this area. This work represents a significant step toward accessible communication technologies that respect the linguistic integrity of sign languages.

Prior Knowledge Distillation Based on Financial Time Series

This paper introduces a novel approach to knowledge distillation in the domain of financial time series analysis. We propose a framework that leverages domain-specific prior knowledge to enhance the performance of compact machine learning models for financial forecasting tasks. Our method systematically extracts and transfers essential patterns, market dynamics, and temporal dependencies from both expert domain knowledge and larger teacher models into smaller, more deployable student networks. Experiments conducted on multiple financial datasets, including stock prices, forex, and cryptocurrency markets, demonstrate that our knowledge distillation approach significantly outperforms traditional model compression techniques, reducing model size by up to 75% while maintaining 96% of the original predictive accuracy. Furthermore, the distilled models show improved generalization during periods of market volatility and regime changes. The incorporation of financial domain priors into the distillation process enables these lightweight models to capture critical market behaviors that might otherwise be lost during compression. Our approach addresses the crucial industry requirements for computational efficiency and interpretability in financial prediction systems while preserving performance on complex time series forecasting tasks.

The Kolmogorov-Arnold Representation Theorem Revisited

This paper provides a contemporary examination of the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, a fundamental result in approximation theory that demonstrates any multivariate continuous function can be represented as a finite composition of continuous functions of a single variable and addition operations. We review the historical development of the theorem from Hilbert's 13th problem to Kolmogorov's surprising solution and Arnold's subsequent refinements. Our analysis addresses recent advances in constructive approaches to the theorem, highlighting improved algorithms for determining the univariate functions required in the representation. We examine the theorem's connections to modern neural network theory, particularly its relationship to universal approximation capabilities of certain network architectures. Additionally, we discuss computational complexity issues that arise in practical implementations and propose extensions that address some of the theorem's known limitations regarding smoothness properties. Our results contribute to both the theoretical understanding of function representation and practical applications in machine learning and high-dimensional approximation problems.

An Adaptive Cluster-based Filtering Framework for Speckle Reduction of OCT Skin Images

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) has emerged as a valuable non-invasive imaging technique for dermatological applications, providing high-resolution cross-sectional images of skin tissue. However, the presence of speckle noise significantly compromises image quality and diagnostic accuracy. This paper presents a novel adaptive cluster-based filtering framework specifically designed for speckle reduction in OCT skin images. Our approach integrates spatial clustering techniques with adaptive filtering mechanisms that dynamically adjust to local tissue characteristics. The proposed framework first segments the OCT image into meaningful clusters based on tissue morphology, then applies optimized filtering parameters tailored to each cluster's statistical properties. Experimental validation conducted on both phantom and in vivo human skin OCT datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional speckle reduction methods, achieving an average signal-to-noise ratio improvement of 8.2 dB while preserving critical tissue boundaries and fine structural details. Quantitative assessment using contrast-to-noise ratio, equivalent number of looks, and edge preservation metrics confirms the framework's effectiveness. The proposed method enhances visualization of dermal-epidermal junction and deeper dermal structures, potentially improving diagnostic capabilities for various skin conditions without introducing artificial features or significant computational overhead.

3D-MAN: 3D Multi-frame Attention Network for Object Detection

We present 3D-MAN (3D Multi-frame Attention Network), a novel approach for 3D object detection in point cloud sequences. Unlike conventional methods that process individual frames independently, our network leverages temporal information across multiple frames to enhance detection accuracy and robustness. The core of our architecture is a multi-frame attention mechanism that dynamically aggregates features across the temporal dimension, allowing the model to reason about object persistence, motion patterns, and occlusion. Our framework consists of three main components: (1) a single-frame feature extractor that processes raw point cloud data, (2) a temporal attention module that establishes correspondences between frames and weighs their contributions, and (3) a detection head that predicts 3D bounding boxes with associated class probabilities. Extensive experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset and KITTI benchmark demonstrate that 3D-MAN significantly outperforms single-frame baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance especially for small, distant, and partially occluded objects. Our ablation studies confirm that the performance gains stem from the network's ability to accumulate evidence across frames while effectively handling challenges such as varying point cloud density and object motion. The proposed approach represents an important step toward robust perception systems for autonomous driving and robotics applications.

Enhanced Techniques for PDF Image Segmentation and Text Extraction

This paper presents novel methodologies for improving image segmentation and text extraction from PDF documents. We introduce a hybrid approach that combines convolutional neural networks with traditional computer vision techniques to accurately identify and separate textual and graphical elements within complex PDF layouts. Our method addresses common challenges including overlapping content, varied font styles, multi-column formats, and low-quality scanned documents. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves 94.7% accuracy in text extraction across a diverse dataset of 5,000 PDF documents spanning academic, business, and technical domains, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods by an average of 8.3%. Additionally, our algorithm reduces processing time by 37% compared to existing solutions while maintaining high precision in preserving document structure and formatting. The proposed framework offers significant improvements for digital document processing workflows, particularly for applications in information retrieval, document analysis, and automated content management systems.

Detection of Morphed Face Images Using Discriminative Wavelet Sub-bands

Face morphing attacks pose a significant threat to facial recognition systems by creating synthetic images that can match multiple identities, potentially compromising identity verification processes at border control and other security applications. This paper presents a novel approach for detecting morphed face images using discriminative wavelet sub-bands. We decompose facial images using multi-level wavelet transformation and identify the most discriminative sub-bands that capture subtle artifacts introduced during the morphing process. Our method exploits the observation that morphing operations leave characteristic traces in specific frequency domains that are not visually apparent but can be detected in the wavelet domain. We propose a feature extraction framework that selectively combines information from these discriminative sub-bands and employs an ensemble classification approach to differentiate between bona fide and morphed facial images. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple public and proprietary datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art detection performance with an average detection accuracy of 97.3% and an equal error rate of 2.1%, outperforming existing methods particularly in cross-dataset scenarios. The proposed technique shows strong resilience against various post-processing operations commonly applied to conceal morphing artifacts, offering a robust solution for operational deployment in security-critical applications.

Time Matters in Using Data Augmentation for Vision-based Deep Reinforcement Learning

Data augmentation techniques have proven highly effective in supervised learning contexts, yet their application to vision-based deep reinforcement learning (RL) remains less explored. This paper investigates the critical role of timing when implementing data augmentation strategies in RL frameworks. Through extensive experiments across multiple environments, we demonstrate that the temporal positioning of augmentation operations—whether applied during collection, training, or inference—significantly impacts agent performance. Our results reveal that augmentation during training can mitigate overfitting and improve sample efficiency, while augmentation during collection enhances exploration and environment generalization. However, we find that poorly timed augmentation can destabilize learning or create distribution shifts that degrade performance. We propose a novel adaptive timing framework that dynamically adjusts augmentation scheduling based on learning progress, achieving 27% improved performance over static approaches. Our analysis provides practical guidelines for effectively incorporating data augmentation into vision-based RL systems, highlighting that when augmentation occurs is as important as how it is implemented.

DeepPerimeter: Indoor Boundary Estimation from Posed Monocular Sequences

This paper presents DeepPerimeter, a novel deep learning approach for estimating indoor structural boundaries from posed monocular video sequences. Accurate floor plan estimation remains challenging due to occlusions, varied lighting conditions, and complex room geometries. Our method leverages temporal information across video frames to overcome these limitations, producing consistent and complete perimeter reconstructions. We introduce a multi-stage architecture that first extracts per-frame boundary features, then aggregates these features across the sequence using a transformer-based temporal fusion module. This is followed by a boundary completion network that infers occluded regions based on visible evidence. Experiments on standard datasets demonstrate that DeepPerimeter outperforms existing methods by 18% in boundary accuracy and 23% in completeness metrics. Additionally, we present a new dataset of challenging indoor environments with ground truth boundaries. Our approach enables applications in augmented reality, indoor navigation, and architectural documentation, while requiring only a standard smartphone camera for input. Code and dataset are available at our project website.

Progressively Unfreezing Perceptual GAN

This paper introduces Progressively Unfreezing Perceptual GAN (PUP-GAN), a novel approach to generative adversarial network training that combines progressive layer unfreezing with perceptual loss functions. While state-of-the-art GANs have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generating high-fidelity images, they often suffer from training instability and mode collapse. Our method addresses these challenges by initially freezing most network layers and gradually unfreezing them during training, allowing the model to learn hierarchical representations in a controlled manner. We incorporate perceptual losses derived from pre-trained visual recognition networks to guide the generator toward producing images that match real data distributions at multiple levels of abstraction. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that PUP-GAN achieves superior Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores and improved training stability compared to conventional GAN architectures. Additionally, our approach reduces computational requirements during early training stages and accelerates convergence. The progressive unfreezing strategy proves particularly effective for high-resolution image synthesis tasks, where managing the complexity of the learning process is crucial for optimal results.

Evolutionary Population Curriculum for Scaling Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces Evolutionary Population Curriculum (EPC), a novel framework for scaling multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to complex environments with large numbers of agents. While MARL has shown promising results in various domains, training agents in environments with many learning agents remains challenging due to non-stationarity, complex strategic interactions, and exponentially growing state-action spaces. Our approach addresses these challenges by dynamically evolving a curriculum of increasingly complex agent populations. EPC begins with small populations where learning is more tractable, then progressively scales to larger populations using an evolutionary selection mechanism that preserves and propagates successful policies. Through a combination of policy distillation, adaptive difficulty adjustment, and strategic diversity maintenance, EPC creates a structured learning pathway that mitigates the inherent instability of many-agent training. We evaluate our method across several challenging multi-agent environments, including strategic team competitions, mixed cooperative-competitive scenarios, and large-scale coordination tasks. Results demonstrate that EPC significantly outperforms existing MARL approaches in both sample efficiency and final performance, successfully scaling to environments with hundreds of interacting agents while maintaining stable learning dynamics. Our analysis reveals that the evolved curriculum automatically discovers critical skills in a sequential manner, enabling agents to master complex behaviors that are unattainable with standard training methods.

HIVE-COTE 2.0: a new meta ensemble for time series classification

Time series classification (TSC) presents unique challenges due to the temporal nature of the data. The Hierarchical Vote Collective of Transformation-based Ensembles (HIVE-COTE) has emerged as a leading algorithm for TSC tasks. In this paper, we introduce HIVE-COTE 2.0, a significant advancement over its predecessor that addresses key limitations while improving classification accuracy and computational efficiency.
