Our new meta-ensemble incorporates refined component classifiers that leverage diverse representations of time series data, including frequency, shapelet, and interval-based features. We introduce a novel weighted probabilistic voting scheme that dynamically adjusts the contribution of each component based on its estimated performance on the problem at hand. Extensive empirical evaluation on the UCR/UEA time series archive demonstrates that HIVE-COTE 2.0 achieves state-of-the-art performance, significantly outperforming both deep learning approaches and the original HIVE-COTE across a wide range of domains. Notably, our implementation reduces runtime by an order of magnitude compared to the previous version while maintaining superior classification accuracy. These improvements make HIVE-COTE 2.0 not only more accurate but also more practical for real-world applications where computational resources are limited.

Deep Image Spatial Transformation for Person Image Generation

This paper presents a novel approach to person image generation using deep image spatial transformation techniques. We address the challenging task of generating realistic person images with arbitrary poses while preserving identity-specific details such as appearance, clothing texture, and facial features. Unlike previous methods that rely heavily on direct pixel synthesis, our framework introduces a spatial transformation network that explicitly models the geometric deformations needed to transfer a source person image to a target pose. By decomposing the generation process into spatial transformation and content refinement stages, our method better handles large pose differences and complex self-occlusions. We propose a multi-scale attention mechanism that guides the transformation process by establishing fine-grained correspondences between source and target body parts. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and human perceptual studies, producing more realistic and identity-consistent results. The proposed technique has significant applications in virtual try-on systems, video generation, and data augmentation for person re-identification.

Hierarchically Compositional Tasks and Deep Convolutional Networks

This paper explores the relationship between hierarchically compositional tasks and the architectural design of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). We demonstrate that many real-world visual recognition problems exhibit a natural hierarchical structure, where complex concepts are composed of simpler sub-components arranged in increasingly sophisticated patterns. Our work establishes a theoretical framework connecting the compositional nature of these tasks to the hierarchical feature extraction mechanisms inherent in deep CNNs. Through extensive experiments on both synthetic and natural datasets, we show that the performance of CNNs improves significantly when their architectural hierarchy—defined by depth, receptive field growth, and feature abstraction—aligns with the compositional structure of the target task. We introduce a novel metric to quantify this alignment and demonstrate its predictive power for model performance across diverse visual recognition challenges. Our findings provide principled guidance for CNN architecture design based on task characteristics and offer insights into why deep convolutional architectures have been so successful in domains with hierarchically structured information. These results have important implications for both the theoretical understanding of deep learning and practical applications in computer vision.

Regularize, Expand and Compress: Multi-task based Lifelong Learning via NonExpansive AutoML

Lifelong learning remains a significant challenge in machine learning, as systems struggle to acquire new knowledge without catastrophically forgetting previously learned tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel framework called "Regularize, Expand and Compress" (REC) that addresses this challenge through a multi-task based approach leveraging NonExpansive AutoML techniques. Our method operates in three distinct phases: first regularizing the model to preserve knowledge of previous tasks, then strategically expanding the network capacity to accommodate new tasks, and finally compressing the expanded network to maintain efficiency. Unlike previous approaches that suffer from either rigidity or unbounded growth, REC achieves a balance between stability and plasticity while maintaining a compact model footprint. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets including CIFAR-100, Omniglot, and CORe50, we demonstrate that REC outperforms state-of-the-art lifelong learning methods by an average of 8.7% in accuracy while using only 35% of the parameters required by comparable approaches. Furthermore, our NonExpansive AutoML component automatically optimizes the architecture for each task sequence, eliminating the need for manual hyperparameter tuning. These results suggest that REC offers a promising direction for developing more adaptive and resource-efficient lifelong learning systems.

A Compact Sequence Encoding Scheme for Online Human Activity Recognition in HRI Applications

This paper presents a novel compact sequence encoding scheme designed to facilitate real-time human activity recognition (HAR) in human-robot interaction (HRI) applications. The proposed approach addresses key challenges in online HAR systems, including computational efficiency, model size, and recognition accuracy under temporal variations. Our encoding scheme transforms multimodal sensor data into compact sequential representations that preserve temporal dynamics while significantly reducing dimensionality. We introduce a hierarchical feature extraction method that captures both local motion patterns and global activity structures, enabling efficient processing on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Experimental evaluation on three public HAR datasets demonstrates that our approach achieves comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art deep learning methods while requiring 78% less memory and 65% reduced inference time. When implemented on a social robot platform, the system maintained real-time performance (24fps) while accurately recognizing 18 different human activities. The results suggest that our compact encoding scheme offers a promising solution for deployment in practical HRI scenarios where responsive and accurate activity recognition is essential for natural human-robot collaboration.

SparseCodePicking: Feature Extraction in Mass Spectrometry Using Sparse Coding Algorithms

Mass spectrometry (MS) is a fundamental analytical technique in proteomics, metabolomics, and related fields, generating complex spectral data that require sophisticated computational approaches for effective analysis. This paper introduces SparseCodePicking, a novel feature extraction framework that leverages sparse coding algorithms to address the challenges of peak detection and feature identification in MS data. Our approach represents mass spectra as sparse linear combinations of basis functions from an optimized dictionary, enabling more robust detection of meaningful spectral features even in noisy, low-intensity, or overlapping peak scenarios. We demonstrate that by learning an appropriate dictionary directly from experimental data, SparseCodePicking can automatically adapt to instrument-specific characteristics and diverse sample types without manual parameter tuning. Comparative evaluations against established methods show that our approach achieves superior sensitivity and specificity in peak detection across multiple MS platforms, with particular advantages in complex biological samples. Furthermore, SparseCodePicking exhibits enhanced performance in the identification of isotope patterns and adduct ions, contributing to improved compound identification. The computational efficiency of our implementation makes it suitable for high-throughput applications. These results suggest that sparse coding provides a powerful mathematical framework for MS data analysis that could significantly advance feature extraction capabilities in metabolomics and proteomics research.

Representation Matters: Improving Perception and Exploration for Robotics

This paper presents a novel approach to representation learning for robotic perception and exploration. We demonstrate that the quality and structure of learned representations significantly impact a robot's ability to understand its environment and make informed decisions. Our framework leverages deep neural architectures to extract meaningful features from high-dimensional sensory inputs, creating compact yet information-rich representations that facilitate downstream tasks. Through extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world robotic platforms, we show that our representation learning approach improves object recognition accuracy by 27%, reduces exploration time in novel environments by 42%, and enhances sample efficiency in reinforcement learning tasks. The key insight of our work is that representations should balance task-specificity with generalizability, enabling robots to transfer knowledge across domains while maintaining performance on specialized tasks. Our approach demonstrates robust performance even under challenging conditions including partial observability, sensor noise, and dynamic environments. These findings underscore the critical role of representation learning in advancing autonomous robotic systems and provide a foundation for developing more capable and adaptable robots for real-world applications.

Towards Robust Interpretability with Self-Explaining Neural Networks

Deep neural networks have demonstrated remarkable performance across various domains but often function as black boxes, limiting their utility in critical applications requiring transparency. This paper introduces Self-Explaining Neural Networks (SENN), a novel framework designed to provide robust interpretability without sacrificing predictive performance. Unlike post-hoc explanation methods, SENNs incorporate interpretability directly into their architecture by learning concept-based representations paired with relevance scores that explicitly contribute to predictions. We formalize the notion of interpretability through three key properties: explicitness, faithfulness, and stability. Our empirical evaluation across image classification, sentiment analysis, and medical diagnosis tasks demonstrates that SENNs achieve comparable accuracy to traditional neural networks while providing interpretations that are more robust to input perturbations and adversarial attacks. Furthermore, we show that the learned concepts often align with human-understandable features without explicit supervision. This work represents a significant step toward machine learning systems that are both powerful and transparently interpretable, addressing a critical need for trustworthy AI in high-stakes decision-making contexts.

Structured Sparse Non-negative Matrix Factorization with L20-Norm for scRNA-seq Data Analysis

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has revolutionized our ability to characterize cellular heterogeneity, but the high dimensionality and sparsity of these datasets present significant computational challenges. In this paper, we introduce a novel dimensionality reduction method called Structured Sparse Non-negative Matrix Factorization with L20-Norm (SS-NMF-L20) specifically designed for scRNA-seq data analysis. Our approach extends traditional non-negative matrix factorization by incorporating an L20-norm regularization term that simultaneously promotes group sparsity and maintains non-negativity constraints, which preserves the biological interpretability of the resulting factors. Unlike existing methods, SS-NMF-L20 effectively captures the inherent hierarchical structure of gene expression patterns while addressing the zero-inflation problem common in scRNA-seq data. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on multiple scRNA-seq datasets spanning diverse tissue types and experimental conditions. SS-NMF-L20 consistently outperforms state-of-the-art dimensionality reduction techniques in cell type identification, rare cell population detection, and trajectory inference tasks. Furthermore, we provide a computationally efficient implementation that scales to datasets containing millions of cells. Our results suggest that SS-NMF-L20 offers a powerful framework for extracting meaningful biological insights from the complex landscape of single-cell transcriptomic data.

A Multi-step and Resilient Predictive Q-learning Algorithm for IoT with Human Operators in the Loop: A Case Study in Water Supply Networks

This paper introduces a novel multi-step predictive Q-learning algorithm designed for Internet of Things (IoT) environments that incorporate human operators in the decision-making loop. The proposed approach enhances traditional reinforcement learning methods by implementing a resilient framework that anticipates system states several steps into the future while accommodating human intervention. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a comprehensive case study of water supply networks, where operational efficiency and fault tolerance are critical. Our method integrates sensor data from IoT devices with human expertise to optimize control decisions under uncertainty and partial observability. Experimental results show that the multi-step predictive capability improves response time to potential failures by 37% compared to conventional Q-learning approaches, while the human-in-the-loop component reduces false alarms by 42% and improves decision accuracy in edge cases. The algorithm demonstrates particular resilience to sensor failures and communication disruptions, maintaining 89% operational efficiency even when 30% of the IoT infrastructure is compromised. This research provides a promising framework for critical infrastructure management where both automated intelligence and human oversight are essential for reliable operation.

Leveraging Pre-Images to Discover Nonlinear Relationships in Multivariate Environments

This study introduces a novel methodology for uncovering complex nonlinear relationships within high-dimensional data structures by leveraging the concept of pre-images in kernel-based learning frameworks. While traditional multivariate analysis techniques often struggle with highly nonlinear dependencies, our approach maps data into a high-dimensional feature space where we identify and reconstruct the pre-images—original data points corresponding to specific feature space representations. By analyzing these pre-images, we demonstrate how intricate relationships that remain obscured in conventional analyses can be systematically revealed. We evaluate our methodology across diverse domains including climate science, financial markets, and biomedical datasets, where nonlinear interactions between variables are prevalent but poorly characterized by linear models. Results show that our pre-image based approach achieves a 37% improvement in predictive accuracy compared to traditional methods when applied to complex systems. Furthermore, we introduce a computational framework that addresses the traditionally ill-posed nature of pre-image problems through regularization techniques and manifold learning. This research provides both theoretical contributions to the understanding of nonlinear feature relationships and practical tools for scientists working with multivariate data across disciplines.

Gaining Insight into SARS-CoV-2 Infection and COVID-19 Severity Using Self-supervised Edge Features and Graph Neural Networks

This study presents a novel computational framework leveraging self-supervised edge features and graph neural networks (GNNs) to gain deeper insights into SARS-CoV-2 infection mechanisms and COVID-19 severity prediction. We constructed multi-modal biological networks integrating host-pathogen protein interactions, gene expression data, and clinical parameters from COVID-19 patients. Our approach employs self-supervised learning to extract meaningful edge features representing the complex relationships between biological entities within these networks. The framework utilizes a custom GNN architecture that captures both local and global network properties to identify critical molecular pathways involved in viral infection and disease progression. Analysis of the learned representations revealed previously uncharacterized interactions between viral proteins and host immune response mechanisms. Furthermore, our model achieved significant improvements in predicting COVID-19 severity (AUC 0.87, 95% CI: 0.83-0.91) compared to conventional machine learning approaches. Feature importance analysis highlighted key molecular signatures associated with severe outcomes, including dysregulation of interferon signaling pathways and specific cytokine profiles. These findings provide valuable insights for therapeutic target identification and patient risk stratification. Our self-supervised GNN framework demonstrates the potential of network-based approaches for understanding complex host-pathogen interactions and may be applicable to other infectious diseases beyond COVID-19.

Context-aware Active Multi-Step Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces a novel framework for reinforcement learning that integrates context awareness with active learning principles in a multi-step decision-making process. Our approach, Context-aware Active Multi-Step Reinforcement Learning (CAMSRL), dynamically adapts exploration strategies based on environmental context signals while actively selecting the most informative experiences to learn from. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning methods that treat all environments uniformly, CAMSRL leverages contextual information to modulate policy selection and value estimation across temporally extended action sequences. We formalize this framework through a hierarchical Bayesian model that captures uncertainty at both the context and action-selection levels. Empirical evaluations across diverse domains—including robotic manipulation, autonomous navigation, and strategic games—demonstrate that CAMSRL achieves significantly improved sample efficiency, faster convergence, and more robust transfer learning capabilities compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our approach reduces the required training interactions by up to 45% while improving final performance by an average of 27%. These results highlight the potential of integrating contextual awareness with active learning principles to address fundamental challenges in reinforcement learning, particularly in complex, dynamic environments where efficient adaptation is critical.

Biased Estimates of Advantages over Path Ensembles

This paper examines the systematic biases that emerge when estimating advantage functions across path ensembles in reinforcement learning and stochastic optimal control frameworks. We demonstrate that conventional methods for advantage estimation can produce significantly biased results when applied to distributions of trajectories rather than individual paths. Through theoretical analysis, we identify the sources of these biases and quantify their magnitude under various sampling conditions. Our findings reveal that these biases are particularly pronounced in high-dimensional state spaces and when using truncated temporal horizons. We propose a novel estimation technique that employs importance-weighted sampling with trajectory-aware normalization, which substantially reduces bias while maintaining computational efficiency. Empirical evaluations across both synthetic control problems and complex robotic tasks demonstrate that our approach yields more accurate advantage estimates, leading to improved policy optimization and faster convergence. These results have important implications for algorithms that rely on advantage estimation, including policy gradient methods and actor-critic architectures.

Eccentric Regularization: Minimizing Hyperspherical Energy without explicit projection

This paper introduces Eccentric Regularization, a novel approach to minimize hyperspherical energy in deep neural networks without requiring explicit projection operations. Traditional methods for optimizing feature embeddings on the hypersphere typically involve computationally expensive normalization steps that can impede training efficiency. Our proposed regularization technique implicitly encourages uniform distribution of features on the hypersphere by penalizing eccentric configurations through a carefully designed loss function. We demonstrate that Eccentric Regularization achieves comparable or superior performance to explicit projection-based methods while significantly reducing computational overhead. Extensive experiments on image classification, face recognition, and metric learning tasks show that our approach not only improves model generalization but also accelerates convergence. Theoretical analysis reveals that our method effectively approximates minimum energy configurations on the hypersphere while maintaining the flexibility needed for representation learning. These results suggest that Eccentric Regularization offers a promising alternative for applications requiring hyperspherical feature distributions without the computational burden of explicit normalization.

Multi-task Transformation Learning for Robust Out-of-Distribution Detection

Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains a critical challenge for deploying machine learning models in real-world scenarios where test data may differ significantly from training distributions. This paper introduces Multi-task Transformation Learning (MTL), a novel framework that enhances OOD detection by simultaneously learning multiple data transformations and their corresponding detection tasks. Our approach leverages the insight that different semantic transformations of input data can reveal distinctive patterns of distribution shift. By jointly optimizing a set of learnable transformations and task-specific detection heads, MTL creates a rich representation space that captures various aspects of distribution boundaries. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and MNIST) demonstrate that MTL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average improvement of 8.3% in AUROC scores on challenging OOD benchmarks. Notably, our method maintains robust performance even under adversarial perturbations and dataset shifts not encountered during training. Ablation studies confirm that the multi-task learning paradigm provides complementary signals that enhance detection capabilities beyond what individual transformation approaches can achieve. The proposed MTL framework offers a principled approach to robust OOD detection that can be readily integrated into existing deep learning pipelines.

A Dataset for Improved RGBD-based Object Detection and Pose Estimation for Warehouse Pick-and-Place

This paper presents a comprehensive RGBD dataset specifically designed to advance object detection and pose estimation for robotic pick-and-place operations in warehouse environments. Despite recent progress in computer vision and robotics, existing datasets often lack the specific challenges encountered in warehouse settings, such as cluttered environments, varying lighting conditions, and diverse object geometries. Our dataset contains over 10,000 RGBD images capturing 50 common warehouse items across multiple poses, occlusion levels, and lighting conditions. The data is meticulously annotated with 3D bounding boxes, 6-DOF poses, and segmentation masks. We establish benchmark results using state-of-the-art detection and pose estimation algorithms, demonstrating that methods trained on our dataset achieve significant improvements in accuracy and robustness compared to those trained on general-purpose datasets. Specifically, we observe a 27% improvement in pose estimation accuracy and a 19% increase in successful grasp attempts when deployed on a real warehouse robotic system. This dataset addresses the gap between existing computer vision capabilities and the practical requirements of autonomous warehouse pick-and-place operations, providing a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in robotics, computer vision, and automated logistics.

A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification

This paper provides an accessible introduction to conformal prediction, a powerful framework for constructing prediction intervals with guaranteed coverage properties regardless of the underlying data distribution. Unlike traditional uncertainty quantification methods that rely on parametric assumptions, conformal prediction offers distribution-free guarantees while remaining computationally efficient and applicable to any predictive model. We begin by explaining the fundamental principles of conformal prediction, including the concept of nonconformity measures and the split conformal approach. Through illustrative examples and visualizations, we demonstrate how these methods can be applied to regression and classification problems. We explore recent advances in the field, including conditional conformal prediction and methods for handling covariate shift, while highlighting practical considerations for implementation. This tutorial aims to bridge the gap between theoretical foundations and practical applications, making conformal prediction accessible to practitioners across various domains who seek reliable uncertainty quantification without restrictive distributional assumptions. Examples in Python accompany the theoretical exposition to facilitate immediate application of these techniques.

ViTGAN: Training GANs with Vision Transformers

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated remarkable success in image synthesis, yet their traditional convolutional neural network architectures may limit their representational capacity. In this paper, we present ViTGAN, a novel approach that leverages Vision Transformers (ViT) for both generator and discriminator components in the GAN framework. Our method replaces conventional convolutional architectures with transformer-based models that capture long-range dependencies and global image context through self-attention mechanisms. We introduce several architectural modifications to adapt the ViT framework for generative tasks, including a specialized positional encoding scheme and a hierarchical transformer structure optimized for image generation. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that ViTGAN achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS), while exhibiting improved training stability compared to convolutional GANs. Additionally, we show that the self-attention mechanisms inherent in transformers enable ViTGAN to generate images with better global coherence and fine-grained details. Our work establishes a promising direction for leveraging transformer architectures in generative modeling and demonstrates their effectiveness in high-quality image synthesis.

3DMNDT: 3D Multi-view Registration Method Based on the Normal Distributions Transform

This paper presents 3DMNDT, a novel approach to 3D multi-view point cloud registration that extends the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) to efficiently handle multiple overlapping views simultaneously. Unlike traditional pairwise registration methods that accumulate errors when aligning multiple scans sequentially, our approach optimizes the global alignment of all views in a unified framework. We represent local surface geometries as probability density functions using a voxelized NDT structure and formulate a multi-view cost function that evaluates the consistency of point distributions across all overlapping regions. The optimization process iteratively refines transformation parameters for each view relative to a common reference frame, achieving global consistency while preserving local geometric details. Experimental evaluation on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates that 3DMNDT achieves superior registration accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, with up to 35% reduction in alignment error and improved robustness to noise and partial overlaps. Additionally, our method exhibits favorable computational efficiency, making it suitable for applications in 3D reconstruction, mapping, and object modeling. The source code is made publicly available to facilitate further research in multi-view registration.

An Introduction to Robust Graph Convolutional Networks

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning representations on graph-structured data, with applications spanning recommendation systems, social network analysis, and molecular property prediction. However, standard GCNs often exhibit vulnerability to adversarial attacks, noisy features, and structural perturbations that compromise their reliability in real-world scenarios. This paper provides a comprehensive introduction to Robust Graph Convolutional Networks, surveying recent advances in developing GCN architectures that maintain performance stability under various forms of adversarial manipulation and data corruption. We categorize robustness techniques into three primary approaches: adversarial training frameworks, architectural modifications with built-in defense mechanisms, and graph purification methods that detect and mitigate malicious perturbations. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that these robust variants significantly outperform standard GCNs when subjected to targeted attacks while maintaining competitive performance on clean data. Additionally, we identify open challenges and promising research directions in the development of robust graph neural networks for safety-critical applications. This introduction serves as a foundation for researchers and practitioners seeking to implement reliable graph-based learning systems in adversarial environments.

Edge of Chaos as a Guiding Principle for Modern Neural Network Training

This paper explores the theoretical and practical implications of operating neural networks at the "edge of chaos" - a critical transition point between ordered and chaotic dynamics that may optimize learning capabilities. We demonstrate that neural networks achieve optimal performance when their parameters are tuned to this critical boundary, characterized by balanced signal propagation and gradient flow. Through extensive experiments across architectures including transformers, convolutional networks, and recurrent models, we show that initialization strategies and regularization techniques that maintain networks near this phase transition consistently yield improved generalization, faster convergence, and enhanced robustness. We formalize this principle mathematically, connecting it to information-theoretic measures and dynamical systems theory, and provide practical guidelines for practitioners to leverage this principle in training deep networks. Our findings suggest that the edge of chaos represents not merely a curious phenomenon but a fundamental principle that can guide the development of more efficient and effective neural network training paradigms. This perspective unifies several seemingly disparate best practices in deep learning and offers new directions for architecture design and optimization strategies.

Show, Attend and Distill: Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching

Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful technique for transferring knowledge from large, computationally expensive teacher models to compact student models. However, conventional distillation approaches often focus on matching final outputs or intermediate representations without explicitly considering the importance of different feature regions. In this paper, we propose a novel attention-based feature matching framework for knowledge distillation called "Show, Attend and Distill." Our approach leverages attention mechanisms to identify and emphasize the most informative regions in the feature maps of the teacher model, guiding the student to focus on these critical areas during training. By incorporating spatial attention maps as transfer bridges between teacher and student networks, our method enables more effective knowledge transfer while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments across multiple architectures and datasets demonstrate that our attention-guided distillation consistently outperforms traditional knowledge distillation methods, achieving higher accuracy with significantly smaller model sizes. The proposed approach not only improves performance metrics but also enhances the interpretability of the distillation process by visualizing which features are deemed most important for the teacher's predictions. Our work contributes a new perspective on knowledge distillation that explicitly models and transfers attention patterns, providing both theoretical insights and practical improvements to model compression techniques.

Scalable Optimization for Wind Farm Control using Coordination Graphs

This paper presents a novel approach to wind farm control optimization using coordination graphs that addresses the computational complexity challenges inherent in large-scale wind farm management. Traditional centralized control methods struggle to scale efficiently as farm sizes increase, leading to suboptimal power production and turbine loading. We introduce a coordination graph framework that decomposes the global optimization problem into locally coupled subproblems, where each turbine coordinates primarily with neighbors significantly affected by its wake. This graph-based representation captures the essential aerodynamic interdependencies while dramatically reducing computational requirements. Our method employs a distributed message-passing algorithm that enables efficient optimization of yaw angles and axial induction factors across the farm. Simulations on wind farms of varying sizes (50-300 turbines) demonstrate that our approach achieves within 2-3% of the theoretical optimal power production while reducing computational time by up to 95% compared to centralized methods. The scalability advantages become particularly pronounced in larger installations, where our method maintains near-linear computational scaling. Additionally, the framework naturally accommodates heterogeneous turbine types and dynamic reconfigurations as wind conditions change. These results suggest that coordination graphs provide a promising foundation for real-time control of next-generation utility-scale wind farms.

Adversarial Generation of Handwritten Text Images Conditioned on Sequences

This paper presents a novel approach to generating realistic handwritten text images using adversarial networks conditioned on character sequences. We introduce a sequence-conditioned generative adversarial network (SC-GAN) architecture that bridges the gap between text recognition and synthesis by learning to generate diverse, authentic-looking handwritten text while maintaining character-level fidelity. Our model incorporates a conditional mechanism that allows fine-grained control over both content and style characteristics of the generated text. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach produces visually convincing handwritten text samples that preserve the intended character sequence while exhibiting natural variations in writing style. The generated images successfully fool both human evaluators and state-of-the-art OCR systems in authenticity tests. Furthermore, we show that our synthetic handwritten text can be used to augment training datasets for text recognition systems, improving their performance by up to 8.7% on benchmark datasets. The proposed method has significant implications for applications requiring synthetic handwritten text, including data augmentation for OCR, historical document processing, and privacy-preserving text synthesis.

An Ode to an Ordinary Differential Equation: Abstract

This paper presents a poetic exploration of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and their profound impact on mathematical modeling across disciplines. Through metaphorical analysis, we examine how ODEs capture the essence of dynamic systems by expressing relationships between functions and their derivatives. We trace the historical development of ODEs from Newton and Leibniz to modern applications in physics, engineering, ecology, and economics. The mathematical beauty of ODEs is highlighted through case studies demonstrating their elegant solutions and the insights they provide into natural phenomena. We discuss how the interplay between analytical methods and numerical approximations has evolved with computational advances, allowing increasingly complex systems to be modeled. This interdisciplinary perspective celebrates ODEs not merely as mathematical tools but as a language that reveals the underlying harmony of change in our universe.

ViViT: Curvature access through the generalized Gauss-Newton's low-rank structure

Curvature information plays a critical role in optimization for deep learning, yet accessing and utilizing this information remains computationally challenging. In this paper, we introduce ViViT (Visual Visualization of Implicit Tensors), a novel approach that exploits the inherent low-rank structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix to efficiently access curvature information in neural networks. Our method leverages the observation that the GGN matrix, while prohibitively large to compute explicitly for modern architectures, often exhibits a surprisingly low effective rank in practical settings. ViViT employs an implicit tensor formulation combined with randomized numerical techniques to extract the dominant eigenspace of the curvature matrix without ever forming the full matrix. We demonstrate that this approach enables practical curvature-aware optimization for networks of unprecedented scale, reducing computational overhead while maintaining the benefits of second-order information. Empirical evaluations across various architectures show that ViViT-based optimization leads to faster convergence, improved generalization, and enhanced robustness to hyperparameter choices compared to first-order methods. Our approach opens new possibilities for incorporating curvature information in large-scale deep learning optimization while providing intuitive visualizations of the loss landscape geometry.

Monte Carlo Dropout Ensembles for Robust Illumination Estimation

Accurate illumination estimation remains a challenging problem in computer vision with significant implications for applications ranging from color constancy to augmented reality. In this paper, we present a novel approach leveraging Monte Carlo dropout ensembles to improve the robustness of illumination estimation under varying conditions. Our method employs a deep neural network architecture where dropout layers remain active during inference, enabling the generation of multiple predictions that collectively form a probabilistic distribution of illumination estimates. This ensemble approach not only provides mean estimates of scene illumination but also quantifies prediction uncertainty, which proves valuable in challenging scenarios with ambiguous lighting conditions. Experimental results on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our approach reduces angular error by 15% compared to deterministic baselines while providing meaningful uncertainty measures that correlate with estimation difficulty. Furthermore, we show that our method maintains robust performance across diverse lighting conditions, including mixed illumination and low-light environments where traditional methods often fail. Our approach requires minimal computational overhead compared to sampling-based alternatives, making it suitable for real-time applications.

Learning to Reach Goals via Iterated Supervised Learning

This paper introduces a novel approach to goal-directed reinforcement learning called Iterated Supervised Learning (ISL). Unlike traditional reinforcement learning methods that rely on reward signals, ISL iteratively transforms goal-reaching problems into supervised learning tasks. Our approach begins with a small set of successful goal-reaching demonstrations and progressively expands this dataset through repeated cycles of policy training and data collection. Each iteration trains a policy to imitate successful trajectories while attempting increasingly challenging goals, effectively bootstrapping the agent's capabilities. We provide theoretical analysis showing that ISL converges to optimal goal-reaching policies under certain conditions and empirically demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse domains including robotic manipulation, navigation, and game environments. Compared to state-of-the-art reinforcement learning and imitation learning methods, ISL achieves superior sample efficiency, better generalization to unseen goals, and greater robustness to environmental variations. Our results suggest that reformulating reinforcement learning problems as iterative supervised learning can significantly improve the scalability and practicality of goal-directed learning systems.

Stack-U-Net: Refinement Network for Image Segmentation on the Example of Optic Disc and Cup

This paper presents Stack-U-Net, a novel deep learning architecture designed for high-precision medical image segmentation, with specific application to optic disc and cup segmentation in retinal fundus images. Our approach builds upon the traditional U-Net framework by introducing a sequential stack of interconnected U-Net modules that progressively refine segmentation outputs. Each module in the stack leverages features from previous stages, allowing the network to hierarchically resolve ambiguities in boundary delineation. We evaluate our method on multiple public datasets, including DRISHTI-GS, RIM-ONE, and REFUGE, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art approaches with average Dice coefficients of 0.967 for optic disc and 0.891 for optic cup segmentation. The proposed architecture shows particular strength in handling challenging cases with low contrast boundaries and pathological variations. Additionally, we perform extensive ablation studies to analyze the contribution of each architectural component. Our Stack-U-Net framework provides a generalizable solution that can be adapted to various medical image segmentation tasks requiring precise boundary detection.

Multi-StyleGAN: Towards Image-Based Simulation of Time-Lapse Live-Cell Microscopy

Time-lapse live-cell microscopy is an essential tool for studying dynamic cellular processes, but its application is constrained by phototoxicity, photobleaching, and the significant resources required for experimental setup and data acquisition. In this paper, we introduce Multi-StyleGAN, a novel deep learning framework that generates realistic time-lapse sequences of cellular dynamics by leveraging the power of StyleGAN architecture with temporal coherence constraints. Our approach conditions image generation on both cell morphology and temporal evolution, enabling the simulation of diverse cellular behaviors across extended time periods. We demonstrate that Multi-StyleGAN can faithfully reproduce complex phenomena such as cell migration, division, and morphological changes while maintaining biological plausibility between consecutive frames. Quantitative evaluation shows that our synthetic sequences are statistically indistinguishable from real microscopy data across multiple metrics, including texture similarity, motion consistency, and biological feature preservation. Furthermore, we show that these synthetic datasets can effectively supplement real data for downstream tasks such as cell tracking and event detection, improving performance by up to 27% when training data is limited. Multi-StyleGAN represents a significant advancement in computational microscopy, offering researchers a powerful tool to simulate cellular dynamics without the limitations of physical imaging, thereby accelerating biological discovery while reducing experimental costs and cellular stress.

A Graph Cut Approach to 3D Tree Delineation, Using Integrated Airborne LiDAR and Hyperspectral Imagery

This paper presents a novel graph cut-based approach for automated individual tree delineation in forest environments using the integration of airborne Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) and hyperspectral imagery. While existing methods often rely on either spectral or structural information alone, our approach leverages the complementary nature of these data sources to improve delineation accuracy. We formulate the tree delineation problem as an energy minimization task within a graph theoretical framework, where LiDAR-derived structural features define the spatial relationships between points, while hyperspectral data contributes species-specific spectral signatures. The proposed method first constructs a weighted graph from the 3D point cloud, with edges weighted according to both structural discontinuities and spectral dissimilarities. A normalized cut algorithm is then applied to segment the graph into individual tree crowns. We evaluate our approach on diverse forest plots in both managed and natural environments, demonstrating significant improvements in delineation accuracy compared to single-sensor approaches. Quantitative assessment shows our method achieves an overall accuracy of 87% in complex multi-layered forest stands. The integration of spectral and structural information proves particularly effective in distinguishing adjacent trees of different species and in resolving understory vegetation. This research contributes to advancing forest inventory techniques and supports more accurate biomass estimation and ecosystem monitoring applications.

Extended Bit-Plane Compression for Convolutional Neural Network Accelerators

This paper presents Extended Bit-Plane Compression (EBPC), a novel compression technique specifically designed for convolutional neural network (CNN) accelerators. As CNNs continue to grow in complexity, the memory bandwidth required to transfer weights and activations has become a critical bottleneck in accelerator performance. EBPC builds upon traditional bit-plane compression methods by exploiting the statistical distribution of values in CNN parameters and feature maps. Our approach extends conventional bit-plane encoding with adaptive quantization and run-length encoding strategies tailored to the characteristics of CNN data patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that EBPC achieves an average compression ratio of 3.8× across popular CNN architectures (ResNet, MobileNet, and EfficientNet), with minimal impact on inference accuracy (less than 0.5% drop). When implemented in hardware, our technique reduces off-chip memory bandwidth by up to 74% and decreases energy consumption by 68% compared to uncompressed baselines, while requiring only 4.2% additional chip area. The proposed method is particularly effective for resource-constrained edge devices, enabling deployment of larger networks with improved throughput under strict memory constraints.

Injecting Hierarchy with U-Net Transformers

Transformer architectures have demonstrated remarkable success across various domains, yet they often struggle to efficiently capture hierarchical structures inherent in many data types. In this paper, we introduce the U-Net Transformer, a novel architecture that explicitly injects hierarchical inductive bias into the standard Transformer framework. Our approach combines the self-attention mechanism of Transformers with the multi-resolution processing capabilities of U-Net architectures, enabling simultaneous modeling of both local and global dependencies. The U-Net Transformer progressively contracts the sequence through a series of downsampling operations to capture high-level abstractions, followed by an expansion path that restores resolution while incorporating fine-grained details. Critically, we maintain skip connections between corresponding levels, allowing the model to preserve information across different hierarchical scales. Experiments across multiple domains—including natural language processing, computer vision, and time series forecasting—demonstrate that our architecture consistently outperforms standard Transformers, especially on tasks requiring multi-scale reasoning. The U-Net Transformer achieves these improvements while reducing computational complexity and memory requirements for long sequences. Our analysis reveals that the model effectively learns to specialize different hierarchical levels for different aspects of the underlying data structure, providing both performance gains and enhanced interpretability.

Exploration in Approximate Hyper-State Space for Meta Reinforcement Learning

Meta Reinforcement Learning (Meta-RL) aims to develop agents that can quickly adapt to novel tasks by leveraging experience from previously encountered tasks. A critical challenge in Meta-RL is efficient exploration during both meta-training and adaptation phases. This paper introduces a novel exploration framework based on the concept of approximate hyper-state spaces, which extends traditional state representations to incorporate task-specific information and uncertainty estimates. We formalize the hyper-state representation as a combination of environmental states, task belief distributions, and adaptation progress indicators. By conducting exploration in this enriched representation space, our approach enables more efficient discovery of task-relevant information compared to conventional state-based exploration strategies. We propose a hierarchical Bayesian approach to maintain and update belief distributions over task parameters and develop an uncertainty-driven exploration bonus that operates in the hyper-state space. Empirical evaluations across diverse meta-learning benchmarks, including MuJoCo locomotion tasks and ProcGen environments, demonstrate that our method achieves faster adaptation, improved sample efficiency during meta-training, and better generalization to out-of-distribution tasks compared to state-of-the-art Meta-RL algorithms. Our analysis reveals that explicitly reasoning about task uncertainty through the hyper-state representation allows the agent to perform more targeted exploration, leading to more effective meta-learning.

Abstract

This study investigates the sensitivity of Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to minimal visual changes in complex patterns. We demonstrate that the quantization error (QE) produced by a trained SOM can effectively detect single-pixel alterations within large random patterns, with sensitivity that varies predictably with both contrast and colour properties. Through systematic experiments with controlled stimuli, we established that the QE signal exhibits a non-linear relationship with contrast levels and displays distinct signatures across different colour channels. Our findings reveal that SOMs inherently develop specialized feature detectors that respond differentially to minute changes based on their visual salience. This property enables the detection of subtle pattern modifications that would be imperceptible to conventional image analysis methods. The contrast and colour-specific nature of the QE signal suggests potential applications in image forgery detection, steganography, visual quality assessment, and as a computational model for human perception of visual change. Our work provides a novel theoretical framework for understanding how topological neural networks encode and respond to minimal disturbances in complex visual information.

Quadratic GCN for Graph Classification

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as powerful tools for graph-based learning tasks, yet their performance on graph classification problems is often limited by their linear aggregation mechanisms. In this paper, we introduce Quadratic Graph Convolutional Networks (QGCN), a novel architecture that enhances the expressive power of traditional GCNs by incorporating quadratic interactions between node features during the aggregation process. Our approach leverages a second-order polynomial mapping that captures more complex structural patterns and feature relationships within graphs. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that QGCNs can distinguish graph structures that are indistinguishable to standard GCNs. We evaluate our method on multiple benchmark datasets across various domains, including social networks, molecular graphs, and protein structures. Experimental results show that QGCN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art graph classification methods, achieving accuracy improvements of up to 5.3% while maintaining computational efficiency. Additionally, we provide visualizations that offer insights into how quadratic feature interactions contribute to improved discriminative capabilities. Our work opens new directions for designing more expressive graph neural networks for classification tasks.

RL for Latent MDPs: Regret Guarantees and a Lower Bound

This paper addresses the problem of reinforcement learning in Latent Markov Decision Processes (LMDPs), where the underlying states are not directly observable. We develop a novel algorithm that efficiently learns optimal policies in such partially observable environments by leveraging the latent structure. Our approach combines spectral methods for state estimation with optimistic exploration strategies to achieve sublinear regret. Specifically, we prove that our algorithm achieves a regret bound of Õ(√(H³S²AT)), where H is the horizon length, S is the number of latent states, A is the action space size, and T is the number of interactions. This matches the optimal dependence on T for tabular MDPs with full observability. We complement our upper bound with a matching lower bound of Ω(√(H³S²AT)), demonstrating the fundamental limits of learning in LMDPs. Experimental results on both synthetic domains and robotics simulation tasks validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our approach compared to existing methods. Our work provides the first comprehensive theoretical understanding of the sample complexity of reinforcement learning in latent MDPs.

PGTRNet: Two-phase Weakly Supervised Object Detection with Pseudo Ground Truth Refining

Weakly supervised object detection (WSOD) aims to train object detectors using only image-level annotations, eliminating the need for costly bounding box labels. While recent approaches have shown promising results, they often struggle with imprecise localization and partial object detection. In this paper, we propose PGTRNet, a novel two-phase framework that addresses these limitations through a pseudo ground truth refinement mechanism. In the first phase, our model generates initial pseudo bounding boxes using a multiple instance learning (MIL) strategy enhanced with spatial attention. The second phase introduces our key innovation: a refinement network that iteratively improves the quality of pseudo ground truth by leveraging both high-confidence detections and contextual information. Our refinement process incorporates a novel consistency loss that ensures stable updates and reduces the risk of catastrophic forgetting during training. Extensive experiments on PASCAL VOC and MS COCO datasets demonstrate that PGTRNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art WSOD methods, achieving improvements of 2.7% and 2.1% in mAP on these benchmarks, respectively. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of our pseudo ground truth refinement approach, particularly for challenging object categories with variable appearances and occlusions.

Beyond Image to Depth: Improving Depth Prediction using Echoes

Accurate depth estimation is crucial for various computer vision applications, yet traditional image-based depth prediction methods often struggle with challenging scenarios such as transparent surfaces, textureless regions, and poor lighting conditions. This paper introduces a novel multimodal approach that leverages acoustic information alongside visual data to enhance depth prediction accuracy. We propose a deep learning framework that fuses echoes captured from emitted audio signals with corresponding RGB images to overcome the inherent limitations of vision-only methods. Our system employs a specialized encoder-decoder architecture with cross-modal attention mechanisms to effectively integrate the complementary information from both modalities. Extensive experiments on our newly collected Echo-Depth dataset demonstrate that our approach achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art image-only depth estimation methods, with particularly notable gains in traditionally challenging scenarios. Ablation studies confirm that acoustic information provides geometric cues that are fundamentally unavailable in visual data alone. This work opens new possibilities for robust depth sensing in real-world applications where conventional methods fall short, including robotics, augmented reality, and autonomous navigation systems.

Towards Interpreting Computer Vision Based on Transformation Invariant Optimization

This paper presents a novel framework for interpreting deep learning models in computer vision through the lens of transformation invariant optimization. While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in visual recognition tasks, their black-box nature limits our understanding of their decision-making processes. We propose that many successful computer vision architectures implicitly learn transformation invariances that are critical to their performance. Our approach formalizes these invariances within an optimization framework, allowing us to decompose complex models into interpretable components that correspond to specific visual transformations (e.g., translation, rotation, scaling). Through extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including ImageNet and COCO, we demonstrate that our framework can (1) accurately predict which transformations a model is invariant to, (2) identify failure cases where invariance assumptions are violated, and (3) guide architectural modifications that enhance robustness to specific transformations. Furthermore, we establish theoretical connections between our optimization-based interpretation and traditional computer vision principles. This work bridges the gap between classical computer vision theory and modern deep learning practices, offering both enhanced interpretability and practical guidelines for designing more robust vision systems.

Building 3D Morphable Models from a Single Scan

Three-dimensional morphable models (3DMMs) have become essential tools in computer vision and graphics for tasks including face recognition, reconstruction, and animation. However, traditional approaches to building these models require large datasets of 3D scans, which are expensive and time-consuming to collect. In this paper, we present a novel framework for constructing 3D morphable models from a single high-quality scan. Our approach leverages recent advances in deep generative modeling to learn the underlying shape and texture variations from a single exemplar. By introducing a deformation-based self-supervised learning strategy, our method synthesizes plausible shape variations while preserving anatomical constraints and semantic consistency. We demonstrate that our single-scan morphable model (SSMM) can effectively represent a wide range of identities despite being trained on minimal data. Extensive experiments show that our SSMM achieves comparable performance to traditional multi-scan models in applications such as 3D reconstruction from images, identity preservation, and expression transfer. This work significantly reduces the barrier to entry for creating customized morphable models and enables new applications in domains where collecting multiple 3D scans is impractical.

Selection of Source Images Heavily Influences the Effectiveness of Adversarial Attacks

This paper investigates how the choice of source images significantly impacts the success rate and transferability of adversarial attacks against deep neural networks. Through extensive experiments across multiple model architectures (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-10), we demonstrate that carefully selected source images can increase attack success rates by up to 37% compared to randomly chosen images. Our analysis reveals that source images with high confidence predictions, distinctive feature representations, and proximity to decision boundaries are particularly effective for generating adversarial perturbations. Furthermore, we show that the relationship between source and target classes plays a crucial role in attack transferability across different models. We propose a novel source image selection strategy that outperforms existing methods in black-box attack scenarios. These findings highlight a previously underexplored vulnerability in adversarial machine learning and suggest that defensive mechanisms should consider the influence of source image selection to improve model robustness against sophisticated attacks.

PyTorchRL: Modular and Distributed Reinforcement Learning in PyTorch

We present PyTorchRL, an open-source reinforcement learning (RL) library built on PyTorch that provides a modular and distributed framework for RL research and applications. PyTorchRL is designed with three key principles: modularity, allowing researchers to easily compose and customize components; scalability, supporting efficient single-machine execution and seamless distributed training across multiple nodes; and reproducibility, emphasizing consistent experimental results through standardized implementations. The library includes implementations of state-of-the-art algorithms across various RL paradigms including model-free, model-based, offline, and multi-agent approaches. PyTorchRL's architecture decouples environment interaction from policy optimization, enabling flexible deployment configurations that can leverage modern hardware accelerators. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that PyTorchRL achieves competitive performance and throughput compared to existing frameworks while providing superior extensibility. By combining the familiar PyTorch ecosystem with specialized RL components, PyTorchRL aims to accelerate research innovation while remaining accessible to both newcomers and experienced practitioners in the field.

Graph Convolutional Policy for Solving Tree Decomposition via Reinforcement Learning Heuristics

Tree decomposition is a fundamental graph-theoretic problem with significant applications in algorithm design, constraint satisfaction, and network analysis. Despite its theoretical importance, computing optimal tree decompositions remains challenging due to its NP-hard nature. This paper introduces a novel approach that combines graph convolutional networks (GCNs) with reinforcement learning to learn effective heuristics for the tree decomposition problem. We formulate the decomposition process as a sequential decision-making task where a GCN-based policy iteratively selects vertices to construct a high-quality decomposition. Our model captures the structural properties of graphs through message-passing neural networks and learns decomposition strategies through policy gradient methods. Experimental results on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms traditional heuristic methods, reducing the treewidth by an average of 15% compared to established baselines. Furthermore, our model generalizes effectively to larger and more complex graphs than those seen during training. This work represents a significant step toward leveraging machine learning techniques to solve computationally intensive graph problems and provides insights into the structural patterns that lead to optimal tree decompositions.

Voice2Series: Reprogramming Acoustic Models for Time Series Classification

This paper introduces Voice2Series, a novel framework that repurposes pre-trained speech recognition models for time series classification tasks. While deep learning has achieved remarkable success in time series analysis, training effective models often requires substantial domain-specific data and computational resources. We demonstrate that acoustic models, originally trained on vast speech corpora, contain transferable knowledge applicable to general time series classification problems. Our approach involves a lightweight adaptation mechanism that transforms arbitrary time series data into a compatible input representation for pre-trained acoustic models, effectively "reprogramming" them without modifying their internal parameters. Experiments across diverse domains—including healthcare, industrial monitoring, and human activity recognition—show that Voice2Series outperforms specialized time series models trained from scratch, particularly in low-data regimes. The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets while requiring significantly less training data and computational resources. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into why speech recognition models transfer effectively to other time series domains. Voice2Series opens new possibilities for leveraging the rich representational capacity of acoustic models across the broader spectrum of time series analysis tasks.

Deep Interactive Region Segmentation and Captioning

This paper presents a novel framework for interactive region segmentation and captioning that combines deep learning approaches for both visual understanding and natural language generation. Our system enables users to select regions of interest within images through intuitive interactions, after which the framework automatically segments the selected region with pixel-level precision and generates descriptive captions for that specific area. We propose a two-stage architecture that integrates a region-aware segmentation network with a context-sensitive captioning model. The segmentation component utilizes a modified Mask R-CNN backbone enhanced with user interaction encoding, while the captioning module employs a transformer-based architecture that conditions text generation on both the visual features of the segmented region and its spatial context within the entire image. Extensive experiments on MS COCO and Visual Genome datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in both segmentation accuracy (improving IoU by 8.3% over previous methods) and caption quality (showing a 12.5% improvement in CIDEr scores). User studies further confirm that our system significantly enhances the efficiency and quality of region-specific image understanding tasks. The proposed framework has promising applications in assistive technologies, content creation tools, and interactive image analysis systems.

Diamond in the Rough: Improving Image Realism by Traversing the GAN Latent Space

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in synthesizing photorealistic images. However, the latent space of these models often contains regions that produce artifacts and unrealistic outputs. This paper introduces "Diamond in the Rough," a novel framework for enhancing the realism of GAN-generated images through strategic traversal of the latent space. We propose an optimization method that iteratively refines latent code vectors by navigating toward regions associated with higher perceptual realism while maintaining the semantic content of the original generation. Our approach combines a realism discriminator with differentiable perceptual metrics to guide this traversal, effectively mining "diamonds" of realistic outputs from the "rough" of the latent space. Extensive experiments on StyleGAN2 and BigGAN architectures demonstrate that our method significantly improves image quality metrics, reduces common GAN artifacts, and enhances overall visual realism as confirmed by human evaluations. The proposed technique requires no additional training of the base GAN models and can be applied as a post-processing step to existing generators. Our findings provide insights into the structure of GAN latent spaces and offer a practical solution for applications requiring high-fidelity image synthesis.

Nighttime Dehazing with a Synthetic Benchmark

Nighttime image dehazing remains a challenging problem in computer vision due to the complex interaction between light sources, atmospheric particles, and low illumination conditions. In this paper, we present a novel approach to nighttime dehazing along with a comprehensive synthetic benchmark dataset to address the scarcity of paired training data. Our benchmark consists of over 10,000 synthetically generated nighttime hazy images with corresponding ground truth clear images, covering diverse scenes, lighting conditions, and haze densities. We propose a physics-based image formation model that accurately simulates the unique characteristics of nighttime haze, including light scattering, glow effects around artificial light sources, and non-uniform illumination. Based on this model, we develop a deep learning architecture that incorporates attention mechanisms to handle the spatially varying nature of nighttime haze while preserving the contrast and color fidelity of the original scene. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on both synthetic and real-world nighttime hazy images, achieving significant improvements in PSNR, SSIM, and perceptual quality metrics. The proposed benchmark enables objective evaluation and facilitates further research in this challenging domain.

Ordinal-Content VAE: Isolating Ordinal-Valued Content Factors in Deep Latent Variable Models

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have proven effective for learning disentangled representations of data, yet they often struggle to properly isolate and represent ordinal-valued content factors. In this paper, we introduce the Ordinal-Content VAE (OC-VAE), a novel extension to the VAE framework specifically designed to identify and model ordinal-valued attributes within complex data distributions. Our approach partitions the latent space into continuous and ordinal subspaces, employing a specialized ordinal encoding mechanism that enforces discrete, ordered representations while maintaining differentiability during training. Through a carefully designed regularization scheme, OC-VAE encourages disentanglement between ordinal content factors and other continuous latent variables. We evaluate our model on synthetic and real-world datasets containing inherent ordinal characteristics such as age progression, intensity levels, and sequential transformations. Experimental results demonstrate that OC-VAE significantly outperforms standard VAEs and other state-of-the-art disentanglement methods in accurately capturing ordinal content factors while preserving reconstruction fidelity. Our approach enables more interpretable representations and controlled generation along ordinal dimensions, showing promise for applications in data augmentation, attribute editing, and causal inference where ordinal factors play a crucial role.

A Novel Framework of the Fuzzy C-Means Distances Problem Based Weighted Distance

This paper presents a novel framework that addresses the inherent limitations of traditional fuzzy c-means (FCM) clustering by introducing a weighted distance approach to the distances problem. While conventional FCM algorithms utilize fixed Euclidean distances that treat all features equally, our proposed framework incorporates a dynamic weighting mechanism that adaptively adjusts feature contributions based on their relevance to cluster formation. We formulate a comprehensive mathematical model that optimizes both cluster centers and distance weights simultaneously through an iterative process. The framework introduces a regularization parameter that controls the degree of weight distribution, preventing degenerate solutions while allowing for feature selection. Extensive experimental validation on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates that our approach significantly outperforms standard FCM and several state-of-the-art variants across multiple evaluation metrics. The results show particular improvement in handling high-dimensional data with irrelevant features and datasets with clusters of varying shapes and densities. This framework provides a flexible foundation for developing more robust and interpretable fuzzy clustering algorithms with enhanced performance in complex data environments.

Automated Classification of Histopathology Images Using Transfer Learning

This study presents a novel approach to the automated classification of histopathology images using transfer learning techniques. Digital pathology has emerged as a transformative field in medical diagnostics, yet the manual interpretation of histopathology slides remains time-consuming and subject to inter-observer variability. We developed and evaluated a deep learning framework that leverages pre-trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) adapted to the specific challenges of histopathological image analysis. Our methodology incorporates several state-of-the-art architectures (ResNet50, DenseNet121, and EfficientNetB4) fine-tuned on a diverse dataset of 15,000 annotated histopathology images spanning multiple tissue types and pathological conditions. The proposed model achieved 94.3% accuracy in multi-class classification tasks, significantly outperforming previous approaches. Furthermore, we implemented an attention mechanism to enhance interpretability, generating heat maps that highlight diagnostically relevant regions. Cross-validation experiments across multiple independent datasets demonstrated robust generalization capabilities, with consistent performance across different staining techniques and scanning platforms. This work represents a significant advancement toward computer-aided diagnostic systems that can assist pathologists in clinical practice, potentially reducing diagnostic timeframes and improving consistency in histopathological assessments.

Is Plug-in Solver Sample-Efficient for Feature-based Reinforcement Learning?

In feature-based reinforcement learning (RL), the plug-in solver approach—where one first estimates the model parameters and then solves for the optimal policy using the estimated model—is widely used due to its simplicity and empirical success. However, the theoretical understanding of its sample efficiency remains limited. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the sample complexity of plug-in solvers in linear Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). We establish both upper and lower bounds on the number of samples required to achieve near-optimal policies. Our analysis reveals that while plug-in solvers can be sample-efficient in certain regimes, they suffer from a fundamental limitation: their sample complexity necessarily scales with the size of the state space in the worst case, even when the feature dimension is small. We further identify conditions under which plug-in methods can achieve dimension-dependent sample efficiency, particularly when the feature representation satisfies certain coverage properties. Through extensive experiments on synthetic and benchmark environments, we validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical implications of our results. This work provides important insights into when plug-in solvers are appropriate for feature-based RL and when alternative approaches might be necessary.

Camera Calibration and Player Localization in SoccerNet-v2 and Investigation of their Representations for Action Spotting

This paper explores the integration of camera calibration and player localization data within the SoccerNet-v2 dataset to enhance action spotting in soccer videos. We present a comprehensive framework that leverages geometric information from camera parameters and spatial player distributions to improve the detection and classification of key events in soccer matches. Our approach begins by developing robust camera calibration techniques that account for the dynamic nature of broadcast soccer footage, followed by accurate player localization methods that track positions relative to the playing field. We then investigate various representation schemes for encoding this spatial-temporal information into feature vectors compatible with existing action spotting architectures. Experiments demonstrate that incorporating calibration and localization data significantly improves action spotting performance, achieving a 7.3% increase in average-mAP compared to baseline methods that rely solely on visual features. Our ablation studies reveal that the combination of homography-based field mapping and density-based player representation provides the most substantial gains for identifying positional play patterns and set-piece events. These findings highlight the importance of geometric understanding in sports video analysis and offer new directions for multimodal approaches to action recognition in team sports.

Fine-Grained 3D Shape Classification with Hierarchical Part-View Attentions

This paper presents a novel approach to fine-grained 3D shape classification through a hierarchical part-view attention mechanism. While existing methods often treat 3D objects as holistic entities, we argue that discriminative features in fine-grained classification scenarios often lie in subtle differences between object parts and their spatial relationships. Our proposed framework, Hierarchical Part-View Attention Network (HPVAN), employs a two-tier attention mechanism that first identifies salient object parts and then focuses on informative views within each part. The network learns to decompose 3D shapes into semantically meaningful components without explicit part supervision, while simultaneously weighting the importance of different viewpoints to capture subtle geometric variations. Extensive experiments on multiple fine-grained 3D shape benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 4.2% higher accuracy on the challenging FinePart-3D dataset. Further ablation studies verify the effectiveness of our hierarchical attention design. Our approach not only improves classification performance but also enhances model interpretability by visualizing the part-view attention maps that highlight discriminative regions used for fine-grained categorization.

Actor-Mimic: Deep Multitask and Transfer Reinforcement Learning

This paper introduces Actor-Mimic, a novel deep reinforcement learning approach that enables both multitask learning and transfer learning in complex domains. Our framework trains a single policy network to emulate the behavior of multiple expert networks, each trained on a different task, by using a policy regression objective that encourages the multitask network to match the output distributions of the expert networks.
